A Detailed Overview of Srimad-Bhagavatam Cantos Eleven and Twelve

# Backward Glance. Cantos 11, 12

## Dedication

His Divine Grace A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada fearlessly sailed to New York in 1965 at the age of sixty-nine. His mission was to spread the chanting of Krsna’s holy names and the teachings of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu. And with him on that almost mythical voy- age was a trunk filled with copies of his own English translations of the First Canto of Srimad-Bhagavatam. While still aboard the Jaladuta, Srila Prabhupada wrote:

*bhagavater katha se taba avatar*  
*dhira haiya sune jadi kane bar bar*

“The words of Srimad-Bhagavatam are Your incarnation, and if a sober person repeatedly receives them with submissive aural reception, then he will be able to understand Your message.”

Even prior to his boarding the Jaladuta, with full faith, he wrote that Srimad-Bhagavatam was “India’s Message of Peace and Goodwill” to the world.

To you, Srila Prabhupada, a great hero who lived, loved, translated, published, and distributed Srimad-Bhagavatam, I dedicate The Backward Glance.

## Introduction

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura once offered a telling reply to a provocative question: Do all panditas in India accept Srimad-Bhagavatam, or do scholars of other schools stand opposed to its authority? His characteristically straightforward response nonetheless surprises: “There is no deliberation in the world which is not against the Bhagavatam. All the different currents of thoughts of jivas averse to God from time immemorial are against it.”

In that same mood, Srila Prabhupada branded his books revolutionary, for they are “an attempt to glorify Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Nothing more. There is no literary career.” (Lecture on Srimad-Bhagavatam 1.8.20, Mayapur, September 30, 1974)

Canto by canto, the Srimad-Bhagavatam draws us onward, encouraging, purifying, and guiding us to stop clutching at straws of matter in our search for happiness and security. Instead, the Bhagavatam implores us to grasp Lord Hari’s lotus feet tightly by hearing about Him and glorifying Him, for those feet are the boat that will ferry us across the dangerous ocean of material existence and transport us to His abode, Goloka Vrndavana.

Thus Srimad-Bhagavatam, from its inception to its close, glorifies Krsna as it carries us forward in its mission to help our love for Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, blossom through hearing and chanting His glories, names, and pastimes.

Suta Gosvami states these truths moments before ending his recitation of the Bhagavatam to the sages at Naimisaranya:

From beginning to end, the Srimad-Bhagavatam is full of narrations that encourage renunciation of material life, as well as nectarean accounts of Lord Hart’s transcendental pastimes, which give ecstasy to the saintly devotees and demigods. This Bhagavatam is the essence of all Vedanta philosophy because its subject matter is the Absolute Truth, which, while nondifferent from the spirit soul, is the ultimate reality, one without a second. The goal of this literature is exclusive devotional service unto that Supreme Truth— Srimad-Bhagavatam is the spotless Puram. It is most dear to the Vaisnavas because it describes the pure and supreme knowledge of the paramahamsas. This Bhagavatam reveals the means for becoming free from all material work, together with the processes of transcendental knowledge, renunciation, and devotion. Anyone who seriously tries to understand Srimad-Bhagavatam, who properly hears and chants it with devotion, becomes completely liberated. (SB. 12.13.11-12, 18)

It is the attempt of The Backward Glance: A Detailed Overview of Srimad-Bhagavatam Cantos Eleven arid Twelve to provide a guiding thread for its readers. By grasping this thread, readers will more easily traverse and absorb the instructive and multifaceted philosophical guidance offered in these final cantos of Srimad-Bhagavatam.

It is my hope that this book will prove itself a useful companion on the path of studying Srimad-Bhagavatam, a friend that will increase both the ease and depth of the journey to the Bhagavatam’s conclusion. I also hope it will assist readers to stay focused on the goal of Srimad' Bhagavatam - the “smiling face of Krsna” presented in Canto Ten - as they gather the ruby-, diamond-, and emeraldlike instructions cantos Eleven and Twelve present.

Those jewels are indeed numerous. Srila Jiva Gosvami, in the Bhakti Sandarbha, quotes from cantos 11 and 12 approximately three hundred and fifty times as he establishes the practices for developing depth in one’s Krsna consciousness.

This book’s title, The Backward Glance, indicates that hearing these cantos, especially the Uddhava'gita in Canto Eleven, chapters 6-29, provide both Maharaja Pariksit, who is soon to leave the world, and ourselves a backward glance at the many essential instructions the king has heard in the Bhagavatam’s earlier cantos as well as at Krsna’s Vrndavana pastimes just recited in Canto Ten.

**About Cantos Eleven and Twelve**

For many devotees, the Eleventh and Twelfth cantos remain mysterious and obscure. This is because they are filled with dense philosophy, have little storyline to maintain a reader’s interest, and were not translated and commentated by Srila Prahhupada, Although these cantos are obviously not light reading, they should neither he made light of nor neglected. They are alive with guidance and inspiration, and they are meant to be studied, their philosophical thread acknowledged, and their points carefully considered and applied.

Although I was bereft of Srila Prabhupada’s translations and pur- ports to the Eleventh and Twelfth canto texts while writing The Backward Glance, I was not orphaned. I had the fortune of holding in my hand the BBT translations and purports to these cantos, as well as the translated commentaries and writings of our acaryas. I therefore offer my most respectful obeisances to the great personages, Srila Jiva Gosvami, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura. I have written this book guided by their words.

I also offer my humble prostrations at the feet of the BBT team who presented these cantos (Hridayananda dasa Goswami, Gopiparana-dhana Dasa, and Dravida Dasa), as well as to Bhanu Swami for his translations of the Bhagavatam commentaries and Srila Jiva Gosvami’s Sat Sandarbha.

**Translations from the Sanskrit in The Backward Glance**

Because I sometimes paraphrased the translations of the acaryas' commentaries, I asked Alaukika Devi Dasi, a fine Sanskrit scholar, to check for accuracy all of the Sanskrit I included. When she needed clarification on a point, she was able to approach Hridayananda dasa Goswami, who kindly answered any questions she sent.

**A Quick Tour Through Cantos Eleven and Twelve**

The Backward Glance divides the chapters of Canto Eleven into five dialogues and those of Canto Twelve into two. The Eleventh Canto’s first dialogue, which comprises chapter 1 of the Eleventh Canto, plants the seed of Sri Krsna’s disappearance along with that of His family members. Dialogue 2 (chapters 2—5 of Canto Eleven) recounts the questions and answers on which many of the philosophical conclusions and devotional practices of the Gaudiya Vaisnavas are based.

Dialogue Three (chapters 6—9 of Canto Eleven) begins the Uddhava-gita, or Krsna’s instructions to Uddhava, His cousin and dearmost friend. In ibis dialogue, Krsna tells Uddhava about a conversation King Yadu had with a saintly and enlightened brahmana avadhuta. The avadhuta taughi the king practical spiritual principles that be bad gleaned from his observation of nature and common occurrences. Dialogue Four begins with a discussion on varnasrama-dharma and passes through jnana before climbing to the summit of devotion. In chapter 12 Krsna opens His heart and reveals to Uddhava the topmost love of the Vrajavasis and specifically, the love of the Vraja gopis. The dialogue then continues through the powerful words of the Hamsa-avatara and ends midway through chapter 14, with Krsna recommending that Uddhava fix his mind on Him in bhakti.

In Dialogue Five (chapters 14-21 of the Eleventh Canto), Krsna gives instructions on meditation, yoga, mystic perfections, and bhakti. These chapters reveal the unlimitedly opulent Supreme Lord, the support of everything in existence. Krsna then details the varnasrama sys- tern, which leads to the path of knowledge - a path one ultimately renounces if one is to attain pure devotional service. Indeed, traversing karma, jnana, and yoga - the entire Vedic path - culminates in attaining Him through bhakti.

Dialogue Six (chapters 22-29 of the Eleventh Canto) ends the Uddhava-gita, with Krsna’s words carrying His dear friend through the jnana required to untangle the knot of material creation; through extreme detachment with focus on accepting one’s fate and remaining dependent on Krsna; through sankbya-yoga; through the modes of material nature and the worship of the Supreme Lord’s Deity form; and through a summary of the jnana path that purposefully leads practitioners to accept Krsna’s shelter and attain Him. Krsna concludes His instructions to Uddhava by discussing bhakti, and then speaks on how to remove envy from the heart. Uddhava feels immense gratitude for the Lord’s having instructed him, and he prays to Krsna for undeviating attachment to His lotus feet. On the Lord’s order and with a heavy heart, Uddhava leaves Krsna’s personal presence in Dvaraka to satisfy the sages of Badarikasrama with the instructions he has just heard.

Finally, in Dialogue Seven (chapters 30-31 of Canto Eleven), the Eleventh Canto ends with the fructification of the seed Krsna planted in chapter 1: the Yadu dynasty and Lord Krsna depart from the earth.

Sukadeva Gosvami begins Canto Twelve - and we begin Dialogue Eight (chapters 1-6 of Canto Twelve) — describing the ever-degrading ruling dynasties of Kali-yuga and listing the age’s ever-increasing, pain-inducing faults. He then prescribes the only workable cure: the kirtana of Krsnas holy names. Maharaja Panksit then hears about the types of universal annihilation and is given a lesson in jnana before fixing his consciousness on the Supreme Personality of Godhead and leaving his body.

Suta Gosvami narrates the remaining chapters of Srimad-Bhagavatam, which in our book forms Dialogue Nine, the final chapter of The Backward Glance. This chapter covers chapters 7-13 of Canto Twelve.

After summarizing the tree of Vedic literature, Suta Gosvami glorifies its ripened fruit, the Srimad-Bhagavatam. Suta concludes the Twelfth Canto by offering his respects to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Lord Vasudeva, who is the all-pervading witness; to Srila Sukadeva Gosvami; and to the Supreme Lord Hari, “the congregational chanting of whose holy names destroys all sinful reactions, and the offering of obeisances unto whom relieves all material suffering.”

**Comparing the Uddhava-gita to the Bhagavad-gita**

Krsna speaks the Bhagavad-gita to Arjuna, His dear friend, just prior to the great war at Kuruksetra. Krsna later speaks the Uddhava-gita to Uddhava, another dear friend, immediately prior to His pastime of leaving the world.

The Bhagavad-gita is composed of eighteen chapters set in the Maha-bharata. The Uddhava-gita has twenty-three chapters set near the end of Srimad-Bhagavatam, providing a philosophical climax to Krsna’s pastimes. Srila Vyasadeva spoke both gitas, and both share a number of themes.

The conclusion of bhakti is clear in the Bhagavad-gita, but Krsna’s emphasis on bhakti in some chapters is less obvious. The conclusion of bhakti is clear in the Uddhava-gita, and almost every chapter proves that bhakti is the goal of every process Krsna explains. \[See graph on p. 617.\]

Arjuna was a man of action, a warrior; Uddhava was an intellectual, an advisor. On perceiving his brilliant intelligence, Uddhava’s spiritual master, Brhaspati, the guru of the demigods, undertook to personally train him. The words Krsna speaks in these two gitas reflects the difference between the two hearers. Another difference is that Krsna sent Uddhava to Vrndavana (SB. 10, chapters 46-47) to solace the Vrajavasis, particularly the gopis, who were burning in a fire of separation from Him. Later, in the Uddhava-gita, Krsna speaks to Uddhava about the depth of the gopis’ love. He does not speak about this most intimate topic with Arjuna, because it was Uddhava, not Arjuna, who bad visited Vrndavana and met Nanda and Yasoda and Vrndavana’s olber residents.

**Reading the Uddhava-gita**

The Uddhava-gita contains wisdom carefully handed down from Sri Krsna to Uddhava. Since association is the key to advancement in Krsna consciousness, a reader should adopt the mentality that reading the Uddhava-gita is taking association with the greatest persons: Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Sri Uddhava, Srila Vyasadeva, Srila Sukadeva Gosvami, Srila Suta Gosvami, Srila Jiva Gosvami, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura, and our Srila Prabhupada.

Before you begin, prayerfully set your mind to benefit from this association. Then read carefully. Again, read more for association than to acquire knowledge. Make note of points that especially strike you as foundational or otherwise important. Keep these points with you and try your best to meditate on and apply them. Pray to Krsna for the intelligence to make use of His instructions for your advancement. Note that Krsna ends the Uddhava-gita, which comprises about 75 percent of Canto Eleven, with these inspiring words: “This process is the supreme intelligence of the intelligent and the cleverness of the most clever, for by following it one can in this very life make use of the temporary and unreal to achieve Me, the eternal reality.” (SB. 11.29.22)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments: “The devotee is the most intelligent of those with intelligence, but he is not intelligent in dissecting difficult scriptures. He is clever among those who are clever, but he is not clever at earning a gold coin in exchange for a penny. What, then, is he clever at? In Bharata-bhumi, the devotee, using his mortal, temporary body, can attain Me, who am without death. He attains Me who possess an eternal form and who exists at all times. He thus attains his true existence. By his bhakti alone he can even control Me.”

## Canto Eleven

## Dialogue 1. Planting the seed of Krsna’s disappearance pastime

**Chapter 1: The Yadu Dynasty Cursed**

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s invocation prayers to his commentary on Canto Eleven are sweet: “I offer respects to Sri Krsna Caitanya. I take shelter of the Lord of Govardhana, who supported Govardhana Hill on His hand, and of Sri Govardhana, the hill that nourishes \[Krsna’s\] cows. Again offering respects to guru and Krsna, the ocean of mercy, I take shelter of Sukadeva, master of the world, eye of the universe. I offer myself and everything I possess to the supremely powerful Lord, who is the life of the gopis, in service to His dear devotees.”

*Texts 1-7: Krsna contemplates His final pastimes*

Sri Sukadeva Gosvami begins the Eleventh Canto of Srimad-Bhagavatam with a summary of the events that culminate in the disappearance of Krsna and Balarama.In the Tenth Canto, we saw Maharaja Pariksit blessedly submerged in the ocean of Krsna’s unlimitedly sweet pastimes.Now we are nearing the last of Maharaja Pariksit’s seven days. He will meet his disappearance soon, and Sukadeva Gosvami wants to help him journey through the door of death and on to the spiritual realm. He therefore provides the king a backward glance at Krsna, beginning with a summary of the reason for Krsna’s descentin order to indicate that the Lord has almost completed His mission.

Srila Sukadeva Gosvami begins: “Lord Sri Krsna, accompanied by Balarama and surrounded by the Yadu dynasty, executed the killing of many demons. Then, further to remove the burden of the earth, the Lord arranged for the great Battle of Kuruksetra, which suddenly erupted in violence between the Kurus and the Pandavas.... On the pretext of the Battle of Kuruksetra, Lord Krsna arranged for all the kings who were burdening the earth to assemble with their armies on opposite sides of the battlefield, and when the Lord killed them through the agency of war, the earth was relieved of its burden.” (SB. 11.1.1-2)

Sukadeva tells Pariksit that Krsna and Balarama and Their family members, the Yadu dynasty, had killed many demons even before Krsna had arranged for the massive destruction of demons during the Battle of Kuruksetra. Sukadeva Gosvami goes on to describe what Krsna was thinking: “Then the unfathomable Lord thought to Himself, ‘Although some may say that the earth’s burden is now gone, in My opinion it is not yet gone, because there still remains the Yadava dynasty itself, whose strength is unbearable for the earth.’”(SB. 11.1.3)

It is interesting to note that the Lord considered His own family members, the Yadu dynasty, an additional burden on the earth, and therefore contemplated their destruction. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura describes Krsna’s thinking in his comments on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.1.4: “Should someone else undertake it to relieve the earth of this burden? The answer is given. Members of the Yadu dynasty cannot even be censured by anyone else, what to speak of killed, because they have taken shelter of Me and have unrestricted power. Arranging for them to go to Prabhasa and to quarrel, I will arrange for their destruction and attainment of Vaikuntha. I Myself will go to Vaikuntha in My portion \[in His form as Narayana, which merged into Krsna when Krsna appeared on earth\]. Just as the wind causes stalks of bamboo to rub against one another and burst into flame, destroying the stalks, before it disappears, so I will arrange for friction among the Yadus, destroy them, and then disappear.”

The reasons Krsna “removed” the Yadu dynasty can he difficult to understand and even sound cruel on His part. The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.1.3 quotes Srila Sridhara Svami to indicate that “it is impossible for anyone, even the Lord’s own family members, to understand His will completely.” In bis purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 1.15.13, Srila Prabhupada explains why there is nothing ultimately cruel in the Lord’s actions: “The setting of the sun does not mean the end of the sun. It means that the sun is out of our sight. Similarly, the end of the mission of the Lord on a particular planet or universe only means that He is out of our sight. The end of the Yadu dynasty also does not mean that it is annihilated. It disappears, along with the Lord, out of our sight.”

Sukadeva Gosvami continues: “No outside force could ever bring about the defeat of this family, the Yadu dynasty, whose members have always been fully surrendered to Me and are unrestricted in their opulence. But if I inspire a quarrel within the dynasty, that quarrel will act just like a fire created from the friction of bamboo in a grove, and then I shall achieve My real purpose and return to My eternal abode.” (SB. 11.1.4)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura’s comments on this verse indicate that the disappearance pastimes of the Yadu dynasty protect Krsna’s pastimes from Mayavada interpretation by showing that Krsna’s own family members, powerful as they were, are not as worshipable as He, and that “even the most powerful living entity can never equal or surpass the Supreme Lord.”

Sukadeva Gosvami goes on to say that once the supreme, almighty Lord made up His mind, “He withdrew His own family on the pretext of a curse spoken by an assembly of brahmanas.” (SB. 11.1.5)

Sukadeva then completes Krsna’s contemplation of the topic, reminding his audience of the relationship between Krsna’s attractiveness and the mission of His descent: “The Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krsna, is the reservoir of all beauty. All beautiful things emanate from Him, and His personal form is so attractive that it steals the eyes away from all other objects, which then seem devoid of beauty in comparison to Him. When Lord Krsna was on the earth, He attracted the eyes of all people. When Krsna spoke, His words attracted the minds of all who remembered them. By seeing the footsteps of Lord Krsna, people became attracted to Him, and thus they wanted to offer their bodily activities to the Lord as His followers. In this way Krsna very easily spread His glories, which are sung throughout the world by the most sublime and essential Vedic verses. Lord Krsna considered that simply by hearing and chanting those glories, conditioned souls born in the future would cross beyond the darkness of ignorance. Being satisfied with this arrangement, He left for His desired destination.” (SB.11.1.6-7)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comments on texts 6 and 7 indicate the unique mercy Krsna bestows by both His descent and His departure: “Krsna, having appeared, attracted the senses of all people, but when He departed, He left them blind, deaf, mute, mad, and paralyzed! Who can call Him merciful? He is the greatest thief! This is a form of vyaja-stuti, or criticism that actually indicates praise. Krsna actually gave liberation to the demons after killing them; to others He gave prema after drowning them in the ocean of His beauty. No one else has offered such unrestricted mercy. After having spread His glories, which are praised by poets, and thinking that people born on earth in the future would easily cross the ocean of samsara on the boat of hearing those glories, Krsna left for His own abode. Considering all this, Krsna made up His mind. This indicates Krsna’s mercy to the people of the future \[as well as those who were present with Him on earth\].”

In Sri Krsna Sandarbha (anuccheda 181), Srila Jiva Gosvami offers two Bhagavatam texts to prove that the earth was not actually overburdened by impious Yadus, but rather, that the Yadus were Krsna’s most exalted devotees:

The Vrsnis were so absorbed in Krsna consciousness that they forgot their own bodies while sleeping, sitting, walking, conversing, playing, bathing, and so on. (SB. 10.90.46)

How could the brahmanas curse the Vrsnis, who were always respectful to the brahmanas, charitable, and inclined to serve senior and exalted personalities and whose minds were always fully absorbed in thought of Lord Krsna? (SB. 11.1.8)

Thus through His appearance, Krsna had arranged that His potent name, form, qualities, and pastimes would remain on earth and forcibly penetrate the wall of indifference toward His devotional service erected by conditioned souls. His purposes complete, Krsna was now ready to depart for His own eternal abode, Goloka Vrndavana.

*Texts 8-24: Planting the seed of the Lord’s disappearance pastime*

In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.1.8-9, Pariksit Maharaja asks Sukadeva Gosvami to speak further about the cursing of the Yadus, because he is shocked to learn that self-satisfied sages would curse Krsna’s family members - those who had accepted service to Krsna as their life. He was also shocked to learn that the Yadus would quarrel among themselves, destroying themselves “like a fire created from the friction of bamboo in a grove.” (SB. 11.1.4)

Sukadeva Gosvami’s response immediately makes it clear that Krsna simply used the sages as agents of His own infallible desire. Sukadeva then narrates the fateful events that led to the mysterious conclusion of the Lord’s pastimes on earth.

Why are the Lord’s pastimes mysterious? All the activities displayed by Krsna, the unborn, unlimited Lord, are, by definition, beyond the scope of the human intellect to comprehend. They are displays of the Lord’s internal energy and therefore closely resemble the actions driven by His maya-sakti, His reflective, external energy. We call such displays lila. Sri Krsna’s actions are lila because they spring from His independent desire and are facilitated by His internal energy. Even a great devotee like Kuntidevi is bewildered by Krsna’s unfathomable pastimes:

O Lord, no one can understand Your transcendental pastimes, which appear to be human and are so misleading. You have no specific object of favor, nor do You have any object of envy. People only imagine that You are partial. Of course, it is bewildering, O soul of the universe, that You work, though You are inactive, and that You take birth, though You are the vital force and the unborn. You Yourself descend among animals, men, sages, and aquatics. Verily, this is bewildering. My dear Krsna, Yasoda took up a rope to bind You when You committed an offense, and Your perturbed eyes overflooded with tears, which washed the mascara from Your eyes. And You were afraid, though fear personified is afraid of You. This sight is bewildering to me. (SB. 1.8.29-31)

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.1.10 quotes Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura on Krsna’s disappearance hid: “Krsna had clearly demonstrated the unsurpassable beauty and strength of His personal form, pastimes, and pleasures to all residents of earth. Thus His incarnation to kill the demons, save the devotees, and reestablish religious principles had been completely successful. When Lord Krsna noticed that His mission was complete, everything having been done perfectly, He desired It) return to His transcendental abode along with the Vrsnis. This the Lord personally arranged lor the Yatlu dynasty to be cursed by the brahmanas— Krsna is always self-satisfied, and yet in order to execute His transcendental pastimes He arranged to destroy His own dynasty for three specific purposes, namely, to reestablish in the heavenly planets those demigods who had taken birth among the Yadus in order to assist Him; to reestablish His plenary Visnu expansions in Their abodes, such as Vaikuntha, Svetadvipa, and Badarikasrama; and to remove Himself and His eternal associates from the vision of those in the material world.”

*Texts 11-15: The Pastime takes root*

In the home of Krsna’s father, Vasudeva, in Dvaraka, many great sages, including ViSvamitra, Asita, Durvasa, Bhrgu, Kasyapa, Vasistha, and Narada, completed a ritual that would create piety and remove the sins of Kali-yuga. Krsna remunerated the sages with gifts and sent them to holy Pindaraka.

There, young Yadava princes teased the sages by dressing Krsna’s son Samba as a pregnant girl. They then impudently grabbed hold of the sages’ feet and asked with feigned humility, “O learned brahmanas, this black-eyed pregnant woman has something to ask you. She is too embarrassed to inquire for herself. She is just about to give birth and is very desirous of having a son. Since all of you are great sages with infallible vision, please tell us whether her child will be a boy or a girl.” (SB. 11.1.13—15)

In his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.1.13, Srila Jiva Gosvami confirms that Krsna is using His intimate devotees, the Yadava princes, in His mission to remove Himself and them from the earth, and that their lack of humility was by His arrangement.

*Texts 16-23: The curse of the sages*

The sages became angry at this impudent testing that was actually ridicule, and replied with a potent curse: “Fools! She will bear you an iron club that will destroy your entire dynasty.”

The boys fearfully uncovered Samba and were shocked to find an iron club in bis cushioned belly! Returning to Dvaraka, the Yadava princes approached Maharaja Ugrasena and bis royal assembly and revealed the club and the foreboding curse. They were afraid to speak directly to Krsna. According to Srila Visvanatha Thakura Maharaja Ugrasena told everyone to feel neither fear nor shame. Without consulting Krsna, the king then had the club ground to powder. “King Ahuka \[Ugrasena\] of the Yadus personally threw the pieces, along with the remaining lump of iron, into the water of the ocean. A certain fish swallowed the iron lump, and the bits of iron, carried back to the shore by the waves, implanted themselves there and grew into tall, sharp canes. The fish was caught in the ocean along with other fish in a fishermen’s net. The iron lump in the fish’s stomach was taken by the hunter Jara, who fixed it as an arrowhead at the end of his shaft. Knowing fully the significance of all these events, the Supreme Lord, though capable of reversing the brahmanas’ curse, did not wish to do so. Rather, in His form of time, He gladly sanctioned the events.” (SB. 11.1.21-24)

## Dialogue 2. The nine Yogendras instruct Vasudeva

**Chapter 2: Maharaja Nimi Meets the Nine Yogendras**

*Texts 1-10: Vasudeva inquires from Narada Muni*

After planting the seed that would sprout into the disappearance of the Yadus, Sri Sukadeva Gosvami continued to inform Maharaja Pariksit of events that occurred later, in Dvaraka: “Eager to engage in the worship of Lord Krsna, O best of the Kurus, Narada Muni stayed for some time in Dvaraka, which was always protected by the arms of Govinda. My dear King, in the material world the conditioned souls are confronted by death at every step of life. Therefore, who among the conditioned souls would not render service to the lotus feet of Lord Mukunda, who is worshipable even for the greatest of liberated souls?” (SB. 11.2.1-2) Narada Muni returned to Dvaraka again and again, even though he had service elsewhere, because in Dvaraka he could satisfy his desire to worship Lord Krsna. One may wonder how Narada Muni could stay in Dvaraka for any length of time, since Daksa had once cursed him, “You may travel all over the universe, but I curse you to have no residence anywhere.”According to Srila Sridhara Svami, Daksa’s curse had no effect on Narada when he was in Dvaraka, because Dvaraka is govinda-bhuja-gupatayam, “protected by the arms of Govinda.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on text 2 calls Krsna most worshipable: “The Lord binds to Him with eagerness even liberated persons such as Narada Muni. Who would not worship Him? The qualification to worship Him is to have senses, like ears - that is, to be sentient. But it’s not only jivas who worship the Lord; even the best of the devatas, Lord Siva, worships Him.”

On one visit to Dvaraka, Narada Muni went to see Vasudeva, who greeted him with respect. Vasudeva then praised Narada for carrying with him the Lord’s mercy potency, because Narada Muni always acts for the benefit of all those whom he meets, whether they appear to be qualified to receive the Lord’s mercy or not: “My lord, your visit, like that of a father to his children, is for the benefit of all living beings. You especially help the most wretched among them, as well as those who are advanced on the path toward the Supreme Lord, Uttamasloka.” (SB. 11.2.4)

Vasudeva continued: Your kindness is even greater than that of the demigods, for the demigods’ “kindness” actually only delivers the results of karma the way a shadow follows a body. But sadhus like you show real mercy to the fallen.

Restating these thoughts, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura categorizes the mercy of saints as more substantial than the mercy of demigods because demigods merely reciprocate with the limited, material desires of their worshipers (SB. 11.2.6). We can extrapolate on the acarya’s words by understanding the gifts saints bestow: guidance, krsna-katha, and blessings that culminate in a soul’s unending spiritual bliss.

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura also discusses this point, comparing the relative statuses of rsis, demigods, and pure devotees. He explains that sadhus among karmis and jnanis who have no knowledge of the Supreme Lord are inferior to demigods, because at least demigods know the Lord’s position and that all souls are meant to serve Him. But pure devotees like Narada are topmost, even above demigods, because they have been empowered to award the highest perfection of life to both the pious and the impious.

*Texts 7-9: Vasudeva’s glorious question*

Vasudeva now inquires from Narada Muni about bhagavata-dharma “O brahmana, although I am satisfied simply by seeing you, I still wish to inquire about those duties which give pleasure to the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Any mortal who faithfully hears about them is freed from all kinds of fear. In a previous birth on this earth, I worshiped the Supreme Lord, Atlanta, who alone can award liberation, but because I desired to have a child, I did not worship Him for liberation. Thus I was bewildered by the Lord’s illusory energy.” (SB. 11.2.7-8)

Vasudeva attained the position of becoming Krsna’s father. What, then, is he afraid of? What could cause this exalted soul fear or anxiety?

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.2.8 explains: “Srila Jiva Gosvami states that from the anxiety of Vasudeva ... it is to be discerned that Vasudeva had heard of the curse of the brahmarias at Pindaraka against the Yadu dynasty and that he could understand from this curse that the Lord’s disappearance from the earth was imminent. Vasudeva understood that the Lord’s manifest pastimes within this universe were coming to an end, and he now lamented that he had not directly taken advantage of the opportunity to worship Krsna to go back home, back to Godhead… Vasudeva lamented that he had desired Krsna to come to him as a son instead of desiring to go back to Krsna, back to Godhead, to serve the Lord in the spiritual sky.... Vasudeva’s statement... should be taken to mean that Krsna’s internal potency bewildered Vasudeva so that he would desire Krsna as his son. This paved the way for the Lord’s appearance as the son of His loving devotees.”

Vasudeva prayed to Narada Muni in the mood of an ordinary man: “My dear lord, you are always true to your vow. Please instruct me clearly, so that by your mercy I may easily free myself from material existence, which is full of many dangers and keeps us constantly bound in fear.” (SB. 11.2.9) Pleased by Vasudeva’s questions, Narada Muni begins his reply. The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.2.11 notes that Narada will first answer Vasudeva’s inquiry by describing the process of devotional service, then later, at the end of their conversation (SB. 11.5.45-49), discuss Vasudeva’s comment that Vasudeva was at fault for not desiring liberation.

*Texts 11-29: The nava-yogendras visit a sacrifice performed by Maharaja Nimi*

Although our questions tend to steer us to various places in maya’s realm, truly good questions lead to krsna-katha and therefore form a glorious gateway to transcendence. As early as the Second Canto (2.1.1), Sukadeva (iosvaini glorified Maharaja Pariksit’s question about the duty ol one about to die, calling it “very beneficial to all kinds of people” and the “prime subject matter lot hearing.” Similarly, Suta Gosvami glorified the six questions Saunaka Rsi asked at the beginning of the Bhagavatam because they caused krsna-katha to be spoken, “so are of relevance for the world’s welfare.” (SB. 1.2.5)

*Texts 11-13: The power of bhagavata-dharma*

Narada Muni glorifies Vasudeva’s question about satisfying the Lord as “correct,” and acknowledges the unique power of bhagavata-dharma, or the eternal soul’s constitutional duty in relation to the Lord: “Such devotional service to the Lord is so potent that its performance can purify the entire universe.” (SB. 11.2.11)

What is bhagavata-dharma1 Narada Muni calls it sat-dharmah and defines it as devotional service characterized by a pure intention to act solely for the Lord’s pleasure: “Pure devotional service rendered to the Supreme Lord is spiritually so potent that simply by hearing about such transcendental service, by chanting its glories in response, by meditating on it, by respectfully and faithfully accepting it, or by praising the devotional service of others, even persons who hate the demigods and all other living beings can be immediately purified. Today you have made me remember my Lord, the supremely blissful Personality of Godhead, Narayana. The Supreme Lord is so auspicious that whoever hears and chants about Him becomes completely pious.” (SB. 11.2.12-13)

Srila Jiva Gosvami indicates that Vasudeva’s question initially drew Narada Muni’s attention from Krsna back to Narayana Rsi, who had acted as Narada’s spiritual master and taught him bhagavata-dharma.

*Texts 14-29: Maharaja Nimi meets the nava-yogendras*

Narada Muni begins by retelling an ancient history, of the meeting between Maharaja Nimi, the King of Videha, and the nava-yogendras, or nine perfected sons of Rsabhadeva. These nine great souls - Kavi, Havir, Antariksa, Prabuddha, Pippalayana, Avirhotra, Drumila, Camasa, and Karabhajana- were devotees in santa-rasa. Being beyond bodily identification, they traveled about “clothed only by the four directions.” They “wandered the earth seeing the entire universe, with all its gross and subtle objects, as a manifestation of the Supreme Lord and as non- different from the self.” (SB. I 1.2.22)

When they arrived at Maharaja Nimi’s sacrifice, all present stood in respect. King Nimi, recognizing the nine sages as great devotees (nardyana-parayanan) and pure carriers of the Lord’s mercy, and overjoyed by their arrival, worshiped them as one would worship the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Then he bowed his head humbly and said, “I think that you must be direct associates of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is famous as the enemy of the demon Madhu. Indeed, the pure devotees of Lord Visnu wander throughout the universe not for their personal, selfish interest, but to purify all the conditioned souls. For the conditioned souls, the human body is most difficult to achieve, and it can be lost at any moment. But I think that even those who have achieved human life rarely gain the association of pure devotees, who are dear to the Lord of Vaikuntha.” (SB. 11.2.28—29)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments, speaking as Maharaja Nimi: “Today I have seen my good fortune. Taking a human birth provides one the rare opportunity to attain liberation. However, meeting the Lord’s associates is rarer, because they bestow bhakti on those whom they meet.”

According to Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura, the eternal servants of the Supreme Lord are controlled by a powerful overflow of mercy, and they descend to the material world as Vaisnavas to deliver the conditioned souls, who are bound by the results of their own mundane work. Such Vaisnavas distribute their mercy in the form of krsna-katha even to those laboriously searching after the impersonal Absolute.

*Texts 30-43: Maharaja Nimi asks a question*

In this and the next four chapters (2-5), Maharaja Nimi will ask the sages nine questions. A different one of Rsabhadeva’s nine sons will respond to each question. The king’s questions and the sages’ answers are summarized in the BBT purport to Bhagavatam 11.2.20-21:

Ql. What is the highest good? (Asked in SB 11.2.30. Answered by Kavi in SB 11.2.33-43.)

Q2. What are the religious principles (dharma), natural proclivities (svabhava), behavior (acara), speech (vakya), and outward symptoms (laksana) of a bhagavata, or Vaisnava? (Asked m SB 11.2.44 Answered by Havir in SB 11.2.45 55.)

Q3. What is the external energy of the Supreme Lord Visnu! (Asked in SB 11.3.1. Answered by Antarlksa in SB 11.3.3-16.)

Q4. How can one become dissociated from this maya! (Asked in SB. 11.3.17. Answered by Prabuddha in SB 11.3.18-33.)

Q5. What is the true identity of Brahman! (Asked in SB 11.3.34. Answered by Pippalayana in SB 11.3.35-40.)

Q6. What are the three types of karma (karma based on the enjoyment of the fruits of work, karma offered to the Supreme Lord, and naiskarmya)! (Asked in SB 11.3.41. Answered by Avirhotra in SB 11.3.43—55.)

Q7. What are the various pastimes of God’s different incarnations! (Asked in SB 11.4.1. Answered by Drumila in SB 11.4.2-23.)

Q8. What is the aim or destination of one who is averse to the Supreme Lord and devoid of bhakti (in other words, a nondevotee)! (Asked in SB 11.5.1. Answered by Camasa in SB 11.5.2-18.)

Q9. What are the respective colors, forms, and names of the four yuga-avataras, or the four incarnations of the Supreme Lord who appear in the four ages, and what is the process of worshiping each of Them! (Asked in SB 11.5.19. Answered by Karabhajana in SB 11.5.20—42.)

*Texts 30-33: What is the highest good? (SB. 11.2.30) and sage Kavi’s reply (SB. 11.2.33-43)*

Recognizing the unlimited value of the association he now has, Maharaja Nimi is too enthusiastic to make polite inquiries or even to observe the ordinary etiquette of waiting for the sages to respond to the words he had spoken as he worshiped them. Instead, since “even half a moment’s association with pure devotees within this world of birth and death is a priceless treasure for any man,” he asks his first quest ion: What is the supreme good! (SB. 11.2.30)Anticipating the sages’ answer, he continues: "How does one engage in bhagavata-dharma, the Lord’s service?”

After the king asks his question he immediately answers it himself, so one may wonder how he can be so sure that bhagavata-dharma is the supreme good. Maharaja Nimi continues, stating that the extraordinary power of bhagavata-dharma is that it brings the Lord under His servant’s control: “When a living entity offers loving service to the Supreme Lord, the Lord is immediately satisfied, and in return He will give even His own self to the surrendered soul.” (SB. 11.2.31) The king’s understanding takes us back to the Tenth Canto, in which we hear of numerous pastimes where Krsna interacts with the Vrndavana-vasis and is controlled by their love.

*Texts 33-43: Sage Kavi replies*

Kavi begins his powerful reply to this question - a question that actually asks him to define a meaningful life- by describing the potency (33-35) and practice (36) of bhagavata-dharma. He then explains that fear is caused by failing to turn to Krsna through bhagavata-dharma (37-38). In text 39 he also gives a prescription for overcoming fear, then describes what those who find themselves free from fear should do as they move toward perfection. Kavi follows this by painting a picture of the ecstasy experienced by a perfected devotee (40), as well as the humble vision one needs in order to advance to this platform (41). Nearing his conclusion, Kavi assures the king that the results of practicing bhagavata-dharma can be directly perceived (42), and in conclusion provides a summary of his answer (43).

*Texts 33-35: The potency of bhagavata-dharma - sage Kavi’s answer in detail*

Kavi begins: Even those whose intelligence is constantly disturbed due to their misidentification with the temporary can become fearless through the constant, devoted worship of the infallible Supreme Lord’s lotus feet (acyutasya padambujopasanam). And even those in ignorance can easily know that Supreme Lord by following bhagavata-dharma, for it is the process the Lord Himself prescribes for those who wish to know Him. “O King, one who accepts this process of devotional service to the Supreme Personality of Godhead will never blunder on his path in this world. Even while running with eyes closed, he will never trip or fall.” (SB. 11.2.15)

Kavi therefore recommends that one practice devotional service as the gateway to the supreme good, partly because devotional service is so powerful, but also, as Srila Sridhara Svami explains in his conimentary on this verse, because it is so easily performed. Krsna Himself emphasizes this point in Bhagavad-gita 9.2,and Srila Prabhupada further emphasizes it in his purport to that text:

The process of devotional service is a very happy one (susukham). Why? Devotional service consists of sravanam kirtanam visnoh (SB. 7.5.23), so one can simply hear the chanting of the glories of the Lord or can attend philosophical lectures on transcendental knowledge given by authorized acaryas. Simply by sitting, one can leam; then one can eat the remnants of the food offered to God, nice palatable dishes. In every state devotional service is joyful… Simply by tasting the tulasi leaves offered to the lotus feet of the Lord, great sages like Sanat-kumara became great devotees. Therefore the devotional process is very nice, and it can be executed in a happy mood. God accepts only the love with which things are offered to Him.

Srila Sridhara Svami clarifies what it means to run on the path of devotional service “with eyes closed”: “Even if running with both eyes closed, a devotee on this path of bhagavata-dharma will not stumble. ‘Closing one’s eyes’ refers to being ignorant \[of the standard Vedic literature\]. As it is said, ‘The sruti and smrti scriptures are the two eyes of the brahmanas.’ Lacking one of them, a brahmana is half blind, and deprived of both he is considered completely blind.”

Sage Kavi’s expression of the potency of sincerely performed devotional service does not endorse self-created, whimsical, or inauspicious actions performed in the name of devotional service. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments: “If one manufactures his own process of devotional service for the sake of attaining the Supreme Lord, such a concoction is highly polluting and will cause total ruination.” And: “The exalted status of a Vaisnava can never be accorded to one who is not following the basic regulations of bhakti-yoga. Nor can it apply to one who is sometimes serving Krsna and sometimes serving the illusory energy, maya, by mental speculation or fruitive activities.”

Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura’s comment on text 35 is conciusive: “In all dharmas other than bhagavata-dharma, one must consider the conditioned soul’s qualification. But a soul surrendered to the Lord is never confounded by error \[or pride\], even if unqualified in all other respects. His feet never stumble and he never falls. Even though wandering in the world at whim, he always resides in an auspicious place by the influence of his unswerving worship. The unique potency of bhagavata-dharma does not appear in any of the other dharmas of the world. There is no comparison between a surrendered individual who has taken shelter of bhagavata-dharma and the practitioner of any other dharma.”

*Text 36: How to perform bhagavata-dharma*

In text 36 of this chapter, Kavi offers further instructions on how to perform bhagavata-dharma: “In accordance with the particular nature one has acquired in conditioned life, whatever one does with body, words, mind, senses, intelligence, or purified consciousness one should offer to the Supreme, thinking, ‘This is for the pleasure of Lord Narayana.’ ”

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura comments that the pious karmis, who are inclined toward devotion, offer the fruits that result from performing their duties to Krsna. This offering is technically called karma-misra bhakti, or devotional service mixed with the desire to enjoy the fruits of one’s work. Because these persons’ activities are mixed with bhakti, they are gradually purified and their activities transformed into acts of pure devotional service.

In his commentary on Bhagavad-gita 9.27, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura speaks of karma-jnana-misra-pradhdni-bhuta-bhakti, devotional service free from attachment to the fruits of one’s work, but which is still tinged with attachment to performing one’s duty. This is slightly different from pure devotional service, wherein one’s activities are inspired only by the desire to give Krsna pleasure.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments on text 36, above, by saying that as materialistic persons perform activities for material happiness, devotees should perform their activities for the Supreme Lord’s pleasure. If done throughout the day, even the usual mundane activities we perform to maintain ourselves become angas of bhakti. So whatever acts we perform according to our nature and necessity should be performed in service to Lord Narayana.

And Srila Jiva Gosvami comments that those who not only offer the Supreme Lord die fruits of their work but also are extremely attracted to hearing and chanting about Him have attained actual devotion, or svarupa-siddha bhakti. When love appears as a consequence of such pious persons’ becoming attached to chanting and hearing about the Lord’s personal qualities, we can know those persons are approaching the mature stage of spiritual life.

*Texts 37-38: The fate of those who fail to turn to Krsna through bhagavata-dharma*

Krsna is the all-inclusive Absolute Truth. Absolute truth, by definition, means that nothing can be separate from or independent of it. So it follows that all souls have a relationship with the Absolute Truth. That relationship is one of service. If one sees one’s life as meant for Krsna’s service and acts according to Kavi’s words in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.2.36, one’s bhakti will sprout and eventually flower. But what do those who deny bhagavata-dharma - their natural service relationship with Krsna - see? Kavi continues: “Fear arises when a living entity misiden- tifies himself as the material body because of absorption in the external, illusory energy of the Lord. When the living entity thus turns away from the Supreme Lord, he also forgets his own constitutional position as a servant of the Lord. This bewildering, fearful condition is effected by the potency for illusion, called maya. Therefore, an intelligent person should engage unflinchingly in the unalloyed devotional service of the Lord, under the guidance of a bona fide spiritual master, whom he should accept as his worshipable deity and as his very life and soul.” (SB. 11.2.37)

Here Kavi describes the result of interacting with Krsna’s deadly and insurmountable maya with the hopes of finding sense pleasure: one becomes afraid. He also prescribes the cure for fear: surrender.

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments that devotees should not be afraid of being bound by samsara. Rather, fear is naturally destroyed for those who even begin to practice bhakti:

No fear exists for those faithful to the Lord and who turn toward Him… Fear arises by the Lord’s maya. As Bhagavad-gita 2.61 states, when memory is lost, intelligence is lost, and when intelligence is lost, one is destroyed. The intelligent person, therefore, having gotten his intelligence by the mercy of the guru’s lotus feet, should fully worship the Lord by pure (ekaya) bhakti devoid of other desires, such as the desires for karma or jnana. Such a person considers the guru to be as dear as the Lord and his own self.

This Eleventh Canto verse is important, and Srila Prabhupada referred to it in a lecture he gave in 1966 on the Caitanya-caritamrta: “We have discussed the sloka, verse, that bhayarh dvitiyabhinivesatah syad isad apetasya viparyaya-smrtih - because we have taken a reverse position for forgetting the Supreme, therefore we are put into anxiety. Because we have taken a reverse position. Who is God? Viparyaya-smrtih. This very word is used. Viparyaya means topsy-turvied. Your memory has become topsy-turvied. Therefore you are suffering.”

Kavi next compares this “topsy-turvied” vision of a conditioned soul to a dream or illusion: “This imaginary experience of a world separate from Krsna can be compared to the acts of dreaming and desiring. When the conditioned soul dreams at night of something desirable or horrible, or when he dayareams of what he would like to have or avoid, he creates a reality that has no existence beyond his own imagination.” (SB. 11.2.38)

And because the central figure in this illusion is the mind, which continuously seeks enjoyment even while it lives in fear, in the same verse Kavi encourages the spiritual aspirant to control the mind, “restricting it from the illusion of seeing things separate from Krsna, and when the mind is thus controlled he will experience actual fearlessness.” (SB. 11.2.38)

Srila Sridhara Svami speaks of how impossible it is for a soul devoid of unalloyed devotion to refrain from grasping at sense pleasures. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura states that one’s ability to control the mind comes from living a life of devotional service to the Lord. So one of the by-products of seriously practicing bhakti is that “the accepting and rejecting mind can stop its thirst for sensory enjoyment apart from Krsna.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s words on this verse are both sober and practical: “‘Shouldn’t those who live without sense enjoyment (garlands and cooling sandalwood paste and women) or who live renounced in the forest he free of fear?’ Do not say this. If they meditate on sense enjoyment, the work! of sense enjoyment, though absent inti uii -lives, remains always on t heir minds.... Therefore one should control the mind, which accepts or rejects one or another action. But one can control the mind only by being devoted to the lotus feet of guru and by no other method.”

Throughout his writings, Srila Jiva Gosvami underlines that those who seriously want to vanquish the fearful dualities of material illusion must hear and chant the Supreme Lord’s glories.

*Texts 38-39: Becoming fearless and acting without fear*

Kavi concludes with a recommendation: one should become fearless by freeing oneself from material dualities. That is, one “should control the mind, restricting it from the illusion of seeing things separate from Krsna, and when the mind is thus controlled he will experience actual fearlessness.” (SB. 11.2.38)

This is liberation. Naturally, one wants to know how liberated souls should act. Kavi says they should renounce all material attachments to home and family and wander fearlessly throughout the world, experiencing neither embarrassment nor shame, hearing and chanting about the Lord, His pastimes, activities, and His holy names (SB. 11.2.39).

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura restates this recommendation in his comment on the verse: “Singing and chanting, free from attachment to anything else, such a person should wander about.” Srila Jiva Gosvami notes, however, that the processes one follows as he chants should be accepted in disciplic succession, which will offer both the instructions one should follow along with references for those instructions from bona fide Vedic scriptures.

Clearly, therefore, when holy persons “wander freely,” neither their wanderings nor their actions are indiscriminate. They should also strictly avoid the association of those uninterested in Krsna consciousness or who are sinfully engaged.

*Text 40: Perfected consciousness*

Kavi next describes the exalted consciousness one attains if he or she follows these instructions: one becomes filled with premaThakti. “By chanting the holy name of the Supreme Lord, one comes to the stage of love of Godhead. Then the devotee is fixed in his vow as an eternal servant of the Lord, and he gradually becomes very much attached to a particular name and form o( the Supreme Personality of Godhead. As his heart melts with ecstatic love, he laughs very loudly or cries or shouts. Sometimes he sings and dances like a madman, for he is indifferent to public opinion.”

Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu (Caitanya-caritdmrta, Adi 7.93) considered this text the essence of the Srimad-Bhagavatam’s instructions. The Lord also spoke of the great pleasure His spiritual master, Sripad isvara Puri, experienced when he heard that the Lord was chanting with sponta- neous devotion, dancing and crying as He recited His diksa-mantra. Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu told the sannyasis of Varanasi what Isvara Puri had said to Him:

It is the nature of the Hare Krsna maha-mantra that anyone who chants it immediately develops his loving ecstasy for Krsna... The conclusion of all revealed scriptures is that one should awaken his dormant love of Godhead. You are greatly fortunate to have already done so... When one actually develops love of Godhead, he naturally sometimes cries, sometimes laughs, sometimes chants and sometimes runs here and there just like a madman. “It is very good, my dear child, that You have attained the supreme goal of life by developing love of Godhead. Thus You have pleased me very much, and I am very much obliged to You. My dear child, continue dancing, chanting, and performing sankirtana in association with devotees. Furthermore, go out and preach the value of chanting krsna-nama, for by this process You will be able to deliver all fallen souls.” (Caitanya-caritamrta, Adi 7.83, 86, 88, 91-92)

Sridhara Svami indicates that Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.2.40 describes the perfectional stage of life as entirely beyond the scope of worldly affairs, for one’s devotional service at this stage is enriched by ecstatic love.

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.2.40 includes Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s description of the inner experience of a soul whose external expressions correspond to those Kavi describes: ‘“Oh, that thief Krsna, the son of Yasoda, has entered the house to steal the fresh butter. Grab Him! Keep Him away!’ Hearing these menacing words spoken by the elderly gopi Jarati, Krsna immediately prepares to leave the house. The devotee to whom this transcendental pastime is revealed laughs in ecstasy. But suddenly he can no longer see Krsna. He then cries in great lamentation, ‘Oh! I achieved the greatest fortune in the world, anil now it has suddenly slipped from my hands!’ Thus the devotee cries loudly, ‘So, my Lord! Where are You? Give me Your answer!’ The Lord answers, ‘My dear devotee, I heard your loud complaint, and so I have again come before you.’ On seeing Lord Krsna again, the devotee begins to sing, ‘Today my life has become perfect.’ Thus overwhelmed with transcendental bliss, he begins to dance like a madman.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura also notes that the words sva-priya-nama-kirtya from text 40 can refer either to a devotee’s chanting of the names of Krsna, who is dear to him, or his chanting of those names of Krsna that are especially dear to him. By either type of chanting a devotee can develop prema (jatanuragah). Yearning to see their Lord, their hearts melt, and in bliss they dance madly, not caring whether people laugh at them, praise them, or respect or disrespect them (loka-bahyah).

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura recommends that when studying text 40, we should also study text 73 of Srila Rupa Gosvami’s Padyavali: “If talkative people rebuke us, we do not care. We will become thoroughly maddened by drinking the intoxicating beverage of the mellows of love for Krsna. We will roll about on the ground. We will dance. We will experience ecstasy.”

*Text 41: The humble vision we need if we wish to make advancement*

Kavi next describes the vision a devotee needs in order to advance toward ecstatic devotional service to Krsna: Ether, fire, air, water, earth, the sun and other luminaries, all living beings, the directions, the trees and other plants, and the rivers and oceans - a devotee should bow down to all of these and offer respect. One should honor everything in existence, seeing it as the Lord’s energy and an expansion of His body.

Seeing Krsna, the source of everything, in all things means one has a personalistic view of the universe. This is the viewpoint of a lover; lovers are so captivated by the beloved that they remember and see only the beloved wherever they look. Those who have this vision can use everything in Krsna’s service, because they are free of the separatist vision that usually imprisons us. “O scion of Bharata, O conqueror of the foe, all living entities are born into delusion, bewildered by dualities arisen from desire and hate.” (Bhagavad-gita 7.27)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura’s comment on this Bhaga-vatam text further extols the glory of using everything in Krsna’s service: “One who has experienced his own true identity understands that all things exist as paraphernalia for giving ecstatic pleasure to the Supreme Lord. Thus one becomes free from the separatist vision in which one sees the world as existing for one’s own enjoyment. In the transcendental state, whatever a devotee sees reminds him of Krsna, and thus his transcendental knowledge and bliss increase.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura offers a text from the Pur anas in his own commentary on text 41: “A devotee sees everyone and everything in relation to Narayana. Everything is an expansion of Narayana’s energy. Just as those who are greedy see everything as a source of moneymaking and those who are lusty see women in everything.”

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura goes on to explain that whatever falls within the vision of those experiencing prema becomes, for them, a manifestation of Syamasundara’s body, and that sadhakas who even contemplate this type of perfection will also be able to see in this way. Because these devotees know that the Lord’s body is the basis of all the material elements, they will offer everything their respect. For devotees, Krsna is the only object of service. Through the words of a resident of Vrndavana, the Padyavali (239) describes the perfection of this vision: “Separation from Krsna is better than meeting Him. When I meet Him there is only one Krsna, but when I am separated from Him, the three worlds are filled with Krsnas.”

*Text 42: Bhaktas perceive the results of practicing bhagavata-dharma*

Moving toward the end of his description of the supreme good, Kavi notes that the practitioners themselves perceive the results of their own devotional service: “Devotion, direct experience of the Supreme Lord, and detachment from other things - these three occur simultaneously for one who has taken shelter of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, in the same way that pleasure, nourishment, and relief from hunger come simultaneously and increasingly, with each bite, for a person engaged in eating.” (SB. 11.2.42)

Sage Kavi compares devotional service to eating, the results of which are perceptible. Using this text as his reference, Srila Prabhupada often spoke of how we can perceive our own progress in Krsna consciousness: “So that is the test; how much you have become advanced in devotional service you can experience yourself. The example is given: Just like a hungry man, if he’s given food, if he eats, then he experiences himself that he’s getting strength, his hunger is being satisfied. These things will be experienced. He hasn’t got to take certificate from others, ‘Whether I am advancing in spiritual consciousness, Krsna consciousness?’ He’ll feel himself. Bhaktih paresanubhava viraktir anyatra syat. This is the test.” (Talks on The Nectar of Devotion, Vrndavana, October 1972)

Similarly, while lecturing in Los Angeles in 1973, Srila Prabhupada said: “There need be no doubt of whether we are spiritually advanced or not. We can test ourselves. Bhaktih paresanubhavo viraktir anyatra ca. When we eat, we can understand for ourselves whether our hunger is satisfied; we don’t have to take a certificate from others. Similarly, we can test for ourselves whether we are in the material world or the spiritual world. If we are jealous or envious, we are in the material world, and if we are not, we are in the spiritual world.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura indicates that happiness comes from devotional service even while one is still practicing, as a sadhaka: “An example is given to show that even at the stage of sadhana, which gives great happiness, one achieves results. When there is bhakti in the form of hearing and chanting about Krsna, the supreme Deity, a sweet experience occurs. At that time, one should also experience detachment from material happiness.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura further analyzes Kavi’s comparison between bhakti and eating: When a person eats, with each mouthful he feels happier, more nourished, and no longer hungry. As a person who eats just a little gets a little satisfaction, a little nourishment, and some relief from his hunger, so a person who worships the Lord just a little, through hearing and chanting, gets a little experience of the Lord and a little detachment from material life. On the other hand, a person who eats a lot becomes fully satisfied, is fully nourished, and finds complete relief from his hunger, just as a person who worships the Lord fully experiences the Lord fully and becomes completely detached from material life. It’s impossible to eat without cessation, but one can worship without cessation. The more one worships, the more capable one becomes of worshiping Him. That is the difference between the mundane example and the transcendental reality.

*Text 43: Kavi concludes his description of the supreme good*

To summarize his response to Maharaja Nimi’s question about the supreme good, and to further glorify the achievements of those who have taken to devotional service which is the supreme good Kavi concludes with these words: “My dear King, the devotee who worships the lotus feet of the infallible Personality of Godhead with constant endeavor thus achieves unflinching devotion, detachment, and experienced knowledge of the Personality of Godhead. In this way the successful devotee of the Lord achieves supreme spiritual peace.” (SB. 11.2.43)

Kavi’s prescription may seem counterintuitive to a conditioned soul: How can the secret of happiness be to renounce one’s own pleasure in order to concentrate on giving pleasure to Krsna ? But this has been the position of the Bhagavatam since its first chapter: “The supreme occupation \[dharma\] for all humanity is that by which men can attain to loving devotional service unto the transcendent Lord. Such devotional service must be unmotivated and uninterrupted to completely satisfy the self.” (SB. 1.2.6)Serving Krsna with devotion is the nature of every soul in its pure state, and to follow that nature is the supreme good, because it is an activity that benefits everyone.

*Question two: How are various types of devotees categorized?*

*(SB. 11.2.44), and Sage Havir’s reply (SB. 11.2.45-55)*

Maharaja Nimi has heard Kavi define the greatest good: offering devoted service to the Supreme Person. He has also heard that potent devotional service turns even the ignorant toward Krsna (34), that the Lord guides and protects His devotees (35), how one can serve regardless of one’s conditioned nature (36), how devotional service saves one from the tragedy of living in fear (37-39), of the exalted and ecstatic consciousness of devotees who live in their relationship with Krsna (40), how the devotees respect everything and everyone because they can see their Lord in everything and everyone (41), of the nourishment devotees receive when they take shelter of the Supreme Lord’s lotus feet (42), and the supreme spiritual peace that results from constantly endeavoring to worship the Lord’s feet (43).

Because devotional service is attained only through association with devotees," the king quite naturally wants to know more about the Lord’s devotees (44). He asks:

1\. By what symptoms can we recognize devotees who are most advanced, least advanced, and those who are in the middle?

2\. What are the devotees’ religious duties (yad-dharmo)? How do devotees behave when they are with others (yadrso nrnam yathticarati), and how do they speak (yad brute)?

3\. Which “visible symptoms” (yaih lingaih) make a devotee dear to the Supreme Lord (bhagavat-priyah)?

**Havir begins his answer**

The second of the nava-yogendras, Havir, offers a preliminary answer to these questions in texts 45-47, where he describes the most advanced devotee, the intermediate devotee, and the least advanced devotee. The final eight texts of his response to Nimi’s questions, texts 48-55, discuss the topmost devotee in more detail, simultaneously answering Maharaja Nimi’s other questions about Vaisnava duties and behavior.

Text 45 gives Havir’s description of the most advanced devotee. The bhagavata-uttamah, he says, sees only the Soul of all souls, the Supreme Lord, in everyone and everything. Text 46 speaks of the intermediate, or madhyama, devotees, who see four categories of persons and treat each differently, offering their love to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, their sincere friendship to other Vaisnavas, and their mercy to the innocent. Madhyama-bhaktas disregard the envious and those inimical toward the Lord.

The least advanced, the materialistic devotees, are called prakrta-bhaktas, and Havir describes them in text 47. These devotees faithfully worship the Deity in the temple, but they do not behave properly toward devotees or anyone else.

Havir’s answer continues until the end of the chapter (text 55). In these remaining eight texts, Havir will describe only the characteristics of the topmost devotees, or bhagavata-uttamas. Sridhara Svami comments in this connection that Havir speaks about the topmost devotee over a number of texts because such devotees are so worthy of honor. Yet Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura comments (on text 46) that envying any devotee — from the least advanced to the most advanced - causes one to revert to impersonalism.

**Qualities of advanced devotees**

1\. They see everything as Krsna’s energy (text 48)

“Even while engaging his senses in contact with their objects, one who sees this whole world as the energy of Lord Visnu is neither repelled nor elated. He is indeed the greatest among devotees.” (SB. 11.2.48)

Superlative devotees are not attracted to the realm of matter even though they interact with it, because they see the universe as inconsequential - the Lord’s external energy. But it’s not that advanced devotees neglect the universe. Rather, as Srila Sanatana Gosvami comments on text 48, because they see the material universe as the Lord’s external energy, they use everything in it in His service. Srila Jiva Gosvami makes a similar point. Grhitvdpindriyair arthan, he indicates, does not mean that the devotees stop acting in the world just because they are serving Krsna. Rather, because they think of nothing but serving their Lord, they do not use their senses and the resources around them for selfish pleasure. Instead, they use them in His service.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura groups texts 48 through 50 together, saying that they describe the different levels of a first-class devotee. This is how Havir partially answers the question Maharaja Nimi posed in text 44: How does one distinguish between one level of devotional realization and another?

Havir continues to describe the consciousness of a bhagavata-uttama: the topmost devotees are never bewildered by the decline of their bodies, the harassments of hunger or thirst, the hankerings of the intelligence for things they can never attain, or life’s other inevitable miseries. How do they remain so steady in their consciousness? “\[S\]imply by remembering the lotus feet of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.” (SB. 11.2.49)

In the Bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 192), Srila Jiva Gosvami notes that an advanced devotee’s steadiness is also described in the Bhagavad-gita (7.28): “Persons who have acted piously in previous lives and in this life and whose sinful actions are completely eradicated are freed from the dualities of delusion, and they engage themselves in My service with determination.”

2\. Advanced devotees have no material desires (text 50)

Sri Havir continues: The Bhagavata-Uttamas have taken exclusive shelter of the Supreme Lord Vasudeva and become free of fruitive activi- ties, which are based on lust for matter. This means they no longer desire to enjoy sense gratification, sex, social prestige, or money. It’s not even possible for these desires to develop within their minds. Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura underlines that those who seriously wish to achieve such Krsna conscious perfection must live in the association of Vaisnavas no matter how they are classified by the varnasrama system. That is, Vaisnava association is essential for all varnas and all asramas.

3\. Advanced devotees are prideless (text 51)

Because they don’t identify with the body but instead identify fully with their position as servants of Krsna, devotees dear to Krsna feel no pride even though they are pious, may come from aristocratic families, or have performed austerities. The Lord’s dearmost devotees are prideless.

The BBT purport to this text quotes Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura: “\[W\]hen a devotee understands that the process of bhakti-yoga is complete in itself and he becomes absorbed in hearing and chanting the glories of the Lord, the supremely merciful Personality of Godhead affectionately lifts such a first-class devotee onto His own lap. The Supreme Lord can be pleased only by unalloyed devotion, and not by any arrangement of the gross body, composed of five material elements, or the subtle body, composed of innumerable speculations and false pride.” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati concludes, “\[O\]ne should carefully give up all false pride and always remember that he is a humble servant of Krsna. As stated by Caitanya Mahaprabhu, amanina manadena kirtaniyah soda, harih.”

4\. Advanced devotees are not possessive (text 52)

The topmost devotees are peaceful and satisfied; they don’t lay claim to things that cause most people to become attached, like wealth and possessions. Nor do they consider their own body better or more important than the bodies of others. Rather, these devotees consider themselves “simply one among all the living beings who are equally part and parcel of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.” Such satisfied Vaisnavas, Havir concludes, are “considered to be at the highest standard of devotional service.” (SB. 11.2.52)

The BBT commentary aptly notes: ‘According to Srila Jiva Gosvami and Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, this verse of Srimad-Bhagavatam does not forbid using a particular object in the Lord’s service, since a devotee is free to use anything favorable for serving Lord Krsna.” It is the sense of personal possessiveness that the great devotee rejects.

Similarly, one should not be unconcerned with others while remaining concerned only with the pain in one’s own body. Lord Kapila gives His mother a similar instruction in Srimad-Bhagavatam 3.29.26-27: “As the blazing fire of death, I cause great fear to whoever makes the least discrimination between himself and other living entities because of a differential outlook. Therefore, through charitable gifts and attention, as well as through friendly behavior and by viewing all to be alike, one should propitiate Me, who abide in all creatures as their very Self.”

5\. Advanced devotees are fixed in remembrance of the Lord’s lotus feet (text 53)

The topmost devotees are unwilling to part from the Lord’s lotus feet, which are sought after by the greatest of demigods, even in exchange for all the wealth and power in the universe. Their remembrance of Krsna is unwavering - their minds do not leave the Lord’s lotus feet for even a fraction of a second. Devotees with this level of focused remembrance are considered vaisnava-agryah, the foremost of the Lord’s devotees.

In the Bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 196), Srila Jiva Gosvami explains that the topmost devotees know that there is nothing greater in existence than the Lord’s lotus feet. The reason these topmost devotees do not move from Krsna’s lotus feet is that those feet are their life and soul and very rarely achieved. As this Eleventh Canto verse states, even the demigods who have already attained rulership over the three worlds seek those lotus feet.

The BBT commentators offer us the words of Srila Sridhara Svami and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura. Sridhara Svami writes: “\[O\]ne may ask, ‘If one were able to gain the opulence of the entire universe in exchange for leaving the Lord’s lotus feet for just half a moment, what would be the harm in leaving the Lord’s lotus feet for such an insignificant amount of time?’ The answer is given by the word akuntha-smrti. It is simply impossible for a pure devotee to forget the lotus feet of the Personality of Godhead, since everything that exists is in fact an expansion of the Supreme Lord. Since nothing is separate from the Supreme Lord, a pure devotee of the Lord cannot think of anything but the Lord. Nor can a pure devotee contemplate ruling or en joying universal opulence; even if given all the opulence of the universe, he would immediately offer it at the lotus feet of the Lord and return to his position as a humble servant of the Lord.”

And from Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura: “\[W\]e can understand from this verse that since none of the material facilities available in any of the universal planetary systems can distract a pure devotee of the Lord, such a devotee can never possibly fall or become inimical to the Lord’s service.”

6\. Because of association with the Lord’s lotus feet, advanced devotees cannot suffer (text 54)

Those who worship the Lord’s lotus feet do not suffer. “The Lord’s lotus feet have performed innumerable heroic deeds, and the beautiful nails on His toes resemble valuable jewels. The effulgence emanating from those nails resembles cooling moonshine, for it instantly relieves the suffering within the heart of the pure devotee, just as the appearance of the moon’s cooling light relieves the burning heat of the sun.” (SB. 11.2.54)

In his comment on this verse, Srila Sridhara Svami indicates the wonder of Lord Krsna’s feet. Decorating those feet are the Lord’s toes, and on His toes sit His gemlike nails, which have a soothing, lustrous effulgence. That effulgence dispels the lust in the devotees’ hearts.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura adds: “Lust for material enjoyment may disturb devotees, but such lust cannot arise in the heart of great devotees, because it has been destroyed by the Lord’s heroic lotus feet. On those lotus feet are His toes, and on His toes are His toenails, which are like jewels that emanate rays as cooling as moonlight. The cooling moon rays emanating from the Lord’s lotus feet destroy the heat of lust. When His feet rise in the hearts of His worshipers they dissipate the pain of lust, just like the moon rises and dissipates the heat of the sun.”

7\. Pure devotees capture the Lord with their love, and He never leaves their hearts (text 55)

As the Lord takes away all the sinful reactions of those who even unknowingly call His name, so **“**when a devotee who has taken shelter of the Lord’s lotus feet chants the holy name of Krsna with genuine love, the Supreme Personality of Godhead can never give up the heart of such a devotee.” Such a soul is known as a “bhagavata-pradhana, the most exalted devotee of the Lord.” (SB. 11.2.55)

Srila Sridhara Svami tells us that Havir spoke this text to convey the essential characteristic of the topmost devotees. Why, he asks, is the Lord unable to leave the hearts of such devotees? Because these devotees have bound the Lord with love.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura mentions that this text answers two of Maharaja Nimi’s questions: How do devotees speak?, and Why does the Lord not leave the temple of His devotees’ hearts? Just as Yasoda bound Krsna to the mortar by the power of her prema, so the Lord, who binds all jivas with the chains of maya, is Himself bound with the chains of His devotees’ prema.

In the Bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 198), Srila Jiva Gosvami comments on the use of the word saksat, “directly.” Saksat, he explains, indicates that when the Lord appears in His devotees’ hearts, there can be no material desires or sinful reactions in the heart along with Him because of the devotees’ constant chanting of His holy names.

**Chapter 3: Liberation from the Illusory Energy**

*Question three: “What is the external energy of the Supreme Lord?” (SB. 11.3.1), and Antariksa’s reply (SB. 11.3.3-16)*
