Because in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.2.48 Maharaja Nimi was told that a devotee of Krsna sees the material universe as the Lord’s illusory potency” (visnor mayam idam pasyan), the king next wants to understand something about the Lord’s powerful maya-sakti, which bewilders even great mystics. He wants to hear this especially because he has personal experience of the power of hearing about the Lord and His energies and knows that such katha is both nectarean and a powerful medicine that removes all distress.

Srila Sridhara Svami describes the sweetness that motivates Maharaja Nimi’s next question and summarizes Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.3.2: “You have become a great devotee, with all the qualities described in the previous chapter. You have achieved everything you desire. I am always suffering the pain of samsara. Therefore I am not yet satiated by your words, which come in the form of the nectar narrations of Lord Hari and which are the medicine for my pain.”

This time the sage Antariksa replies. He begins with a description of the three modes of material nature. The primeval Soul, he says, awards the eternal, conditioned soul varying bodies, propensities, and types of intelligence, so that they can attain either sense enjoyment or liberation according to their individual desires. That Lord also enters their bodies, activating them to facilitate the mistaken identification of body for self, along with the consequent attempt to find mundane pleasure.Impelled by these deep-rooted desires, the embodied soul then wanders the world, experiencing happiness and distress and using its free will again and again to entangle itself further in karmic reactions.

According to Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, maya’s influence is so strong that the conditioned souls think they are enjoying even in hell. According to their karma, the bound living entities transmigrate helplessly from body to body until the Supreme Lord, through His energy as time, annihlilates the cosmos. During that cosmic annihlilation there is first drought, then unbearable heat, then the universe burns. “Beginning from Patalaloka, a fire grows, emanating from the mouth of Lord Sankarsana. Its flames shooting upward, driven by great winds, it scorches everything in all directions.” (SB. 11.3.10)

Next come the rains with “drops as long as the trunk of an elephant.” That rainfall submerges the universe. “Then Vairaja Brahma, the soul of the universal form, gives up his universal body.” (SB. 11.3.12) Depending on the quality of his consciousness, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains, Brahma either enters the spiritual world, attains liberation, or merges with the unmanifest material nature. Both the gross and subtle universal elements then give up the qualities that distinguish them and, reversing the process of creation, reform themselves first into their source element and then into their orginal source, the mahat-tattva.

Having completed his description of the Lord’s maya, sage Antariksa concludes, “This illusory potency, consisting of the three modes of material nature, is empowered by the Lord for the creation, maintenance, and annihilation of the material universe. Now, what more do you wish to hear?” (SB. 11.3.16)

*Question four: “How can one become dissociated from maya?"*

*(SB. 11.3.17), and Prabuddha’s reply (SB. 11.3.18-33)*

The sage Antariksa’s description of the Lord’s ferocious, devastating, and insurmountable material energy inspires Maharaja Nimis next question, here, formulated by Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura: How can... cripple-minded people cross over maya in the easiest way possible, since by nature they are lazy when it comes to spiritual matters?”

Prabuddha responds: One should note the fleeting happiness, always mixed with sorrow, that results from a life centered on sex, wealth, and the objects one acquires with wealth. “Similarly, how can one gain ultimate or permanent happiness from one’s so-called home, children, relatives, and domestic animals, which are all maintained by one’s hard-earned money?” (SB. 11.3.19)

“Therefore,” the sage explains, “any person who seriously desires real happiness must seek a bona fide spiritual master and take shelter of him by initiation. The qualification of the bona fide guru is that he has realized the conclusions of the scriptures by deliberation and is able to convince others of these conclusions. Such great personalities, who have taken shelter of the Supreme Godhead, leaving aside all material considerations, should be understood to be bona fide spiritual masters.” (SB. 11.3.21)

Prabuddha next describes how the disciple, having found a bona fide spiritual master, should accept that guru’s shelter: “Accepting the bona fide spiritual master as one’s life and soul and worshipable deity, the disciple should learn from him the process of pure devotional service. The Supreme Personality of Godhead, Hari, the soul of all souls, is inclined to give Himself to His pure devotees. Therefore, the disciple should learn from the spiritual master to serve the Lord without duplicity and in such a faithful and favorable way that the Supreme Lord, being satisfied, will offer Himself to the faithful disciple.” (SB. 11.3.22)

Qualities helpful to spiritual advancement are listed next: One should pull one’s mind away from matter and associate with one’s spiritual master and other saintly devotees. One should be merciful to those who are less advanced, friendly toward one’s peers, and serve one’s superiors.One should also be clean, studious, simple, celibate, nonviolent, and equal-minded in the face of the material dualities, like heat and cold and happiness and distress. One should meditate and, living in a secluded place, be fully detached and satisfied in every situation. One should faithfully follow sastra. Rigidly controlling the mind, speech, and body, a disciple should always speak the truth and bring the mind and senses under full control.

In texts 27-32, Prabuddha describes the potent practices that form the essence of the hluikli path, the boat by which souls cross the vast ocean of nescience: “One should hear, glorify, and meditate on the wonderful transcendental activities of the Lord. One should specifically become absorbed in the appearance, activities, qualities, and holy names of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Thus inspired, one should perform all of one’s daily activities as an offering to the Lord. One should perform sacrifice, charity, and penance exclusively for the Lord’s satisfaction. Similarly, one should chant only those mantras which glorify the Supreme Personality of Godhead. And all one’s religious activities should be performed as an offering to the Lord. Whatever one finds pleasing or enjoyable he should immediately offer to the Supreme Lord, and even his wife, children, home, and very life air he should offer at the lotus feet of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.” (SB. 11.3.27-28)

With whom should a disciple associate, and how should he behave with others? Prabuddha continues: “One who desires his ultimate self-interest should cultivate friendship with those persons who have accepted Krsna as the Lord of their life. One should further develop an attitude of service toward all living beings. One should especially try to help those in the human form of life and, among them, especially those who accept the principles of religious behavior. Among religious persons, one should especially render service to the pure devotees of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. One should learn how to associate with the devotees of the Lord by gathering with them to chant the glories of the Lord. This process is most purifying. As devotees thus develop their loving friendship, they feel mutual happiness and satisfaction. And by thus encouraging one another they are able to give up material sense gratification, which is the cause of all suffering. The devotees of the Lord constantly discuss the glories of the Personality of Godhead among themselves. Thus they constantly remember the Lord and remind one another of His qualities and pastimes.” (SB. 11.3.29—31)

In the BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.3.30, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura is quoted on the effect inspired by devotee association: “Oh, you have given up sense gratification. Starting today, I shall also give it up.”

What is the result of devotedly following the practices of sadhana-bhakti? We give the Lord pleasure, which deeply purifies us and ultimately leads us to prema-bhakti: “In this way, by their devotion to the principles of bhakti-yoga, the devotees please the Personality of Godhead, who takes away from them everything inauspicious. Being purified of all impediments, the devotees awaken to pure love of Godhead, and thus, even within this world, their spiritualized bodies exhibit symptoms of transcendental ecstasy, such as standing of the bodily hairs on end. Having achieved love of Godhead, the devotees sometimes cry out loud, absorbed in thought of the infallible Lord. Sometimes they laugh, feel great pleasure, speak out loud to the Lord, dance, or sing. Such devotees, having transcended material, conditioned life, sometimes imitate the unborn Supreme by acting out His pastimes. And sometimes, achieving His personal audience, they remain peaceful and silent.” (SB. 11.3.31-32)

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on text 32 reveals the visions and moods that bring about the ecstatic symptoms listed above:

Rudanti: The devotees cry, thinking, “Another day has passed, and still I could not obtain Krsna. Then what will I do, where will I go, from whom shall I inquire, and who can possibly help me reach Krsna?” Hasanti: It is late at night, the sky is dark, and Krsna is determined to steal from the house of one of the elderly gopis. He is hiding underneath a tree in the corner of a courtyard belong- ing to one of the cowherd men. Although Krsna thinks that He is completely concealed, He suddenly hears a voice from one of the elderly members of the family. “Who are You there? Who are You, I say?” Thus Krsna has been caught, and He begins to flee the courtyard. When this humorous scene is revealed to the devotee, the devotee begins to laugh heartily. Nandanti: When Krsna actually reveals His transcendental form to the devotee, the devotee experiences the highest transcendental bliss. Vadanti: The devotee says to the Lord, “O Krsna, after so many days I have finally achieved You.”

Prabuddha concludes, in text 33, by describing the prema-soaked methodology arising from devotees’ sincere practices as “complete devotion to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Narayana.” It is this type of complete bhakti that effortlessly propels one across the insurmountable ocean of illusion.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains: “Learning about the performances of bhakti ends with text 31. Following that, teachings are presented about the cherished goal, prerna, in order to inspire the devotee to develop that stage, thinking, ‘When will I develop symptoms of ecstasy?’ By prema-bhakti arising from sadhana-bhakti one will easily cross beyond maya, as crossing maya is only prema-bhakti’s secondary result.”

*Question five: “What is the true identity of Brahman!”*

*(SB 11.3.34), and Pippalayana Rsi’s reply (SB 11.3.35-40)*

Maharaja Nimi next asks (in text 34)to hear specific information about Lord Narayana, the supreme personality who is the Absolute Truth (brahmanah) and Supersoul (paramatmanah), and whose service liberates one from illusion. Why has he asked about Lord Narayana? In their response to the king’s first question, the sages have already established that serving the Lord is the supreme good. In question four they explained that bhakti is the easiest way to cross beyond the Supreme Lord’s otherwise insurmountable illusory potency.

According to Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura, the word nistha (used in text 34, and translated there as “the transcendental situation”) can also be translated as “firm faith.” In this sense, Nimi Maharaja is asking how one develops perfect faith in the Supreme Lord (bhagavan-nistha).

*Text 35: The Supreme Brahman is the ultimate cause*

Sri Pippalayana responds to this question. He begins: “The Supreme Personality of Godhead is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of this universe, yet He has no prior cause. He pervades the various states of wakefulness, dreaming, and unconscious deep sleep and also exists beyond them. By entering the body of every living being as the Supersoul, He enlivens the body, senses, life airs, and mental activities, and thus all the subtle and gross organs of the body begin their functions. My dear King, know that Personality of Godhead to be the Supreme.” (SB. 11.3.35)

The sage’s opening words define how Lord Narayana functions as the Supreme Person (the three purusa avataras) in the same order the king inquired about them; that is, he first mentions Lord Narayana, then the Lord as the Absolute Truth Brahman, whose existence pervades all three states of consciousness, and finally as Paramatma, who enters the hearts of all living beings.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains that the fact that the Supreme Personality of Godhead has multifarious manifestations does not compromise His position as the one without a second. The Absolute Truth is paramavyomamatha, or “the Lord of the spiritual sky,” and He appears as two-armed Syamasundara as well as in four-armed, eight-armed, and thousand-armed forms.

Because the king is already aware that the Absolute Truth is worshiped as a person, the sage offers him a description of Brahman, because this aspect of the Supreme is difficult to understand.

*Text 36: Understanding from indirect statements made in the Vedas that Brahman has personal form*

Pippalayana explains: The Absolute Truth cannot be “penetrated” by one’s senses, intelligence, life airs, or perceived in the direct statements of the Vedas. But, he asserts, one can understand that the Absolute Truth exists by studying the many indirect references to Him in the Vedic literature. If He didn’t exist, “the various restrictions found in the Vedas would have no ultimate purpose.” (SB. 11.3.36)

Srila Madhvacarya offers an example of an indirect description of the Absolute Truth from the Brahma-tarka: “The transcendental bliss of the Absolute Truth cannot be compared to the ordinary happiness of the material world.” This implies that the Absolute Truth offers a degree of happiness that cannot be compared to anything in the material world.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura cites the Taittiriya Upanisad (2.4.1), offering another such example: “Words and mind cannot approach the Lord.” This implies that there’s a Lord to be approached. He goes on to present a number of other indirect references to the Absolute Truth from other Vedic literatures including these two from the Kena Upanisad (1.4 and 2.3.9): “Know that Brahman, which cannot be expressed by words and from which words arise,” and “Mind cannot measure it, and one cannot see it with the eye.” “If Brahman did not exist,” Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains, “negative statements about it would be meaningless.”

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura next offers a thought-provoking comment that describes how devotees can see the Lord’s form even though it is imperceptible: “Although the Lord’s body is spiritual, His form becomes visible in the material world by His inconceivable krpa-sakti. His form is described with words like ‘blue like the petals of a blue lotus.’ The Lord’s body is the color of a spiritual lotus petal, but we have experienced only material lotuses.” How, then, can one hope to see the spiritual using only material eyes and experiences? Visvanatha continues: “However, the spiritual form on which a devotee meditates using a material description becomes visible to that devotee by the Lord’s inconceivable mercy. This form is not revealed by the devotee’s material mind and words \[but by the Lord Himself\].”

*Text 37: The characteristics of Brahman*

Pippalayana now describes the Absolute Truth, or Brahman, as the primal source of everything in existence, from the three modes of material nature to the conditioned souls’ senses to their happiness and distress. Yet, Pippalayana explains, Brahman is still transcendental - that is, ever beyond matter. Brahman is clearly the source of everything, and it is ultimately neither undifferentiated nor devoid of potencies or qualities. Otherwise, even calling it “undifferentiated” assigns it a quality.

Pippalayana continues: From Brahman “the manifestation of the material world takes place as the subtle cause and as the material effect visible in the appearance of gross material objects. Brahman, which is the source of all subtle and gross manifestations, is simultaneously transcendental to them, being absolute.” (SB. 11.3.37)

The BBT purport quotes Srila Sridhara Svami: “Karyarh karanad bhinnam na bhavati: ‘The result is not different from its cause.’ Therefore, since the Absolute is eternal existence, this material world, being the potency of the Absolute, must also be accepted as real, although the various manifestations of the material world are temporary and thus illusory.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura also commented on this text. He writes: “The svarupa of Brahman is difficult for people to perceive, but it exists without doubt because all material objects are Brahman, since they are produced of Brahman. Srud says brahmaivedam sarvam: everything is Brahman (Brhad-aranyaka Upanisad 2.5.1).”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura continues: “That from which these powerful energies arise is called Brahman. The gross effect (sat) and the subtle cause (asat) are all Brahman. Why? Because Brahman is the cause of the sat and the asat. ‘You should know that the Brahman that pervades the universe is my condensed effulgence.’ (Hari vamsa) The meaning is ibis: that which is superior to everything, the Supreme Brahman, ‘divides up’ as this universe; it becomes divided into the mahat-tattva and other elements. ‘You should know that this Brahman is my effulgence.’ The Bhagavad-gita (14-27) confirms this: brahmano hi pratisthaham, ‘I am the basis of Brahman.’ Like the intense light of the sun, Brahman is the effulgence of the Lord’s body. In the sruti statement, yasya bhasd sarevam idam vibhdti (‘by His light the universe shines’), yasya refers to Krsna.”

*Text 38: Further characteristics of Brahman*

Pippalayana goes on to describe Brahman as eternal and everywhere at all times (sarvatra). Brahman is pure consciousness, unborn, and neither grows nor decays. Because individual souls experience themselves as unchanging even through the changes undergone by their material body - birth, youth, middle age, old age and death - they can also be understood to be Brahman. Srila Sridhara Svami notes in his comment on text 38: “\[A\]lthough the Lord’s external potency is subject to transformations such as birth, growth, decay, and death, one should not foolishly conclude that the Lord’s internal potency, the living entity, is also subject to these changes. Both the living entity and the material nature are ultimately Brahman, being expansions of the Supreme Brahman.”

The BBT purport writers remind us, though, that unlike Brahman, the individual soul is not “everywhere at all times.” Rather, “The soul is not born, nor does he die. Yet in our present conditioned state we falsely identify with the birth and death of the body. Therefore, because an all-pervading soul would never fall into illusion, sarvatra cannot indicate that the individual soul is all-pervading. Illusion implies an incomplete understanding of reality, which would not be possible for an all-pervading entity. Therefore, the word sarvatra is understood to mean that the pure spiritual soul exists in all material conditions.”

That we are not the Supreme Lord but eternal souls, His parts and parcels, is foundational to Gaudiya Vaisnava philosophy, but when, one may wonder, will I directly perceive the truth of it? The BBT purport quotes the Moksa-dharma section of the Mahabharata that Srila Madhvacarya included in his comment on this text: “The living entity, known as jiva, is not different from Me, for he is My expansion. Thus the living entity is eternal, as I am, and always exists within Me. But you should not artificially think, ‘Now I have seen the soul.’ Rather, I, as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, will bestow this benediction upon you when you tire actually qualified.”

*Text 39: “Little Brahman,” the individual embodied soul*

Sage Pippalayana describes the individual soul as appearing in a body; the body is then born through the agency of an egg, embryo, seed, or perspiration. The soul remains an individual regardless of the specifics of its embodiment. Pippalayana gives an example to illustrate how the individual identity continues despite the soul’s apparently changing external circumstances: “When we are absorbed in deep sleep without dreaming, the material senses become inactive, and even the mind and false ego are merged into a dormant condition. But although the senses, mind, and false ego are inactive, one remembers upon waking that he, the soul, was peacefully sleeping.” (SB. 11.3.39)

*Text 40: Conclusion - serve the Supreme Brahman and fix His lotus feet in your heart*

One may ask why we return to material existence after experiencing, in sleep, a fleeting glimpse of eternality. Pippalayana answers this question as he concludes his description of Narayana, the Supreme Brahman, and tells us how to attain Him: “When one seriously engages in the devotional service of the Personality of Godhead, fixing the Lord’s lotus feet within one’s heart as the only goal of life, one can destroy the innumerable impure desires lodged within the heart as a result of one’s previous fruitive work within the three modes of material nature. When the heart is thus purified one can directly perceive both the Supreme Lord and one’s self as transcendental entities.” (SB. 11.3.40)

Being always in Krsna’s presence requires a pure heart - a heart free of material desires. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura notes that text 40 indicates the sangati, or “coming together” of the successive logical steps developed in preceding texts: one should become a pure devotee of the Personality of Godhead and worship the Lord’s lotus feet.

*Question six: “What are the three types of karma? ” (SB. 11.3.41), and Avirhotra Rsi’s reply (SB. 11.3.43-55)*

King Nimi next asks the nava-yogendras for a practical way to purify oneself so one can approach the Lord: “O great sages, please speak to us about the process of karma-yoga. Purified by this process of dedicating one’s practical work to the Supreme, a person can very quickly free himself from all material activities, even in this life, and thus enjoy pure life on the transcendental platform.” (SB. 11.3.41) The king also wondered why, when he had asked the same question of the Four Kumaras, they had remained silent.

In his comment on text 41, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura states that in the previous verse, the king heard that bhakti and jnana destroy the dirt in the heart created from one’s previous activities, and that one thus becomes naiskarmya, or freed from the desire to enjoy the fruits of his activities. He now wants to hear how this state can be attained through karma-yoga, because karma-yogis are quickly freed from the material, contaminating, and binding aspects of their work as they perform fruitive activities.

Srila Jiva Gosvami notes that the Kumaras did not answer the king’s question because when he asked it, he was still a child, and so was incapable of fully understanding their answer. In the BBT purport to text 43, the idea that the king was too young is qualified in an instructive way: “The four sons of Lord Brahma declined to answered the question of King Nimi since at that time the king was a mere child and therefore not capable of seriously surrendering to the process of hearing through disciplic succession.” Now the king is older and quite capable of “seriously surrendering” to the authority of the Vedas in disciplic succession, and so the sage Avirhotra will answer him.

Sage Avirhotra states that the science of action can only be understood as it is presented in the Vedic scriptures, and not by speculating about it. It is essential, he adds, that one first understand the entire purpose of the Vedas if one hopes to understand their specific recommendations on fruitive acts. One gains this essential understanding by hearing the Vedas from the proper authorities.

By prescribing materialistic, fruitive acts, the Vedic injunctions lead the foolish children of this world (balanam anusasanam) to ultimately reject those acts, just “as a father promises his child candy so that the child will take his medicine.” (SB. 11.3.44) This is the hidden purpose (paroksa-vada) behind the Vedic prescriptions of fruitive activities.

The BBT purport to text 44 explains paroksa-vada: “If a father tells his child, ‘You must take this medicine by my order,’ the child may become fearful and rebellious and reject the medicine. Therefore the father entices his child by saying, ‘I am going to give you a delicious piece of candy. But if you want this candy, first just take this little hit of medicine, and then you can have the candy.’ Such indirect persuasion is called paroksa-vadah, or an indirect description that conceals the actual purpose.”

The sage continues: Following the Vedas allows the materially attached to find pleasure without degrading themselves through unrestricted, sinful, and irreligious acts. Like the candy offered to the child who has taken his medicine, these Vedic fruitive prescriptions are meant only to stimulate interest and faith in the Vedas. Of course, better than this is to perform one’s prescribed duties with detachment, offering the results of one’s work to the Supreme Lord (nihsango ’rpitam isvare). Still, the Vedas are supremely merciful (parama-karuniko vedah), because they offer a gradual process by which one can become purified.

In text 47, Avirhotra gives a prescription for greater surrender and thereby quicker success: “One who desires to quickly cut the knot of false ego, which binds the spirit soul, should worship the Supreme Lord, Kesava, by the regulations found in Vedic literatures such as the tantras.” (SB. 11.3.47) The Pancaratra and other Vaisnava tantras give explicit and detailed instructions on how to worship Lord Kesava. This level of Vedic knowledge and practice is not for “the childlike and foolish” but for the learned transcendentalists.

Avirhotra now places before Maharaja Nimi an essential principle to be applied in his worship of the Lord: “Having obtained the mercy of his spiritual master, who reveals to the disciple the injunctions of Vedic scriptures, the devotee should worship the Supreme Personality of Godhead in the particular personal form of the Lord the devotee finds most attractive.” (SB. 11.3.48) By approaching the form of the Lord that best evokes one’s bhakti and then worshiping Him with whatever one has acquired through one’s activities, one is simultaneously purified of material attachment and more deeply attracted to one’s worshipable Lord. This is a practical description of the value and method of Deity worship.

In the next seven texts - from text 49 to the end of the chapter, text 55 - sage Avirhotra will describe the pancaratriki process, or the regulations for worshiping the Lord in His form as a Deity. These include cleanliness, pranayama, marking the body with tilaka, gathering the items to be used in the worship, establishing the Deity, sitting before Him, bathing the Deity with scented water, worshiping I lim with maul ras, and offering incense, fragrant oils, fine clothing, decorations, ornaments, and lamps. One should then honor the Deity with prayers and bow down before Him.

The sage concludes his description of the worship with this: “The worshiper should become fully absorbed in meditating upon himself as an eternal servant of the Lord and should thus perfectly worship the Deity, remembering that the Deity is also situated within his heart.” (SB. 11.3.54)The worshiper should then “take the remnants of the Deity’s paraphernalia, such as flower garlands, upon his head and respectfully put the Deity back in His own place.” Concluding the worship, the devotee should recognize that the Supreme Soul is not only in the Deity but is all-pervading, present in fire, the sun, water, in the hearts of the guests one receives in one’s home, and in one’s own heart. If one worships using the processes and in the mood Avirhotra prescribes, one will “very soon achieve liberation.” (SB. 11.3.55)

**Chapter 4: Drumila Explains the Incarnations of Godhead to King Nimi**

*Question seven: “What are the various pastimes of God’s different incarnations?” (SB. 11.4.1), and Drumila Rsi’s reply (SB. 11.4.2-23)*

Maharaja Nimi has now heard that the supreme good is bhagavata-dharma: one should act to satisfy the Lord. He has also learned how to practice bhagavata-dharma and been told about the perfection bhagavata-dharma bestows (question one: SB. 11.2.33-43). Next, he heard about the three grades of devotees, defined as those who practice bhagavata-dharma, and learned especially about the qualities of the topmost devotees, the bhagavat-uttamas (question two: SB. 11.2.45-55). Having heard (in SB. 11.2.48) that the topmost devotee sees the world neutrally, as the Lord’s maya energy (rumor mayam idam pasyan), the king asked and was told (question three: SB. 11.3.1-16) about the nature of this insurmountable illusory energy. The fortunate person who desires to cross beyond tire material world will, the king was told, accept initiation from a bona fide spiritual master and fully engage in the powerful and sweet practices of bhakti (question four: SB. 11.3.17—33).

Nimi Maharaja then heard of the Lord’s three aspects, Bhagavan, Paramatma, and Brahman, and especially about Brahman (question live: SB. 11.3.58). Following this description, the king learned about Deity worship as an adjunct to karma-yoga, and noted that one should worship the form of the Lord one finds most attractive (SB. 11.3.48) by bowing down before Him and honoring Him with prayers (question six: SB.11.3.53).

Now, in order to learn more about the Lord he is meant to worship, Maharaja Nimi asks question seven, about the Lord’s qualities and pastimes in His past, present, and future descents. This time, the yogendra Drumila replies. Drumila begins by telling the king that it is impossible to fully describe the Supreme Lord’s attractive qualities: “Anyone trying to enumerate or describe fully the unlimited qualities of the unlimited Supreme Lord has the intelligence of a foolish child. Even if a great genius could somehow or other, after a time-consuming endeavor, count all the particles of dust on the surface of the earth, such a genius could never count the attractive qualities of the Personality of Godhead, who is the reservoir of all potencies.” (SB. 11.4-2)

*Texts 3-5: Garbhodaka-sayi Visnu enters the universe*

Drumila then offers the king a taste from one drop of the ocean of the Lord’s innumerable incarnations, beginning with a description of the purusa-avatara Garbhodaka-sayi Visnu’s entrance into the material elements and His subsequent role in the universe’s creation. Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu reasons, “By tasting a drop of seawater one can get a general idea of the flavor of the ocean. Similarly, by submissively hearing about the Personality of Godhead one can acquire a qualitative understanding of the Absolute Truth, although quantitatively one’s knowledge can never be complete.” (SB. 11.4.2, purport)

“When the primeval Lord Narayana created His universal body out of the five elements produced from Himself and then entered within that universal body by His own plenary portion, He thus became known as the Purusa.... In the beginning, the original Supreme Personality manifested the form of Brahma through the material mode of passion in order to create this universe. The Lord manifested His form as Visnu, the Lord of sacrifice and protector of the twice- born brahmanas and their religious duties, to maintain the universe. And when the universe is to be annihilated the same Supreme Lord employs the material mode of ignorance and manifests the form of Rudra. The created living beings are thus always subject to the forces of creation, maintenance, and destruction.” (SB. 11.4.1-5)

*Texts 6-16: The glories of Nara-Narayana Rsi*

Drumila next speaks of Nara-Narayana Rsi, the Lord’s avatar a as the peaceful, austere twin sageswho taught the performance of detached devotional service (naiskarmya-laksanam). Observing His austerities, Indra, who could not see His potency, feared that Nara-Narayana Rsi would gain enough yogic power to replace him as the king of heaven. To protect himself, Indra sent Cupid and his associates to tempt the sage to break His vows. “As the charming breezes of spring created a most sensuous atmosphere, Cupid himself attacked the Lord with arrows in the form of the irresistible glances of beautiful women.” (SB. 11.4.7)

But Lord Nara-Narayana Rsi is completely self-satisfied, unlike most tapasvis, and so He does not respond to Cupid’s enticements; He shows no interest in them, nor does He become proud or angry. Instead, aware of Indra’s offensive behavior, He laughs. “Do not fear, O mighty Madana \[Cupid\], O wind god, and wives of the demigods,” He said. “Rather, please accept these gifts I am offering you and kindly sanctify My asrama by your presence.” (SB. 11.4.8) Sri Nara-Narayana Rsi then tells Cupid and the demigods that their visit has fulfilled the purpose of His asrama because He has had the opportunity to receive such respectable persons.

His words shame Cupid and the demigods who were present, and they bow their heads before Him. Then they offer Him praise (texts 9-11) in hopes of invoking His compassion. Although ordinary living beings such as themselves tend to be disturbed by material pride and anger, they say, Lord Nara-Narayana Rsi is always transcendental, unaffected by the things of this world. It is not surprising that they, as fallible demigods, could not appreciate His glories. Although they place obstacles before those who hope to reach the Lord’s abode, the Lord is “the direct protector” of His devotees, allowing them to step over all obstacles.

The BBT purport includes Srila Jiva Gosvami’s encouraging comment: “\[T\]he continuous obstacles presented by the demigods form a kind of ladder or stairway upon which the devotee steadily progresses back to the kingdom of God.”

The demigods continue their praise: Through severe austerities, some sages successfully conquer the alluring influences we place before them, successfully crossing beyond the ocean of sense gratification. Yei these same sages “foolishly drown in a cow’s hoofprint when conquered by useless anger. Thus they exhaust the benefit of their difficult austerities in vain.” (SB. 11.4.11)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments on text 11: “Those who perform austerities but do not worship You, being averse to serving You, have two destinations. They either become controlled by us \[the demigods\] or controlled by anger— Just as a person who is drowning gives up whatever treasure he is carrying on his head, so these tapasvis destroy their difficult austerities by cursing in anger, thus making their austerity useless for either liberation or enjoyment.”

As the demigods praised the all-powerful Lord, He suddenly showed them His mystic potencies, which took the forms of “many women, who were astonishingly gorgeous, decorated with fine clothes and ornaments, and all faithfully engaging in the Lord’s service.” (SB. 11.4.12) Gazing on the fascinating and mystical beauty of the women the Lord had created, and inhaling their fragrance, the demigods became completely bewildered, their pride in their own beauty demolished.

The Lord smiled slightly. To encourage the demigods, who were now bowing down before Him, He said, “Please choose one of these women - whomever you find suitable - and she will become the ornament of the heavenly planets.”

“Vibrating the sacred syllable om, the servants of the demigods selected Urvasi, the best of the Apsaras. Placing her in front of them out of respect, they returned to the heavenly planets.” (SB. 11.4.15)

When Indra heard of the supreme power of Nara-Narayana Rsi, he was suddenly aware of his offense, and he became both astonished and fearful.

*Texts 17-23: Further incarnations of the Lord*

Drumila then tells of other incarnations in which the Lord both performs amazing pastimes and benefits the world by teaching the science of self-realization. Included among them are Hamsa-avatara (the swan incarnation), Dattatreya, the Four Kumaras, the mighty Rsabhadeva, Hayagriva, Matsya, Varahadeva, Kurma, a succession of Manvantara avataras, Parasurama, Ramacandra, Krsna and Balarama, Buddha, and Kalki, who appears at the end of the age of Kali.

The BBT commentary to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.4-22 notes: “Srila Jiva Gosvami has pointed out that the description of the incarnations to deal with sudran, or low-class men, refers to both Buddha and Kalki. Those who misuse Vedic sacrifice to engage in gross sense gratification, such as the sinful killing of animals, are certainly in the category of sudra, as are the so-called political leaders of Kali-yuga who perform many atrocities in the name of state management.”

Drumila summarizes his points by reminding the king: “O mighty-armed King, there are innumerable appearances and activities of the Supreme Lord of the universe similar to those I have already mentioned. In fact, the glories of the Supreme Lord are unlimited.” (SB. 11.4.23)

**Chapter 5: Narada Concludes His Teachings to Vasudeva**

*Question eight: “What is the aim and destination of the nondevotee?” (SB. 11.5.1), and Camasa Rsi’s reply (SB. 11.5.2-18)*

Maharaja Nimi now places his eighth question before the nava-yogendras, a question both critical and compassionate: “\[K\]indly explain to me the destination of those who for the most part never worship the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Hari, who are unable to quench their material desires, and who are not in control of their own selves.” (SB. 11.5.1)

Camasa Rsi’s reply begins with a short description of varnasrama-dharma, a system that ensures people’s spiritual and material welfare. He explains how a person’s work is regulated according to the material modes he has acquired. The system of occupational and spiritual duties is, the Rsi explains, generated from the Supreme Lord’s universal form to purify those who are not spontaneously attracted to His service. Varnasrama is meant to be a compassionate system in that it ensures that everyone in society worships the “source of their own creation”; failing to do so, and disrespecting the Lord, causes one to fall into a hellish life of suffering (SB. 11.5.2-3).

Camasa Rsi then appeals to the king to give his mercy to those who are not averse to the Lord’s service but who have little opportunity to learn about. Him. In this group he includes “women, sudras, and other fallen classes,” and says that they “always deserve the mercy ol great personalities like yourself.” (SB. 1 1.5.4) By speaking these words, Camasa Rsi has indirectly indicated the good fortune of those who do have the opportunity to hear and chant about Krsna. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura clarifies the recommendations the Rsi makes to help those bereft of Krsna conscious opportunities: “Those who are distant from topics of the Lord, who are devoid of the good fortune of associating with devotees or distant from kirtana of the Lord (or who are deaf), should first receive Your mercy in the form of instructions on bhakti and then in the form of the dust of Your lotus feet on their heads.”

Camasa Rsi’s point is that by following the general varnasrama system of spiritual and material elevation given by Krsna to guide human society, one can get one’s needs fulfilled without resorting to the soub killing dangers of materialism.

He has also defined the essence of varnasrama: to hear and chant about Lord Hari. Ultimately, it is only this essence that gives life and purpose to the regulatory formulas of varnasrama-dharma.

But every system can be circumvented by the crooked. In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.5.5—18, Camasa Rsi tells Maharaja Nimi of the re- suits obtained by materialists, along with the misery that awaits those who try to defeat the true purpose of the varnasrama system. The varnasrama principles bring both material and spiritual elevation, and those who cheat in the name of their position in the varnasrama system have a dark future, even if they ve been initiated according to the Vedas.

“On the other hand, brahmanas, members of the royal order, and vaisyas, even after being allowed to approach the lotus feet of the Supreme Lord, Hari, by receiving the second birth of Vedic initiation, can become bewildered and adopt various materialistic philosophies. Ignorant of the art of work \[karmany akovidah\], such arrogantly proud fools, enchanted and enlivened by the sweet words of the Vedas, pose as learned authorities and offer flattering entreaties to the demigods.” (SB. 11.5.5—6)

In the Bhagavad-gita (2.42-43) Krsna condemns superficial following of the Vedic formulas: “Men of small knowledge are very much attached to the flowery words of the Vedas, which recommend various fruitive activities for elevation to heavenly planets, resultant good birth, power, and so forth. Being desirous of sense gratification and opulent life, they say that there is nothing more than this.”

Such persons are actually avoiding the Vedas even as they appear to follow them. “In the minds of those who are too attached to sense enjoyment and material opulence, and who are bewildered by such things, the resolute determination for devotional service to the Supreme Lord does not take place.” (Bhagavad-gita 2.44) In text 46 of the Gita, Krsna hints at what Camasa Rsi says in text 6 of this fifth chapter of the Eleventh Canto: “All purposes served by a small well can at once be served by a great reservoir of water. Similarly, all the purposes of the Vedas can be served to one who knows the purpose behind them.”

The rsi’s description now becomes frightening: “Due to the influence of the mode of passion, the materialistic followers of the Vedas become subject to violent desires and are excessively lusty. Their anger is like that of a snake. Deceitful, overly proud, and sinful in their behavior, they mock the devotees who are dear to Lord Acyuta.” (SB. 11.5.7)

*Texts 8-18: Camasa Rsi’s remaining descriptions*

The Rsi continues: “The materialistic followers of Vedic rituals, giving up the worship of the Lord, instead practically worship their wives, and thus their homes become dedicated to sex life. Such materialistic householders encourage one another in such whimsical behavior. Understanding ritualistic sacrifice as a necessary item for bodily maintenance, they perform unauthorized ceremonies in which there is no distribution of foodstuffs or charity to the brahmanas and other respectable persons. Instead, they cruelly slaughter animals such as goats without any understanding of the dark consequences of their activities. The intelligence of cruel-minded persons is blinded by false pride based on great wealth, opulence, prestigious family connections, education, renunciation, personal beauty, physical strength, and successful performance of Vedic rituals. Being intoxicated with this false pride, such cruel persons blaspheme the Supreme Personality of Godhead and His devotees.” (SB. 11.5.8-9)

Such persons neither want nor receive pleasure from hearing about I le whom the Vedic literatures elaborately glorifies, that all-pervad- mg, supreme worshipahle object and absolute controller of everything. “They prefer to waste their time discussing their own mental concoctions, which inevitably deal with gross material sense gratification such as sex life and meat-eating.” (SB. 11.5.10)

Camasa Rsi next places the Vedic rituals that allow for sex, meat-eating, and intoxication in perspective: the Vedic prescriptions that address these so-called pleasurable activities are meant for the gradual attainment of renunciation. “In this material world the conditioned soul is always inclined to sex, meat-eating, and intoxication. Therefore religious scriptures never actually encourage such activities. Although the scriptural injunctions provide for sex through sacred marriage, for meat-eating through sacrificial offerings, and for intoxication through the acceptance of ritual cups of wine, such ceremonies are meant for the ultimate purpose of renunciation.” (SB. 11.5.11) But materialists tend to abhor renunciation. They prefer to use their wealth to enhance their families rather than to increase their knowledge and philosophical understanding of life’s true goal. Still, despite their attempts to embrace continuous and unending pleasure, “they fail to see that insurmountable death will soon destroy the frail material body.” (SB. 11.5.12)

Camasa Rsi now advises the king on the proper application of these often misused scriptural prescriptions: “According to the Vedic injunctions, when wine is offered in sacrificial ceremonies it is later to be consumed by smelling, and not by drinking. Similarly, the sacrificial offering of animals is permitted, but there is no provision for wide- scale animal slaughter. Religious sex life is also permitted, but only in marriage for begetting children, and not for sensuous exploitation of the body. Unfortunately, however, the less intelligent materialists cannot understand that their duties in life should be performed purely on the spiritual platform.

“Those sinful persons who are ignorant of actual religious principles, yet consider themselves to be completely pious, without compunction commit violence against innocent animals who are fully trusting in them. In their next lives, such sinful persons will be eaten by the same creatures they have killed in this world.” (SB. 11.5.13-14)

The strict law of nature that orders the murdered to kill his killer is described in Srimad-Bhagavatam 4.25.7-8: “O ruler of the citizens, my dear King, please see in the sky those animals which you have sacrificed, without compassion and without mercy, in the sacrificial arena. All these animals are awaiting your death so that they can avenge the injuries you have inflicted upon them. After you die, they will angrily pierce your body with iron horns.”

Camasa Rsi next questions the goodness of those who appear pious hut who only superficially follow the Vedas: Such souls, due to their love for their own bodies, ate proud, foolish, and envious of others, including of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. They gradually descend into hell. “Those who have not achieved knowledge of the Absolute Truth, yet who are still beyond the darkness of complete ignorance, generally follow the threefold path of pious material life, namely religiosity, economic development, and sense gratification. Not having time to reflect on any higher purpose, they become the killers of their own soul. The killers of the soul are never peaceful, because they consider that human intelligence is ultimately meant for expanding material life. Thus neglecting their real, spiritual duties, they are always in distress. They are filled with great hopes and dreams, but unfortunately these are always destroyed by the inevitable march of time. Those who have turned away from the Supreme Lord, Vasudeva, being under the spell of the Lord’s illusory energy, are eventually forced to give up their so-called homes, children, friends, wives, and lovers, which were all created by the illusory potency of the Supreme Lord, and enter against their will into the darkest regions of the universe.” (SB. 11.5.16-18)

*Question nine: “What are the respective colors, forms, and names of the four yuga-avataras and what is the process of worshiping each of Them?” (SB. 11.5.19), and Karabhajana Rsi’s reply (SB. 11.5.20-42)*

Hearing of the misfortune and suffering awaiting those who fail to worship the Lord, Maharaja Nimi wonders how they can be saved, but when he realizes that only Krsna’s mercy can save them, he poses his final question: “In what colors and forms does the Supreme Personality of Godhead appear in each of the different ages, and with what names and by what types of regulative principles is the Lord worshiped in human society?” (SB. 11.5.19) By exploring the specific details of the Lord’s appearances and the appropriate methods of worshiping Him, King Nimi hopes to attract conditioned souls to take up that worship and thus receive the Lord’s mercy.

Sn Karabhajana replies to this question, beginning by describing the four yuga-avatar as, or the Lord’s descents in each age in order to teach the yuga-dharma: “In each of the four yugas, or ages — Krta, Treta, Dvapara, and Kali — Lord Kesava appears with various complexions, names, and forms and is thus worshiped by various processes.” (SB. 11.5.20)

The sage begins (in texts 20-22 of this chapter) with the yuga-avatara for Satya-yuga. Satya- or Krta-yuga is a golden age in which people are peaceful, nonenvious, friendly toward all creatures, and always consistent and steady in their behavior. They worship the Supreme Personality through austere forms of meditation, which is the appropriate process of worship in that age, and by internal and external sense control. During Satya-yuga the Supreme Lord descends in the form of an austere brahmacarl wearing a black deerskin and tree bark, a sacred thread, and carrying prayer beads, a danda, and a water pot. He is four-armed, and His hair is matted and His complexion white (sukla). He is known by the names “Hamsa, Suparna, Vaikuntha, Dharma, Yogesvara, Amala, Isvara, Purusa, Avyakta, and Paramatma.” (SB. 11.5.23)

In the next age, Treta-yuga, discussed in texts 24-26, those fixed in religiousness and “sincerely interested in achieving the Absolute Truth worship Lord Hari, who contains within Himself all the demigods ... by the rituals of sacrifice taught in the three Vedas.” (SB. 11.5.25)He too has four arms, but His hair is golden and His complexion red (rakta). He embodies knowledge of worship through Vedic sacrifice. His symbols are the ladle, spoon, and other sacrificial implements, and He is known as “Visnu, Yajna, Prsnigarbha, Sarvadeva, Urukrama, Vrsakapi, Jayanta, and Urugaya.” (SB. 11.5.26)

In the third age, Dvapara-yuga (described in texts 27-30), the Lord appears with a complexion the color of a dark blue flower (syamah). He wears yellow garments, is ornamented with the Srivatsa mark,and carries His personal weapons such as the Sudarsana cakra. Those who want to know this supreme enjoyer will reverentially worship Him in His Deity form in the mood of honoring a great king, following the prescriptions of both the Vedas and the tantras.

Sages glorify the Supreme Lord in the mood of honoring a great king with the following prayer: “Obeisances to You, O Supreme Lord Vasudeva, and to Your forms of Sahkarsana, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. O Supreme Personality of Godhead, all obeisances unto You. O Lord Narayana Rsi, O creator of the universe, best of personalities, master of this cosmos and original form of the universe, O Supersoul of all created entities, all homage unto You.” (SB. 11.5.29-30)

Jiva Gosvami points out in his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.5.31 that Krsna appears at the end of Dvapara-yuga, but great sages glorify Him at the onset of the age in anticipation of His appearance.

*Texts 31-42: The avatara for the fourth age, Kali-yuga*

*Text 32: Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu is the Kali-yuga avatara*

Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.3.30-32 describes Kali-yuga: “When there is a predominance of cheating, lying, sloth, sleepiness, violence, depression, lamentation, bewilderment, fear, and poverty, that age is Kali, the age of the mode of ignorance. Because of the bad qualities of the Age of Kali, human beings will become shortsighted, unfortunate, gluttonous, lustful, and poverty-stricken. The women, becoming unchaste, will freely wander from one man to the next. Cities will be dominated by thieves, the Vedas will be contaminated by speculative interpretations of atheists, political leaders will virtually consume the citizens, and the so-called priests and intellectuals will be devotees of their bellies and genitals.” These four texts (SB. 12.3.30-33), which grant both a perspective on contemporary “progress” and a vision of the future, comprise a short description of the chaos and horrors of Kali-yuga.

But who is the avatara for the Age of Kali? Some say no avatara descends and that the Lord appears only in Satya-yuga, Treta-yuga, and Dvapara-yuga - and therefore He is known as Triyuga (SB.7.9.38). Sastra indicates the absence of kla-avaldras (the Lord coming to perform specific pastimes) in Kali-yuga, but states that the Lord does descend as a yuga-avatara to teach the yuga-dharma, the specific religious practice suitable for this age. During Krsna’s name-giving ceremony, Garga Muni tells Nanda Maharaja that in the past his son had bodies of three different colors, according to the age. These colors were white, red, and yellow. In this age \[Dvapara-yuga\] He has accepted a blackish body (SB. 10.8.13).

As Srimad-Bhagavatam 7.9.38 states, the Supreme Lord comes in a covered form in Kali-yuga (channah kalau yad abhavas tn-yugo ’tha sa tvam) and does not proclaim Himself the Lord. “In this way, my Lord, You appear in various incarnations as a human being, an animal, a great saint, a demigod, a fish, or a tortoise, thus maintaining the entire crea- I ion in different planetary systems and killing the demoniac principles. According to the age, O my Lord, You protect the principles of religion, in l be Age of Kali, however, You do not assert Yourself as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and therefore You are known as Triyuga, or the Lord who appears in three yugas."

Srila Prabhupada’s purport to this Seventh Canto text explains why Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu chose to remain channah, covered: “In all the yugas but Kali-yuga, the Lord appears in various incarnations and asserts Himself as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, but although Lord Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu, who appears in Kali-yuga, is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, He never asserted Himself as such. On the contrary, whenever Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu was addressed as being as good as Krsna, He blocked His ears with His hands, denying His identity with Krsna, because He was playing the part of a devotee. Lord Caitanya knew that in Kali-yuga there would be many bogus incarnations pretending to be God, and therefore He avoided asserting Himself as the Supreme Personality of Godhead.”

Thus the sage Karabhajana indicates that the Supreme Lord does descend and is worshiped in Kali-yuga, despite the horrific nature of the age. He begins (in SB. 11.5.32) by describing the Kali-yuga avatara and the dharma He promulgates:

*krsna-varnam tvisakrsnam*

*sangopdngastra-parsadam*

*yajnaih sarikirtana-prayair*

*yajanti hi su-medhasah*

In the Age of Kali, intelligent persons perform congregational chanting to worship the incarnation of Godhead who constantly sings the names of Krsna. Although His complexion is not blackish, He is Krsna Himself. He is accompanied by His associates, servants, weapons, and confidential companions.

Here is an analysis of how this verse indicates Caitanya Mahaprabhu:

*krsna-varnam tvisakrsnam*

Meaning one: Internally, His complextion is blackish (krsna-varnam), but externally He possesses a luster (tvisa) that is akrsnam, not blackish (but golden). Krsna-varnam also means that He is of the same category (varnam) as Krsna.

Meaning two: krsna-varnam means He repeatedly chants the names of Krsna, because vaniayati means He “utters” or “describes.”

*sangopangastra-parsadam*

Meaning one: Sri Jiva Gosvami states, “His limbs (sa-ahga, upa-anga) are always decorated with ornaments of sandalwood and with sandal-wood paste.” His weapon (astra) is His all-attractive personal beauty, and by that beauty He subdues the people of Kali-yuga.

Meaning two: Srila Prabhupada translated this line of the text in Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, Madhya 6.103: “\[Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu\] is always associated with His plenary expansions \[such as Sri Nityananda Prabhu\] and personal expansions \[such as Gadadhara\], as well as His devotees and associates \[such as Svarupa Damodara\].” These associates are the weapons (astra) with which He fights the Age of Kali.

*yajhaih sahkirtana-prdyair*

The method by which the Lord and His associates fight is primarily (.prayair) the religious sacrifice (yajha) specifically recommended in the Age of Kali, or the congregational chanting of the holy names, sri-krsna-sankirtana.

*yajanti hi su-medhasah*

Those who are intelligent (su-medhasah) will worship (yajanati) the Supreme Lord through the above-mentioned methodology of sri-krsnasahkirtana.

Srila Jiva Gosvami opens the Sat Sandarbha, his six theological treatises that conclusively delineate the Gaudiya Vaisnava philosophy, practices, and goal, with Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.5.32, which serves as his mahgalacarana, or “auspicious invocation.” He follows that verse with a beautiful verse of his own composition that effectively summarizes the meaning of Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.5.32:

*antah krsnam bahir gauram darsitahgadi-vaibhavam*

*kalau sahkirtanddyaih smah krsna-caitanyam asritah*

I take shelter of Lord Sri Krsna Caitanya Mahaprabhu, who is outwardly of a fair complexion but is inwardly Krsna Himself. In this Age of Kali He displays His expansions \[angas and upangas\] by performing congregational chanting of the holy name of the Lord. Srila Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami includes this verse in his Sri Caitanya-caritamrta as Adi Alla 3.81. Srila Prabhupada’s purport to this text adds to our understanding of it:

Antah krsna refers to one who is always thinking of Krsna. This attitude is a predominant feature of Srimati Radharani. Even though many devotees always think of Krsna, none can surpass the gopis, among whom Radharani is the leader in thinking of Krsna. Radharani’s Krsna consciousness surpasses that of all other devotees. Lord Caitanya accepted the position of Srimati Radharani to understand Krsna; therefore He was always thinking of Krsna in the same way as Radharani... Sri Krsna Caitanya, who was outwardly very fair, with a complexion like molten gold, simultaneously manifested His eternal associates, opulences, expansions, and incarnations. He preached the process of chanting Hare Krsna, and those who are under His lotus feet are glorious.

The Mahabharata’s Visnu-sahasra-nama-stotra is also quoted in Sri Gaitanya'Caritamrta (as Madhya 6.104) to identify Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu as the Supreme Personality of Godhead:

*suvarna-varno hemango*

*varangas candanangadi*

*sannyasa-krc chamah santo*

*nistha-santi-parayanah*

The Lord \[in His incarnation as Gaurasundara\] has a golden complexion. Indeed, His entire body, which is very nicely constituted, is like molten gold. Sandalwood pulp is smeared all over His body. He will take the fourth order of spiritual life \[sannyasa\] and will be very much self-controlled. He will be distinguished from Mayavadi sannyasis in that He will be fixed in devotional service and will spread the sahkirtana movement.

And an upapurana is also quoted:

*aham eva kvacid brahman*

*sannyasasramam asritah*

*hari-bhaktim grahayami*

*kalau papa-hatan naran*

O learned brahmana, sometimes I accept the renounced order of life to induce the fallen people of the Age of Kali to accept devotional service to the Lord. (Caitanya-caritamrta, Adi 3.83)

*Texts 33-34: Prayers glorifying the Kali-yuga avatara*

Karabhajana Rsi now presents prayers to glorify the Supreme Lord, Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu, the Kali-yuga avatara. Both prayers end vande maha-purusa te caranaravindam, homage to the lotus feet of the maha- purusa, that great person known as Mahaprabhu. Text 33 can be summarized in a simple way: “Your lotus feet are the most suitable boat by which one may cross the ocean of material existence and attain love for Krsna.”

*dhyeyam soda paribhava-ghnam abhista-doham*

*tirthaspadam siva-virinci-nutam saranyam*

*bhrtyarti-ham pranata-pala bhavabdhi-potam*

*vande maha-purusa te caranaravindam*

“My dear Lord, You are the Maha-purusa, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and I worship Your lotus feet, which are the only eternal object of meditation. Those feet destroy the embarrassing conditions of material life and freely award the greatest desire of the soul, the attainment of pure love of Godhead. My dear Lord, Your lotus feet are the shelter of all holy places and of all saintly authorities in the line of devotional service and are honored by powerful demigods like Lord Siva and Lord Brahma. My Lord, You are so kind that You willingly protect all those who simply bow down to You with respect, and thus You mercifully relieve all the distress of Your servants. In conclusion, my Lord, Your lotus feet are actually the suitable boat for crossing over the ocean of birth and death, and therefore even Lord Brahma and Lord Siva seek shelter at Your lotus feet.” (SB. 11.5.33)

The first sentence in the translation - “My dear Lord, You are the maha-purusa, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and I worship Your lotus feet, which are the only eternal object of meditation” - correlates with the fourth line of the Sanskrit: vande maha-purusa te caranaravindam.

The second sentence in the translation - “Those feet destroy the embarrassing conditions of material life and freely award the greatest desire of the soul, the attainment of pure love of Godhead” - correlates with the first line of the Sanskrit: dhyeyam sada paribhava-ghnam abhista-doham.

We can interpret this line as “Your lotus feet destroy material life and award pure love of Krsna.” The BBT purport, discussing the words dhyeyam sada, “always to be meditated on,” states that there are no hard and fast rules in this age for chanting Krsna’s holy names and that one should always (sada) chant them. Paribhava-ghnam indicates that the chanting of the holy names is so powerful it will destroy the disturbed, quarrel-filled existence of those who have taken birth in Kali-yuga. As the BBT purport indicates, “Once this false identification (with the body) is broken, one can be blissful in any adverse material condition.”

The third sentence in the translation - “My dear Lord, Your lotus feet are the shelter of all holy places and of all saintly authorities in the line of devotional service and are honored by powerful demigods like Lord Siva and Lord Brahma” - correlates with the second line of the Sanskrit: tirthaspadarh siva-virihcimutam saranyam. This line too can be summarized simply: “Holy places, saintly devotees, and powerful demigods find shelter at and honor Your lotus feet.”

The BBT purport defines tlrthaspadam as “the lotus feet of Caitanya Mahaprabhu, the shelter of all holy places.” This allows devotees to visit the supreme holy place - the lotus feet of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu - no matter where they are in the world. Srila Narottama dasa Thakura sings of this in his Prema-bhakti-candrika (song 2): “The struggle to travel to various holy pilgrimage places is simply the mind’s mistake, because to make spiritual advancement all one actually needs is the lotus feet of Lord Govinda. Abandoning pride and envy, and with firm faith in your heart, always worship Lord Govinda without deviation.”

The words siva-virinci-nutam saranyam indicate that even powerful Siva and Brahma carefully worship the lotus feet of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu to find safety and shelter. These words also indicate that Lord Siva and Lord Brahma, as Advaita Acarya and Haridasa Thakura, will worship Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu.

The fourth sentence in the translation — “My Lord, You are so kind that You willingly protect all those who simply bow down to You with respect, and thus You mercifully relieve all the distress of Your servants” - correlates with the third line of the Sanskrit: bhrtyarti-ham pranata-pala bhavabdhi-potam. And this line also has a simple summary: “You offer shelter to and remove the distress of those who bow down to You with respect.” The BBT purport states: “The words bhrtyarti-ham pranata-pala indicate that if one simply bows down without duplicity at the lotus feet of the Lord (pranata), then the Lord will give such a sincere candidate all protection. This verse does not mention that one need be an exalted devotee of the Lord” to bow down or to receive that protection, and Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments that Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu “protects anyone who simply bows down with the thought of doing service.” Therefore, bhavabdhi-potam: the Lord’s lotus feet are “a suitable boat for crossing the ocean of material existence.” This is stated in the final line of the translation: “In conclusion, my Lord, Your lotus feet are actually the suitable boat for crossing over the ocean of birth and death, and therefore even Lord Brahma and Lord Siva seek shelter at Your lotus feet.” We can summarize this as “Your lotus feet are therefore the most suitable boat for crossing over material existence.”

A simple summary of text 34, before we read the verse: “Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu, as a renounced sannyasi, internally cherishes His own loving sentiments in the mood of Srimati Radharani feeling separation from Sri Krsna, and He liberally awards mercy to all conditioned souls. One should therefore worship His lotus feet.”

*tyaktva su-dustyaja-surepsita-rajya-laksmim*

*dharmistha arya-vacasa yad agad aranyam*

*mayd-mrgam dayitayepsitam anvadhavad*

*vande maha-purusa te caranaravindam*

“O Maha-purusa, I worship Your lotus feet. You gave up the association of the goddess of fortune and all her opulence, which is most difficult to renounce and is hankered after by even the great demigods. Being the most faithful follower of the path of religion, You thus left for the forest in obedience to a brahmana’s curse. Out of sheer mercifulness You chased after the fallen conditioned souls, who are always in pursuit of the false enjoyment of illusion, and at the same time engaged in searching out Your own desired object, Lord Syamasundara.” (SB. 11.5.34)

The first sentence of the translation - “O Maha-purusa, I worship Your lotus feet - correlates with the fourth line of the Sanskrit: vande maha-purusa te caranaravindam. According to different deary as, this text can refer either to Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu, Sri Krsna, or Lord Ramacandra. As no qualitative difference exists between Them, that the acaryas have different opinions creates no true contradiction. In Kali-yuga, however, we should choose to worship Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu, the maha-purusa glorified in this verse as the bestower of the yuga-dharma for Kali-yuga: sri-krsna-sankirtana. This point will soon be clarified.

The second sentence of the translation - “You gave up the association of the goddess of fortune and all her opulence, which is most difficult to renounce and is hankered after by even the great demigods” - correlates with the first line of the Sanskrit: tyaktva su-dustyaja-surepsita-rajya-laksmim. This line can be summarized as “You renounced Your own opulent material situation.” The BBT purport gives us the comments of Srila Jiva Gosvami, who tells us how these words indicate both Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu and Sri Krsna:

Caitanya Mahaprabhu had the pleasure of marrying the goddess of fortune. No ordinary woman of the material world, no matter how gorgeous she may be, can in any way compare with the beautiful goddess of fortune. Everyone in the universe, including Lord Brahma, is searching after the goddess of fortune. Therefore it is stated here, surepsita (anxiously desired by the demigods)— According to Srila Jiva Gosvami, this verse also describes the incarnation of Lord Krsna Himself in His original blackish form. Thus the words surepsita-rajya-laksmim indicate sri-mathura-sampattim, or the opulence of Mathura. Mathura is described in Vedic literature as the reservoir of all opulence because of the touch of the Lord’s lotus feet in that precinct. But Krsna, although taking birth in the opulent city of Mathura, transferred Himself to the forest village of Vrndavana. In this case the word drya-vacasa indicates the order of Lord Krsna’s original parents, Vasudeva and Devaki.

The third sentence of the translation - “Being the most faithful follower of the path of religion, You thus left for the forest in obedience to a brahmana’s curse” - correlates with the second line of the Sanskrit: dharmistha drya-vacasa, yad agad aranyam. The BBT purport explains how this text also indicates Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu:

Caitanya Mahaprabhu appeared as a great philosopher-brahmana, and thus He is certainly dharmisthah. In Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, in the seventeenth chapter of the Adi-lila, it is described that a certain brahmana, who was well known for being harsh and cursing others, could not enter the kirtana hall where Caitanya Mahaprabhu was performing kirtana because the door was locked. Being very agitated and breaking his brahmana’s thread, he cursed Caitanya Mahaprabhu the next day on the bank of the Ganges, saying, “I shall now curse You, for Your behavior has greatly aggrieved me. You shall be bereft of all material happiness.” However, Caitanya Mahaprabhu felt great jubilation within Himself, since His mission was vairagya-vidya-nija-bhakti-yoga- to give up the illusion of material sense gratification and staunchly engage twenty-four hours a day in the devotional service of the Lord. Therefore, Caitanya Mahaprabhu took this curse as a blessing, and soon after, the Lord took sannyasa. Thus it is stated in this verse that by the words of the Aryan, the brahmana (arya-vacasa), Caitanya Mahaprabhu took sannyasa (yad agad aranyam) and went traveling through the different forests of India on the way to Vrndavana, and later South India. Caitanya Mahaprabhu wanted especially to preserve the prestige of the brahmana class, and therefore He decided to keep the brahmana’s curse intact.

The BBT purport also indicates how the words in this line indicate Krsna’s appearance: “\[T\]he word arya-vacasa indicates the order of Lord Krsna’s original parents, Vasudeva and Devaki. In Srimad-Bhagavatam (10.3.22, 29) both Vasudeva and Devaki express their fear at the threat of Karhsa, who had already killed all of Krsna’s elder brothers. The word arya-vacasa thus indicates that with great love they requested Krsna to kindly make some arrangement to avoid Karhsa. And Krsna, to obey their order, transferred Himself to the forest village of Vrndavana (yad agad aranyam).'’

The fourth sentence of the translation - “Out of sheer mercifulness You chased after the fallen conditioned souls, who are always in pursuit of the false enjoyment of illusion, and at the same time engaged in searching out Your own desired object, Lord Syamasundara” - correlates to the third line of the Sanskrit: maya-mrgarh dayitayepsitam anvadhavad. It can be summarized, “You, the Supreme Lord in the mood ol Kudhuruni, remain overwhelmed in your mood of ecstatic separation from Krsna. While internally in that mood, You freely distributed Your mercy to those in illusion.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura also claims this line as a description of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu: “He gave up His beloved Laksmi, who was more difficult to give up than His life airs (asu-dustyaja), and whose faithful presence with her husband was desired by the devatas. He went to the forest. Why? He went on the word of the brahmana who tore his sacred thread while cursing him, ‘May the happiness of Your family life be destroyed!’ He was the best among all persons following dharma and thus accepted the curse of the brahmana, thinking, ‘The word of the brahmana should not go in vain.’ What did He do in the forest? He sought out persons who were chasing may a - wife, sons, and wealth; He pursued men absorbed in samsara. Out of His great compassion (dayitaya), He desired to embrace (svabhipsitam) such persons drowning in the ocean of samsara in order to drown them in the ocean of prema. This indicates Lord Caitanya’s causeless mercy.”

The BBT purport also explains how these words point to Sri Krsna:

The words maya-mrgam indicate the special, exalted relationship between Srimati Radharani and Sri Krsna. Maya also indicates the internal potency of Krsna, yoga-maya. The original form of Krsna’s internal potency is Srimati Radharani. Due to the inconceivable love of Srimati Radharani, Lord Krsna becomes easily controlled by Her. Thus, mrgam, or ‘animal,’ in this case indicates krida-mrgam, or ‘a toy animal.’ Just as a beautiful young girl may play with so many dolls or stuffed animals, similarly Lord Krsna becomes just like a doll in the hands of the most beautiful young girl, Srimati Radharani. According to Srila Jiva Gosvami, Srimati Radharani performed innumerable types of worship in order to bind Krsna more and more to Her, because Srimati Radharani cannot live without Krsna. Thus, due to Srimati Radharani’s aradhana, or worship, Krsna can never leave Vrndavana. He runs here and there in Vrndavana, protecting the cows, playing with His friends, and engaging in countless intrigues of love with Srimati Radharani and the gopis. Thus the word anvadhavat indicates Krsna’s boyish activities, His running throughout the transcendental land of Vrndavana, tightly under the control of the love of Snmati Radharani.

How the entire text describes the Lord’s incarnation of Ramacandra is also explained in the BBT purport:

Srila Sridhara Svami has explained how this verse also describes the incarnation of Lord Sri Ramacandra.... In the great capital of Ayodhya all of the citizens loved Ramacandra more than can be described. In this context arya-vacasa means that by the order of His father, who was just like His guru, Ramacandra gave up everything and went to the forest. There He exhibited His great affection for Mother Sita and chased after maya-mrgavn, or the illusory deer that had been created by the trick of Ravana. That this golden deer was especially desired by Srimati Sitadevi is indicated by the word dayitayepsitam.

In addition to interpreting text 34 as referring to Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura also points out how it can indicate Sri Ramacandra: “O great purusal I offer respects to the lotus feet of You who gave up Sita, who was worshiped by the devatas, and hard to give up. I offer respects to You who, fixed in dharma, went to the forest, obeying the words of Your father, and who pursued a false deer desired by Sita.”

The BBT purport ends by combining these different interpretations and pointing to a grand conclusion: “Corroborating the explanation of this verse, the followers of Caitanya Mahaprabhu also worship Him in His six-armed form of sad-bhuja. Two arms carry the water pot and danda of the sannyasi Caitanya Mahaprabhu, two arms carry the flute of Lord Krsna, and two arms carry the bow and arrow of Sri Ramacandra. This sad-bhuja form is the actual purport of this verse of Srimad-Bhagavatam.”

*Text 35: In each age, it is appropriate to worship the yuga-avatara for that age*

“Thus, O King, the Supreme Lord Hari is the giver of all desirable benefits of life. Intelligent human beings worship the particular forms and names that the Lord manifests in different ages.”

Unlike in his description of the other three yuga-avataras,Sukadeva, like Sri Prahlada Maharaja (see SB. 7.9.38), keeps the Kali-yuga avatara channah, or covered, because the people of Kali-yuga are too degraded to properly receive an avatara. The BBT purport adds:

In his Laghu-Bhagavatamrta (Purva-khanda 1.25), Rupa Gosvami states: “The Supreme Lord Hari is described in terms of His color and names as sukla \[white, or the most pure\] in Satya-yuga, and as red, dark blue, and black respectively in Treta, Dvapara, and Kali.” Thus, although in each age various names suitable for glorifying the Lord are given, such as Hamsa and Suparna in Satya-yuga, Visnu and Yajna in Treta-yuga, and Vasudeva and Sankarsana in Dvapara-yuga, similar names are not given for Kali-yuga, although such names exist, in order to avoid disclosing cheaply the truth of the incarnation of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu. In Kali-yuga human society is infested with hypocrisy and superficiality. There is a strong tendency toward imitation and fraud in this age. Therefore the incarnation of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu is revealed in Vedic literature in a confidential, discreet way, so that it will be known to the authorized persons, who can then propagate the mission of the Lord on the earth. We actually see in this modern age that many foolish and ordinary persons claim to be God or incarnations, avataras, etc.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura quotes the Laghu-Bhagavatamrta (1.4.25) in his commentary, and then explains, “In Satya-yuga the Lord is also called Hamsa and Suparna. In Treta-yuga he is called Visnu and Yajna. In Dvapara-yuga he is called Vasudeva and Sankarsana. These have been mentioned in the previous verses. In Kali-yuga, other names also exist, as in previous ages, but are not mentioned to maintain the secret of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s appearance.”

Srila Baladeva Vidyabhusana responds to this Laghu-Bhagavatamrta text: “In that Kali-yuga, when golden-colored Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu appears, the regular, black-colored avatara resides within Him.”

Baladeva’s comment indicates that Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu Himself does not descend in every Kali-yuga hut comes only once in each day of Brahma. In each Kali-yuga a yuga-avatara does descend, but Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu comes in His original form - as Krsna experiencing separation in the mood of Srimati Radharani - only once in each day of Brahma. At that time, the juga-avatara enters Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu as He chants Krsna’s holy names and distributes to everyone the loving mood of Stimuli Radharani in Vfndavana.

*Texts 36—40: Benefits of birth in the Age of Kali*

Having now heard about all four yugas, ending with the dark, sinful Age of Kali, Karabhajana unexpectedly glorifies Kali-yoga: “Those who are actually advanced in knowledge are able to appreciate the essential value of this Age of Kali.” Why? “Such enlightened persons worship Kali-yuga because in this fallen age all perfection of life can easily be achieved by the performance of sankirtana.” (SB. 11.5.36)

By sankirtana, a soul who has wandered through matter from one body to another “can attain the supreme peace and free oneself from the cycle of repeated birth and death.” (SB. 11.5.37) Additionally, even those born in Satya-yuga eagerly desire to be born in Kali-yuga, because in that age many devotees of Lord Narayana appear in a variety of places (although they are “especially numerous in South India”). These souls who drink the holy waters of the South Indian (Dravida-desa) holy rivers “will almost all be purehearted devotees of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Vasudeva.” (SB. 11.5.40)

It’s therefore clear that the fortunate Kali-yuga awards one the opportunity to participate in sankirtana (which counteracts the degradations of the age), easily bestows love for Krsna, and allows one entrance into the divine realm of Goloka Vrndavana.
