As will be stated later in Bhagavatam (12.3.52) but is quoted as follows in the purport to SB. 11.5.36, “Whatever is achieved in Satya-yuga by meditation, in Treta by offering ritual sacrifices, and in Dvapara by temple worship is achieved in Kali-yuga by chanting the names of Lord Kesava congregationally.”

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.5.37 quotes a statement supporting the importance of sankirtana in Kali-yuga from the Skanda Purana: maha-bhagavata nityam kalau kurvanti kirtanam, “During Kali-yuga the great devotees of the Lord always engage in kirtana, chanting the Lord’s holy names.”

Yet the opportunity to chant Krsna’s names is not limited to a birth in Kali-yuga; chanting Krsna’s holy names to attain perfection was practiced in other ages as well. For example, Srimati Devahuti long ago glorified the potent and purifying nature of chanting Krsna’s names when she said to her son, Kapila: “Oh, how glorious are they whose tongues are chanting Your holy name! Even if born in the families of dog-eaters, such persons are worshipable. Persons who chant the holy name of Your Lordship must have executed all kinds of austerities and fire sacrifices and achieved all the good manners of the Aryans. To be chanting the holy name of Your Lordship, they must have bathed at holy places of pilgrimage, studied the Vedas, and fulfilled everything required.” (SB. 3.33.7)

The BBT purport to texts 11.5.38-40 offers many wonderful sastric statements from books such as the Skanda Parana, Padma Parana, Sri Visnu Parana, Vaisnava-cintamani, and Srimad-Bhagavatam to indicate that chanting Krsna’s holy names is effective at all times and in all places and not only in Kali-yuga. Why, then, one may rightfully ask, is sri-krsna-sankirtana especially recommended for Kali-yuga?

The purport to text 37 describes how Kali-yuga has one special opulence - intense suffering - and how this suffering helps souls who are miserable transform their pain:

According to Sridhara Svami, even in previous ages such as Satya- yuga it was not possible for the living entities to achieve the perfection that is available in Kali-yuga. Srila Jiva Gosvami has explained this as follows. In former ages such as Satya-yuga human beings were perfectly qualified and easily performed even the most difficult spiritual processes, meditating for many thousands of years practically without eating or sleeping. Thus, although in any age one who completely takes shelter of the Lord’s holy name gets all perfection, the highly qualified inhabitants of Satya-yuga do not consider that merely moving the tongue and lips, chanting the Lord’s holy name, is a complete process, and that the Lord’s holy name is the only shelter within the universe— In Satya-yuga sinful life is practically unheard of, and therefore people are not afflicted with the terrible reactions seen in Kali-yuga, such as world war, famine, plague, drought, insanity, etc. Although in Satya-yuga people always worship the Personality of Godhead as the ultimate goal of life and meticulously follow His laws, called dharma, they do not feel themselves to be in a helpless condition, and thus they do not always experience intense love for the Lord.

However, in Kali-yuga living conditions are so unbearable, modern governments are so obnoxious, our bodies are so ridden by physical and mental disease, and even self-preservation is so troublesome, that the conditioned souls intensely cry out the holy name of Krsna, begging for relief from the onslaught of this age.... Thus, due to their helpless and pathetic condition, the living entities in Kali-yuga have great impetus to surrender fully to the holy name of Krsna, putting all of their hope and faith in the Lord’s holy name. Kali-yuga is therefore the best age because in this age, more than in Satya-yuga or other ages, the conditioned souls become disgusted with the kingdom of illusion and surrender fully to the Lord’s holy name. This status of full surrender is called paramam santim, or supreme peace.

Perceptive souls in Satya-yuga are therefore willing to undergo the intense austerity of living in Kali-yuga so they can associate with devotees and gain the facility to develop love for Krsna through sri-krsna-sankirtana.

*Texts 41—42: The glories of the surrendered*

In two texts, Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.5.41 and 42 - and in conclusion - Karabhajana Rsi extolls the uniquely glorious position of souls who have given up everything other than the shelter of the Lord’s lotus feet.

*Text 41: A soul surrendered to Krsna is freed from all worldly obligations*

“O King, one who has given up all material duties and has taken full shelter of the lotus feet of Mukunda, who offers shelter to all, is not indebted to the demigods, great sages, ordinary living beings, relatives, friends, mankind, or even one’s forefathers who have passed away. Since all such classes of living entities are part and parcel of the Supreme Lord, one who has surrendered to the Lord’s service has no need to serve such persons separately.”

A soul fully surrendered to serving Krsna is freed from the obligations of ordinary persons. Fully surrendered souls owe no karmic debts, just as those who water the roots of a tree automatically water its branches and leaves. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments, “Smrti says pariksinam rnartham karma karayet: one should perform karmas for destroying debts. That is not so for the devotee who has surrendered completely to Mukunda. It is just like a person who, on being accepted as die servant of the emperor of the earth, cannot be the servant of the ruler of one stale.”

Visvanatha Cakravarti supports his statement with Krsna’s words as they are spoken in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.20.9: “As long as one is not satiated by fruitive activity and has not awakened his taste for devotional service by hearing and chanting about the Supreme Lord, one has to act according to the regulative principles of the Vedic injunctions.”

Sukadeva Gosvami, narrating the words of Karabhajana Rsi, thus encourages full detachment in Maharaja Pariksit; because the king will die soon, it’s important that Pariksit Maharaja understands that his only real duty is to hear about Krsna and remain fully under the Lord’s protection.

The next text, 42, will describe how the fully surrendered soul is dear to the Lord.

*Text 42: A soul surrendered to Krsna does not need to perform purificatory atonement processes*

“One who has thus given up all other engagements and has taken full shelter at the lotus feet of Hari, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, is very dear to the Lord. Indeed, if such a surrendered soul accidentally commits some sinful activity, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is seated within everyone’s heart, immediately takes away the reaction to such sin.”

The BBT purport quotes Lord Krsna’s words from the Bhagavad-gita (9.30),along with an example to support the text’s conclusion:

Although the beloved child may accidentally commit an abominable activity, the loving father forgives the child, taking into consideration the actual good intentions of the child. Thus, although the devotee of the Lord does not try to exploit the Lord’s mercy by requesting the Lord to free him from any future suffering, the Lord, by His own initiative, frees the devotee from the reactions to accidental falldowns.

This causeless mercy of the Lord upon His devotee is His param-aisvaryam, or supreme opulence. Gradually the faithful devotee becomes free, even from accidental falldown, because simply by remembering the lotus feet of the Lord, what to speak of by actively rendering service to Him, his heart is purified. Although the surrendered devotees of the Personality of Godhead may sometimes appear to be affected by mundane attitudes, they are inevitably protected by the merciful Lord and are never actually defeated in life.

Through his explanation of this text, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura deepens still further our understanding of the Lord’s heartfelt reciprocation with His devotee’s surrender and service: “Having negated all prescribed karma, now the sage negates atonement for committing sinful acts. A person who has given up the thoughts of his obligation to worship the devatas should not have a tendency to commit sin. If by illusion however this does happen, the Lord destroys the reaction. ‘But it is seen that masters punish their servants when the servants commit sin. The Lord should also punish his servants.’ The devotee will not be punished because he is dear to the Lord. That is the Lord’s great quality (paresah). ‘Must not the devotee perform worship to destroy the reaction to sin?’ No. The Lord is in the heart of all beings, and due to His inherent powers (vastu-saktis), He does not depend on the devotee having to request this.”

*Texts 43-52: Narada Muni concludes his conversation with Vasudeva. The nine Yogendras depart (texts 43-45) and Narada Muni glorifies Vasudeva’s good fortune (texts 46-50)*

“Narada Muni said: Having thus heard the science of devotional service, Nimi, the King of Mithila, felt extremely satisfied and, along with the sacrificial priests, offered respectful worship to the sagacious sons of Jayanti.” (SB. 11.5.43) The sages then disappeared before everyone’s eyes, and the fortunate King Nimi began to practice what he had learned from the sages.

Narada then tells Vasudeva, “O greatly fortunate Vasudeva, simply apply with faith these principles of devotional service which you have heard, and thus, being free from material association, you will attain the Supreme.” (SB. 11.5.45)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura tells us that Vasudeva was an eternally perfected associate of the Supreme Lord - the father of Krsna - hut because of his humble absorption in the mood of an ordinary man longing for devotional perfection, Narada Muni spoke to him as if he were in fact ordinary. In texts 46-50, however, Narada speaks more accurately about Vasudeva’s position: “Indeed, the whole world lias become filled with the glories of you ami your good wife because the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Lord Hari, has taken the position of your son.” This was due to Vasudeva’s extraordinary devotion to the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Narada continues: “My dear Vasudeva, you and your good wife Devaki have manifested great transcendental love for Krsna, accepting Him as your son. Indeed, you are always seeing the Lord, embracing Him, speaking with Him, resting with Him, sitting together with Him, and taking your meals with Him. By such affectionate and intimate association with the Lord, undoubtedly both of you have completely purified your hearts. In other words, you are already perfect.” (SB. 11.5.46-47)

If kings inimical to Krsna such as Sisupala, Paundraka, and Salva achieved liberation by always thinking of Him in envy, “what then can be said of the benedictions offered to those who constantly fix their minds on Lord Krsna in a favorable, loving mood?” (SB. 11.5.48)

Even foolish sinners like Sisupala and Duryodhana, who showered abuse on the Lord, were cleansed of their sins simply by remembering Krsna. Somehow or other their minds were absorbed in Him, and so they attained liberation.

What doubt, then, is there about the destination of those who are overwhelmed by devotional feelings for the Lord?

The BBT purport to text 48 explains Vasudeva’s ecstasy in more detail: “Vasudeva was also feeling anxiety because on the one hand he was aware that Krsna is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, hut at the same time he treated the Lord as his beloved son— In this way Vasudeva was feeling that undoubtedly he had offended the Lord in his attempt to train Lord Krsna as his son. However, Lord Krsna is actually pleased when a pure devotee becomes absorbed in parental love for Him and thus devotedly tries to care for Him just as loving parents care for a small child.”

When Krsna had released Vasudeva and Devaki from prison after Kamsa’s death (SB. 10.44.50-51 and 10.45.1), they had a similar conflicting mixture of parental love and reverence. In this regard Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments (10.44.51): “Remembering the events of Krsna’s birth and seeing the power He displayed on killing Kamsa, Vasudeva and Devaki, seeing Him as the Lord, could not embrace Him. Conscious of custom (which does not allow parents to bow to their children), neither did they offer their obeisances. They remained fearful and paralyzed; they simply stood." At that time, seeing His mother and father standing stunned and immobile with folded hands, Krsna spread the influence of His yoga-maya, which caused a more satisfying and ecstatic exchange.

Narada Muni now encourages Vasudeva simply to think of Krsna as his son: “Do not think of Krsna as an ordinary child, because He is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, inexhaustible and the Soul of all beings. The Lord has concealed His inconceivable opulence and is thus outwardly appearing to be an ordinary human being.” (SB. 11.5.49) His mission was to remove the earth’s burden and protect the saintly devotees, and to both demons and devotees He mercifully awards liberation, simultaneously spreading His fame throughout the universe.

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.5.49 provides details: ‘“Due to your love for Krsna you may think that He is an ordinary human being. You are appearing like a human being, and Lord Krsna is simply reciprocating with you. In order to encourage you to love Him as your son, He is placing Himself under your control. And thus, His inconceivable power and opulences are being concealed from you. Don’t assume, however, that there is actually a dangerous situation because of the events of this material world. Although Krsna appears to be under your control, He is eternally the supreme controller. Therefore, do not consider Him to be a human being. He is always the Supreme Personality of Godhead.’ ... when Vasudeva was filled with anxiety due to the dangerous situation created by the brahmana’s curse, Narada immediately reminded him that such anxiety was unnecessary, since all these events were under the direct control of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura adds, “You should think of Krsna with attachment, not indifference. Do not think that Krsna is the Supreme Lord and is just making a show of being your son, although He is not. Think ‘He is my son.’ ‘But how can the Lord become the son of a mortal like me?’ He hides His powers by His maya, His mercy, and i hen, as a human, He becomes the son of you, another human. But even then, He remains supreme with all powers undiminished . . . Actually Krsna’s human form is His svarupa \[actual form\]; it is not illusory.”

“Sri Sukadeva Gosvami continued: Having heard this narration, the greatly fortunate Vasudeva was completely struck with wonder. Thus he and his most blessed wife Devaki gave up all illusion and anxiety that had entered their hearts.” (SB. 1 1.5.51)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains, “The Lord appeared to kill the kings who were a burden to the earth, to protect the devotees, and to give pleasure to both by giving sayujya to the demons and prema to the devotees. Thus the Lord cannot be accused of being biased or hateful. Vasudeva and Devaki thus gave up their ignorance concerning Krsna’s awarding liberation to demons.”

*Text 52: Phala-sruti, the great fortune that results from attentively meditating on the sages’ instructions*

“Anyone who meditates on this pious historical narration with fixed attention will purify himself of all contamination in this very life and thus achieve the highest spiritual perfection.”

## Dialogue 3. The Uddhava-gita begins: knowledge gained by observing the world

*Canto eleven: chapters 6-9*

**Chapter 6: The Yadu Dynasty Retires to Prabhasa**

*Texts 1-6: The demigods approach Sri Krsna in Dvaraka*

In the first chapter of the Eleventh Canto, Sri Krsna planted a seed in the form of the sages’ curse that would fructify into an all-consuming fratricidal battle and lead to the Yadus’ return to the spiritual world. This event would be followed by Krsna’s own departure from the earth. But first, the demigods who control the universe will arrive in Dvaraka hoping to meet Krsna. Brahma, Siva, Indra, and others - along with their respective followers - have come for a specific purpose.

But to begin, in text 4, Sukadeva Gosvami includes in his description of their arrival his own praise of Krsna’s form: “By His transcendental form, Krsna, the Supreme Lord, enchanted all human beings and spread His own fame throughout the worlds. The Lord’s glories destroy all contamination within the universe.” (SB. 11.6.4)

On beholding the Lord’s splendid form, the demigods cover it with fragrant, heavenly garlands. They then add their own voices to Sukadeva’s praise. But their prayers, spoken now near the close of Krsna’s pastime's, begin to resemble the prayers they spoke when they welcomed His descent into the world.Both sets of prayers are made about universal affairs - naming Krsna the cause of everything in the material world, and describing Him as transcendental to the material creation. Again they point out that His lotus feet award His devotees protection, shelter, and the fulfillment of all desires.

*Texts 7-19: The prayers of the demigods*

*Texts 7-13: The glorious lotus feet of Krsna*

The demigods call Krsna the Supreme Personality of Godhead and the transcendental cause of all causes. His lotus feet are the goal of all transcendentalists, and faithful meditation on those feet is the sadhana mystic yogis perform.

Commenting on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.6.7, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains why the demigods see themselves as most fortunate: “Persons desiring liberation meditate on those lotus feet but do not see them. We, however, have seen those feet and thus we offer them our respects. What great fortune we have!”

The demigods continue: Even though there are other ways to make spiritual advancement, these methods can’t equal the purification and spiritual attainment that having faith in You and Your glories offers. “Our Lord, those pure souls who have developed a powerful transcendental faith in Your glories achieve a purified state of existence that can never be attained by those lacking such faith.” (SB. 11.6.9)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on this prayer expands our understanding of the demigods’ words: “Just as everyone should worship Your lotus feet, so they should hear and remember Your glories. O worshipable Lord, one does not become purified through knowledge or other processes, because generally the heart is left contaminated by pride. O best among the avataras with purified (suddha-sattva) bodies! One becomes purified when one has a higher and more abundant faith in hearing, remembering, and glorifying Your fame. Such faith is nourished when one hears the sastra.’’

Then in text 10, the demigods again glorify the Lord’s lotus feet as the object of meditation for yogis and of worship for devotees. Indeed, they say, You are worshiped by the followers of karma and jnana. “Your lotus feet are just like a blazing fire that burns to ashes all the inauspicious desires for material sense gratification.” (SB. 11.6.10)

They continue: “O almighty Lord, You are so kind to Your servants that You have accepted the withered flower garland that we have placed on Your chest. Since the goddess of fortune makes her abode on Your transcendental chest, she will undoubtedly become agitated, like a jealous co-wife, upon seeing our offering also dwelling there. Yet You are so merciful that You neglect Your eternal consort Laksmi and accept our offering as most excellent worship.” (SB. 11.6.12)

According to text 6 of this chapter, the demigods offered Krsna flower garlands from the heavenly planets. In their purport to text 12, the BBT commentators explain the mood in which the demigods speak these words: “Srila Jiva Gosvami has pointed out that any garland worn by the Lord cannot be faded because all of the Lord’s personal paraphernalia is completely transcendental and spiritually opulent. Similarly, there is no possibility that mundane jealousy could appear in the character of the goddess of fortune, who is as transcendental as Lord Krsna Himself. Therefore the statements of the demigods are to be understood as humorous words inspired by intense love of Godhead.”

The demigods continue, “O merciful Lord, may Your lotus feet always act as a blazing fire to consume the inauspicious desires within our hearts.” (SB. 11.6.12) The Lord’s lotus feet fill the demons with fear and the demigods with courage. “We are sincerely trying to worship You, our Lord; therefore may Your lotus feet kindly free us from all of our sinful reactions.” (SB. 11.6.13)

*Texts 14-17: The unequaled transcendental position of Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead*

The demigods make further points in their prayers: Even we demigods struggle with the material nature and are fully controlled by Your crushing time potency. You, O Lord, are transcendental to both the material nature and to those souls attempting to exploit it. You are the ultimate cause of the universe and its regulator. No one controls You, and so You are the Supreme Personality of Godhead. You are the primal source and controller of material existence. You are superior to all individual jivas, and superior even to Maha-visnu. You control all living entities, the modes of nature, and the living beings’ senses. In contrast to Your position, yogis and philosophers “are disturbed and frightened simply by remembering the material objects that they have supposedly renounced in their pursuit of enlightenment.” (SB. I 1.6.17)

The demigods then offer an example of one of Krsna’s transcendental interactions, which to those unaware of Krsna’s potency may appear mundane: “My Lord, You are living with sixteen thousand exquisitely beautiful, aristocratic wives. By their irresistible coy and smiling glances and by their lovely arching eyebrows, they send You messages of eager conjugal love. But they are completely unable to disturb the mind and senses of Your Lordship.” (SB. 11.6.18)

In text 17 it is stated that nothing material can attract the Lord’s senses. Text 18, however, informs us that the Lord “has no desire to enjoy even spiritual sense gratification.” Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura adds a further perspective: “The Lord was not under the control of His queens, even though they are spiritual energies and not mundane. He wanted to show that He is not under the control of His energies. However, the Ujjvala-nilamani states that among the queens, some are filled with prema. This is shown when Krsna falls under the control of His queen, Satyabhama, and steals the parijata tree from Svarga. Thus He is controlled by prema but not by lust, mundane or extraordinary. This text can also mean that Krsna is not as disturbed by His queens as He is disturbed by the gopis. In any case, the text indicates that Krsna is controlled by His queens to the extent of their prema."

*Text 19: The demigods’ conclude that krsna-katha and krsna-caranamrta are tremendously purifying*

The demigods conclude their prayers: “The nectar-bearing rivers of discussions about You, and also the holy rivers generated from the bathing of Your lotus feet, are able to destroy all contamination within the three worlds. Those who are striving for purification associate with the holy narrations of Your glories by hearing them with their ears, and they associate with the holy rivers flowing from Your lotus feet by physically bathing in them.” (SB. 11.6.19)

*Texts 20-27: Brahmas prayers*

At the beginning of the Tenth Canto, Lord Brahma had asked the Lord of Svetadvipa, on Bhumidevi’s behalf, to remove the earth’s distress.The Supreme Lord (isvaresvarah) had agreed to descend as sva-kala-saktya, His time potency, to diminish the earth’s burden. Now 125 years later in Dvaraka, Brahma humbly informs Krsna that His mission on behalf of the demigods has been completed and it’s time for Him to depart: “My Lord, You have reestablished the principles of religion among pious men who are always firmly bound to the truth. You have also distributed Your glories all over the world, and thus the whole world can be purified by hearing about You. Descending into the dynasty of King Yadu, You have manifested Your unique transcendental form, and for the benefit of the entire universe You have executed magnanimous transcendental activities. My dear Lord, those pious and saintly persons who in the Age of Kali hear about Your transcendental activities and also glorify them will easily cross over the darkness of the age. My dear Lord, there is nothing remaining at this time for Your Lordship to do on behalf of the demigods. You have already withdrawn Your dynasty by the curse of the brahmanas. O Lord, You are the basis of everything, and if You so desire, kindly return now to Your own abode in the spiritual world. At the same time, we humbly beg that You always protect us. We are Your humble servants, and on Your behalf we are managing the universal situation. We, along with our planets and followers, require Your constant protection.” (SB. 11.6.22-24, 26-27)

*Texts 28-32: Sri Krsna’s response*

*Texts 33-41: His words to the senior members of the Yadu dynasty*

Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, replied that He still had to take care of one last burden: His own family members, the powerful and expansive Yadu dynasty. “Now due to the brahmanas’ curse, the annihilation of My family has already begun. O sinless Brahma, when this annihilation is finished and I am en route to Vaikuntha, I will pay a small visit to your abode.” (SB. 11.6.31)

According to the BBT purport to text 31, we can understand the imminent destruction of the Yadu dynasty as follows: “The Yadu dynasty entered into the hidden or confidential Dvaraka in the spiritual world, which is not manifested here on the earth. In other words, Dvaraka, the Lord’s abode, is manifest on the earth, and when (he earthly Dvaraka is apparently removed, the eternal Dvaraka in die spiritual world remains as it is. Since the members of the Yadu dynasty are eternal associates of the Lord, there is no question of their destruction."

In his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.6.29-30, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura provides more detail about why Krsna’s dynasty had to leave the earth:

The Yadus cannot be defeated in strength or enthusiasm in battle. They want to spread out over the world since there are so many of them, but I have confined them to Dvaraka by My inconceivable potency; otherwise, the whole of the earth planet is insufficient to contain them all— The Yadus are proud because they are both My family members and My servants (mamaka). Transgressing proper etiquette, they are like an ocean overrunning the shore. Although the earth does not consider My Yadus a burden, since they follow dharma, I am the master of this earth, and it is I who should remove this weight from her, just as a husband removes the wife’s heavy ornaments when she is very well decorated. It’s easy to bear the weight of something one strongly desires to own, but it is also possible for something to simply be too heavy to bear. If a greedy merchant suddenly obtains a pile of gold, even though he wants to possess that gold he will still find its weight difficult to transport.

On hearing Krsna’s reply, Brahma and the other demigods left for their abodes. As soon as they were gone Dvaraka was rocked by powerful forces. Sri Krsna turned to the senior members of the Yadu dynasty and, urgency in His voice, said: “My dear respected elders, we must not remain any longer in this place if we wish to keep our lives intact. Let us go this very day to the most pious place Prabhasa.We have no time to delay.” (SB. 11.6.35) The Yadus accepted Krsna’s instructions and immediately yoked their horses to their chariots and prepared to depart by boat from their island city.

Why would Krsna tell the Yadus to leave holy Dvaraka to perform pious activities somewhere else? Our acaryas quote sastra to prove that nothing inauspicious can occur in Dvaraka. Indeed, Brahma has just indicated (in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.6.22) that the world is purified and protected simply by hearing krsna-katha and glorifying Krsna. What need was there to go anywhere?

In his comment on text 35, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura reveals Krsna’s purpose: “Let Dvaraka remain with all My eternal associates! Unseen by others, the devatas previously entered the Yadus. Now, by My yogic power, I will extract them and lake them to Prabhasa. I will then make them fight one another by My maya and send them back to Svarga, while I, in My form as the son of Vikuntha and other forms (merged in Me), will go to Vaikuntha above Brahmaloka and other spiritual abodes. In My complete form, however, I and My associates will remain eternally in Dvaraka.”

*Texts 40-49: Uddhava’s request to Krsna*

Krsna considered Uddhava His cousinand faithful follower, His dearest and most intelligent friend. Uddhava, with his vast intelligence, had already noted the omens in Dvaraka and seen the Yadavas preparing to go to Prabhasa; and he understood what these implied. He therefore privately approached his friend, the Personality of Godhead, controller of the universe, and bowed his head at His lotus feet. Folding his hands in reverence, Uddhava opened his heart. “O my Lord, O supreme God among all the demigods, real piety is invoked simply by hearing and chanting Your transcendental glories. My Lord, it appears that You will now withdraw Your dynasty, and thus You Yourself will finally give up Your pastimes within this universe. You are the supreme controller and the master of all mystic power. But although You are fully capable of counteracting the brahmanas’ curse against Your dynasty, You are not doing so, and Your disappearance is imminent.” (SB. 11.6.42)

Uddhava knew that bathing at Prabhasa was far less powerful than simply seeing Krsna. He knew that it was Krsna who empowers both the piety and the words of the brahmanas. He knew Krsna could have easily said, “Let this curse not act” and the brahmanas’ curse would have been neutralized. He could therefore only conclude that Krsna wanted io leave the universe, using the curse as the cause.

His voice choked with devotion, Uddhava continued, “O Lord Kesava, my dear master, I cannot tolerate giving up Your lotus feet even for a fraction of a moment. I urge You to take me along with You to Your own abode. O my dear Krsna, Your pastimes are supremely auspicious for mankind and are an intoxicating beverage for the ears. Tasting such pastimes, people forget their desires for other lungs. My dear Lord, You are the Supreme Soul, and thus You are most dear to us. We are Your devotees, and how can we possibly reject You or live without You even for a moment? Whether we are lying down, sitting, walking, standing, bathing, enjoying recreation, eating, or doing anything else, we are constantly engaged in Your service.” (SB. 11.6.43-45)

In his comments on texts 44 and 45, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura expands on Uddhava’s mood as he contemplated living without Krsna: “Upon hearing Krsna’s pastimes, people give up their desires for sons, wife, and finally liberation, but they cannot give up those pastimes. How, then, can I give You up? How can Your devotees ever give You up, whom we constantly serve by massaging Your feet whether you are lying down or sitting?”

Uddhava is different from sages who, desiring liberation through jnana, perform austerities to end their interactions with matter. Uddhava doesn’t serve Krsna out of fear of maya or the sufferings this world inflicts; he serves only out of his love for Krsna, devoid of any desire for karma or jnana.

In text 46, Uddhava describes how devotees effortlessly attain liberation: “Simply by decorating ourselves with the garlands, fragrant oils, clothes, and ornaments that You have already enjoyed, and by eating the remnants of Your meals, we, Your servants, will indeed conquer Your illusory energy.” (SB. 11.6.46)

Jnanis, on the other hand, get a different result from their practices: “Naked sages who seriously endeavor in spiritual practice, who have raised their semen upward, who are peaceful and sinless members of the renounced order, attain the spiritual abode called Brahman.” (SB. 11.6.47)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura writes, speaking as Uddhava: “Such sages go to that light (Brahman). Let them. But we do not want that attainment. We wish to remain intoxicated by drinking the nectar of the sweet smile on Your moonlike face.”

Considering himself an ordinary human being, Uddhava concludes, “O greatest of mystics, although we are conditioned souls wandering on the path of fruitive work, we will certainly cross beyond the darkness of this material world simply by hearing about Your Lordship in the association of Your devotees. Thus we are always remembering and glorifying the wonderful things You do and the wonderful things You say. We ecstatically recall Your amorous pastimes with Your confidential conjugal devotees and how You boldly smile and move about while engaged in such youthful pastimes. My dear Lord, Your loving pastimes are bewilderingly similar to the activities of ordinary people within this material world.” (SB. I 1.6.48-49)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura summarizes the devotional practices that Uddhava and the demigods, in their prayers, recommend in this chapter: “We will not cross with the naked sages! We will cross maya with Your devotees, who have a similar nature to us. By which method? By the light from Your Sudarsana cakra in the form of remembering and glorifying Your pastimes, we will easily cross the darkness of maya.”

One’s prayers reflect the depth of one’s consciousness. The three sets of prayers in this chapter - those of the demigods, of Lord Brahma, and of Sri Uddhava - ring forth, a clear call to the reader to take the “backward glance” Krsna offers in this canto. Readers of the Eleventh Canto may come to recognize the significance of Krsna’s Tenth Canto pastimes, which they have just heard. Krsna-katha is both the means to conquer over matter and the lotus-like vehicle that carries us back to Krsna. Krsna’s pastimes, enacted with His beloved devotees, should be the object of our absorption; we should recall, reflect on, and recount them again and again.

**Chapter 7: Lord Krsna Instructs Uddhava**

*Texts 1-13: Krsna replies to Uddhava*

Uddhava has inferred that Krsna will soon end His earthly pastimes and so he begs Krsna not to leave him behind. Krsna’s reply is first informative (1-2), then predictive (3-4), and finally instructive (5): “O greatly fortunate Uddhava, you have accurately revealed My desire to withdraw the Yadu dynasty from the earth and return to My own abode in Vaikuntha. Thus Lord Brahma, Lord Siva, and all other planetary rulers are now praying for Me to resume My residence in Vaikuntha. Answering the prayer of Lord Brahma, I descended within this world along with My plenary portion, Lord Baladeva, and performed various activities on behalf of the demigods. I have now completed My mission here. Now due to the brahmanas’ curse the Yadu dynasty will certainly perish by fighting among themselves; and on the seventh day from today the ocean will rise up and inundate this city of Dvaraka. O saintly Uddhava, in the near future I will abandon this earth. Then, being overwhelmed by the Age of Kali, the earth will he bereft of all piety. My dear Uddhava, you should not remain here on the earth once I have abandoned this world. My dear devotee, you are sinless, but in Kali-yuga the people will be addicted to all types of sinful activities; therefore do not stay here.” (SB. 11.7.1-5)

Continuing (in texts 6-12), almost surprisingly, Krsna teaches Uddhava about jnana and vairagya, knowledge and detachment. He encourages Uddhava to remain aloof from material entanglement and to focus his consciousness on Him. Maya, He says, causes one to see the illusory creation as real and the material experience as eternal. But all of this is temporary and without value. To avoid maya, Uddhava should subdue his mind and senses and see everything that exists as in Krsna.

He should also be equally disposed to all and wander the earth free from mundane dualities, like good and bad. He should be fully satisfied and peaceful by developing knowledge of the true self with the help of Vedic knowledge. He should remain pure, peaceful, fixed in knowledge, and kind toward all living beings. Seeing Me in everything, Krsna tells Uddhava, you will never again fall into the cycle of birth and death.

Uddhava is an eternal associate of Krsna, and Krsna will later name him as His representative among the devotees (SB. 11.16.29). Krsna had also personally sent him to Vraja to associate with His beloved Vrajavasis, especially the gopis. In text 46 of the sixth chapter, we learned of Uddhava’s devotion-soaked method for crossing the ocean of nescience: “Simply by decorating ourselves with the garlands, fragrant oils, clothes, and ornaments that You have already enjoyed, and by eating the remnants of Your meals, we, Your servants, will indeed conquer Your illusory energy.” (SB. 11.6.46) Why, then, is Krsna now instructing Uddhava in jnana and vairagya? And why will Krsna teach this loving devotee about karma, jnana, and yoga in the twenty-four chapters that we now know as the Uddhava-gita?

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura responds to these questions in his comments on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.7.6: “The Lord thought within Himself, ‘I have fulfilled the desires of My devotees on earth who yearned to see Me— (But) I have not fulfilled the longing of the great sages of Badarikasrama such as Nara-Narayana. And now the limit of My 125 years of manifested pastimes has expired. I should send Uddhava to Badarikasrama, since he is equal to Me and is another form of Myself. I will give them bhakti-yoga, like a valuable jewel, as a gift, along with jnana and vairagya, which are expressed by the term bhaga, in My name Bhagavan. Then their desires will be satisfied. Although Uddhava already has jnana and vairagya arising from his full prcrna for Me anti has no desire for Me lo teach I lim about jfiana and vairagya as separate processes, I will produce a desire in him, since this is My desire.’ ... Considering in this way, the Lord then created a desire for bhakti-yoga along with jnana and vairagya in Uddhava’s heart.”

A related question: Why does Krsna speak about karma, jnana, and yoga so close to the conclusion of Srimad-Bhagavatam - especially after His most intimate pastimes with His devotees have already been presented in the Tenth Canto? There are a number of ways to answer this question, but here are four:

1\. Bhakti fulfills the purpose of the Vedic literature

Krsna will say later in the Uddhava-gita (SB. 11.20.6): “My dear Uddhava, because I desire that human beings may achieve perfection, I have presented three paths of advancement - the path of knowledge \[jnana\], the path of work \[karma\], and the path of devotion \[bhakti\]. Besides these three there is absolutely no other means of elevation.”

As Krsna continues His instructions to Uddhava, we’ll see that the successive chapters of the Uddhava-gita clearly reveal that all three paths culminate in bhakti (SB. 11.20.31-33), and that of all the ways to practice bhakti, that practiced by the residents of Vrndavana, especially the gopis, is topmost (SB. 11.12.10-13). In the Uddhava-gita Krsna presents these truths to express the fulfillment of the ultimate purpose of the Vedic literature.

2\. The Vedic system is liberal and inclusive

The Vedic system is both liberal and inclusive. Although Krsna’s powerful presentation in the Uddhava-gita clarifies the purpose behind the sastric injunctions and points all practitioners, no matter which path they’ve chosen, to bhakti, Krsna nevertheless allows for the exercise of free will.

It’s interesting to note that immediately before Maharaja Pariksit’s passing (SB. 12.6), Sukadeva Gosvami teaches him jnana (SB. 12.5). Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura briefly explains Sukadeva’s purpose in his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.6.1: “Understanding t lie mind of the jnanis present, Sukadeva Gosvami made them happy hy presenting teachings on jnana.”

Thus those who want the goals of karma and jnana may still fulfill their desires within the framework of the Vedic culture, finding in the Vedic literature justification for their faith, practices, and goals. This is Vedic liberality and inclusiveness - that the system supports a graduated spiritual development.

3\. It protects the confidentiality of bhakti

Paroksa-vada rsayah, paroksah mama ca priyam: “The Vedic seers and mantras ... deal in esoteric terms, and I \[Krsna\] also am pleased by such confidential descriptions.” (SB. 11.21.35)

The Vedic literature, including Srimad-Bhagavatam, uses paroksa-vada, or indirect, esoteric statements that allow for multiple interpretations. This protects the intimacy and confidentiality of bhakti from those who lack faith in and realization of its supreme position and worth. In addition, with the shift back to philosophy in the Eleventh Canto, the intimacy of the lilas discussed in the Tenth Canto are again hidden from sight.

4\. Krsna has a tendency to speak knowledge and philosophy

Commenting on Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.82.47, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura indicates the gopis’ conclusion about why Krsna spoke philosophically to them at Kuruksetra despite the long period of separation between them: ‘“He who taught us dharma at the beginning of the rasa-lila (SB. 10.29) despite our not being intellectuals, and who taught us jnana, intellectual knowledge, through Uddhava (SB. 10.46-47), is now again teaching us jnana. We should know that this is His nature and it’s hard for Him to give it up.’ That was the gopis’ conclusion about Him.”

*Texts 13-18: Uddhava asks for further instruction*

On hearing Krsna’s instructions, Uddhava replied: O Supreme Soul, for my benefit You explained how to give up the material world by taking sannyasa (becoming renounced). But such renunciation is difficult for those attached to matter. Please tell me how I can easily carry out Your instructions, for I am foolishly attached to my body and relationships. How can I see everything and everyone equally and wander the world with no attachment other than to You? My dear Lord, You reveal Yourself to Your devotees, and I can see no more perfect teacher than You who can explain to me perfect knowledge. Even the demigods headed by Brahma are bewildered by Your illusory potency and accept their bodies and the expansions of their bodies as the highest truth. My Lord, I am weary of material life and tormented by its distresses. I surrender to You, my perfect master. “You are known as Narayana, the true friend of all living beings.” (SB. 11.13.18)

*Texts 19-23: Krsna’s prelude to the teachings of Dattatreya Muni - gaining spiritual insights through one’s own intelligence*

Sri Krsna begins His reply to His dear devotee Uddhava: “Generally those human beings who can expertly analyze the actual situation of the material world are able to raise themselves beyond the inauspicious life of gross material gratification. An intelligent person, expert in perceiving the world around him and in applying sound logic, can achieve real benefit through his own intelligence. Thus sometimes one acts as one’s own instructing spiritual master.” (SB. 11.7.19-20)

Krsna then tells Uddhava (texts 21-23) that of all the forms of life on earth, the human form is dear to Him, because although He can never be captured by the ordinary, mundane senses, human beings can search for Him as He is indirectly manifest in His creation, using logical inference.

The BBT purport to text 20 provides a prelude to the instructions found in this seventh chapter: “\[A\] sensitive, reasonable person can acquire real knowledge and happiness simply by carefully observing the world around him. By observing the happiness and distress of other living entities, one can understand what is beneficial and what is destructive.”

The purport to text 19 quotes Srila Sridhara Svami as saying, “\[E\]ven if one has not received the instruction of a bona fide spiritual master, one can understand by direct and indirect analysis that the material world is not a place of enjoyment. Direct analysis means one’s personal experience and indirect analysis means hearing and reading of the experience of others.” Srila Jiva Gosvami concurs, and his comments are quoted in the BBT purport to text 20: “\[T\]he knowledge acquired by one’s own perception and intelligence leads one to appreciate the value of the representative of Lord Krsna.”

Why will knowledge gained in this way lead one to understand that he needs a guru who represents Lord Krsna? Srila Visvanatha Cakravartt Thakura (cited in the purport to text 23) makes it clear that although much that is helpful in spiritual life can be understood solely through one’s intelligence, Krsna Himself can only be understood through bhakti, which must be performed under the direction of a merciful spiritual master:

One in a human form who engages in bhakti-yoga directly searches for Me, Krsna, by such bhakti-inspired activities as hearing and chanting. Bhakyaham ekaya grahyah: I am only attained by bhakti (SB. 11.14.21).

“But can’t they also see You by searching for You through inference, since it is You who stimulates their intelligence?”

“No,” Krsna says, “I cannot be attained by inference using the intelligence or various indicators.”

But one can infer the existence of the dependent jiva, and since the jiva’s senses and intelligence must have a cause, one can somewhat infer the presence of the antaryami, the Supersoul,who instigates the jiva’s senses and intelligence. However, Svayam Bhagavan Krsna cannot be inferred in the same way, since His form, qualities, pastimes, and powers are inconceivable and beyond the ability of the intelligence to conceive.

The quality of one’s mind dictates how and what we perceive. For example, jnanis see the world as impersonal; business-minded people see the world as filled with financial potential; and abstract artists see the world as filled with juxtaposed, mutable forms.

Uddhava has already told Krsna that he won’t be able to bear His separation. So Krsna will teach Uddhava how to see Him - and how to feel His presence - even after He returns to the spiritual world. “In this chapter, Lord Krsna is training Uddhava to see the Lord’s personal form in the course of his daily experiences in the material world. The Lord has already indicated to Uddhava that Uddhava will travel throughout the world in samadhi, or trance, and now Lord Krsna is preparing Uddhava to travel as a true sannyasi, seeing the Personality of Godhead everywhere.” (SB 11.7.21, purport)

*Texts 24-31: King Yadu meets the saintly brahmana avadhuta*

Krsna now narrates a historical conversation between the powerful Maharaja Yadu and an avadhuta,or one who is no longer hound to follow the scriptural injunctions that govern behavior, because he has already transcended material nature.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments (SB. 11.7.24) that sages narrate this story to illustrate how one can infer the presence of the Paramatma (but not of Svayam Bhagavan Krsna).

In Srimad-Bhagavatam 9.18.38, Maharaja Yayati asked his son Yadu to exchange his youth for the king’s old age. Yadu replied, “My dear father, you have already achieved old age, although you also were a young man. But I do not welcome your old age and invalidity, for unless one enjoys material happiness, one cannot attain renunciation.” (SB. 9.18.40)

In his purport to Yadu’s reply, Srila Prabhupada notes the religious underpinnings of Maharaja Yadu’s seemingly irreligious refusal: “Maharaja Yadu was ready to accept his father’s order and exchange youth for old age because he was confident that the youth taken by his father would be returned. But because this exchange would delay his complete engagement in devotional service, he did not want to accept his father’s old age, for he was eager to achieve freedom from disturbances. Moreover, among the descendants of Yadu would be Lord Krsna. Therefore, because Yadu was eager to see the Lord’s appearance in his dynasty as soon as possible, Yadu refused to accept his father’s proposal. This was not irreligious, however, because Yadu’s purpose was to serve the Lord.”

Desiring both service and honest, mature renunciation, Maharaja Yadu refused to become prematurely old, choosing to pursue renunciation later in his life. He did renounce later (see Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.9.33), and the association and instruction that inspired him to do so appeared in the form of the avadhuta brahmana, about to be described.

Maharaja Yadu noted that the avadhuta appeared both young and learned; he seemed free of fear and anxiety, enlightened, unbound by societal norms, and yet he seemed to be a madman. Maharaja Yadu wondered how the avadhuta had managed to become enlightened, espe- i lally because he appeared not to be doing any kind of spiritual practice. So i he king asked, “Although all people within the material world are burning in the great forest fire of lust and greed, you remain free and are not burned by that fire. You are just like an elephant who takes shelter from a forest fire by standing within the water of the Ganges River. O brahmana, we see that you are devoid of any contact with material enjoyment and that you are traveling alone, without any companions or family members. Therefore, because we are sincerely inquiring from you, please tell us the cause of the great ecstasy that you are feeling within yourself.” (SB. 11.7.29-30)

*Texts 32—76: Learning from the first ten of the avadhuta s twenty-four spiritual masters*

The avadhuta found the king’s piercing intelligence and humble attitude attractive, and so he chose to reply. “My dear King, with my intelligence I have taken shelter of many spiritual masters. Having gained transcendental understanding from them, I now wander about the earth in a liberated condition. Please listen as I describe them to you. O King, I have taken shelter of twenty-four gurus, who are the following: the earth, air, sky, water, fire, moon, sun, pigeon, and python; the sea, moth, honeybee, elephant, and honey thief; the deer, the fish, the prostitute Pingala, the kurara bird, and the child; and the young girl, arrow maker, serpent, spider, and wasp. My dear King, by studying their activities I have learned the science of the self. Please listen, O son of Maharaja Yayati, O tiger among men, as I explain to you what I have learned from each of these gurus.” (SB. 11.7.32-36)

Thus the avadhuta indicated that he had gained his realizations through intelligent observation of the world, not from another person. A sampling of what he learned follows.

1\. The earth (text 37)

From the earth the avadhuta learned that those who are aggressive toward him are acting helplessly under the control of the laws of nature - ultimately, they are controlled by the hand of God. So from the earth he learned both tolerance and steadfastness, and even in difficulty he remains focused on his spiritual progress. Clearly, one has to be tolerant if he wishes to remain fixed on any path.

2\. The mountain and the tree (texts 38 and 39)

From the mountain he learned to devote himself to serving others and to make their welfare the reason for his existence. “Similarly, as the disciple of the tree, he should learn to dedicate himself to others.” (SB. 11.7.38)

Srila Visvanaiha Cakravarti Thakura comments: "One can move a tree from one place to another, replant it, and water it. These qualities of the tree are not seen in a mountain, although mountains, too, teach us to dedicate ourselves to others. But a yogi should emulate the tree by accepting such disturbances without protest.”

The avadhuta grouped the earth, mountain, and tree together. Then he moved on to the air (wind).

3\. The wind (or air) (texts 39-41)

The avadhuta brahmana has observed that the ever-shifting wind picks up and leaves both foul and fragrant aromas without becoming attached to either. Nor does the air actually mix with the aromas it carries. Thus from the wind he has learned detachment, regardless of whether he is in contact with something pleasant or something unpleasant.

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments that as the air doesn’t mix with either good or bad fragrances, although it is aware of them as it meets them, so the yogi is similarly aware of contact with the qualities of his body but neither identifies with nor becomes attached to them. Rather, he sees himself - the atma - as different from his body. The wind is attached neither to the dark cave nor to the blazing fire.

4\. The sky (ether) (texts 42-43)

The sky extends itself over everything and everything rests in the sky, hut like the wind, the sky doesn’t mix with anything nor can it be divided by anything. From the sky, under which the mighty wind blows up clouds and storms, the avadhuta has learned that despite how it seems, neither the soul nor the Supersoul mix with anything.

5\. Water (text 44)

Water, the avadhuta brahmana says, has taught him many things. “\[A\] saintly person is just like water because he is free from all contamination, gentle by nature, and by speaking creates a beautiful vibration like that of flowing water. Just by seeing, touching, or hearing such a saintly person, the living entity is purified, just as one is cleansed by contact with pure water. Thus a saintly person, just like a holy place,.purifies all those who contact him because he always chants the glories of the Lord.” (SB. 1 1.7.44)

So, the avadhuta brahmana says, he has learned to be pure and gentle, and when speaking, to be like a saintly person who carries water’s purifying potency by chanting the Lord’s glories. As pure water is transparent, so saintly persons are transparent, and when you look through to their hearts, you see the Personality of Godhead there.

6\. Fire (texts 45-47, 49)

The avadhuta brahmana learned detachment from fire. As fire bums to ashes everything one feeds it, so the reactions to food one eats are similarly burned to ashes.

“Such naturally liberated sages accept foodstuffs that are offered to them by destiny, and if by chance they happen to eat contaminated food, they are not affected.” (SB. 11.7.45) As fire sometimes burns openly and at other times is concealed in a pot, so when saintly persons reveal their position by serving as spiritual masters, they burn to ashes their disciples’ reactions by accepting their offerings. Also, as ashes may be stirred into flame, the ever-present Supreme Personality of Godhead can be stirred into manifesting His presence when His devotees repeatedly chant and hear His glories.

7\. The moon (text 48)

As the moon does not change itself regardless of its phase, so the soul does not change no matter what phase of life the body it inhabits is experiencing.

8\. The sun (texts 50—51)

From the sun the brahmana has learned to accept material objects and then return them to the correct person at the right time for the right purpose. The sun evaporates seawater, which has flowed into the sea from the earth in the form of rivers, and returns it to the earth in the form of rain at the right time. Similarly, saintly persons accept things at the right time and then return them appropriately. They do not become attached to those things, nor do they think, “This was obtained by me” or “I gave this thing to another.” Thus they remain free either while accepting or relinquishing objects.

The sun also taught the brahmana another lesson. Despite being reflected in many objects, the sun remains the same. Similarly, the eternal soul remains unchanged regardless of the bodies through which its consciousness is reflected.

9\. The pigeon (texts 52-74)

The doors of liberation are opened wide to those with a human body, but if a human being simply devotes himself to family like the foolish bird in this story, he is to be considered one who has climbed to a high place only to trip and tumble back down. This is what the avadhuta brahmana learned from the foolish pigeon, who was so attached to his family members that he too became caught in the hunter’s net.

**Chapter 8: The Story of Pingala**

*Texts 1-42: The avadhuta brahmana describes nine more gurus*

10\. The python (texts 1-4)

“O King, the embodied living entity automatically experiences unhappiness in heaven or hell. Similarly, happiness will also be experienced, even without one’s seeking it. Therefore a person of intelligent discrimination does not make any endeavor to obtain such material happiness.” (SB. 11.8.1)This the avadhuta brahmana learned from the python. On a practical level, this means accepting whatever food comes by destiny without regard to its quality or quantity. It also means not striving for anything material while remaining alert to and active in the pursuit of one’s spiritual interests.

11\. The ocean (texts 5-6)

The ocean is deep, and from the ocean the brahmana learned that depth means one doesn’t overflow (rejoice) during times of abundance or dry up (feel morose) during times of lack.

12\. The moth (texts 7-8)

The moth taught him to he detached from the desire to see a woman’s form. “One who has lailed to control his senses immediately feels attraction upon seeing a woman’s form, which is created by the illusory energy of the Supreme Lord. Indeed, when the woman speaks with enticing words, smiles coquettishly, and moves her body sensuously, his mind is immediately captured, and thus he falls blindly into the darkness of material existence, just as the moth maddened by the fire rushes blindly into its flames.” (SB. 11.8.7)

The purport to the next text continues this point: “However, the foolish relationship based on material sex attraction begins by seeing, and thus rupa, or form, is very prominent in the process of ruining one’s intelligence.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura takes this idea and extrapolates it into a principle: “The moth teaches that attachment to form is the cause of destruction. This is explained in two verses. Although each of the five senses contributes to one’s becoming attracted to a woman - or any other sense object - sight is the first to fall victim. Thus form is the chief sense object.”

13\. Honeybees (texts 9-12)

The avadhuta next explains what he has learned from two different types of honeybees, the bhramara (which wanders from flower to flower) and the maksika (which accumulates honey in its hive). From the first he has learned to accept just a little from a number of places and not to become attached to others’ generosity. He has also learned to eat only enough to keep body and soul together so as not to become a burden on others’ kindness. “Thus one should not imitate the greedy honeybee who eagerly collects more and more honey ... \[because if he collects\] more and more delicious foodstuffs, that which he has collected will indeed ruin him.” (SB. 11.8.11-12)

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.8.12 underlines this point: “A saintly mendicant should be like the bhramara bee, because if he imitates the maksika bee, his spiritual consciousness will be ruined.”

In his comment on text 9 of this chapter, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura describes the bhramara’s madhukari, or practice of begging a small amount from a number of houses: “Just as a bee that stays in one lotus because of greed for its special fragrance becomes trapped when the petals close at night, the sage, taking shelter of one house because of its good qualities becomes trapped there by illusion. Therefore one should accept a little from each house and eat only to keep the body alive. One commits violence against the householders by taking too much or too little.”

The BBT purport to text 11 also notes the danger inherent in overcollecting, but adds an additional, important point: “One who is interested in making spiritual progress should avoid such a situation; however, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura points out that for the purpose of spreading Krsna consciousness one may accumulate an unlimited amount of material opulence. This is called yukta-vairagya, or using everything in the service of Krsna.”

In text 11, the avadhuta adds another lesson from the honeybee: Like a bee approaching a flower and taking just pollen, I too have learned to accept only the essence from all sastra (SB. 11.8.10).

14\. The elephant (texts 13-14)

From the elephant the avadhuta has learned to avoid wanting to exploit the body of a woman. He tells Maharaja Yadu that even a mighty bull elephant that wants to touch a she-elephant can be lured into a covered hole or killed by a more powerful competitor. He therefore recommends that a sadhu never touch a woman - or even a wooden form in the shape of a woman - not even with his foot!

15\. More bees (texts 15—16)

“The greedy man is like the bee who struggles to produce a large quantity of honey, which is then stolen by a man who will enjoy it personally or sell it to others. No matter how carefully one hides bis hard-earned wealth or tries to protect it, there are those who are expert in detecting the whereabouts of valuable things, and they will steal it.” (SB. 11.8.15)

From the BBT purport: “\[T\]he word artha-vit indicates one who by hook or by crook is expert in stealing the hard-earned wealth of other people. Tire bees work frantically to produce honey, but they will not enjoy their honey. As Lord Krsna states, mrtyuh sarva-haras caham: ‘I will come as death personified and steal everything.’ (Bhagavad-gita 10.14) Somehow or other one’s hard-earned material opulence will be stolen., and therefore, as mentioned in this verse, one should not work uselessly like the foolish honeybee.”

The avadhuta concludes this point in text 16, comparing mendicants like brahmacaris and sannyasis to beekeepers who “are entitled to enjoy the property painstakingly accumulated by householders dedicated to family enjoyment.”

16\. The deer (text 17-18)

The avadhuta explains that a hunter’s flute can attract and lure a deer to its death. One serious about spiritual progress should therefore carefully study the deer’s example and avoid mundane songs. The avadhuta offers the innocent sage Rsyasrnga, mentioned in the Mahabharata, as an illustration of his point. Rsyasrnga, who had been raised by his father to be a perfect brahmacari and kept for his whole life from even seeing a woman, was lured by the “singing, dancing, and musical entertainment of beautiful women \[and\] fell totally under their control, just like a pet animal.” (SB. 11.8.18)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura adds in his comment to text 17 that instead of listening to mundane songs, one should listen to the Bhagavad-gita.

17\. The fish (19-21)

Noting that death awaits a fish lured into biting a fisherman’s baited hook, the avadhuta has learned not to surrender to the tongue’s powerful urges. Even starving the tongue through fasting does not weaken the tongue’s power. “Although one may conquer all the other senses, as long as the tongue is not conquered it cannot be said that one has controlled his senses. However, if one is able to control the tongue, then one is understood to be in full control of all the senses.” (SB 11.8.21) Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments (on text 20) that we should try to control the tongue, because through that one sense the other four senses are empowered. How do we control the tongue? “By developing a taste for loudly chanting the name of the Lord.”

The BBT purports adds to this prescription that we eat only prasada. As Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura sings, “But You, dear Krsna, are very kind and have given us such nice prasada just to control the tongue. Now take this prasada to your full satisfaction and glorify Their Lordships Sri Sri Radha-Krsna - and in love call for the help of Lord Caitanya and Lord Nityananda.”

18\. The prostitute Pingala (texts 22-42)

The avadhuta brahmana tells us that after a long night, greedy Pingala found no customer, and this made her lament. But from her disappointment she gained detachment, which slashed at and destroyed her material desires. Happiness then filled her heart. Pingala then sang what is known as the Pingala-gita (texts 30-42 of this chapter):

Just see how greatly illusioned I am! Because I cannot control my mind, just like a fool I desire lusty pleasure from an insignificant man. I am such a fool that I have given up the service of that person who, being eternally situated within my heart, is actually most dear to me. That most dear one is the Lord of the universe, who is the bestower of real love and happiness and the source of all prosperity. Although He is in my own heart, I have completely neglected Him. Instead I have ignorantly served insignificant men who can never satisfy my real desires and who have simply brought me unhappiness, fear, anxiety, lamentation, and illusion. Oh, how I have uselessly tortured my own soul! I have sold my body to lusty, greedy men who are themselves objects of pity. Thus practicing the most abominable profession of a prostitute, I hoped to get money and sex pleasure. This material body is like a house in which I, the soul, am living. The bones forming my spine, ribs, arms, and legs are like the beams, crossbeams, and pillars of the house, and the whole structure, which is full of stool and urine, is covered by skin, hair, and nails. The nine doors leading into this body are constantly excreting foul substances. Besides me, what woman could be so foolish as to devote herself to this material body, thinking that she might find pleasure and love in this contraption?

Certainly in this city of Videha I alone am completely foolish. I neglected the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who awards us everything, even our original spiritual form, and instead I desired to enjoy sense gratification with many men. The Supreme Personality of Godhead is absolutely the most dear one for all living beings because He is everyone’s well-wisher and Lord. He is the Supreme Soul situated in everyone’s heart. Therefore I will now pay the price of complete surrender, and thus purchasing the Lord I will enjoy with Him just like Laksmulevi.

Men provide sense gratification for women, hut all these men, and even the demigods in heaven, have a beginning and an end.

They are temporary creations who will be dragged away in time. Therefore how much actual pleasure or happiness could any of them ever give to their wives? Although I most stubbornly hoped to enjoy the material world, somehow or other detachment has arisen in my heart, and it is making me very happy. Therefore the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Visnu, must be pleased with me. Without even knowing it, I must have performed some activity satisfying to Him. A person who has developed detachment can give up the bondage of material society, friendship, and love, and a person who undergoes great suffering gradually becomes, out of hopelessness, detached and indifferent to the material world. Thus, due to my great suffering, such detachment awoke in my heart; yet how could I have undergone such merciful suffering if I were actually unfortunate?

Therefore, I am in fact fortunate and have received the mercy of the Lord. He must somehow or other be pleased with me. With devotion I accept the great benefit that the Lord has bestowed upon me. Having given up my sinful desires for ordinary sense gratification, I now take shelter of Him, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. I am now completely satisfied, and I have full faith in the Lord’s mercy. Therefore I will maintain myself with whatever comes of its own accord. I shall enjoy life with only the Lord, because He is the real source of love and happiness. The intelligence of the living entity is stolen away by activities of sense gratification, and thus he falls into the dark well of material existence. Within that well he is then seized by the deadly serpent of time. Who else but the Supreme Personality of Godhead could save the poor living entity from such a hopeless condition? When the living entity sees that the entire universe has been seized by the serpent of time, he becomes sober and sane and at that time detaches himself from all material sense gratification. In that condition the living entity is qualified to be his own protector.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments on text 42 of this sequence: ‘“Will you worship the Lord to gain deliverance?’ ‘No,’ Pingala said. ‘When a jiva sees the world as being devoured by time he becomes detached from material enjoyment. He then becomes his own protection from samsara. Because I now have this nature, I have automatically been delivered from samsara. From now on I will simply worship the Lord with prema alone.’ ”

Having completed Pingala’s song, the avadhuta finishes with his own instructions to Maharaja Yadu: “Material desire is undoubtedly the cause of the greatest unhappiness, and freedom from such desire is the cause of the greatest happiness.” (SB. 11.8.44) Pingala understood this and, free from all material desires, happily went to sleep.

**Chapter 9: Detachment From the Material**

19\. The hawk (kurara) (texts 1-2)

A hawk was carrying meat in its beak, but was attacked by another hawk. In fear, it relinquished the meat and so was saved. Although the hawk’s detachment was, at first, forced, it subsequently became actually detached and felt true happiness.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura summarizes the lesson from the kurara: “From attachment to what is most dear, one suffers. He who is without desire is learned and attains unlimited happiness.”

20\. The child (text 3-4)

The avadhuta brahmana tells Maharaja Yadu that free from anxiety and detached from honor, dishonor, and family, he wanders the world like a child, absorbed and satisfied in himself (the atma). “In this world two types of people are free from all anxiety and merged in great happiness: one who is a retarded and childish fool and one who has approached the Supreme Lord, who is beyond the three modes of material nature.” (SB. 11.9.4)

21\. The girl (texts 5-10)

lo keep her conch shell bangles from colliding and alerting her guest that she had no servant, a young girl who had to stir her own pots removed all hut one bracelet on each wrist. So the avadhuta said, he had learned that living with others causes people to collide in the form of frivolous talk and quarrels. Staying alone, on the other hand, leaves one free from conflict.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura clarifies this image in his comment on text 10, fitting it to devotees: “Just as the poor, husbandless girl took off her bracelets to stop the jangling, so juana-yoga makes sages who practice jnana live alone. Just as a married princess, on meeting her husband, wears her bracelets so they will make a pleasing sound, Bhaktidevi makes the devotees who accept her shelter associate with one another, creating a rasa of making sounds of sweet nama-kirtana. They do not remain alone. The Lord says, ‘These devotees, who are engaged in service to My feet, following scriptural rules, who desire only the taste of My beauty, who, gathering together, relish My pastimes among themselves, never desire to become one with Brahman’ ” (SB. 3.25.34).

22\. The arrow maker (texts 11-13)

To successfully practice yoga, one’s mind must become steady, detached, and fixed on the goal of one’s practice. Free from the modes of material nature, especially passion and ignorance, but even goodness, ultimately, one can firmly fix his consciousness on the Supreme Absolute Truth. This the avadhuta learned from the arrow maker, whose concentration on fashioning a perfectly straight arrow caused him to miss the king and his retinue, complete with bugles and kettledrums, even though the king passed nearby.

23\. The serpent (texts 14-15)

“A saintly person should remain alone and constantly travel without any fixed residence. Being alert, he should remain secluded and should act in such a way that he is not recognized or noticed by others. Moving without companions, he should not speak more than required.” (SB. 11.9.14)

Fearing an attack by humans, snakes live alone. Similarly, fearing the attack of materialistic persons, the avadhuta has learned to live in seclusion. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura compares the instruction the avadhuta gleaned from the young girl to what he learned from the serpent: “The young girl is a guru for giving up even the association of other yogis. The snake is a guru for giving up the association of materialists. The sage moves about alone, distrusting society, without a fixed residence, always alert. He lives alone and goes unnoticed by the public. He has no companion and speaks little.”

The BBT purport to text 14 adds: “\[A saintly person\] should also avoid having a fixed residence and should wander unnoticed by others.” One may ask, “Where then should I live?” The avadhuta replies to this in text 15 when he indicates that a sadhu is indifferent to materialistic endeavor: “When a person living in a temporary material body tries to construct a happy home, the result is fruitless and miserable. The snake, however, enters a home that has been built by others and prospers happily.” (SB. 11.9.15)

The BBT purport to text 15 is also relevant, because it underscores the importance of devotees using matter in Krsna’s service: “Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura points out that although materialistic persons take unlimited pains to invent and mass-produce electricity, automobiles, airplanes, etc., ultimately these things are meant for the convenience of the Vaisnavas who are preaching Krsna consciousness. The karmis will always go to such trouble, and the devotees will always offer such laborious productions to the Supreme Personality of Godhead by engaging them in His loving service. The devotees, being concerned with the ultimate perfection of life, do not personally struggle for material advancement.”

24\. The spider (texts 16-21)

In texts 16—20 the avadhuta describes the Supreme Lord’s relationship to i he universe: with no outside assistance Lord Narayana creates, maintains, and destroys the material universe. He remains alone after universal annihilation and is the supreme worshipable object and controller.

His body is composed of the totality of spiritual bliss, and as the shelter and reservoir of all potencies, He “exhibits the fullest meaning of the word ‘liberation.’” (SB. 11.9.18)

Then in text 21 the avadhuta compares the self-sufficient Supreme Personality of Godhead to a spider, for both create from themselves, willi nothing external to themselves. As the Lord in time winds up His creation within Himself, so the spider does the same by swallowing its web. As the BBT purport to text 21 concludes, “transcendental knowledge is visible everywhere for one whose eyes are opened in Krsna consciousness.”

25\. The wasp (texts 22-23)

Seeing a terrified insect trapped by a pesaskrt wasp in its hive, the avadhuta brahmana notes that the “insect constantly meditated upon his captor, and without giving up his body, he gradually achieved the same state of existence as the wasp. Thus one achieves a state of existence according to one’s constant concentration.” (SB. 11.9.23)

The lesson is explicitly stated in text 22: “If out of love, hate, or fear an embodied soul fixes his mind with intelligence and complete concentration upon a particular bodily form, he will certainly attain the form that he is meditating upon.”

The BBT’s purport to text 23 clarifies this unique example: “Since the weaker insect in this story did not physically change his body, how can it be said that he achieved the same state of existence as the wasp? Actually, by constant meditation upon a particular object one’s consciousness becomes filled with its qualities. Due to extreme fear the smaller insect was absorbed in the characteristics and activities of the large wasp and thus entered into the existence of the wasp. Due to such meditation, he actually took the body of a wasp in his next life. Similarly, although we are conditioned souls, if we absorb our consciousness in Lord Krsna we can become liberated even before giving up our present body.”

The avadhuta now adds his own body as his twenty-fifth guru. Being his constant companion, this guru may instruct us in the absence of all other teachers.

26\. The body (texts 25-27)

From his body the avadhuta has learned detachment, because his body will come to a painful end. “Thus, although using my body to acquire knowledge, I always remember that it will ultimately be consumed by others, and remaining detached, I move about this world.” (SB. 11.9.25)

Not only at death hut also during life, my body teaches me detachment because it never awards peace, the avadhuta says. Like a man with many wives who simultaneously demand his attention and affection, the avadhuta has learned that his senses also each demand attention, pulling him in different directions.

Finally, “As a tree before dying produces the seed of a future tree, the dying body manifests the seed of one’s next material body in the form of one’s accumulated karma. Thus assuring the continuation of material existence, the material body sinks down and dies.” (SB. 11.9.26) All of these bring detachment from the body.

In his comment on text 26, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura poses a question: “The body, the best among all the gurus, gives bhakti-yoga, detachment, and discrimination. Although temporary, it should be served with the greatest attachment. To do otherwise would be a sign of ingratitude. That being true, why do you remain unattached to your body?”

“That’s true,” the avadhuta replies, “but the body is such an amazing guru that when served with great attachment, it does not at all teach discrimination and detachment. Rather, it throws a person into the huge blind well of samsara!”

The BBT purport to text 27 adds, “\[O\]ne should merely offer, without attachment, the bare necessities to the guru of one’s body. One should keep one’s body fit and working in the simplest possible way, and that is the sum and substance of service to this so-called guru. If one desires to faithfully serve the body, one should consider that the body pulls the consciousness of the conditioned soul in many ways at once, and thus for the servant of the body there is no possibility of understanding God or even of becoming peaceful.”

*Texts 28-33: The avadhuta speaks to Maharaja Yadu about the importance of human life*

The avadhuta then tells Maharaja Yadu that of all the species the Supreme Lord has created within which a conditioned soul may live, only the human species has the intellectual ability to perceive the Absolute Truth. Thus the human form of life, which is rarely at- mined and can award perfection, pleases the Lord. Sober human beings should work quickly to achieve the ultimate perfection of life, as long as their body, which is always subject to death, has not fallen down and died. After all, sense gratification is available even in the most abominable species of life, whereas Krsna consciousness is possible only for human beings.
