The avadhuta brahmana says, having thus learned from my many gurusI now wander the earth, my consciousness focused internally, lie (ached, and without false ego. “Although the Absolute Truth is one without a second, the sages have described Him in many different ways. Therefore one may not be able to acquire very firm or complete knowledge from one spiritual master.” (SB 11.9.31)

After explaining what he had learned from his twenty-five gurus, the wise brahmana avadhuta, who was actually the incarnation Dattatreya Rsi, “accepted obeisances and worship from the King and felt pleased within himself. Then bidding farewell, he left exactly as he had come.” (SB. 11.9.32)

Krsna concludes this segment of His instructions to Uddhava by describing the effect the avadhuta’s instructions had on Maharaja Yadu: “O Uddhava, hearing the words of the avadhuta, the saintly King Yadu, who is the forefather of our own ancestors, became free from all material attachment, and thus his mind was evenly fixed on the spiritual platform.” (SB. 11.9.33)

## Dialogue 4. Bhakti, the supreme and recommended process

*Canto eleven: chapters 10-14*

**Chapter 10: The Nature of Fruitive Activity**

Sri Krsna has completed His instructions centered on the words of the avadhuta brahmana, and Uddhava has heard about the value of becomiug detached from matter and absorbed in meditation on the Supersoul. He has also learned about the depth of that absorption from the examples given of Pingala and the arrow maker. All of these instructions have highlighted what it means to be a sadhu. Now Krsna will teach Uddhava about varnasrama-dharma, because by following varnasrama according to die standard Vedic sastras, a person’s consciousness is gradually elevated to that of a sadhu. As the BBT purport to Bhagavatam 11.10.1 says, “Now the Lord describes the practical means for achieving such a saintly position.” The first thirteen texts in this chapter concisely define the essential practices and purpose of varnasrama. A qualified disciple surrendering to a qualified guru will break free from material ignorance and the attachments to which such ignorance gives birth. After attaining proper knowledge, that disciple will attain a spiritual destination appropriate to his or her realization of God as Brahman, Paramatma, or Bhagavan.

As Krsna describes varnasrama-dharma to Uddhava, it becomes clear that the true path of varnasrama requires one to be detached, determined, disciplined.

*Texts 1-13: The process of developing saintly consciousness by following varnasrama-dharma*

*Texts 1-5: Initial principles for advancement*

First, Krsna lists principles that will build the firm spiritual foundation on which He will then build His teachings about varnasrama: “Taking full shelter in Me, with the mind carefully fixed in the devotional service of the Lord as spoken by Me, one should live without personal desire and practice the social and occupational system called varnasrama.” (SB. 11.10.1)

A review of these instructions - Uddhava should:

1\. Take full shelter in Krsna in devotional service (sva-dharmesu mad-asrayah).

2\. Practice the Vedic social and occupational system, varnasrama-dharma (varnasrama-kulacaram samacaret).

3\. While doing the above, act dutifully without attachment or personal, fruitive desires (akamatma).

These three instructions are essentially the same three recommendations Krsna gives to Arjuna in the Bhagavad-gita (2.47): “You have a right to perform your prescribed duty, hut you are not entitled to the fruits of action. Never consider yourself the cause of the results of your activities, and never be attached to not doing your duty.” In His instructions to Uddhava, however, Krsna adds that Uddhava should take shelter of Him (mat-asrayah).

Without making specific prescriptions, Krsna continues to offer foundational principles for practitioners of the varnasrama system.Next, He criticizes the value of performing duties motivated by the desire for material pleasure: one who follows the varnasrama system should act dutifully, free from attachment to sense pleasure, because those pleasures are as ephemeral as dreams. Material pleasure is temporary and doomed to end. It cannot possibly bring happiness.

Instead of allowing the desire for sense enjoyment to drive one’s work, Krsna recommends an alternative, especially for those on a spiritual path: “One who has fixed Me within his mind as the goal of life should give up activities based on sense gratification and should instead execute work governed by the regulative principles for advancement. When, however, one is fully engaged in searching out the ultimate truth of the soul, one should not accept the scriptural injunctions governing fruitive activities. One who has accepted Me as the supreme goal of life should strictly observe the scriptural injunctions forbidding sinful activities and, as far as possible, should execute the injunctions prescribing minor regulative duties such as cleanliness.” (SB. 11.10.4-5)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura, quoted in the BBT purport to text 4, goes straight to the point: “\[A\]ny attempt to enjoy the material world, either religiously or irreligiously, ultimately will be full of contradictions. One should come to the platform of desirelessness, pure love of Godhead, and thus solve all of the problems of life.”

One may wonder, But how can I become free of material desire? Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura answers this relevant question in his comment on text 2 of this section: “By meditation on his spiritual goal in relation to the happiness derived from sense objects, he should see that all mundane endeavors give opposite results.” That is, whenever we act on our desires in order to feel pleasure, whether that pleasure is immediate or in the future, we inevitably suffer. We should “see this repeatedly. Becoming convinced of this truth, a wise person, who no longer desires those opposite results, loses his desire for material things.”

*Texts 5-6: Qualified guru, qualified disciple*

*Text 5: The qualified guru*

In text 5, the Supreme Lord recommends accepting a spiritual master and then hearing from and serving him. The spiritual master should guide one’s advancement. In text 5, Krsna lists the guru’s qualifications as being “full in knowledge of Me as I am,” peacefulness, and, by his spiritual advancement, he is “not different from Me.” Nondifference refers to the spiritual master’s surrender to actions harmonious to fulfilling the Lord’s desires, such as His mission.

*Text 6: The qualified disciple*

The Lord then lists the qualities of a qualified disciple as freedom from false prestige, never considering himself the doer, and always being active and never lazy. Disciples should give up all sense of proprietorship over sense objects, including their spouse, children, home, and society. They should feel a loving friendship with their guru, remain fixed in service and clear in their direction. Always desiring to advance their spiritual understanding, they should free themselves of envy. They should also avoid frivolous conversations.

*Texts 7-11: Results of surrender*

Sri Krsna next delineates the good results sincere disciples achieve when they surrender to a realized, pure spiritual master: detachment from matter due to seeing one’s self-interest (text 7); knowledge of the fact that the self is separate from both the gross and subtle bodies and subsequent release from the wheel of samsara (texts 8-10); the gradually increasing ability to approach the transcendental Lord in the heart while simultaneously understanding that the material world has no independent reality (text 11).

*Texts 12-13: The destruction of both avidya and vidya*

In texts 12-13, Krsna concludes His list of the results one achieves by properly following varnasrama-dharma: by following the work prescribed by the Vedas, even with a fruitive mindset, one achieves detachment and knowledge.The Lord makes it clear that the fire of knowledge (vidya) gained from an expert (visarada) guru burns ignorance (avidya, or the pure soul’s misidentification with the gross and subtle bodies) to ashes. This avidya arises from maya and forces the eternal soul to suffer repeated birth and death. With ignorance destroyed, vidya herself is also destroyed, “just as fire ceases when the stock of fuel has been consumed.” (SB. 11.10.13)

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.10.13 explains the destruction of vidya for the advancing devotee: “As one advances to the perfectional stage of Krsna consciousness, experiencing the presence of the Lord everywhere, one’s attention shifts to the transcendental platform. At that time, pure knowledge itself, one’s constant technical awareness of illusion, diminishes, just as fire diminishes and is extinguished after consuming its stock of fuel.”

In his comment on the same text, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura further explains the destruction of both knowledge (vidya) and ignorance (avidya). There he explains that knowledge can be compared to fire. Vidya, the pure knowledge coming from the Lord, destroys maya made of avidya, or ignorance in the form of identification with the subtle and gross bodies - the bondage of samsara. After also destroying avidya’s qualities, vidya itself is destroyed, just as a fire goes out when its fuel is exhausted. Then, by pure bhakti, which has also been practiced along with vidya (jnana-misra-bhakti), one attains santi-rati and then residence on the Lord’s planet. On the other hand, jnanis who performed bhakti-yoga in order to obtain knowledge (bhakti-misra-jnana) merge into the Paramatma after avidya and vidya are destroyed.

To describe why the jnana-misra-bhaktas are thought of here as practicing pure devotional service, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains more in his comments on Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 3.1.15: “Bhakti does not appear when obstacles such as lust and anger and their constant influence are present. \[These devotees\] practice with a suitable form of detachment - yukta-vairagya - without giving up the desire for liberation. Although they have a desire for liberation, this does not destroy their pure bhakti, because they desire liberation from samsara in order to destroy their lust and anger, not to merge into the Lord. Moreover, they worship with a desire for liberation only during the first stage of their practice.”

*Texts 14—34: Sri Krsna speaks against Jaimini Rsi’s Karma-mimamsa*

Earlier in the Bhagavatam,Suta Gosvami tells his audience the importance of performing duties prescribed by the Vedas: “All occupational engagements are certainly meant for ultimate liberation.” In an almost revolutionary way, Suta Gosvami then goes on to describe what one should never be motivated by when performing one’s duties: “\[Duties\] should never be performed for material gain. Furthermore, according to sages, one who is engaged in the ultimate occupational service should never use material gain to cultivate sense gratification.”

After having just explained that the purpose of work according to die Vedic system is to develop both knowledge and bhakti, Krsna will now explain what work according to the Vedic system is not about. This is similar to how Suta Gosvami spoke in the First Canto. Krsna begins, however, in text 14, by asserting that the knowledge about work He has just given Uddhava is “perfect.” Yet, Krsna tells us, there are philosophers (Karma-mimamsakas) “who challenge My conclusion. They state that the natural position of the living entity is to engage in fruitive activities, and they see him as the enjoyer of the happiness and unhappiness that accrue from his own work. According to this materialistic philosophy, the world, time, the revealed scriptures, and the self are all variegated and eternal, existing as a perpetual flow of transformations. Knowledge, moreover, cannot be one or eternal, because it arises from the different and changing forms of objects; thus knowledge itself is always subject to change. Even if you accept such a philosophy, My dear Uddhava, there will still be perpetual birth, death, old age, and disease, since all living entities must accept a material body subject to the influence of time.” (SB. 11.10.14-16)

Can one become happy engaging in fruitive activities in the form of continuous, pious Vedic performances as the Karma-mimamsakas assert? Is it true that the world, time, the sastras, knowledge, and the self are eternal, “existing as a perpetual flow of transformations”? As Krsna notes, even if Uddhava were to accept such a philosophy, he would have to admit that there, one still has to face a perpetual cycle of birth, death, old age, and disease, and that these are the results of having to accept a material body “subject to the influence of time.” Therefore continuous and unending happiness on the material level, as the Karma-mimamsakas strive for through the continuous performance of pious Vedic rites, is simply not possible.

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.10.14-16 includes a lengthy comment by Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura. He begins by giving Krsna’s reasons for talking about the philosophers who challenge His conclusions: “My dear Uddhava, I have clearly established the actual goal of life in the instructions I have just imparted to you. There are those, however, who challenge My conclusions, especially the followers of Jaimini Kavi. If you are favorable to their understanding and thus do not accept My instructions, then kindly hear the following explanation.”

Jaimini Kavi (Rsi) was a disciple of Srila Vyasadeva and the philosopher who established the Karma-mimamsa darsana, the earliest of the six sad-darsanas, or traditional schools of Vedic philosophical thought. The Karma-mimarhsa school was later called the Purva-mimamsaschool, and it was based on chanting the Vedic mantras contained in the fruitive, ritualistic, or karma-kandiya, sections of the Vedas and their supplements, the Brahmanas. The Purva-mimamsa school is credited with establishing the standards for bow to systematically interpret Vedic texts. Calling it “Purva-mimamsa” differentiated it from the Uttara-mimamsa school,which was based on study of the Vedantasutra and the Upanisads.

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura then describes the points that form the basis of the Karma-mimamsa philosophy:

1\. It’s natural for people to seek their own pleasure and to perform fruitive actions to ensure their own success.

2\. The happiness and distress people experience is simply the fruit of their work.

3\. The ingredients that comprise people’s pleasure are eternal. That includes the material world, time, the scriptures that teach people how to enjoy, and people’s own subtle bodies.

4\. Since everything in existence is part of a perpetual flow of creation and destruction, everything is eternal in the sense that it continually reappears. For example, although a specific beautiful object - a sunset, perhaps - may not always be here, there will always be a beautiful sunset somewhere in existence. In this sense, the world never perishes. Therefore, it is not necessary for jivas to cultivate detachment from the material world simply because the things in it appear temporary or made from maya.

5\. If people carefully execute the rituals prescribed in scripture, they can amass the required piety to remain in contact with the things that give them pleasure, life after life.

6\. Because the world has always existed, there’s no need to posit the existence of a creator. The world and the things in it are real, substantial (yatha), not made of maya. There is no eternal soul-knowledge. Rather, knowledge relates to one becoming aware of different forms and the differences between those forms. In this sense, the atma is not the eternal form of knowledge but a transformation of knowledge. Thus it’s possible to know only about this world and what it contains. Knowing is eternal, but knowledge is not eternally fixed; that is, knowledge is subject to change because the material elements are constantly changing. Like the state of knowing, consciousness is also eternal but inconstant, subject to the changing configurations of matter.

7\. Neither renunciation nor liberation is the goal of life. Rather, the goal is to follow the prescriptions in the scriptures in order to achieve perpetual sense pleasure.

*Texts 17-34: Krsna challenges the Karma-mimamsd promise of perpetual happiness*

In texts 17-34, Krsna refutes the idea of perpetual material happiness, as Jaimini Rsi and his followers have proposed. I have summarized Krsna’s points below.

Texts 17-18: Everyone in this world wants to be completely happy, but no one is, and no one can control his or her destiny fully in order to ensure a perpetual state of material happiness. For example, there are apparently happy fools while more intelligent people are miserable. Don’t intelligent people have a better chance at understanding how to become happy than fools? But everyone is under the control of destiny, and being under such control indicates that there are forces more powerful than ourselves. Can we expect to be completely happy when we can only partially control what happens to us?

Texts 19-20: Even if we could avoid unhappiness and remain happy, we still die. There is nothing we can do to avert our own death or the death of any other being. Can those condemned to death find pleasure in the material objects before them?

Text 21: Even the kind of happiness one finds in heaven is not true happiness, for its fulfillment is inevitably spoiled by obstacles like jealousy, envy, decay, and fear of death.

Texts 22-29: Even perfectly performed pious fruitive activities cannot give us full satisfaction; even those already enjoying heavenly delights are powerless to stop the crushing wheel of time. On the other hand, sinful, irreligious acts breed in us lower, material desires, that lead to pain now and in the future. So neither pious nor impious actions can fill the Jiva with true happiness. “What possible happiness can there be for one who engages in activities inevitably terminating in death?” (SB. 11.10.29)

Texts 30-33: From Brahma, who is in the topmost position in the material world, with a lifetime spanning thousands of billions of years, to those dwelling in hell, every conditioned soul in the universe fears Krsna in His form as time. Whether he or she is pious or impious, time works on every soul according to the results of his or her actions. The path of fruitive work (karma) creates reactions and is therefore by definition fraught with misery.

In anuccheda 81 of the Bhagavata Sandarbha, Srila Jiva Gosvami quotes Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.10.30: “In all the planetary systems, from the heavenly to the hellish, and for all of the great demigods who live for one thousand yuga cycles, there is fear of Me in my form of time. Even Brahma, who possesses the supreme lifespan of 311,040,000,000,000 years, is also afraid of Me.” He then states that the Supreme Lord lives in Vaikuntha, where He surpasses the karmic miseries inherent in time. These miseries are present throughout the three worlds, but there is no misery in Vaikuntha, where the Lord lives in a blissful, fearless, and secure form. One cannot approach Vaikuntha through the mind, through processes like brahmacarya, or in any way other than through devotion to Vaikuntha-natha.

Texts 33-34: Krsna concludes that forgetting Him, the living entities, lost in illusion, will see the forces that control this world - their kar- mic destiny — as if it is disconnected from or independent of Him. How, then, will they avoid unending varieties of experiences in material ex- istence? Not seeing the Lord, they will experience fear as His energies impose on them the results of their own fruitive actions and their subsequent temporary moments of happiness and grief. This is why the jivas describe Krsna according to His unstoppable potencies - as “all-powerful time, the Self, Vedic knowledge, the universe, one’s own nature, religious ceremonies, and so on” (SB. 11.10.34) — and not directly, as Sri Krsna, Govinda, or any of His sweet names.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, concluding his explanation of Sri Krsna’s rejection of Karma-mimamsa, writes: “Those who dedicate themselves to material rituals are filled with lamentation and are bewildered.” (SB. 11.10.33) Rather than using the Vedic laws to practice karma simply to obtain material pleasure, the jiva should instead “strive for freedom from the bondage of karma.”

*Texts 35-37: Uddhava inquires further*

Sri Krsna has just clarified for Uddhava that the purpose of the Vedas - and by extrapolation, the purpose of Vedic culture - is liberation, not sense pleasure. Uddhava then asks an intelligent question about how one goes about becoming liberated: “O my Lord, a living entity situated within the material body is surrounded by the modes of nature and the happiness and distress that are born of activities caused by these modes. How is it possible that he is not bound by this material encirclement? It may also be said that the living entity is ultimately transcendental and has nothing to do with the material world. Then how is he ever bound by material nature? O my Lord, Acyuta, the same living entity is sometimes described as eternally conditioned and at other times as eternally liberated. I am not able to understand, therefore, the actual situation of the living entity. You, my Lord, are the best of those who are expert in answering philosophical questions. Please explain to me the symptoms by which one can tell the difference between a living entity who is eternally liberated and one who is eternally conditioned. In what various ways would they remain situated, enjoy life, eat, evacuate, lie down, sit, or move about?” (SB. 11.10.35-37)

In other words, Uddhava is asking how material existence binds the jiva, and to understand this he wants to know the nature of both the bound and the free. Are the liberated souls among us - and he gives the examples of Dattatreya and Bharata, who were liberated yet maintained gross and subtle bodies and performed all the activities of any embodied jiva - also controlled by the material modes? If so, how can we understand that they are liberated?

In his comment on texts 35-37, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura adds something more to Uddhava’s question: “Or, if it is argued that the soul is spiritual and never truly mixes with material nature, how then is it possible for any soul to become bound?”

In text 36, Uddhava also asks about the symptoms by which we can differentiate between eternally bound souls (nitya-haddha) and eternally-liberated souls (nitya-mukta).And finally, in text 37, how souls can sometimes be designated eternally bound and at other times eternally free.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura rephrases Uddhava’s question in his comment on texts 36-37: “What qualities should I seek in a liberated person, since existing, enjoying, eating, evacuation, sleeping, sitting, and going are actions related to material identity? Since perfectly liberated persons like Dattatreya and Bharata carry out daily activities like the completely bound Jivas, they seem to be the same. This is confusing. It is impossible for me to understand the difference. You must tell me.”

So Uddhava has now heard about the actual Vedic process of performing prescribed duties and now inquires about the forces that bind - or free - the soul, as well as the symptoms of both bound and liberated souls. In the next chapter, Krsna will speak about the nature of an eternal soul’s bondage.

**Chapter 11: The Symptoms of Conditioned and Liberated Living Entities**

*Texts 1-4: Krsna replies through an analogy of a dream*

Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, begins by answering Uddhava’s first question: “My dear Uddhava, due to the influence of the material modes of nature, which are under My control, the living entity is sometimes designated as conditioned and sometimes as liberated. In fact, however, the soul is never really bound up or liberated, and since I am the Supreme Lord of maya, which is the cause of the modes of nature, I also am never to be considered liberated or in bondage.” (SB. 11.11.1)

As the BBT purport explains, Krsna considers Uddhava’s question “somewhat superficial, since the pure spirit soul is never entangled in the material energy of the Lord” and “the living entity is never actually baddha, or bound up, since he merely imagines a false connection with the material world. Because there is ultimately no permanent connection between t he living entity and matter, there is no actual liberation. The living entity, being eternally transcendental to the inferior material energy o! the Lord, is eternally liberated. Lord Krsna reveals that in one sense the living entity is factually not bound up and thus cannot be liberated.”

Krsna uses the analogy of a dream to explain this point: “Just as a dream ... has no actual substance, similarly, material lamentation, illusion, happiness, distress, and the acceptance of the material body under the influence of maya are all creations of My illusory energy. In other words, material existence has no essential reality.” (SB. 11.11.2)

Let’s consider Krsna’s dream reference. A banker may be dreaming that a tiger is chasing him and will soon claw open his flesh and devour him. He becomes terrified. In the dream he feels horror, and runs to escape his death. But even while he’s running, he may suddenly realize that he’s only dreaming and could escape his phantom tiger (and his fear) simply by waking up. Krsna’s point is that both states of the banker’s consciousness happen in dreams - his fleeing from the tiger in his night dream and his escaping by waking himself up.

A friend watching the sleeping banker may see the man’s legs churning and perspiration breaking out on his face. He knows that the sleeping man is a banker and that there is no tiger. He also knows his friend will at some point awaken and go on with his banking duties, completely free of his fear-filled nightmare.

Krsna’s emphasis on the idea that “the soul is never really bound up or liberated” is offered from the viewpoint of the observer, and it speaks to an important point: We have a real life that is eternal and filled with bliss, one lived in relation to Him. Not only is that life far different from the ever-shifting dreamlike phantasmagoria we usually call reality, it is also far different from the ways we use to awaken ourselves from the dream. For example, I may pinch myself, but that pinching is not my awakened state. Rather, it is only something I do to help myself wake up.

We have to be ignorant to accept a dream as reality. If we want relief from the dream, we first need knowledge (vidya), by which we mean both the conscious awareness that we are dreaming as well as knowledge about how to wake ourselves up. But neither ignorance (avidya) nor awareness of one’s ignorance (vidya) are the real (awakened) life of the soul; both are connected to Krsna’s dream-producing material energy, maya.

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.11.3: “Maya has three means of action: pradhana, avidya, anti vidya. Pradhana creates the coverings (upadhis, literally, “frauds,” or the gross and subtle bodies) over the soul. We think these are real. Avidya imposes on the soul the sense that the body is the self (adhyasa), which is a false idea. Vidya destroys this false sense of identity. These are the products of these three aspects of maya.”

So speaking as an observer, objective and philosophical, Krsna expressed in text 1 that the jiva is incapable of being either bound or liberated, but now, in texts 3 and 4, He speaks from the vantage point of the jiva’s consciousness and describes the soul’s bondage (baddhah) and liberation (muktah): “O Uddhava, both knowledge \[vidya\] and ignorance \[avidya\], being products of maya, are expansions of My potency. Both knowledge and ignorance are beginningless and perpetually award liberation and bondage to embodied living beings. O most intelligent Uddhava, the living entity, called jiva, is part and parcel of Me, but due to ignorance he has been suffering in material bondage since time immemorial. By knowledge, however, he can be liberated.” (SB. 11.11.3-4)

Srila Sridhara Svami writes: “\[A\]lthough the Lord has explained in the first verse of this chapter that the living entity is never actually in bondage - and therefore never actually liberated - one may apply the terms ‘bondage’ and ‘liberation’ if one remembers that the living entity is eternally a transcendental fragment of the Personality of Godhead.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura sheds more light on how vidya and avidya function: “Bondage and liberation of My sakti, the jiva, both of which are only apparent - that is, appearing to be true, but unreal - are caused by My avidya-sakti, which imposes the idea of the body on the soul, and My vidya-sakti, which removes that imposition and brings liberation. This is brought about under the influence of My maya-sakti, which functions for My pastime of creating and destroying the universe.”

In his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.11.22, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura writes: “With the destruction of vidya, one attains bhakti, which surpasses vidya.” Thus Visvanatha indicates that the vidya to which Krsna is referring comes from His external energy, His maya-sakti, which may award liberation by breaking the soul’s identification with the body but cannot award full engagement in Krsna’s personal service. On the other hand, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti’s comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.11.7 indicates the presence of a superior vidya, a sakti of His internal energy: “Vidya-maya refers to the cit-sakti, not to the vidya belonging to maya-sakti.” Thus it appears from the comments of Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura that both Krsna’s external and internal energies have vidya-saktis, but they have different functions.

Or the point can be viewed from the perspective that Krsna’s external energy (Durgadevi) is a manifestation of His internal energy (Laksmidevi). From this point of view, as Srila Prabhupada writes in his purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 1.3.34: “The same energy acts as His external, internal, and marginal energies, and by His omnipotency He can perform anything and everything through the agency of any of the above energies. He can turn the external energy into internal by His will.”

*Texts 5-17: Two separate divisions of souls - the Supersoul and the individual soul, and conditioned and liberated souls*

*Texts 5-7: Division one - Distinguishing between the Supersoul and the individual soul*

In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.10.36-37, Uddhava asked Krsna to describe the symptoms of both liberated and conditioned souls. Now, after describing bondage and liberation from different points of view, Krsna will describe two kinds of liberated souls: the unlimited, supremely liberated Supersoul and the minute, liberated jiva soul: “\[I\]n the same material body we find opposing characteristics, such as great happiness and misery. That is because both the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is eternally liberated, as well as the conditioned soul are within the body. I shall now speak to you about their different characteristics.” (SB. 11.11.5)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains the sequence of Krsna’s words: “Uddhava asked about the qualities of the liberated jiva (SB 11.10.36-37). We hear statements like ‘This jiva is in bondage and that jiva is liberated,’ ‘The jiva is in bondage and Paramatma is liberated,’ or ‘That jivatma is without sin.’ Please first hear about the difference between the jiva and the Paramatma, which Krsna will explain in one and a half verses. In one body there are two who possess opposite natures. One is blissful and the other full of lamentation. The first is the controller and the second the controlled.”

In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.11.6-7 Krsna now compares the Supersoul and the conditioned, bound, individual jiva soul to two birds on one tree. They are friends and of a similar nature. “One of them, however, is eating the fruits of the tree, whereas the other, who does not eat the fruits, is in a superior position due to His potency.” The bird that does not eat is omnipotent and understands both His position as well as the position of the “eating bird,” the minute, individual soul. The all- knowing “bird” is the Supersoul, the Personality of Godhead, and He is eternally liberated and full of perfect knowledge. The “eating bird” is covered by ignorance and is thus called eternally conditioned.

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.11.6 describes these two birds further: “As birds are different from the tree on which they sit, so the Paramatma and jiva are different from the body. They are similar because both are conscious entities. They are friends because they are related. They live together in the tree without apparent reason, since one bird, the jiva, is interested in making a nest and eating the tree’s fruit and the other bird, the Paramatma, has no such interest... In this tree (the body), the jiva-bird creates his nest (house) based on his attachments and aversions and thus enjoys (and suffers) the karma-fruit produced of his body. The second bird, the Paramatma, although He does not eat, being satisfied in His own bliss, is the stronger of the two because of His knowledge potency (jnana-sakti) and other potencies.”

*Texts 8-17: Division two - conditioned and liberated souls*

In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.11.8, Krsna defines both liberated souls (“although living within the material body, sees himself as transcendental to the body”) and conditioned souls (“although not identical with his material body but transcendental to it, thinks himself to be situated in the body, just as one who is dreaming sees himself as situated in an imaginary body”). In text 9, the Supreme Lord continues His description of liberated souls: “An enlightened person who is free from the contamination of material desire does not consider himself to be the performer of bodily activities; rather, he knows that in all such activities it is only the senses, born of the modes of nature, that are contacting sense objects born of the same modes of nature.” Krsna tells us in text 10, that conditioned souls “situated within the body created by his previous fruitive activities,” think “‘I am the performer ol action. Bewildered by false ego, such a foolish person is therefore hound up by fruitive activities, which are in fact carried out by the modes of nature.”

Kisna then speaks more on the topic of liberated souls in seven verses, from texis 11-17 of this chapter.From this overall section of ten verses (8 through 17), we can summarize the differences between conditioned and liberated souls as follows:

Conditioned souls: See themselves as the body, just as those who are dreaming consider themselves nondifferent from the body they assume in their dreams (text 8). They think themselves the performer of their activities and thereby become bound to the wheel of samsara by their karmic reactions (text 10).

Liberated souls: See themselves as souls. They no longer identify with the body, just as dreamers who have awoken no longer identify with the body they assumed in a dream (text 8). They have no material desires and do not think themselves the performer of their physical activities; rather, they know that those activities are carried out by the modes of nature (text 9). They are detached from the body, witnessing its actions as objective observers, leaving them free from karmic entanglement (text 11). Like dreamers who have awakened from their dreams, they are fully detached from the body and everything around it. Their knowledge and direct experience of their spiritual identity cuts to pieces any doubts they may have about their identity as souls. They no longer look at the world with material eyes (texts 12-13).They remain free of material desire, aloof from matter, even though they continue to live in their bodies (text 14). They are neither angry when attacked nor satisfied when worshiped (text 15). They see with equal vision and are unaffected by material estimations of good and bad. They keenly observe others’ actions but don’t criticize them (text 16).They are detached in all material circumstances. They wander freely, taking pleasure in self-realization, although appearing externally mad (text 17 ).(According to Srila Jiva Gosvami, text 17 describes a type of discipline recommended for jnana-yogis, who try to understand themselves as different from their body by using their intelligence.)

*Texts 18-25: The goal of the Vedic literature - absorption of the consciousness in the glories of Krsna*

In the previous chapter, Krsna established that the goal of the Vedas is to reach above the attempt to achieve perpetual material pleasure. Rather, one should perform one’s duties detached from the fruits of one’s actions, because detached action gives birth to knowledge. In texts 11-17 of this eleventh chapter, Krsna described the nature of souls who have been liberated from nuiya after gaining such knowledge. Now Krsna will describe a further evolution of consciousness that one can achieve by following the Vedic path.

But first He condemns studying the Vedas without a desire to achieve Him - it’s like “a man who works very hard to take care of a cow that gives no milk. In other words, the fruit of one’s laborious study of Vedic knowledge will simply be the labor itself. There will be no other tangible result. My dear Uddhava, that man is certainly most miserable who takes care of a cow that gives no milk, an unchaste wife, a body totally dependent on others, useless children, or wealth not utilized for the right purpose. Similarly, one who studies Vedic knowledge devoid of My glories is also most miserable.” (SB. 11.11.18-19)

The BBT purport states: “The previous examples are given to illustrate the uselessness of laboriously studying Vedic knowledge that does not glorify the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Srila Jiva Gosvami comments that the spiritual vibration of the Vedas is meant to bring one to the lotus feet of the Supreme Lord, Krsna. Many processes for achieving the Supreme Truth are recommended in the Upanisads and other Vedic literature, but because of their innumerable and seemingly contradictory explanations, commentaries, and injunctions, one cannot achieve the Absolute Truth, the Personality of Godhead, merely by reading such literature. If, however, one understands Sri Krsna to be the ultimate cause of all causes and reads the Upanisads and other Vedic literature as glorification of the Supreme Lord, then one can actually become fixed at the Lord’s lotus feet.”

Krsna previously instructed Uddhava to fix his consciousness on the Supreme, hut Uddhava, according to Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, wants to know Krsna’s intention more precisely: “Should I focus on the Supreme, following the guidance of scriptures promoting tat warn asi - that the jiva and Brahman are one? Or do you mean something else?” Krsna’s reply in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.11.20 is clear: “Focus on Me.” “My dear Uddhava, an intelligent person should never take to literatures that do not contain descriptions of My activities, which purify the whole universe. Indeed, I create, maintain, and annihilate the entire material manifestation.” (SB. 11.11.20)

In the Paramatma Sandarbha (105) Srila Jiva Gosvami quotes Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.11.18 to indicate that ultimately the Lord is not impersonal but very much a person: “\[T\]his scripture named Bhagavatam, the essence of all the Vedas, accepts as its very principle that we should meditate on this highest form of Bhagavan.... The Lord has a spiritual body. He is greater than anything made of earth. He is greater than the sky and greater than the heavens. He has a spiritual abode. He is more beautiful than any great or beautiful object.”

Considering still further, Krsna tells Uddhava to focus on Him by hearing of His childhood activities: “Among all My pastime incarnations, the most beloved are Krsna and Balarama.” (SB. 11.11.20)

In the Bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 69), Srila Jiva Gosvami notes that there are descriptions that far surpass talks about the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the cosmos and Brahman, all of which are described in the Upanisads. These words are “the nectar-words describing Lord Hari, for they make the heart melt, the body tremble, the hairs of the body erect, and they fill the eyes with tears.”

Krsna continues: “Any so-called knowledge that does not recognize these activities of Mine is simply barren and is not acceptable to those who are actually intelligent.” (SB. 11.11.20)

Jiva Gosvami, writing in the Bhakti Sandarbha (anucchedas 68-69), concurs: Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.11.19-20, he says, teaches one to avoid even Vedic utterances if lila-katha about Krsna is absent.

Krsna then offers ultimate instructions for those practicing jnana-yoga, or the path of knowledge: Based on what I have just said, give up the false conception of material variety that illusion imposes on the soul. In this way, cease your material existence. “The mind should be fixed on Me, since I am all-pervading \[mano mayy arpya sarva-ge\].” (SB. 11.11.21)

In essence, Krsna is teaching Uddhava the goal of the Vedas and of his spiritual practice: focus your consciousness on Me and attain Me. Although one may fix his mind on Krsna and practice bhakti to merge with Krsna’s effulgence, the impersonal Brahman, and thus gain the liberation called sayujya-mukti, this is not what Krsna recommends. Rather, Krsna says, know Me as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the source of everything that exists. Fix your mind on Me and attain Me.

In addition, just knowing that Krsna is the Supreme Absolute Truth will naturally cause us to stop seeing material objects as if they are separate from Him and meant for our petty, self-centered pleasures. “Know that I am all-pervading (mano mayy arpya sarva-ge),” Krsna tells Uddhava. He says, since I am everywhere and in everything, look for Me in all things and fix your mind on Me.

The BBT purport to 11.11.21 clarifies why one who has this knowledge can easily fix his mind on Krsna: “Everything is ultimately an expansion of Krsna, and therefore there is really no other object of meditation besides Krsna. But, the purport adds, “\[T\]he Lord now comes to the ultimate conclusion, Krsna consciousness, pure love of Godhead. Without such love there is no question of eternally fixing one’s mind on the Lord.”

Thus Krsna establishes bhakti as the ultimate process and the supreme, most evolved goal of the path of knowledge. In the Bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 70), Srila Jiva Gosvami comments that jnana only reaches its perfection in bhakti, and that one should hear of Krsna’s everpresent transcendental activities (lila-katha), fix his mind on Him, and attain peace.

But what do we do if our bhakti is insufficient to fix our mind on Krsna, even when we accept that Krsna is the all-pervading Supreme Lord, the source of everything in existence? Understanding this dilemma, and after establishing bhakti as the topmost level of consciousness, Krsna offers a practical, less-advanced alternative: “My dear Uddhava, if you are not able to free your mind from all material disturbance and thus absorb it completely on the spiritual platform \[dharayitum mano brahmana\], then perform all your activities as an offering to Me, without trying to enjoy the fruits \[mayi sarvani karmani nirapeksah samacara\].” (SB. 11.11.22)

The BBT purport comments that Krsna’s description of the path of knowledge has culminated in a description of pure bhakti (text 22) and that the Lord will explain how to practice bhakti in texts 23-25.

*Texts 23-25: Establishing the Pure Processes of bhakti*

Krsna begins to open His heart and reveal bhakti, the summit of all the methodologies presented in the Vedas and the heart of the Vedic culture. Bhakti is the perfection of all dharmas. “My dear Uddhava, narrations of My pastimes and qualities are all-auspicious and purify the entire universe. A faithful person who constantly hears, glorifies, and remembers such transcendental activities, who through dramatic performances relives My pastimes, beginning with My appearance, and who takes full shelter of Me, dedicating his religious, sensual, and occupational activities for My satisfaction, certainly obtains unflinching devotional service to Me, the eternal Personality of Godhead.” (SB. 11.11.23—24)

How can one gain faith in the power of bhakti and also learn how to practice it? Krsna answers these important questions in text 25: “One who has obtained pure devotional service by association with My devotees always engages in worshiping Me. Thus he very easily goes to My abode, which is revealed by My pure devotees.” (SB. 11.11.25)

Krsna will again emphasize the importance of associating with devotees in the opening texts of the next chapter, Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.12.1-7.

*Texts 26-28: Uddhava asks more about bhakti*

Krsna has put karma and jnana in the perspective of bhakti, and Uddhava now acknowledges the Lord’s unlimited greatness: You are the ruler of the universal controllers, the Lord of Vaikuntha, and the almighty God of the universe. He adds, “I am Your devotee, and because I love You I have no other shelter than You.” (SB. 11.11.27)

Uddhava asks Krsna two more questions: “My dear Lord, O Supreme Personality of Godhead, what type of person do You consider to be a true devotee, and what type of devotional service is approved by great devotees as worthy of being offered to Your Lordship?” (SB. 11.11.26) After his declaration of allegiance to his Lord, Uddhava then concludes: “My dear Lord, as the Absolute Truth You are transcendental to material nature, and like the sky You are never entangled in any way. Still, being controlled by Your devotees’ love, You accept many different forms, incarnating according to Your devotees’ desires.” (SB. 11.11.28)

By glorifying Krsna as the Absolute Truth, free from entanglement in the material world, controlled by His devotees’ love, and taking forms according to the desires of His devotees, Uddhava states the principle that defines the uniquely attractive, supremely powerful Personality of Godhead: that fully independent Supreme Lord is conquered by His devotees’ bhakti. In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.12.1, Krsna will Himself tell us that the bhakti of His devotees conquers Him, the unconquerable. But first, we will learn who is a true devotee.

*Texts 29-32: The true devotee*

Krsna lists twenty-eight exalted qualities naturally possessed by His devotees. Of these twenty-eight, one is central: “O Uddhava, a saintly person is merciful and never injures others. Even if others are aggressive he is tolerant and forgiving toward all living entities. His strength and meaning in life come from the truth itself, he is free from all envy and jealousy, and his mind is equal in material happiness and distress. Thus, he dedicates his time to work for the welfare of all others. His intelligence is never bewildered by material desires, and he has controlled his senses. His behavior is always pleasing, never harsh, and always exemplary, and he is free from possessiveness. He never endeavors in ordinary, worldly activities, and he strictly controls his eating. He therefore always remains peaceful and steady. A saintly person is thoughtful and accepts Me as his only shelter \[mat-sarana\]. Such a person is very cautious in the execution of his duties and is never subject to superficial transformations, because he is steady and noble, even in a distressing situation. He has conquered over the six material qualities - namely hunger, thirst, lamentation, illusion, old age, and death. He is free from all desire for prestige and offers honor to others. He is expert in reviving the Krsna consciousness of others and therefore never cheats anyone. Rather, he is a well-wishing friend to all, being most merciful. Such a saintly person must be considered the most learned of men. He perfectly understands that the ordinary religious duties prescribed by Me in various Vedic scriptures possess favorable qualities that purify the performer, and he knows that neglect of such duties constitutes a discrepancy in one’s life. Having taken complete shelter at My lotus feet, however, a saintly person ultimately renounces such ordinary religious duties and worships Me alone. He is thus considered to be the best among all living entities.” (SB. 11.11.29-32)

Although devotees may possess many exalted qualities, the central point of the devotional consciousness is mat-sarana, unalloyed surrender to Krsna. If devotees possess that one quality yet fail to exhibit the other twenty-seven, they are still considered saintly.

Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura devotes the fourth chapter of Sri Harinama Cintamani to help his readers chant Krsna’s holy names without offense. There he teaches that the most harmful offense against the holy names is sadhu-ninda, criticism of Vaisnavas, and lists the same twenty-eight qualities described here. Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura adds: "These symptomatic characteristics can he divided into two categories: svarupa-laksana, or those qualities of a substance that are primary, inherent, and of its essence, and tatastha-laksana, the qualities that are secondary, only becoming visible when the substance comes in contact with another object. A sadhu’s quality of mat-saranah, accepting Krsna as his only shelter, is his svarupa-laksana, and all the other twenty-seven qualities are tatastha.”

When one has the svarupd'laksana, the mood of surrender to Krsna, the secondary characteristics of a sadhu will develop naturally. But even if they don’t develop, Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura emphasizes that such a person is still to be respected as a sadhu, and one should avoid blaspheming him. True saintliness depends only on a devotee’s full surrender to Krsna, and, as Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura notes, “The scriptures expound the quality of complete surrender to Lord Krsna as the hallmark of a sadhu, and such a surrendered soul alone can chant purely Krsna’s name.”

In his comment to texts 29-31, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura describes mixed bhakti. He refers to devotees who want to develop these exalted qualities but have not yet attained a pure desire to please Krsna. This is a key point. And as the purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.11.29-32 states, for those who learn to desire only Krsna’s pleasure, “the other twenty-seven qualities automatically appear.”

In text 32,the final text in the description of a devotee’s qualities, Sri Krsna indicates that one who, after understanding the good aspects of practicing the dharma He has taught along with the negative aspects of not practicing it, gives up all duties other than fully surrendered devotional service to Him: “Having taken complete shelter at My lotus feet, however, a saintly person ultimately renounces such ordinary religious duties and worships Me alone. He is thus considered to be the best among all living entities \[mam bhajeta sa tu sattamah\].” (SB. 11.11.32)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains Krsna’s mood and reasoning: “Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.11.32 describes the devotee practicing pure bhakti. It has been said that one who does not give up dharma is the best. But he who completely gives up all dharma because of faith in pure bhakti to Me is actually the best (mam bhajeta sa tu sattamah). But can we say that such a person who is worshiping Me and who therefore gives up the Vedic path of dharma because he is certain that bhakti alone is the highest way to please Me, is acting out of ignorance of or disregard for the Vedas? No. Such a person understands the good points of performing dharma, such as that it will purify his existence, and the negative side of not performing dharma, and gives up all prescribed dharma with firm faith that all things are perfected by bhakti to Me. That is the meaning given by Sridhara Svami.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura then offers evidence, quoting Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.2.42and 5.18.12to indicate that those who practice pure bhakti will develop all good qualities, even if they do not yet possess them. Finally, he says, “He who reaches the highest stage is the best, since he becomes endowed with all good qualities and devoid of all bad qualities. But even without reaching the perfect stage (not yet having developed all good qualities), the devotee at the state of sadhana should also be considered the best. He is better than the previously mentioned devotees because from the beginning he has accepted pure bhakti.”

Krsna will now continue the progression He has begun as He put knowledge (and developing the above qualities) in the perspective of perfected devotional service - that is, service in which one has already developed a personal relationship with Krsna. “My devotees may or may not know exactly what I am, who I am, and how I exist, but if they worship Me with unalloyed love, then I consider them to be the best of devotees.” (SB. 11.11.33)

Pure love for Krsna controls the unlimitedly powerful and independent Lord, capturing Him and stopping Him from taking even one step outside Sri Vrndavana.Krsna is dependent on His devotees’ pure love, dependent on Nanda Maharaja and Mother Yasoda, on His friends, and the gopis. The BBT commentators write: “Although one may develop innumerable saintly qualities, without love of Krsna one will not achieve complete success. One must understand the Personality of Godhead as He is and love Him. Even if one is not capable of analytically understanding the position of God, if one simply loves Krsna, then one is certainly perfect. Many of the residents of Vrndavana had no idea that Krsna is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, nor did they know of Krsna’s potencies or incarnations. They simply loved Krsna with their hearts and souls, and therefore they are considered most perfect.”

*Texts 34-41: The processes of devotional service*

In this eleventh chapter, Krsna’s instructions have taken us up the yoga ladder from karma to jnana and now to bhakti. He has ended His discussioin on the qualities of saints and established the superiority over all others of I hose who have surrendered to Him in devotional service. Krsna has especially glorified those who love Him with full hearts. Thus He has completed His answer to Uddhava’s first question (SB. 11.11.26): What type of person do You consider a true devotee?

In the next eight textsKrsna will answer Uddhava’s second question: What type of devotional service is approved by great devotees as worthy of being offered to Your Lordship? Here, Krsna will enumerate the purifying bhakti practices that bring about detachment from false pride and prestige and attachment to Him.

Sri Krsna says:

One may purify oneself by seeing, touching, worshiping, serving, and offering prayers of glorification and obeisances to My form as the Deity and to My pure devotees. One should also glorify My transcendental qualities and activities, hear with love and faith the narrations of My glories and constantly meditate on Me. One should offer to Me whatever one acquires, and accepting oneself as My eternal servant, one should give oneself completely to Me. One should always discuss My birth and activities and enjoy life by participating in festivals, such as Janmastami, which glorify My pastimes. In My temple, one should also participate in festivals and ceremonies by singing, dancing, playing musical instruments and discussing Me with other Vaisnavas. One should observe all the regularly celebrated annual festivals by attending ceremonies, pilgrimages and making offerings. One should also observe religious vows such as Ekadasi and take initiation by the procedures mentioned in the Vedas, Pancaratra and other, similar literatures. One should faithfully and lovingly support the installation of My Deity, and individually or in cooperation with others one should work for the construction of Krsna conscious temples and cities as well as flower gardens, fruit gardens and special areas to celebrate My pastimes. One should consider oneself to be My humble servant, without duplicity, and thus should help to clean the temple, which is My home. First one should sweep and dust thoroughly, and then one should further cleanse with water and cow dung. Having dried the temple, one should sprinkle scented water and decorate the temple with mandalas. One should thus act just like My servant.

A devotee should never advertise his devotional activities; therefore his service will not be the cause of false pride. One should never use lamps that are offered to Me for other purposes simply because there is need of illumination, and similarly, one should never offer to Me anything that has been offered to or used by others. Whatever is most desired by one within this material world, and whatever is most dear to oneself — one should offer that very thing to Me. Such an offering qualifies one for eternal life. (SB. 11.11.34-41)

*Texts 42—49: Krsna, the all-pervading Lord — worshiping Krsna in the material elements*

Where can one see Krsna and worship Him? In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.11.42, Krsna designates some appropriate places where He can be seen, in the sun, fire, brahmanas, cows, Vaisnavas, the sky, wind, water, the earth, the individual soul, and all living entities.

The BBT purport to this text illumines Krsna’s purpose in speaking this verse: “Unless one understands that Lord Krsna is all-pervading and that everything is resting within the Lord, one’s Krsna consciousness is third class and materialistic— Lord Krsna speaks this verse to clarify His supremacy as the all-pervading Personality of Godhead and to show the path of complete self-realization.”

The BBT’s purport to the next texts adds, “By maintaining steady consciousness of the Lord in His all-pervading feature, one can remain in a worshipful mood twenty-four hours a day. Thus, one will naturally try to engage all material and spiritual elements in the loving service of Lord Krsna.”

So how do we worship the Lord in these manifestations? Krsna answers this question in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.11.43-45:

The sun: Krsna is worshiped through selected Vedic mantras.

Fire: Krsna is worshiped by offering oblations of ghee into the sacrificial fire.

Brahmanas: Krsna is worshiped by respectfully receiving brahmanas as guests, even if they arrive uninvited.

Cows: Krsna is worshiped by offering cows grass, suitable grains, and other paraphernalia for their pleasure and health.

Vaisnavas: Krsna is worshiped by offering Vaisnavas loving friendship and honoring them in all respects.

The sky: Krsna is worshiped through steady meditation within the inner space of the heart.

Air: Krsna is worshiped by knowing that prana is the chief among all elements.

Water: Krsna is worshiped by offering to the Lord water mixed with flowers and tulasi leaves. According to Srila Jiva Gosvami, He is also worshiped by offering water and other suitable items back into water, their source (Bhakti Sandarbha, anuccheda 295).

Earth: Krsna is worshiped by the proper application of confidential seed (bija) mantras.

Living entities: Krsna is worshiped by offering living entities food and other enjoyable substances, being respectful, and maintaining equal vision toward others by seeing the Supersoul in each of them. (Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura adds that without selfish desire, one should offer the same things to oneself as well, understanding that one’s body and atma are the home of the Supersoul.)

Sri Krsna continues: Worship Me personally in these places by using the processes I have just described. “\[M\]editate on My peaceful, transcendental form with four arms holding a conch shell, Sudarsana disc, club, and lotus flower. In this way, one should worship Me with fixed attention.” (SB. 11.11.46)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura states that his comments in this regard are general and need to be applied appropriately. For example, worshipers of Rama or other Deities should use those Deities’ respective mantras to meditate on their Lord’s form in these places.

Conclusion: Krsna consciousness is the goal of both jnana and karma

Krsna’s conclusion is clear: realizing Him and offering Him devotional service is the topmost knowledge. The Lord also previously (SB. 11.10.1-5) instructed Uddhava that taking shelter of Him in devotional service, while accepting Him rather than temporary material pleasure as the supreme goal of life, is also the goal of performing one’s prescribed duties in the varnasrama system. Reiterating this point, Krsna directly says that one should perform Vedic yajnas and pious karmas with one’s attention fixed on Him and only for His pleasure: “One who has executed sacrificial performances and pious works for My satisfaction, and who thus worships Me with fixed attention, obtains unflinching devotional service unto Me.” (SB. 11.11.47)

And such devotional service automatically bestows on one a jnani’s highest attainment: By the excellent quality of his service such a worshiper obtains realized knowledge of Me.” (SB. 11.11.47)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura adds, in Krsna’s voice, “I remember that person who serves with intense sadhana.”

Stopping to summarize before taking His discussion of the Vedic path to its pinnacle, Krsna informs Uddhava that “I am personally the ultimate shelter and way of life for saintly liberated persons, and thus if one does not engage in My loving devotional service, which is made possible by associating with My devotees,then for all practical purposes, one possesses no effective means for escaping from material existence \[prayena bhakti-yogena sat-sangena vinoddhava\].” (SB. 11.11.48)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on this text is concise: There is no way to be delivered from samsara other than by bhakti, which is generally attained by association with devotees. Pure bhakti can only be attained by Vaisnava association; there is no other way to achieve it.”

Krsna concludes chapter 11 by inviting Uddhava to hear secrets still more confidential and mysterious: “My dear Uddhava, O beloved of the Yadu dynasty, because you are My servant, well-wisher, and friend, I shall now speak to you the most confidential knowledge. Please hear as I explain these great mysteries to you.” (SB. 11.11.49)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura expands Krsna’s thought: Sridhara Svami says the Lord will explain that methods like Sankhya and yoga depend on other practices and their results are unpredictable. On the other hand, association with devotees is independent, powerful, and produces results without fail.”

Krsna’s heart opens more fully to Uddhava, like a lotus flower blooming, as He continues to speak about the power of Vaisnava association. Srila Jiva Gosvami explains in the bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 242), that the “most confidential knowledge” Krsna will reveal to Uddhava (SB. 11.12.10-13) is that the vraja-gopikas are His unequaled devotees.

**Chapter 12: Beyond Renunciation and Knowledge**

*Texts 1-7: The power of Vaisnava association*

Krsna has been gradually offering Uddhava a gradation of spiritual truths. That progression will soon reach its summit. He begins this final ascent by revealing in seven texts how to attain the topmost destination of all spiritual journeys, His most confidential, dearest abode.

In the previous chapter (SB. 11.11.25 and 48), the Lord called Vaisnava association “the source of bhakti." Now He eulogizes such association further: “My dear Uddhava, by associating with My pure devotees one can destroy one’s attachment for all objects of material sense gratification. Such purifying association brings Me under the control of My devotee. One may perform the astanga-yoga system, engage in philosophical analysis of the elements of material nature, practice nonviolence and other ordinary principles of piety, chant the Vedas, perform penances, take to the renounced order of life, execute sacrificial performances, and dig wells, plant trees, and perform other public welfare activities, give in charity, carry out severe vows, worship the demigods, chant confidential mantras, visit holy places, or accept major and minor disciplinary injunctions, but even by performing such activities one does not bring Me under his control.” (SB. 11.12.1-2)

The Supreme Personality of Godhead is all-powerful, ever-blissful, fully satisfied, and the cause of all causes. As He depends on no one, and as everything in existence depends on Him, He is the only truly independent being. Nevertheless, He is controlled by His pure devotees’ love for Him. But Krsna says still more: associating with His pure devotees makes one detached from matter and fixed instead in love for Him.

The power of associating with My pure devotees is incomparable, Krsna says in the opening texts of chapter 12. Nothing else compares; nothing else - not practicing astanga-yoga, analyzing the material elements (sankhya-yoga), practicing nonviolence, performing pious acts, studying the Vedas, practicing penances or renunciation or severe vows or doing yajnas, digging wells, planting trees or other acts of public welfare, worshiping the demigods, chanting Vedic mantras, going on pilgrimage, following scriptural rules — can bring Him under control. He is only controlled by love, and love can only be developed by practicing bhakti, which is performed in the association of His devotees.

The BBT purport to these texts offers some perspective on Sri Krsna’s words: “\[T\]hese secondary activities also please Lord Krsna, but to a lesser extent. Specifically, they please the Lord when performed by devotees rather than by ordinary materialistic persons.... In other words, such practices as sacrifice, austerity, and philosophical study may help one become fit for rendering devotional service, and when such activities are performed by devotees aspiring for spiritual advancement, they become somewhat pleasing to the Lord.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura adds: “I am not attained by these methods. But by careful application, association of devotees can control Me even before the appearance of bhakti. That alone can control Me. And what to speak of after bhakti has made its appearance! ... Because yoga and other processes are mixed with some bhakti, they also control Me to a small degree… \[But\] those methods do not control Me as much as does the association of devotees… The association of devotees destroys all material attraction because it controls the Lord.”

In the next four texts (3-6), to demonstrate the power of Vaisnava association Krsna offers more than thirty examples of devotees who attained bhakti through association with His devotees. These examples include the gopis of Vrndavana, Banasura, and the yajha-patnis, and they illustrate that any living entity, even those entangled in the lower modes of nature, will be purified and attain the Lord’s abode through devotee association. The BBT purport notes the special achievements of the gopis and even Banasura to show that a devotee’s surrender conquers the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Like the gopis, some of the thirty listed attained pure love for Krsna. Others simply attained salvation. The BBT purport notes that the wives of the Vedic brahmanas had association with women sent by Lord Krsna to sell flower garlands and betel nuts and heard about the Lord from them.” Thus they too were purified and attained Goloka Vrndavana.

Krsna concludes His glorification of the association of His pure devotees: “The persons I have mentioned did not undergo serious studies of the Vedic literature, nor did they worship great saintly persons, nor did they execute severe vows or austerities. Simply by association with Me and My devotees, they achieved Me.” (SB. 11.12.7)

Practicing the items mentioned in the opening texts of this chapter, such as studying the Vedic literature, the BBT purport to text 7 explains, pleases the Supreme Personality of Godhead only somewhat. But these acts are still “secondary to the essential process of associating with the Supreme Personality of Godhead and His pure devotees. By other processes one may gain the association of the Lord and His devotees, which will actually give the perfection of life.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura states on Krsna’s behalf, “Association with devotees is equivalent to association with Me.” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura adds his emphasis to this apparently simple point in his comment on text 6: “Simply by the influence of Vaisnava association, all one’s incompetence is destroyed and one becomes qualified to attain the service of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.” In his comment on text 7, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura writes, “Without following any other sadhana one can attain the Supreme Lord simply by the influence of devotees.”

*Texts 8-15: The heart of Krsna*

Now Krsna reveals to Uddhava the most secret of secrets - the truth dearest to His heart. Krsna’s words will remind Uddhava of something he experienced earlier:the extreme love of the Vrajavasis for Krsna. Because the Vrajavasis love Krsna to the ultimate degree, they all easily attain Him. This is true whether they are “gopis, cows, unmoving creatures such as the twin arjuna trees, animals, living entities with stunted consciousness such as bushes and thickets, and even snakes such as Kaliya.” Krsna says “all \[these\] achieved the perfection of life by unalloyed love for Me and thus very easily achieved Me \[kevalena hi bhavena gopyo gavah\].” (SB. 11.12.8)

In the Krsna Sandarbha (anuccheda 177), Srila Jiva Gosvami explains more about how some gopis and cows gained the required loving mood (bhavena) to attain Krsna, the Supreme Brahman, by associating with eternally perfected residents of Vrndavana.

Krsna next presents a stark conrrast to the attainment of these Vrajavasis: “Even though one engages with great endeavor in the mystic yoga system, philosophical speculation, charity, vows, penances, ritualistic sacrifices, teaching of Vedic mantras to others, personal study of the Vedas, or the renounced order of life, still one cannot achieve Me.” (SB. 11.12.9) Clearly, it is only by practicing bhakti (and no other process), which is attained by associating with Krsna’s devotees, that one can gain Krsna s association in Goloka Vrndavana.

*Texts 10-13: The most exalted consciousness*

Although the Vrajavasis’ love for Krsna is unparalleled, the vraja-gopikas' love stands supreme in both its focus and its intensity. To Uddhava, His dearest friend, Krsna now expresses something He previously concealed deep in His heart. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments about this sequence of texts (SB. 11.12.10-13) in his commentary on the next two texts, 14-15:“By His unsteadiness He unveils the tears of love for the gopis that although deeply concealed, burn always in His heart. These tears reveal the highest limit of the control the gopis’ bhakthyoga has over Him and the gopis’ superexcellent state of Krsna consciousness, which cannot rest concealed within them.”

Even when Krsna apparently left Vrndavana and the gopis were separated from Him, they remained fully attached to Him as they attained higher and higher stages of love for the Supreme Personality of Godhead. They found no substitute source of happiness. Krsna declares: The residents of Vrndavana, headed by the gopis, were always completely attached to Me with deepest love. Therefore, when My uncle Akrura brought My brother Balarama and Me to the city of Mathura, the residents of Vrndavana suffered extreme mental distress because of separation from Me and could not find any other source of happiness.” (SB. 11.12.10)

Srila Jiva Gosvami writes that Krsna was actually associating with the gopis again by the time He spoke these words to Uddhava: “Filled with intense pain from separation because of deep love, they did not see (during those times) any person other than Me, such as their own sakhis, as a source of happiness. This means that now they see happiness as they are no longer separated from Me. All the nights being without Me were like a kalpa, but now those nights are not so. There is no separation now.” (Krsna Sandarbha, anuccheda 175)

The love of the gopis is so extreme that they experience the many nights i hey spend with Krsna as if they last a fraction of a moment, and one night even one moment - separate from Him as intolerable — a trillion years. Krsna describes the quality of their love in text 11: Dear Uddhava, all of those nights that the gopis spent with Me, their most dearly beloved, in the land of Vrndavana seemed to them to pass in less than a moment. Bereft of My association, however, the gopis felt that those same nights dragged on forever, as if each night were equal to a day of Brahma.” (SB. 11.12.11)

Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu expressed this exact mood of the gopis’ experience of separation from Krsna:

*yugayitarh nimesena*

*caksusa pravrsayitam*

*sunyayitarh jagat sarvam*

*govinda-virahena me*

“My Lord Govinda, because of separation from You, I consider even a moment a great millennium. Tears flow from My eyes like torrents of rain, and I see the entire world as void.” (Caitanya-caritamrta, Antya 20.39)

Srila Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami expands on Mahaprabhu’s transcendentally intense sentiments, which were actually those of Srimati Radharani, despite that among his readers, there would be those with material consciousness who would not be able to penetrate their meaning: “In My agitation, a day never ends, for every moment seems like a millennium. Pouring incessant tears, My eyes are like clouds in the rainy season. The three worlds have become void because of separation from Govinda. I feel as if I were burning alive in a slow fire. Lord Krsna has become indifferent to Me just to test My love, and My friends say, ‘Better to disregard Him.’” (Caitanya-caritamrta, Antya 20.40-42)

Krsna then compares the consciousness of the gopis to that of great yogis absorbed in samadhi, and to rivers that merge with the ocean. In what sense does the consciousness of His beloved gopis remind Him of entranced yogis? In the highest stage of trance, a yogi remains unaware of the names and forms of this world, his own body, and his past and future lives. Great yogis, Krsna says, “merge into self- realization, like rivers merging into the ocean, and are thus not aware of material names and forms.” Like them, “the gopis of Vrndavana were so completely attached to Me within their minds that they could not think of their own bodies, or of this world, or of their future lives. Their entire consciousness was simply hound up in Me.” (SB. 11.12.12)

In the Bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 278), Srila Jiva Gosvami differentiates the various levels of meditation on the Supreme Lord’s name, form, qualities, and pastimes according to their depth of absorption. He also recommends proceeding in meditation by following that order - meditating first on the Supreme Lord’s name, then His form, then His qualities, and then His pastimes. He calls the first stage smaranam, or occasional remembrance of the Supreme Lord “in one way or another.” The second stage is dharana, a more focused concentration on the Lord. The third is dhyana, where one specifically and consciously meditates on the Lord’s name, form, qualities, and/or pastimes. The fourth is called dhruvanusmrti, where one’s meditation on the Lord becomes a constant flow of nectar. The fifth and final stage is samadhi, or trance, where the Lord alone is present in one’s thoughts, and one is not even aware of oneself.

Clearly, the vraja-gopikas' meditation on Krsna is akin to the samadhi of the greatest yogis. Indeed, the extreme depth of their meditation on Krsna, the Absolute Truth, proves that they are the topmost yogis.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on this twelfth text of the chapter further explains Krsna’s comparison: “\[W\]hen one experiences intense emotions, one forgets everything else, although one is not in a state of illusion. That is shown in this verse. The minds of the gopis were bound to constant association with Krsna… By His constant association He bound up the gopis with great strength.” By the word bound Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura means the paralysis caused by Krsna’s colorful pastimes. “(This paralysis) is the strong rope of intimate association, which binds the functions of the gopis’ minds to become like desire-cows to fulfill Krsna’s wishes. The gopis even lost awareness of their own bodies. While going to the rasa dance they knew not where they were nor from where they had come. They were aware of neither this world nor the next... They were like sages in samadhi. While experiencing Brahman, a sage remembers nothing. However the gopis experienced Krsna, not Brahman. Thus the example is useful in showing the forgetfulness of the gopis, hut is not meant to indicate that the yogis’ attainments and those of the gopis are equal. A vast difference exists between the gopis’ prema and the sages’ nirvana, since the gopis love Krsna with a feeling of possessiveness and the sages love Him without that feeling.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura next explains Krsna’s comparison of the gopis’ consciousness to rivers entering the ocean. He also explains the glory of the gopis’ mamata, or sense of possessiveness, in relation to Krsna: “For a woman, seeing her husband or sons, even if they possess no good qualities, gives her more happiness than seeing the moon, whose presence awards bliss and destroys suffering. Why? Because she has a greater feeling of possessiveness for her husband and sons than she does for the moon. Then what to speak of the bliss of one who is experiencing an unlimited sense of possessiveness toward Krsna, the Supreme Brahman, who is decorated with all good qualities and by His very nature awards unending bliss? Such possessiveness toward Krsna causes the greatest nectar for devotees.

“‘The bliss of Brahman realization accumulated by samadhi lasting for half of Brahma’s life cannot compare to one drop of the ocean of the happiness of bhakti.’ (Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 1.1.38) Brahman is attached to the devotees and is under their control, but Brahman is not attached to the sages and so is not under their control. The comparison of the gopis to rivers is not meant to illustrate the absolute nondifference of the gopis and Brahman. Instead, it illustrates the state of relishing rasa: just as rivers entering an ocean do not know their own names or forms, the gopis, while relishing rasa, lose awareness of their names and forms.”

Srila Jiva Gosvami comments on the gopis’ mood, as Krsna describes it in this text 12, in the Krsna Sandarbha (anuccheda 176): “Not distinguishing between the prakata (manifest) and aprakata (unmanifest) pastimes, and attaining the aprakata pastimes, the gopis remained in this world as names and forms only \[since their minds were with Krsna\] ... They remained in a state of mahabhava, which was difficult for them to bear, and which had become manifested due to extreme longing due to separation. Sometimes, when I came to see them, the gopis, having attained My association, were extremely happy. Thus their minds were bound again by that union, and they didn’t know whether the pastimes were aprakata or prakata.”
