After describing that the intensity of the gopis’ focus on Krsna caused them to forget all else, Krsna next describes what they attained as well as the central cause of their success: “All those hundreds of thousands of gopis, understanding Me to be their most charming lover and ardently desiring Me in that way, were unaware of My actual position. Yet by intimately associating with Me, the gopis attained Me, the Supreme Absolute Truth.” (SB. 11.12.13)

The intensity of the gopis' love for Krsna covered their knowledge of His supreme position. Think of rite mother of the Prime Minister worrying that her son may not have time to eat properly. Both gopis and mother have a sweet intimacy in their respective relationships that overrides their sense of the beloved’s power. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments: “The gopis remained unaware of My constitutional potencies that possess \[unlimited\] power, for they experienced only My great sweetness.”

Again, Srila Jiva Gosvami comments in the Krsna Sandarbha (anuccheda 177), this time explaining the reason for the gopis’ attainment: In that condition \[of having attained the Supreme Brahman, Bhagavan\], others - hundreds of thousands of gopis in Gokula - attained Krsna by association with His eternal consorts.... because that association quickly generates a similar bhava. It was said previously ‘by intense bhava the gopis and cows attained Him.’ ... Thus they attained Me.”

With these four texts (10—13), Krsna ends His description of the gopis and their unique, all-consuming love for Him. The Supreme Lord will now slowly draw this topic to a close by giving Uddhava a general instruction in text 14: “Therefore, My dear Uddhava, abandon the Vedic mantras as well as the procedures of supplementary Vedic literatures and their positive and negative injunctions. Disregard that which has been heard and that which is to be heard.” (SB. 11.12.14)

The Vedas prescribe occupational duties (dharma) for gradually elevating those who practice varnasrama. The actual purpose of these duties has been noted by Srila Suta Gosvami in Srimad-Bhagavatam 1.2.8, where he states, notpadayed yadi ratim srama eva hi kevalam: “They are only so much useless labor if they do not provoke attraction for the message of the Personality of Godhead.” Krsna herein tells Uddhava to cast off these prescriptions and their inevitable gradual progression in order to immediately capture the essence of the Vedas.“Simply take shelter of Me alone, for I am the Supreme Personality of Godhead, situated within the heart of all conditioned souls. Take shelter of Me wholeheartedly, and by My grace be free from fear in all circumstances.” (SB. 11.12.15)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti’s Thakura’s comment on text 15 tells us that Krsna praised the pure bhakti-yoga living in the hearts of the gopis anti others as being very rare. The Lord wished to inspire Uddhava with that same degree of pure bhakti, and therefore instructed Uddhava to give up all rules and prohibitions, prescribed and forbidden acts.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura then asks whether Krsna wants Uddhava to take sarmyasa. Krsna says no. Rather, He wants Uddhava to give up both the activities prescribed for sannyasis (renunciation and the cultivation of jnana) and householders (regulated enjoyment and karma). Nor does Krsna want Uddhava to hanker to hear about dharma later; rather, He wants Uddhava to forget everything he’s already heard about dharma. Krsna is saying, “If you fear sin and the continuation of your samsara because you are neglecting karma and jnana, I am here to deliver you from these two fears.”

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.12.14-15 summarizes: “Sri Uddhava inquired from Lord Krsna about the symptoms of saintly persons and liberated souls, and the Lord has replied in terms of different levels of spiritual advancement... Lord Krsna also mentioned that He is captured by His loving devotees and even by those who sincerely associate with His loving devotees. Among all the devotees, the gopis of Vrndavana were described by the Lord as having achieved such a rare state of pure devotional service that Lord Krsna personally feels constantly indebted to them... The Lord has elaborately explained to Uddhava the system of philosophical analysis of the material world, and now He clearly concludes that it is useless for Uddhava to waste time in fruitive activities or mental speculation. Actually, Lord Krsna is hinting that Uddhava should assimilate the example of the gopis and try to advance further in Krsna consciousness by following in the footsteps of the cowherd damsels of Vraja.”

Krsna’s sending Uddhava to Vraja as His messenger (SB. 10.46-47) had in fact already fulfilled the Lord’s desire for Uddhava. In Vraja, Uddhava had witnessed with awe the brilliant intensity of the love of the Vrajavasis, especially the love of the gopis. Having seen the quality of Vraja-bhakti, he had felt humblerand more focused on his own desire to love Krsna. During each of the many daysin his Vrndavana stay, Uddhava praised, honored, and encouraged the gopis with the following song:“Oh, let me be fortunate enough to be one of the bushes, creepers, or herbs in Vrndavana, because the gopis trample them and bless them with the dust of their lotus feet.” (SB. 10.47.61)

*Texts 16-24: Uddhava’s confusion and Krsna’s reply*

*Text 16: Uddhava’s question*

In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.7.16, Uddhava asked Krsna to recommend a specific course for him to follow, but now having heard many levels of instruction from Krsna, Uddhava still doesn’t feel be understands his path. So he responds to Krsna’s intimate glorification of the vraja gopikas with words that imply that he needs to hear more: “O Lord of all masters of mystic power, I have heard Your words, but the doubt in my heart does not go away; thus my mind is bewildered.” (SB. 11.12.16)

The BBT purport to this text clarifies the tone of Uddhava’s inquiry, which is born of his intimate friendship with Sri Krsna:“According to Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, Uddhava is stating here, ‘My dear friend Krsna, first You recommended that I perform worldly activities within the varnasrama system, and then You advised that I reject such activities and take to the path of philosophical research. Now rejecting the path of jnana, You recommend that I simply surrender unto You in bhakti-yoga. If I accept Your decision, in the future You may again go back to Your original point and recommend worldly activities.”’

Srila Jiva Gosvami explains more about Uddhava’s doubt: “Although hearing and understanding Your words, I still have doubts. I cannot understand what you said because Your statements \[describing the love of the gopis\], such as the ones You made in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.12.10, bewilder my mind. Wondering, ‘Alas, how will they meet You?’ \[attaining Krsna’s unmanifest (aprakata) pastimes and not being able to distinguish those pastimes from His manifest (prakata) pastimes\], I cannot maintain my composure.” (Krsna Sandarbha, anuccheda 178)

*Texts 17-24: Krsna responds to Uddhava’s confusion Context for Krsna’s reply*

Krsna replies to Uddhava in eight texts - Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.12.17 through 24. The BBT purport to text 17 gives Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s explanation of Krsna’s reply: “‘My dear Uddhava, when I told you that analytic knowledge is to be practiced, pious duties are to be performed, devotional service is obligatory, yoga procedures must be observed, austerities are to be executed, etc., I was instructing all living entities, using you as My immediate audience. That which I have spoken, am speaking now, and will speak in the future should be understood as guidance for all living entities in different situations.

How could you possibly think that you were meant to practice all the different Vedic processes? I accept you as you are now, My pure devotee. You are not supposed to execute all these processes.’ Thus according to Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, the Lord, with lighthearted and encouraging words, reveals to Uddhava the deep purpose behind the variety of Vedic procedures.”

In these texts, Krsna explains to Uddhava His specific relationship with the Vedas, His relationship with everything a conditioned soul perceives, His relationship with the universe, and His relationship with the innumerable bodies a soul accepts during its long-term material existence. Finally, Krsna describes His relationship with the Vedic opus.

*Texts 17-18: Krsna speaks of His relationship to the Vedas*

It is I who gives life to all jivas. I am situated in the heart with the life air, and I can be perceived in My subtle form in the heart by one’s mind, and it is I who am manifest as the various sounds of the Vedas.

*Texts 19-20: Krsna speaks of His relationship with everything conditioned souls perceive in matter*

The working senses, the knowledge-acquiring senses, the mind, intelligence, and false ego, subtle pradhana, the three modes of nature - “all these should be understood as My materially manifest form.” (SB. 11.12.19) Everything in the cosmos in its unlimited variety has its source in Me.”

*Texts 21-23: Krsna speaks about the universe and the countless bodies the conditioned souls* *have accepted since beginningless time; Krsna speaks about the purpose of the Vedic literature*

The entire universe rests on My potencies and exists within Me. The succession of bodies that have sustained the jiva’s material existence is like a tree: “\[A\]s a tree first blossoms and then produces fruit, similarly the tree of material existence, one’s material body, produces the various results of material existence.” (SB. 11.12.21) One who understands that this tree in its variety of forms is a manifestation of the potency of the one Supreme Lord actually knows the meaning of the entirety of the Vedic literature.

*Text 24: Krsna concludes*

“With steady intelligence you should develop unalloyed devotional service by careful worship of the spiritual master, and with the sharpened ax of transcendental knowledge you should cut off the subtle material covering of the soul. Upon realizing the Supreme Personality of Godhead, you should then give up that ax of analytic knowledge.” (SB. 11.12.24)

Having earlier opened His heart to Uddhava and revealed the unlimitedly deep devotion through which the Vrajavasis keep Him, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, under their control, Krsna, who is extremely grave, has now again carefully hidden His secret behind a veil of philosophy. He has returned to speaking of His position, the purpose of the Vedas, and how to approach Him through detachment and the analytic study of material existence. As He indicated earlier,these instructions are not for Uddhava; they are meant to gather all hearers of the Bhagavatam, regardless of inclination or advancement, to this great work’s ultimate conclusion.

The BBT purport to SB. 11.12.24 announces that conclusion: “Lord Krsna has clearly explained in this chapter that the cowherd damsels of Vrndavana were not interested in an analytical approach to life. They simply loved Lord Krsna and could not think of anything else. Lord Gaitanya Mahaprabhu taught that all His devotees should follow in the footsteps of the cowherd damsels of Vraja in order to develop the highest intensity of selfless love of Godhead. Lord Krsna has elaborately analyzed the nature of the material world so that the conditioned souls, who are trying to enjoy it, can cut down the tree of material existence with this knowledge.”

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.12.18 notes one audience Krsna wishes to address. He will later send Uddhava to carry His Uddhava-gita to these persons (SB. 11.29.41—44): “By My mercy, I am now giving these methods to you, the most qualified person, who is equal to Me. The sages in Badarikasrama will be success- bill having received this knowledge from you.”

**Chapter 13: The Hamsa-avatara Answers the Questions of the Sons of Brahma**

*Texts 1-7: Transcending the modes of nature by using the modes of nature*

**How to gain knowledge**

Comparing the unending cycle of repeated births and deaths to a great lice, Sii Lisna advised Uddhava to cut the soul free from its subtle material coverings with the sharp ax of transcendental knowledge. In the next seven texts, He will teach Uddhava how to do this.

“The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: The three modes of material nature, namely goodness, passion, and ignorance, pertain to material intelligence and not to the spirit soul. By development of material goodness one can conquer the modes of passion and ignorance, and by cultivation of transcendental goodness one may free oneself even from material goodness.” (SB. 11.13.1)

Krsna tells Uddhava that to conquer the lower modes of passion and ignorance, one should cultivate goodness. We will want to liberate ourselves from mundane goodness, but we should still cultivate this higher mode because goodness results in the kind of knowledge that allows us to wield the ax of detachment and cut off material existence.By virtue of the clear vision knowledge in the mode of goodness confers, goodness becomes a steppingstone to transcendence.

Srila Prabhupada made this same point in a March 1976 lecture on Srimad-Bhagavatam 7.9.39: “So first of all we have to try to come to the platform of goodness. There are three platforms: tamo-guna, rajo-guna, and sattva-guna. So immediately we cannot come to the pure guna, suddha-sattva. Sattvam visuddham vasudeva-sabditam, vasudeva platform… Just like Vasudeva is the father of Krsna, so there is vasudeva platform also. Unless one comes to the vasudeva platform, there is no question of Krsna, because Vasudeva can beget Krsna, or Vasudeva. Vasudevah sarvam iti. So actually we have to come to the platform of vasudeva, vasudeva-sabditam, and that is suddha-sattva. But it is not immediately possible. Therefore gradually, from the platform of tamo-guna and rajo-guna, we have to come to the sattva-guna.”

Krsna continues: “When the living entity becomes strongly situated in the mode of goodness, then religious principles, characterized by devotional service to Me, become prominent. One can strengthen the mode of goodness by cultivation of those things that are already situated in goodness, and thus religious principles arise. Religious principles, strengthened by the mode of goodness, destroy the influence of passion and ignorance. When passion and ignorance are overcome, their original cause, irreligion, is quickly vanquished.” (SB. 11.13.2-3)

What can one do to increase the mode of goodness in one’s life? Krsna says: “According to the quality of religious scriptures, water, one’s association with one’s children or with people in general, the particular place, the time, activities, birth, meditation, chanting of mantras, and purificatory rituals, the modes of nature become differently prominent.” (SB. 11.13.4) So dealing with these items in the mode of goodness causes goodness to arise in one’s consciousness. Therefore, Krsna says, sages have always “praised and recommended those in the mode of goodness, criticized and rejected those in the mode of ignorance, and shown indifference to those in the mode of passion.” (SB. 11.13.5) After all, goodness gives rise to jnana and is therefore required until we realize ourselves as eternal souls, thereby ending our identification with the body.

One may ask how it is possible for the mode of goodness to carry one to transcendence, since it is still a mundane mode. Aren’t the choices one makes in the mode of goodness still arising from one’s material intelligence?

Krsna answers this doubt with an example: Wind may cause bamboo stalks in a forest to rub together and, with the friction generated between the stalks, ignite a fire that consumes the source of its birth, the bamboo forest. The fire will automatically be extinguished when it runs out of fuel. Similarly, the modes of nature cause the gross and subtle bodies that encase a soul. When both subtle and gross bodies are used to cultivate goodness and knowledge, like the fire destroying the bamboo that caused it, they destroy the cause of their own birth, the actions of the modes of nature (SB. 11.13.6-7).

*Text 8: Uddhava inquires further*

Uddhava asks a probing question about the value of knowledge. He has noted that intellectually knowing what is correct does not guarantee that one will act on that knowledge: “My dear Krsna, generally human beings know that material life brings great future unhappiness, and still they try to enjoy material life. My dear Lord, how can one in knowledge act just like a dog, an ass, or a goat?” (SB. 11.13.8)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura expands on Uddhava’s examples of animals that don’t learn from what they already know: a dog, i bough beaten, hankers for a man’s leftover food; a donkey, though kicked again and again, attempts to enjoy a female donkey; and a goat, although having seen other goats slaughtered and recognizing that it too is about to be killed, goes on enjoying eating the grass.

*Texts 9-14: Coming under the control of may a and the process of freedom*

By nature, every soul is a servant of Krsna (Caitanya-caritamrta, Madhya 20.108), but some souls choose to turn their backs on Krsna, sending them to Maya’s realm (Caitanya-caritamrta, Madhya 20.117). But each soul is eternally and irrevocably Krsna’s servant, so to survive in illusion it must cover its identity. It establishes a false ego (ahankara), a made-up sense of existence separate from Krsna. Essentially, this false identity becomes the soul’s imprisonment in the material creation. When the creation unfolds, false ego combines with each of the three modes of material nature (goodness, passion, and ignorance). When false ego combines with goodness, the mind is created. Mind wraps around the false ego, still further covering the soul (SB. 3.26.27). Material nature then generates a still grosser covering for the already encased soul: a material body for it to inhabit. This body is built around whatever desires fill the mind (SB. 3.26.23-24) and so is unique to each soul.

Uddhava asked Krsna why we act foolishly even though we have knowledge. Krsna explains in texts 9 and 10 how we act against our own best interest: “My dear Uddhava, a person bereft of intelligence first falsely identifies himself with the material body and mind \[caused by ahankara, or false ego\], and when such false knowledge arises within one’s consciousness, material passion, the cause of great suffering, pervades the mind, which by nature is situated in goodness.” (SB. 11.13.9)

According to Bhagavad-gita 14-7 identifying with the body forces the mind from its natural resting place in goodness and fills it with material desires - a symptom of the mode of passion. “Then the mind, contaminated by passion, becomes absorbed in making and changing his plans for material advancement.” (SB. 11.13.10)

Bhagavad-gita 14.9 tells us that the symptoms of the mode of passion are unlimited desires, all sorts of plan-making, and endless activities meant to fulfill our desires. “Thus, by constantly thinking of the modes of material nature, a foolish person is afflicted with unbearable material desires.” (SB. 11.13.10) What does one achieve from all this? The Bhagavad-gita (2.62 and 14.6) tells us that we achieve misery, not happiness, from both our contemplation of material desires and our attempts to fulfill them.

In his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.13.10, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura characterizes the mind in passion: “The mind first decides ‘This must be enjoyed.’ Then it decides more emphatically, ‘I really must enjoy this.’ Desire that is difficult to suppress arises from absorption in an object’s qualities. ‘Oh! What a beautiful form it has! What good character!”’

The BBT purport adds: “The mind is created from the mode of goodness, as described in Sankhya philosophy, and the natural, peaceful situation of the mind is pure love of Krsna, in which there is no mental disturbance, disappointment, or confusion. Artificially, the mind is dragged down to a lower platform in passion or ignorance, and thus one is never satisfied.”

Next, Krsna distills the above process into a powerful principle that answers Uddhava’s question about why despite having knowledge someone acts against his or her self-interest: “One who does not control the material senses comes under the control of material desires and is thus bewildered by the strong waves of the mode of passion. Such a person executes material activities, although clearly seeing that the result will be future unhappiness.” (SB. 11.13.11)

The Lord now offers a cure: “Although the intelligence of a learned person may be bewildered by the modes of passion and ignorance, he should again carefully \[atandritah\] bring the mind under control. By clearly seeing the contamination of the modes of nature, he does not become attached.” (SB. 11.13.12)

Maintaining a conscious distance between themselves and their material thoughts, learned persons recognize danger and respond by evoking a sense of detachment within themselves as they carefully bring their mind under control. In text 12, Krsna specifically uses the word atandritah to indicate that this is done “carefully” or “alertly.”

How do the “careful” and “alert” act? Krsna explains: “A person should be attentive and grave and never lazy or morose \[anirvinnah\]. Mastering the yoga procedures of breathing and sitting properly, one should practice fixing the mind on Me at dawn, noon, and sunset, and thus gradually the mind should be completely absorbed in Me.” (SB. 11.13.13)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura adds: “The word atandritah from the previous verse is now explained. In what should the mind be engaged.? In Me. If the mind is not under control, one should not give un one’s efforts to coni ml it.”

In the next text Krsna presents the essence of purification and attainment: “The actual yoga system as taught by My devotees, headed by Sanaka-kumara, is simply this: Having withdrawn the mind from all other objects, one should directly and appropriately absorb it in Me.” (SB. 11.13.14)

Texts 15-21: Uddhava’s question leads to two questions from the Four Kumar as

Krsna’s concise description of yoga intrigues Uddhava, who asks Krsna to speak about the teachings of Sanaka-kumara. Krsna then tells Uddhava of the pastime in which the Four Kumaras - Sanaka, Sananda, Sanatana, and Sanat-kumara - asked their father a question.

The Four Kumaras were the first children born to Brahma at the dawn of creation. All four took birth from his mind. Desiring to remain brahmacaris, they refused their father’s order to produce progeny.At first, they roamed the universe as powerful impersonalist sages, but later they became attracted to the fragrance of the tulasi leaves decorating Lord Vaikuntha-natha’s lotus feet. Overwhelmed by that fragrance and His beauty, they became devotees.

These four ever-youthful sages asked Brahma how to perform yoga and about yoga’s supreme goal. Their question was both practical and difficult to answer: “O Lord, people’s minds are naturally attracted to material sense objects, and similarly the sense objects in the form of desire enter within the mind. Therefore, how can a person who desires liberation, who desires to cross over activities of sense gratification, destroy this mutual relationship between the sense objects and the mind? Please explain this to us.” (SB. 11.13.17)

In other words, how do we separate the mind from its sense objects? The two seem inseparably linked. Is it possible for there to exist a mind free of form, taste, touch, smell, and sound? The mind is under the control of the material modes. When passion is dominant in the mind especially, an object that we have seen advertised may enter the mind and become fixed there, where it proceeds to cloud our vision. Although we think that we see reality objectively, we are full of biases based on our preconceived concepts or the concepts that arise from our response to the raw data we perceive with our senses. If this were not true, then why would there he different reports from eyewitnesses at a car crash? Do devotees and cattle ranchers see the same thing when they look at a cow? Is our perception affected by love or hate or even how someone looks at us? Does the love or hate of an object of our perception actually affect or change us in some way? Which view of a chair leg is real? My view when I see it from a distance of a meter? The view seen through a microscope that reveals materials from which the chair leg is composed? The leg seen through an electron microscope? The termite’s view? Where does the mind end and the actual object - the objective object - begin?

This is a difficult question to answer, and the Four Kumaras ask it of their father, guru, and great Vedic authority, Lord Brahma. This question is important to them because their primary practice is meditation. It is important that they know how to cleave their minds from the myriad sense objects that plague them, and they expect that after they learn the technique, they will be able to peacefully meditate on the Absolute Truth.

But clearly this question is relevant to all devotees. Yet a bhakta’s situation in this regard is far more secure than that of a jnani. Bhaktas see the world as Krsna’s, as meant for His service. Therefore their senses are also meant to be used in Krsna’s service. The devotees’ senses must be engaged, because engaging the senses in Krsna’s service is the definition of bhakti (Caitanya-caritamrta, Madhya 19.170).

A jnani, on the other hand, sees sense objects as maya, illusion, something to be feared, because sense objects draw the mind away from its one-pointed focus. A jnani s senses should never contact sense objects, because a jnani’s path requires full renunciation. How difficult it is, then, to be a contemplative, meditative, and renounced jnani or sankhya-yogi when sense objects are continuously invading the mind. We can see how serious a problem this is, because it is not neophyte meditators who are asking the question, but the practice’s greatest adepts.

Knowledge springs from the mode of goodness, and despite the I act that the Four Kumaras embody both goodness and knowledge,they were unable to answer this question and therefore deferred to i heir father, Brahma, who contemplated their question deeply, hut was also unable to reply, since he found himself attached to the activities of creation (passion) and identified himself as “the creator.” Thus he realized-that he too had not been successful in separating his mind from the objects of his senses.

Sri Krsna continues: “Lord Brahma desired to attain the answer to the question that was puzzling him, and thus he fixed his mind on Me, the Supreme Lord. At that time, in My form of Hamsa, I became visible to Lord Brahma.” (SB. 11.13.19)

The BBT purport presents the Lord’s incarnation as the most beautiful swan: “Hamsa means ‘swan,’ and the specific ability of the swan is to separate a mixture of milk and water, extracting the rich, milky portion. Similarly, Lord Krsna appeared as Hamsa, or the swan, in order to separate the pure consciousness of Lord Brahma from the modes of material nature.”

Brahma and his four exalted sons immediately came forward and worshiped the Hamsa-avatara. Eager to understand the yoga system, the Four Kumaras humbly placed Brahma before them and innocently asked, Ko bhavan!” (“Who are You?”).

*Texts 22-24: The Hamsa-avatara clears up misconceptions about the Absolute Truth*

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.13.22 considers the first three texts the Hamsa-avatara speaks as responses to the possible misconceptions embedded in the question “Ko bhavan!” (“Who are You?”): “In asking ‘Who are You?’ are you thinking I am a jiva! Or do you think I am a material body? Or do you think I am the Supreme Lord?’ Hamsa first dismisses the idea that He is a jiva.”

Text 22 states: “My dear brahmanas, if, when asking Me who I am, you believe that I am also a jiva soul and that there is no ultimate difference between us - since all souls are ultimately one without individuality - then how is your question possible or appropriate? Ultimately, what is the real situation or resting place both of yourselves and of Me?”

In other words, the Hamsa-avatara considers the “ko bhavan?” question absurd if it’s asked from the misconception of impersonalism. “If I am a jiva and you are a jiva and we are ultimately one, what’s the meaning of your question? Why ask Me who I am? You could just as easily have asked yourself!”

The Hamsa-avatara’s next words are aimed at dismantling the misconception that the body is the self: “If by asking Me ‘Who are You?’ you were referring to the material body, then I must point out that all material bodies are constituted of five elements, namely earth, water, fire, air, and ether. Thus, you should have asked, “Who are you five?” If you consider that all material bodies are ultimately one, being constituted essentially of the same elements, then your question is still meaningless, since there would be no deep purpose in distinguishing one body from another. Thus, it appears that in asking My identity, you are merely speaking words, without any real meaning or purpose.” (SB. 11.13.23)

In defense of a question they see as innocent, were the Four Kumaras to respond, “You addressed us as vipras, brahmanas \[in text 22\], so were You not also referring to us in relation to our material bodies? If so, then what is our fault in asking You this question?”

The BBT purport to text 23 quotes Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, who replies sharply on behalf of the Hamsa-avatara: “The Lord states, ‘My addressing you as brahmanas is merely an exhibition of words if we are ultimately not different. I merely reciprocated with how you approached Me. Therefore, if we are ultimately one, neither My statement nor your question has any real meaning. I can conclude, therefore, by your question to Me, that you are actually ajnana, not very intelligent. So why are you asking after ultimate knowledge? Aren’t you embarrassed?”’

In text 24 the Lord considers the question “ko bhavdn ?” inappropriate even if addressed to Him with the understanding that He is the Supreme Lord: “Within this world, whatever is perceived by the mind, speech, eyes, or other senses is Me alone and nothing besides Me. All of you please understand this by a straightforward analysis of the facts.”

This third response means that nothing is ultimately separate from the Supreme Personality of Godhead.Since He is both the Kumaras’ mind and other senses, as well as their sense objects, what isn’t Him? In this way, the Lord shows both His immanence and His transcendence. That conception that nothing in existence is separate from the Lord will especially prove important when the Hamsa-avatara begins to actually answer the Kumaras’ deep query.

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.23 gives readers access to Srila Madhvacarya’s explanation, which “points out in this regard that the question of the sages was not appropriate, since they bad already seen their father, Lord Brahma, worshiping the lotus feet of Lord Hamsa. Since their spiritual master and father was worshiping Lard I lamsa, (bey should have immediately understood the Lord’s position, and their question is thus meaningless.”

The same purport also notes: “The Lord is testing the intelligence of the sages by pointing out various contradictions in their questions— We can clearly see that the Lord is paving the way for a deep discussion of spiritual knowledge.”

*Texts 25-26: The Hamsa-avatara’s preliminary addresses to the difficult question posed by the Kumaras*

In his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.13.25, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura has the Four Kumaras humbly restate their origb nal question: “Our dear Lord, if it is indeed true that we are unintelligent, still Your Lordship has stated that You are actually everything because everything is the expansion of Your potency. Therefore, You are also the mind and the sense objects, which are the subject matter of our question. The material sense objects always enter into the functions of the mind, and similarly, the mind always enters into the material sense objects. Thus it is proper that we inquire from Your Lordship how the mind and sense objects can be separated from each other. Please be merciful and give us the answer.”

Hamsa-avatara begins His reply in texts 25 and 26: Yes, the mind tends to enter into the material sense objects, and the sense objects tend to enter into the mind - He agrees with the basic tenet of the question. He continues: But both mind and sense objects are external designations that cover the soul, which is My part and parcel; the mind, the senses, the sense objects, and the jivas are all My energy.

In the BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.13.25, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura expands the meaning of the Lord’s statement: “My dear sons, it is a fact that the mind enters into the material sense objects and the sense objects into the mind… Since it is the natural

function of the material mind and sense objects to mutually interact, how can you possibly prevent such a mutual attraction? Since both the material mind and sense objects are the cause of anarthas and therefore useless, both should be completely given up. Automatically, then, you will be free from all material duality.”

An impersonalist accepts these instructions by the Hamsa-avatara and attempts to stop the troublesome mind from functioning. Practically, this means trying to strip the mind of all content - for example, all thoughts, including any thoughts about sense objects. But this is not possible, because il is the natural function of the mind to interact with sense objects. And again, not only are the sense objects “in the mind,” the mind is also in the sense objects, affecting them. This is the crux of the Kumaras’ question: “How can they be separated?”

So the Hamsa-avatara continues: A person who has achieved Me and knows himself as nondifferent from Me \[mat-rupah\] realizes that constant sense gratification causes the mind and sense objects to mutually enter within each other. “Having understood My transcendental nature, he gives up both the material mind and its objects.” (SB. 11.13.26)

No longer seeing the mind or sense objects as instruments for pleasure, intelligent persons stop meditating on or interacting with them as if they were meant for their enjoyment. “Srila Sridhara Svami points out that the symptom of the material mind is the tendency to consider oneself to be the ultimate doer and enjoyer.” (SB. 11.13.25, purport) Acting on sense gratification, rather than increasing pleasure compounds the problem by causing the mind and sense objects to become inextricably interwoven.

In his comment on text 26, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura describes the process the Hamsa-avatara recommends to the Four Kumaras - a recommendation that will carry a jndnl to the path of devotion: “However, it is not necessary for jnanis to endure such difficulty in separating the mind from the sense objects. A jnani can abandon them both by realizing he is nondifferent from Me, being of My nature. But the devotee, fixed on serving Me as his highest goal, becomes absorbed in My form, qualities, pastimes, and rasa, and so the sense objects withdraw naturally from his mind. It is then not difficult to separate the sense objects from the mind. But jnanis do not desire to absorb their minds in Me.”

Devotees conceive of the problem of the troublesome mind and its interaction with sense objects differently than do jnanis. Rather than struggling to make the mind stop all of its actions, devotees try to renounce the kinds of false self-conceptions that cause their illusioned sense of independence and separateness from Krsna. Because devotees cultivate an attitude of devotion, they naturally want to use both mind and sense objects for Krsna’s pleasure, so the impossible task of forcing the mind and sense objects apart becomes the easier task of absorbing the mind in thoughts of Krsna, the all-attractive source and therefore unit ing principle behind both mind and sense objects. For a true devotee, this mental absorption is effortless and natural; sadhakas who are serious about attaining bhakti must try to raise their consciousness to this platform through appropriate, purifying practices - and specifically, by hearing about Krsna.

In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.13.26, the Hamsa-avatara uses the phrase mat-rupah to direct the consciousness toward the Lord. The BBT pun port explains: “The word mad-rupah in this verse indicates absorption of the mind in the form, qualities, pastimes, and associates of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Immersed in such ecstatic meditation, one should render devotional service to the Lord, and this will automatically drive away the influence of sense gratification.” Renouncing false ego and accepting that one’s true ego identity is as a devoted servant of Krsna, the materialistic, selfish, self-indulgent mind changes and is illumined by surrender and devotion.

*Texts 27-30: The Lord as the fourth state of consciousness is the key to transcendence, because everything is from Him; all other visions of reality are as illusory as a dream*

Here, the same practical question may again arise. The mind and sense objects are inextricably connected. One may want to see everything in existence in relationship to Krsna and focus on His all-attractive form, qualities, and pastimes, but then one faces that primal habit that practically defines a soul as conditioned: one contemplates sense objects as if they were meant for one’s pleasure. This inclination can overturn the boat of sincere desire to serve God. It has certainly overturned the boat of many in the past. Is there an additional methodology to help the mind become detached from the objects of the senses?

*Text 27: Awaken the detached witness*

The Hamsa-avatara responds with instructions based on jnana. First, He differentiates between the three states of consciousness (what we know about ourselves) and the fourth state, or the unknown jiva: “Waking, sleeping, and deep sleep are the three functions of the intelligence and are caused by the modes of material nature. The living entity within the body is ascertained to possess characteristics different from these three states and thus remains as a witness \[saksitvena\] to them.” (SB. 11.13.27)

In the opening seven texts of chapter 13, Krsna advised Uddhava to avoid passion and ignorance and cultivate goodness as a means to develop knowledge. By the sharpened ax of that knowledge, one should then cut off one’s attachment to the tree of material existence. Remember, goodness is recommended not as an ultimate position for conditioned souls but as a state that allows their consciousness to be awake, clear, and aware of what is real and present before them. This is far different from the mode of passion, which draws the mind away from the present and into the future, planning and desiring things it doesn’t yet have. Practically, those dominated by passion live alone with their plans in a fantasy world. The mode of ignorance moves conditioned souls into the past, enveloping them in darkness, inactivity, pain, lamentation, misery, and ever deepening levels of spiritual illiteracy. Krsna therefore recommends that we cultivate the mode of goodness, for the knowledge and detachment born of this mode offer conditioned souls the ability to break their full identification with the mind and its ever-changing fluctuations.

Those who have cultivated the mode of goodness can create a moment of distance between themselves and their thoughts; they can witness their thoughts without identifying with them as they flow moment to moment through their minds. A witness sees the thought, “I want to buy a new purple car” as “interesting - my mind now thinks it wants to buy a new purple car.” When the mood of “witnessing” is evoked, the mode of goodness tends to increase and the mind slows. One has opened a space, even a very small one, and provided a little more freedom to choose. Let me repeat that: with increased goodness, free choice expands and one may note, “Alluring as any thought may appear, I am not that thought. The thought is simply mine, something passing through the doorway of my mind.”

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura notes that three of the jiva’s four states of consciousness are caused by the three modes of nature, but the jiva is separate from them: “Why? It is confirmed that the Jiva merely witnesses those states.” Or, as the BBT purport to text 27 explains, “Real freedom means saksitvena, or to exist as a witness to the functions of illusion.”

The jnana-inspired practice of witnessing one’s thoughts with detachment comes when one is established in the mode of goodness. “Such an advantageous position is achieved by development of Krsna consciousness.” (SB. 11.1 3.27, purport) Clearly, for a devotee, a mind established m the inode of goodness is an ideal container to hold one’s chanting of Krsna s holy names, because one’s chanting will he attentive.

But still more wonderful than simply witnessing one’s thoughts is attentively hearing Krsna’s holy names - or even one of His names. Attentive chanting cultivates the mode of goodness, hut also transcendental goodness, suddha-sattva, the natural environment in which a soul can blossom into a blissful relationship with Krsna.

By prescribing intelligent and detached observation of thoughts in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.13.27, Krsna actually proposes a way to increase our awareness that we are different from the three states of consciousness - wakefulness, sleep, and deep sleep - born of the modes of material nature. It is this “other” in ourselves, this witness, who maintains our sense of identity as we are awake through our days and asleep through our nights. We are eternal, unchanging souls, but these states of consciousness come and go; they are temporary.

Krsna has already stated (SB. 11.13.25) that souls covered by the mind and sense objects are “part and parcels of Me.” Now He develops the point further: “The spirit soul is trapped in the bondage of material intelligence, which awards him constant engagement in the illusory modes of nature.” (SB. 11.13.28)

Goodness, passion, and ignorance bind the eternal soul through his intelligence and cause the three states of material consciousness. We can think of these illusory states either as the typical daily cycle of being awake (goodness), asleep and dreaming (passion), and asleep without dreaming (ignorance); or we can think of a typical daily cycle while awake - conscious of what is before us at the moment (goodness), rapt in plan-making (passion), or lost in lamentation, intoxication, or misery (ignorance). However we choose to understand these three states of consciousness, all three states require absorption in unending illusion.

*Texts 28-31 - Wake from the dream: fix your mind on Me*

After describing how the soul is absorbed in illusion, in the next text the Hamsa-avatara offers the Kumaras a positive alternative to the tyranny of the modes:The soul is trapped by the three modes of nature, which continuously engage him in illusion. But I am beyond the three states of consciousness the modes generate. If you wish to be free of illusion, become situated in Me, and that will stop your consciousness from entangling itself in the modes. If you choose this path, you will automatically become detached from both the mind and the material sense objects.

The BBT purport to text 28 explains that text 28 answers the question the Four Kumaras asked in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.13.17.

The Hamsa-avatara continues in text 29: Desires born of the false ego bind the soul and award him exactly the opposite of what he desires. So renounce your constant anxiety about how to enjoy material life, and fix your consciousness in Me.

The purport to text 29 quotes Srila Sridhara Svami’s description of what causes the soul to be bound: “Because of false ego, one is bound up in the network of illusion. To unbind the soul, the Hamsa-avatara recommends thinking always of Krsna while remaining detached from the spirit of enjoyment, which is born of the false ego. Thinking of Krsna purifies the consciousness of even the desire for liberation. Devotional service motivated by a desire to be freed from material existence is not pure devotional service but service mixed with the material mode of goodness, according to Kapila Muni in Srimad-Bhagavatam 3.29.10. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.13.29: “Giving up the false identification with the body, being situated in Me, who is the form of bliss, one can even give up his fear of samsara."

The Hamsa-avatara adds, in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.13.30-31: Fix your mind on Me alone. See everything as existing in Me. If you see anything as separate from Me, know that your perception is caused by incomplete knowledge. Your perception is incorrect, like when a man dreams he is awake. It’s a misconception to think that anything can be separate from Me, because nothing can exist apart from Me. If you suffer from this misconception, it will make you feel separate from Me, and that will make you engage in fruitive activities.

*Texts 32-33: Awakening from the dream, method one - stop identifying with the three states of material consciousness*

The Hamsa-avatara now offers an understanding that will help us wake Irom the dream of material existence: by remembering and contemplating the succession of wakefulness, dreaming, and deep sleep, one c an see how his identity continues throughout and beyond these stages of consciousness. Understanding this, one must control one’s senses and escape from the bodily concept of life. These three states of consciousness exist in Him, are caused by the modes of nature, and are the result of ignorance. Once we have ascertained the truth of our existence as a soul, we should use the sharp sword of this knowledge, acquired through logic, the instructions of sages, and the Vedic literature, and cut off the false ego, the breeding ground of doubt. “All of you should then worship Me \[bhajata ma\], who am situated within the heart.” (SB. 11.13.33)

Thus the Lord tells the Kumaras that one can become aware of the soul by seeing it as different from the three states of consciousness one experiences. Then one should use that knowledge to break his false identification with those states of consciousness. Now free from illusion, and with one’s hard-won knowledge and detachment, one should simply focus the mind on the Supreme Lord and worship Him.

*Texts 34-35: Awakening from the dream, method two - the material world is temporary, the soul eternal*

Next, the Hamsa-avatara describes a second understanding that can wake us from absorption in the dream of material life: “One should see that the material world is a distinct illusion appearing in the mind, because material objects have an extremely flickering existence and are here today and gone tomorrow. They can be compared to the streaking red line created by whirling a fiery stick. The spirit soul by nature exists in the single state of pure consciousness. However, in this world he appears in many different forms and stages of existence. The modes of nature divide the soul’s consciousness into normal wakefulness, dreaming, and dreamless sleep. All such varieties of perception, however, are actually maya and exist only like a dream.” (SB. 11.13.34)

Here is this point reworded: We should see our perception of the material world as a mental construct; that is, that what we understand as “real” and “reality” are always in flux. Material objects have only a flickering, temporary existence. Still, they appear real, just as whirling a fiery stick appears to create a red circle of fire. The spirit soul, on the other hand, which by nature is pure and eternal, appears as if in different physical forms with different stages of existence. In addition, the three modes of nature divide the soul’s consciousness into three states (wakefulness, dreaming sleep, and deep sleep). But all of these varieties are just maya; they are temporary and no different than a dream. “Having understood the temporary illusory nature of material things, and thus having pulled one’s vision away from illusion, one should remain without material desires. By experiencing the happiness of the soul, one should give up material speaking and activities. If sometimes one must observe the material world, one should remember that it is not ultimate reality and therefore one has given it up. By such constant remembrance up till the time of death, one will not again fall into illusion.” (SB. 11.13.35)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura comments on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.13.35: “The living entity, while living in the external energy of the Lord, should give up any anxiety for sense gratification and should not act for his personal enjoyment. Rather, one should search out spiritual bliss through devotional service to the Supreme Lord. By reviving one’s relationship with Lord Krsna, one will understand that if one accepts any material object for one’s personal enjoyment, attachment will inevitably develop, and thus one will be bewildered by illusion. By gradually developing one’s spiritual body, one will no longer desire to enjoy anything within the material world.”

So the Lord has offered a second way to escape from the tyrannical grip of the mind and sense objects: see that everything one experiences in this world is flickering and temporary and therefore illusory, even though it appears to be real. The three states of consciousness the spirit soul experiences as if they were real are also impermanent and born of maya. The soul, however, is eternal and should remain free from the desire for matter so it can experience a more natural happiness. The soul should always remember these points and not fall again into illusion.

*Texts 36-37: The consciousness of realized souls*

In his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.13.36, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura notes that texts 36 and 37 describe one who is still living in a material body but has been liberated through jnana. Sri Krsna now describes to Uddhava how such a soul acts and thinks: “Just as a drunken man does not notice if he is wearing his coat or shirt, similarly, one who is perfect in self-realization and who has thus achieved his eternal identity does not notice whether the temporary body is sitting or standing. Indeed, if by God’s will the body is finished or if by God’s will he obtains a new body, a self-realized soul does not notice, just as a drunken man does not notice the situation of his outward dress.” (SB. I 1.1 1.36) Such a person continues to live in his body as long as his karma keeps him alive. He is perfectly situated in yoga and never again surrenders to the material body and its manifold manifestations, knowing it to be just like a body he may see in a dream (SB 11.13.37).

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura asks an interesting question at this point: Since such a person is still in a body, is he in danger of again becoming attached and entangled? He answers his own question with a strong “No!” “He is like a person who has woken up. He does not experience the dream body \[as his own self\] again.”

*Texts 38-40: The Hamsa-avatara now answers the Kumaras’ original question: “Ko bhavan?” (“Who are You?”)*

The Hamsa-avatara has completed His explanation of jnana, by which one distinguishes the soul from the body; Saiikhya, by which one uses philosophy to distinguish matter from spirit; and astanga-yoga, by which one links with the Supreme. From the BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.13.39: “Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura points out that the sons of Brahma were struck with wonder at the presentation of the Supreme Personality of Godhead and were thinking, ‘What wonderful knowledge we have just heard.’ The Lord, recognizing their astonishment, spoke this verse to confirm their understanding of Him.”

In texts 11.13.38-40 the Hamsa-avatara reveals His identity because He has given the directive (in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.13.33) to focus the mind on Him: “Please understand that I am the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Visnu, and that I have appeared before you desiring to explain your actual religious duties. O best of the brahmanas, please know that I am the supreme shelter of the yoga system, analytic philosophy, virtuous action, truthful religious principles, power, beauty, fame, and self-control. All superior transcendental qualities, such as being beyond the modes of nature, detached, the well-wisher, the most dear, the Supersoul, equally situated everywhere, and free from material entanglement - all such qualities, free from the transformations of material qualities, find their shelter and worshipable object in Me.”

The BBT purport to text 40 adds: “Srila Madhvacarya has quoted from the Kala-samhita as follows. ‘The demigods are not actually perfectly endowed with transcendental qualities. Indeed, their opulences are limited, and therefore they worship the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the Absolute Truth, who is simultaneously free of all material qualities and completely endowed with all transcendental qualities, which exist in His personal body.”

Clearly, the Absolute Truth is a person, and the Srimad-Bhagavatam’s exposition of His eternal names, forms, qualities, and pastimes allows devotees to absorb their minds fully in Him. Such absorption is ultimately what the Hamsa-avatara recommends. Not only will absorption in thoughts of Krsna separate the mind from the sense objects, but it will carry one to perfectly serving Him in Goloka Vrndavana. Without their having practiced jnana, studied Sankhya, or perfectly practiced astanga-yoga, Krsna has certified that the gopis of Vrndavana are the ultimate masters of this process: “My dear Uddhava, just as great sages in yoga trance merge into self-realization, like rivers merging into the ocean, and are thus not aware of material names and forms, similarly, the gopis of Vrndavana were so completely attached to Me within their minds that they could not think of their own bodies, or of this world, or of their future lives. Their entire consciousness was simply bound up in Me.” (SB. 11.12.12)

*Texts 41-42: The pastime ends*

Lord Sri Krsna concludes by indicating to Uddhava what the Four Kumaras did after imbibing the Hamsa-avatara’s instructions: “My dear Uddhava, thus all of the doubts of the sages headed by Sanaka were destroyed by My words. Fully worshiping Me \[sabhajayitva\] with transcendental love and devotion, they chanted My glories with excellent hymns \[paraya bhaktyagrnata samstavaih\]. The greatest of sages, headed by Sanaka Rsi, thus perfectly worshiped and glorified Me \[tam aham pujitah samyak, samstutah paramarsibhih\], and as Lord Brahma looked on, I returned to My own abode.” (SB. 11.13.41-42)

In text 41 above, Krsna uses the words sabhajayitva paraya, bhakty-agrnata samstavaih, and in the following text, He says tam aham pujitah samyak, samstutah paramarsibhih. These words indicate that the sages understood the meaning of the Hamsa-avatara’s words and, after hearing from Him, worshiped Him full-heartedly with devotion, chanting His glories with beautiful prayers. The jnana inherent in their natures along with the jnana the Lord had spoken inspired them to respond with bhakti. Therefore as Brahma looked on, they engaged in still more bhakti by worshiping and glorifying the Lord, who had descended as the Hamsa-avatara to instruct them in transcendental knowledge.

**Chapter 14: Lord Krsna Explains the Yoga System to Sri Uddhava**

*Texts 1-11: Krsna puts the Vedic paths into perspective*

*Texts 1-2: Uddhava inquires of Krsna*

Uddhava has just heard from Krsna the instructive answers the Hamsa-avatara gave the Four Kumaras in response to their pertinent question about separating the mind from its sense objects. The Hamsa-avatara established bhakti as the supreme methodology to achieve that goal, but He delivered His instructions in a philosophical fashion due to the Kumaras’ background in jnana and their intellectual natures. To ensure that the supreme position of bhakti is clearly understood, Uddhava now asks Krsna to clarify the many recommendations He has made since Uddhava’s initial inquiry: “My dear Krsna, the learned sages who explain Vedic literature recommend various processes for perfecting one’s life. Considering these varieties of viewpoint, my Lord, please tell me whether all these processes are equally important, or whether one of them is supreme. My dear Lord, You have clearly explained the process of unalloyed devotional service, by which a devotee removes all material association from his life, enabling him to fix his mind on You.” (SB. 11.14.1-2)

Surely Uddhava already knows the answer to this question because he has already expressed the process for transcendence he has personally accepted: “Simply by decorating ourselves with the garlands, fragrant oils, clothes, and ornaments that You have already enjoyed, and by eating the remnants of Your meals, we, Your servants, will indeed conquer Your illusory energy.” (SB. 11.6.46) Uddhava’s process is devotional service, and he is a pure devotee. Why, then, does he ask this question?

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.2 explains Uddhava’s intention: “Are You saying that devotional service is the best process? Well, You have already revealed that unalloyed devotional service is topmost because by this process one’s mind becomes attracted to You. Please clarify whether this process is best according to everyone, or this is only Your opinion.”

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.1 also explains why Uddhava asks for more clarification, but discusses his question from a different point of view: “Not all Vedic processes lead directly to the ultimate goal, pure love of God; some only gradually elevate the consciousness of the living entity. For the purpose of giving a general outline of the process of self-realization, sages may discuss the various methods of elevation. But when the time comes to ascertain the most perfect process, the secondary methods must be cleared from the path.”

The purport to text 2 adds: “In discussing the relative advantages of different spiritual processes, one must immediately ascertain the goal of spiritual life and then isolate the process that actually awards this goal. Processes must be defined in terms of primary and secondary functions. A method that gives one the highest perfection is primary, whereas processes that merely assist or enhance the primary function are considered secondary.”

**The primary and secondary practices in bhakti**

At this point, one may ask about the use of secondary processes to help the primary, or direct, process of bhakti. Krsna has actually recommended some of them in the opening seven texts of chapter 13, where He instructed Uddhava to cultivate the material mode of goodness as an aid to transcending material goodness and attaining pure goodness (suddha-sattva) - the spiritual consciousness in which Krsna is revealed.

In the Bhakti Sandarbha (anucchedas 217-34), Srila Jiva Gosvami discusses three kinds of bhakti: aropa-siddha bhakti, sanga-siddha bhakti, and svarupa-siddha bhakti. Aropa-siddha bhakti, or “attributive bhakti,” refers to one’s performing work that has no inherent connection with Krsna and then offering the fruits of that work to Him. By imposing (aropa) on one’s work the desire to make it an offering to Krsna, the work is considered an act of devotion - that is, the work develops the quality of bhakti by having the desire to make it an offering imposed on it. But because of the lack of “inherency” in aropa-siddha bhakti - that is, that the work itself did not spring from the desire to please Krsna - it is referred to as secondary. Because the bhakti is superimposed onto the work, there is a tendency to remain attached to the fruits of the work while performing aropa-siddha bhakti.

Sanga-siddha bhakti refers to using karma or jnana, neither of which by nature possesses the potency of bhakti, to help one perform devotional service. Because Krsna’s potency is not inherent in these other processes, sanga-siddha bhakti, too, is referred to as secondary. Cultivating the mode ol goodness, as Krsna instructs in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.13.1-7, is an example of using jnana to help one’s devotional practices and is therefore an example of sanga-siddha bhakti. Management skills used in the service of preaching Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s message is an example of using karma to assist one’s bhakti. Because this form of bhakti is, like aropa-siddha bhakti, not completely pure, there is a tendency to become attached to the secondary practices of karma and jnana and to use them independently of service or even in a way that opposes Krsna’s pleasure.

In the Bhakti Sandarbha (anucchedas 228-30), Srila Jiva Gosvami calls the practice of devotional service that is purely motivated but mixed with karma, jnana, or both, bhakti-matra-kama.

Svarupa-siddha bhakti, by contrast, is the practice of devotional processes that inherently contain the potency of bhakti. For example, hearing and chanting about Krsna, along with practicing the other seven limbs of devotional service listed in Srimad-Bhagavatam 7.5.13-14, is an example of practicing svarupa-siddha bhakti.In the Bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 217) Sri Jiva asserts that the items of svarupa-siddha bhakti are the primary practices of devotional service. As Krsna is inherently present in His name and pastimes, practicing svarupa-siddha bhakti forcefully carries one forward in bhakti even if it is performed unknowingly. In anuccheda 234, Sri Jiva explains that he described aropa-siddha bhakti and sanga-siddha bhakti to give his readers “broad knowledge.” He adds that the root of these types of bhakti is svarupa-siddha bhakti.

Svarupa-siddha bhakti gives life to aropa-siddha bhakti and sanga-siddha bhakti. In the Caitanya-caritdmrta (Madhya 19.155), Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu said to Sanatana Gosvami, ihan mali sece nitya sravanadi jala: “Although remaining in the material world, the gardener regularly sprinkles the creeper with the water of hearing and chanting.” In his purport to this Caitanya-caritamrta verse, Srila Prabhupada describes hearing and chanting about Krsna: “It is not that at a certain stage one can stop chanting and hearing and become a mature devotee. If one stops, one certainly falls down from devotional service. Although one may be very much exalted in devotional service, he should not give up the watering process of sravana-kirtana."

In Mayapur on September 29, 1974, Srila Prabhupada spoke on Srimad-Bhagavatam 1.8.19. During his lecture, some devotees stood up and began to leave. Srila Prabhupada’s response was strong:

Why they arc going? They are busy in some other work? Ugra-karma. Without hearing, what he will do, nonsense? Sravanam kirtanam, this is our main business. Sravanam. If you don’t hear, what you will do? You will do simply sense gratification. That’s all.

So this is difficulty — that we are not very much interested in hearing. And that is the main business. Our bhakti begins: sravanam kirtanam visnoh. We have to hear and we have to speak. But if we are not interested in hearing and speaking, then it will become simply formula. That’s all. And gradually it will be stopped. Unless there is life of sravanam kirtanam, these big, big buildings, temples, will become burden. So if we are, if we want to create burden for future, then we may give up this hearing and chanting and sleep very nicely. It will be burden. Galagraha. Not srovigraha but gala-graha. Galagraha. Sri-vigraha means worshipable Deity. So if we give up this sravanam kirtanam visnoh, then it will be thought that “Our Guru Maharaja has given a burden in the neck, galagraha.” This is the danger. So we must be very much alert in sravanam kirtanam. Otherwise all this labor will be futile. This building will be only the nest, nest for the doves and the pigeons. That is the danger.

*Texts 3-11: Krsna begins His reply to Uddhava*

Sri Krsna now begins His description of the timeless, independent, and supreme process - bhakti - that He spoke of at the creation: Because Vedic knowledge was lost at the time of annihilation, “I spoke the Vedic knowledge to Brahma because I Myself am the religious principles enunciated in the Vedas.” (SB. 11.14.3)

Srila Sridhara Svami comments on this text: “Because bhakti brings the greatest results, it is therefore the principal practice. Living beings who, according to their natures, imagine that other results, such as the heavenly planets, to be topmost, also imagine other practices to be principal. In order to distinguish bhakti from these other practices, the Lord speaks these seven verses \[SB. 11.14-3—9\] about the purpose of the Vedas (which contain various practices prescribed according to the nature of the practitioner).”

Lord Brahma spoke the same knowledge to Manu, and “the seven great sages headed by Bhrgu Muni then accepted the same knowledge from Manu.” (SB. 11.14.4) These forefathers generated many species in the universe, along with the species’ respective leaders, who appeared with their different natures and desires each generated from the three modes of material nature. “Therefore, because of the different characteristics of the living entities within the universe, there are a great many Vedic rituals, mantras, and rewards.” (SB. 11.14.7)

From the BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.5-7: “Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura explains that this verse describes the varieties of forgetfulness of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. The different Vedic mantras and rituals are especially meant for the different species of intelligent beings throughout the universe; but this proliferation of Vedic formulas indicates only the variety of material illusion and not a variety of ultimate purpose.”

Krsna continues to develop His point: “Thus, due to the great variety of desires and natures among human beings, there are many different theistic philosophies of life, which are handed down through tradition, custom, and disciplic succession. There are other teachers who directly support atheistic viewpoints.” (SB. 11.14.8)

From the BBT purport to text 8: “Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura has given a most interesting example, as follows. The water of the Ganges is always pure and very sweet. On the banks of that great river, however, there are several types of poisonous trees whose roots drink up the Ganges water from the soil and use it to produce poisonous fruits. Similarly, those who are atheistic or demoniac utilize their association with Vedic knowledge to produce the poisonous fruits of atheistic or materialistic philosophy.”

Krsna then describes the many branches that sprout from the Vedic tree: “The intelligence of human beings is bewildered by My illusory potency, and thus, according to their own activities and whims, they speak in innumerable ways about what is actually good for people. Some say that people will be happy by performing pious religious activities. Others say that happiness is attained through fame, sense gratification, truthfulness, self-control, peace, self-interest, political influence, opulence, renunciation, consumption, sacrifice, penance, charity, vows, regulated duties, or strict disciplinary regulation. Each process has its proponents.” (SB. 11.14.9-10)

Until this point, Krsna has simply added detail to the question initially raised by Uddhava: “Of the processes You have mentioned, which is supreme?” Before Krsna answers this question (Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.12—28), He will now emphatically condemn as ineffective all the above paths and their proponents: “All the persons I have just mentioned obtain temporary fruits from their material work. Indeed, the meager and miserable situations they achieve bring future unhappiness and are based on ignorance. Even while enjoying the fruits of their work, such persons are filled with lamentation.” (SB. 11.14.11)

*Texts 12-28: Krsna unequivocally recommends devotional service*

The Supreme Lord Krsna will first speak to Uddhava about what His devotees attain (12-13) and how those attainments minimize the fruits of other paths (14). Then He will tell Uddhava of His love for His devotees (15-16). Then in twelve texts (17-28), Krsna will glorify bhakti and conclusively point to bhakti - full absorption of the mind in devotion to Him - as the supreme and only process He can truly recommend.

*Texts 12-13: The happiness attained by Krsna’s devotees*

Krsna has just rejected the various Vedic paths, and now, in contrast to those He named, He will explain the actual purpose of the Vedas by glorifying the happiness of His devotees: “O learned Uddhava, those who fix their consciousness on Me, giving up all material desires, share with Me a happiness that cannot possibly be experienced by those engaged in sense gratification. One who does not desire anything within this world, who has achieved peace by controlling his senses, whose consciousness is equal in all conditions, and whose mind is completely satisfied in Me finds only happiness wherever he goes.” (SB. 11.14.12-13)

In his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.13, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura writes: “The devotee’s mind and all his senses are satisfied by Me, who possesses great sweetness of astonishing sound, touch, form, taste, smell, pastimes, and mercy̮̮Wherever a person with great, indestructible wealth bound in his cloth goes he finds happiness, wealth, and enjoyment. \[A devotee\] possesses nothing \[material\], but because he has attained Me, the great and indestructible treasure, he finds happiness everywhere.”

Devotional service alone can award the supreme result, krsna-prema. Why? Because Krsna is inclined to give Himself only to His devotees. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura writes: “Those who are fixed in material processes like sense control, mental control, and knowledge, and eveji the jnams, who are fixed in material sattva, do not even attain Brahman \[whal to speak of Me\]!”

Because the material paths contain no bhakti, the Supreme Personality of Godhead is disinclined to reveal Himself to those who practice them. In Srimad-Bhagavatam 4-31.12, Sri Narada Muni rejects them as “useless”: “Transcendental practices that do not ultimately help one realize the Supreme Personality of Godhead are useless, be they mystic yoga practices, the analytical study of matter, severe austerity, the acceptance of sannyasa, or the study of Vedic literature. All these may be very important aspects of spiritual advancement, but unless one understands the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Hari, all these processes are useless.”

In addition to krsna-prema, which is the unique result awarded by bhakti, practitioners of other processes remain dependent on bhakti if they want the results of their own paths.Srila Prabhupada’s BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 4.31.12 notes: “\[W\]ithout a touch of devotional service, jnana, yoga, and Sankhya philosophy cannot give one their promised desired results. The impersonalists wish to merge into the Supreme Brahman; however, merging into the Supreme Brahman also requires a touch of devotional service... In all processes - karma, jnana, or yoga - bhakti is required. That is the purport of this verse.”

*Text 14: Bhakti minimizes the value of the results awarded by other paths*

Krsna then states that the results His devotees attain through intense, focused, devotion minimizes the value of any benefits bestowed by karma or jnana: “One who has fixed his consciousness on Me desires neither the position or abode of Lord Brahma or Lord Indra \[paramesthyam\], nor an empire on the earth, nor sovereignty in the lower planetary systems, nor the eightfold perfection of yoga, nor liberation from birth and death. Such a person desires Me alone.” (SB. 11.14.14)

Srila Jiva Gosvami speaks of Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.14 in the Priti Sandarbha (anuccheda 23). There he notes that the four items the text mentions, beginning with paremesthya, gradually become less and less significant. In other words, if the higher goal is rejected, then there is no question of wanting the lower goals. Yoga siddhis and liberation are last on the list because they are considered the lowest.

In his comment on this verse, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura reveals how Krsna is thinking: “He has offered himself to Me. Because of the rule, ye yatha mam prapadyante tarns tathaiva bhajamy aham, ‘As all surrender to Me, I reward them accordingly’ (Bhagavad-gita 4.11), I offer Myself to him. My devotee does not want anything except Me, and I therefore remain always visible to him through all his senses. For a person who is continuously tasting sweet juice, the taste of mud holds no attraction.”

*Texts 15—16: The love of Krsna for His devotees*

Lord Sri Krsna has just described how fixed His devotees are on loving Him; now He describes His love for such devotees: “My dear Uddhava, neither Lord Brahma, Lord Siva, Lord Sankarsana, the goddess of fortune, nor indeed My own selfis as dear to Me as you are.” (SB. 11.14.15)

The BBT purport to this text offers us guidance: “Srila Madhvacarya cites from Vedic literature the example that a gentleman sometimes neglects his own interest and that of his children to give charity to a poor beggar- Similarly, the Lord gives preference to a helpless devotee who depends completely on His mercy. The only way to obtain the Lord’s mercy is through His causeless love, and the Lord is most lovingly inclined toward those devotees who are most dependent on Him, just as ordinary mothers and fathers worry more about their helpless children than about those who are self-sufficient. Thus even if one lacks any material qualification, one should simply depend upon the Supreme Personality of Godhead, without any other interest, and surely one will achieve the highest perfection of life.”

Sri Krsna next venerates His devotees and their exalted qualities: “With the dust of My devotees’ lotus feet I desire to purify \[puyeya\] the material worlds, which are situated within Me. Thus, I always follow the footsteps of My pure devotees, who are free from all personal desire, rapt in thought of My pastimes, peaceful, without any feelings of enmity, and of equal disposition everywhere.” (SB. 11.14.16)

In his comment on text 16 Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura offers readers the remarks of two great acaryas specifically on the word puyeya (I may be purified”): “Sridhara Svami explains the word puyeya as follows: I he Lord thinks ‘Let the universe, which exists within Me, become purified.’ Jiva Gosvami says puyeya means ‘Let me become purified of tin- fault of not being able to repay the devotion of My followers.’ Srila Jiva continues describing Krsna s thoughts: ‘Actually, bhakti cannot exist without taking the dust from the feet of the devotees, and without bhakti, one cannot experience the sweetness of rasa with Me. I have established this rule. Therefore, I also should become absorbed in the full sweetness of rasa with Me through bhakti, like a devotee.’ ”

The BBT purport expands the meaning of text 16 by quoting Srila Madhvacarya: “Lord Krsna follows the footsteps of His devotees to purify them. As the Lord walks along behind His pure devotees, the wind blows the dust of the Lord’s feet in front of His devotees, who then become purified by contact with such transcendental dust.”

In Srimad-Bhagavatam, Canto 10, chapter 81, a question could have been raised about Krsna’s interaction with Sudama Brahmana. There, we hear how Sudama walked home from Dvaraka after spending the night in the palace of his school friend Krsna. Why did Krsna allow the weak, thin, impoverished Sudama Brahmana to walk home?Why didn’t He at least send His friend home in a chariot? The words Krsna just spoke in text 16 express His affectionate respect for His dear brahmana devotees, and they indicate that the Lord wished the dust raised by Sudama’s feet as he walked to purify His kingdom.

*Texts 17-28: The glories of bhakti*

Krsna will now illuminate more aspects of the glories of bhakti.

*Text 17: Bhakti awards Krsna’s devotees material detachment and a happiness unknown to those who suffer from material attachment*

How can the Lord reciprocate with His pure devotees when they love Him so fully and He loves them so deeply? Krsna answers this question in the next text: “Those who are without any desire for personal gratification, whose minds are always attached to Me, who are peaceful, without false ego and merciful to all living entities, and whose consciousness is never affected by opportunities for sense gratification - such persons enjoy in Me a happiness that cannot be known or achieved by those lacking such detachment from the material world.” (SB. 11.14.17)

Devotees effortlessly and naturally achieve the detachment that jnanis and other renunciants strenuously strive to attain. Additionally, what the devotees attain is far superior to detachment from matter. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comments on text 18 indicate that the devotee Krsna has just described is on the exalted platform of bhava-bhakti, the stage right before prema, or full love of God. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura s comments on text 17, however, describe the mentality of such an exalted devotee: “Since the happiness of experiencing Krsna’s form and qualities can be attained only by bhakti and by no other process, no other process is then recommended. So Lord Krsna spoke this verse. Lord Krsna also describes the devotees as being without material possessions. But, one may object, even the jnanis are without material possessions. To overrule this objection Krsna replies, ‘But My devotees minds are attached to Me. They are affectionate to all jivas, because they want all jivas to taste bhakti-rasa. And so people in general consider them great. Pure devotees do not feel sense enjoyment entering their intelligence even when sense enjoyment is present. Only they know the happiness they relish in serving Me; others cannot know it. Why? Because this happiness arises only in those who have no expectation of material enjoyment or liberation.’”

*Text 18: Material desires cannot defeat Krsna’s devotees*

Does Krsna appreciate only those devotees who are on the most exalted platform? What if a devotee is focused and fixed in service to Krsna yet struggles with some material attachment? How will Krsna reciprocate with such a soul? Will the Lord protect him? Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.18 is Krsna’s reply to this poignant and relevant inquiry: “My dear Uddhava, if My devotee has not fully conquered his senses, he may be harassed by material desires, but because of his unflinching devotion for Me, he will not be defeated by sense gratification.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura is reassuring: “Putting aside words describing a devotee who has developed bhava, a devotee even at the beginning of bhakti is also successful. By practicing strong, resolute bhakti, what to speak of unflinching bhakti, the devotee cannot be overcome by material enjoyment. Krsna’s words also suggest the following.
