A jnani who commits a sinful act will be criticized, and his position as a jnani will be denied (SB. 11.18.40-41).” But devotees who commit sin are not criticized, and their position as devotees is not denied (Bhagavad-gita 9.30).

Visvanatha Cakravarti continues: “Although a devotee may be distressed by sense objects, he will not he overcome by them… One attacked by the weapons of an enemy remains undefeated because of his bravery. Or, on the day that one takes a powerful medicine to reduce a fever, the fever may still be active, but it is no longer a real cause of suffering since it is in the process of being destroyed and will be completely destroyed by the next day.”

*Text 19: bhakti removes a devotee’s sinful reactions*

Krsna continues to describe the potency - and thus superiority - of the bhakti path: “My dear Uddhava, just as a blazing fire turns firewood into ashes, similarly, devotion unto Me completely burns to ashes sins committed by My devotees.” (SB. 11.14.19)

Srila Sridhara Svami states that even the Supreme Personality of Godhead is amazed at the glory and wonder of devotional service: “O Uddhava, please hear this great wonder!” And Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura offers further inspiration to encourage readers to sincerely serve Krsna. The Lord (in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.19) says: “bhakti destroys the sins committed by a devotee who cannot even control his senses… Addressing Uddhava, he implies that Uddhava should be joyful (uddhava means ‘joyful’) on hearing this.”

*Texts 20-24: Only bhakti can conquer Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead*

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.20 gives extra meaning to the words Krsna speaks in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.20-23: “\[Someone may say,\] ‘Just as bhakti is the means to attain You, so other processes like jnana and yoga should also be a means to attain You, since they contain a little portion of the excellence of bhakti.’ Krsna answers this doubt: ‘These \[other\] processes are not the means to attain Me. I am attained by strong bhakti unmixed with karma and jnana.”’

*Text 20: Only bhakti brings Krsna under control*

Krsna then asserts: “My dear Uddhava, the unalloyed devotional service rendered to Me by My devotees brings Me under their control. I cannot be thus controlled by those engaged in mystic yoga, Sarikhya philosophy, pious work, Vedic study, austerity, or renunciation.” (SB. 11.14.20)

Here, Krsna may be thinking of His many exalted devotees, but His backward glance must ultimately rest on the unique devotion of the Vrajavasis. Their devotion must be the fullest even among Krsna’s unalloyed devotees, for it controls Krsna most completely. Unlimitedly powerful and opulent Krsna remains in debt to the gopis (SB. 10.32.22), fearful of Mother Yasoda (SB. 1.8.31), and defeated by His cowherd boyfriends in sport as they play in the forests of Vrndavana (SB. 10.18.23).

*Texts 21-24: Bhakti’s unique power to purify*

Krsna’s next words point to the immensely purifying potency of bhakti: “Only by practicing unalloyed devotional service \[bhaktyaham ekaya grahya\] with full faith in Me \[sraddhaya\] can one obtain Me, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. I am naturally dear to My devotees, who take Me as the only goal \[man-nistha\] of their loving service. By engaging in such pure devotional service, even the dog-eaters can purify themselves from the contamination of their low birth. Neither religious activities endowed with honesty and mercy nor knowledge obtained with great penance can completely purify one’s consciousness if they are bereft of loving service to Me.” (SB. 11.14.21-22)

In his comment on text 21, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura compares the purifying power of bhakti to that of karma and jnana: “I am obtained by bhakti alone (bhaktyaham ekaya grahya), not by other processes. Although it is said that one can attain Brahman by practicing jnana, it should be understood that the secondary bhakti in jnana is what gives the attainment of Brahman. Thus jnana and karma do not give attainment of the Lord. They are useful only in destroying sin. But they are not even as powerful in destroying sin as bhakti… The last two lines of the verse \[the final sentence in the BBT’s English translation\] indicate that bhakti destroys even prarabdha-karma, \[the karmic reactions one is destined to experience in the present lifetime\].”

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.22 adds: “Although pious religious work, truthfulness, mercy, penances, and knowledge partially purify one’s existence, they do not remove the root of material desires. Thus the same desires will reappear at a later time.” The purport to text 21 notes that the bhakti rendered “must have Lord Krsna as the only goal (man-nistha), be rendered with full faith (sraddhaya), and be unalloyed, or without selfish motivation (ekaya)."

Krsna attests to the powerful results one gains by acting in ecstatic bhakti by first making a negative statement: “If one’s hairs do not stand on end, how can the heart melt? And if the heart does not melt, how can tears of love flow from the eyes? If one does not cry in spiritual happiness, how can one render loving service to the Lord? And without such service, how can the consciousness be purified?” (SB. 11.14.23)

He now offers the positive: The capacity of pure, ecstatic devotees to help others is unlimited, because they carry in their heart Krsna, the unlimited Supreme Personality of Godhead. “A devotee whose speech is sometimes choked up, whose heart melts, who cries continually, and sometimes laughs, who feels ashamed and cries out loudly and then dances - a devotee thus fixed in loving service to Me purifies the entire universe.” (SB. 11.14.24)

In the Bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 147) Srila Jiva Gosvami explains that if bhakti can purify the universe, by definition it can also purify individuals within the universe. He also comments in the Paramatma Sandarbha (anuccheda 93) on how an exalted devotee purifies the universe: “Some devotees in this world gather and express their prema for the Lord to one another. They collect some mrdanga players unknown to them and dance madly in bliss on hearing the Lord’s qualities. By this action, they destroy all inauspiciousness in the universe and increase its auspiciousness.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comments that these last two texts (Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.23-24) again show how unique is the purifying power of bhakti. In his comment on text 23, he writes: “Thus niskama-karma, yoga, and other processes purify the heart to some degree according to many scriptural proofs. However, neither direct realization of the Lord nor the full removal of contamination will occur after practicing these processes. Prema-bhakti burns up such contamination, but the fire of jnana does not.” And on text 24: “What is astonishing about a person in prema-bhakti delivering himself is that he also delivers the whole world. A prema-bhakti’s words become garbled and his heart melts, causing him to weep continually in longing for his Lord. Such a devotee sometimes laughs, sometimes becomes shy, sometimes sings loudly, and sometimes dances. By the use of the word “sometimes” (kvacit) we understand that these symptoms of prema may come and go, hut it does not refer to the state of his heart, which remains constantly melted.”

*Text 25: Purified and inspired by devotional service, one attains the spiritual world*

By virtue of their devotion to Krsna such souls are pure, free from all contamination. Their matchlessly pure desire to serve Krsna determines their destination. Krsna continues: “Just as gold, when smelted in fire, gives up its impurities and returns to its pure brilliant state, similarly, the spirit soul, absorbed in the fire of bhakti-yoga, is purified of all contamination caused by previous fruitive activities and returns to its original position of serving Me in the spiritual world.” (SB. 11.14.25)

Only bhakti, and not karma or jnana, explains Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, purifies the soul fully; it is the fire that completely purifies gold, and not the water that simply washes its surface.

*Text 26: Chanting and hearing about Krsna allows one to see Krsna*

More from Krsna on the glorious effects of bhakti: “When a diseased eye is treated with medicinal ointment it gradually recovers its power to see. Similarly, as a conscious living entity cleanses himself of material contamination by hearing and chanting the pious narrations of My glories, he regains his ability to see Me, the Absolute Truth, in My subtle spiritual form.” (SB. 11.14.26)

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.26, and explains how Krsna is thinking: “In proportion to the purification of the soul through pure bhakti, and in proportion to one’s hearing, chanting, and remembering, one attains various degrees of realization of My sweetness.”

*Texts 27-28: The process and goal of bhakti - full devotional absorption in Krsna consciousness*

Krsna names the principle by which one becomes entangled in maya’s web. One may use this same principle to free oneself: “The mind of one meditating upon the objects of sense gratification is certainly entangled \[anusmaratah\] in such objects, but if one constantly remembers Me, then the mind is absorbed in Me.” (SB. 11.14.27)

Again, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s completes Krsna’s (bought: “Just as the mind attached to thinking of sense objects becomes absorbed in the sweetness of those sense objects, the mind attached to thinking of Me becomes absorbed only in My sweetness.”

The BBT purport to text 27 offers us some advice: “One should not think that one can attain complete transcendental knowledge of Krsna by mechanically engaging in worship of the Lord. Lord Krsna states here that one must endeavor constantly to keep the Lord within one’s mind. Anusmaratah, or constant remembrance, is possible for one who always chants and hears the glories of Lord Krsna— One who constantly thinks of the objects of material gratification becomes attached to them; similarly, one who constantly keeps Lord Krsna within his mind becomes absorbed in the Lord’s transcendental nature and thus becomes qualified to render personal service to the Lord in His own abode.”

Concluding, Sri Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, sums up His glorification of bhakti: “Therefore, one should reject all material processes of elevation, which are like the mental creations of a dream, and should completely absorb one’s mind in Me. By constantly thinking of Me, one becomes purified \[mad-bhava-bhavitam\].” (SB. 11.14.28)

Both Krsna’s words and the comment written by Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura are a plea: “Since other processes and results are just as temporary as objects in a dream, give them up and concentrate your mind in pure bhakti on Me.... Absorb your mind, which is endowed with bhava, by thinking of Me (mad-bhava-bhavitam) and Me alone.”

The purport to text 28 ends with these words: “The Lord here concludes His analysis of different processes of human perfection.”

*Texts 29-30: Krsna’s caution*

Before ending His discussion on “Bhakti, the Supreme and Recommended Process,” Krsna cautions Uddhava in two texts: although bhakti purifies, careless actions still cause material bondage. Sri Krsna says: “Being conscious of the eternal self, one should give up association with women and those intimately associated with women. Sitting fearlessly in a solitary place, one should concentrate the mind on Me with great attention. Of all kinds of suffering and bondage arising from various attachments, none is greater than the suffering and bondage arising from attachment to women and intimate contact witli those attached to women.” (SB. 11.14.29—30)

Krsna’s point is simple and clear. The tendencies opposed to bhakti that may overpower bhakti come from association with the opposite sex. For a conditioned soul, whether in a man’s body or a woman’s, association with the opposite sex stimulates the false ego, which lures the soul into the misunderstanding that he or she is the central enjoyer. Locked into that mood leaves one in the unnatural position of competing with Krsna, his back turned toward Krsna, and forgetful that He is the purusottama, the best person and supreme enjoyer. Weedlike desires born of passion start out as ideas of future pleasure, then sprout in the consciousness until they seem to take it over. But what is the fruit of this type of self-indulgence? Dissatisfaction and further entanglement in material desires, frustration, and bondage in the horrific realm of birth and death. Although what Krsna is suggesting is contrary to the flow of Kali-yuga thought and life, we should heed it because it speaks to our self-interest.

In chapters 10-14, Krsna led Uddhava up the yoga ladder to bhakti through His words on Vedic karma and jnana. By expressing His affection for the vraja-gopikas and acknowledging that He can never repay them, and by again and again speaking of the glories of bhakti, we cannot fail to understand that bhakti is the topmost rung of the yoga ladder.

Although Canto 11, chapter 14 continues until text 45, Krsna ends this section of the Uddhava-gita with a caution for His bhaktas. In doing so, the Supreme Lord told us to sit “fearlessly in a solitary place” and “concentrate the mind on Me with great attention.” Uddhava heard Krsna’s glorification of bhakti as well as His caution. Uddhava’s response in text 31 inspires the Lord to shift to another topic. “Sri Uddhava said: My dear lotus-eyed Krsna, by what process should one who desires liberation meditate upon You, of what specific nature should Iris meditation be, and upon which form should he meditate? Kindly explain to me this topic of meditation.”

## Dialogue 5. Krsna, the Goal of the vedic path

*Canto eleven: chapters 14-21*

**Chapter 14: Texts 31-46**

*Text 31: Uddhava inquires of Krsna*

In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.29, Krsna summarized His instructions to Uddhava on the supreme Vedic practice: one should withdraw the mind from (he dreamlike material existence and absorb it in thoughts of Him. Uddhava responded with a cluster of questions centered on meditation: “My dear lotus-eyed Krsna, by what process should one who desires liberation \[mumuksuh\] meditate upon You, of what specific nature should his meditation be, and upon which form should he meditate? Kindly explain to me this topic of meditation.” (SB. 11.14.31)

Why does Uddhava ask these questions? What do they have to do with what Krsna has just told him? Is it because he wants liberation? No. I Jddhava already described his own path of devoted service to Krsna in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.6.46. He knows the bhakti path will free him from l he fierce ocean of illusion. He also already informed Krsna that he plans to “cross beyond the darkness of this material world simply by hearing about Your Lordship in the association of Your devotees.” (SB. 11.6.48-49) So Uddhava is not asking his questions about meditation for himself. Nor is he asking for other bhaktas. He has just heard the glories of bhakti and already feels assured about his path. Instead, he is asking about the path of the mumuksuhs, or those who want liberation.

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.31 gives two reasons why Uddhava turns Krsna’s attention from bhakti to meditation:

1\. “\[O\]ne cannot fully appreciate the beauty and perfection of bhakti-yoga unless one sees its superiority to all other processes. Through comparative analysis, the devotees become fully ecstatic in their appreciation of bhakti-yoga.”

2\. Uddhava “is asking questions for the benefit of those who are not on the platform of love of Godhead. Uddhava wants to hear this knowledge for his personal appreciation and so that those who pursue salvation, or liberation, can be protected and redirected to the path of pure devotional service to the Supreme Lord.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura describes Uddhava’s question as being about methods of bhakti meditation for those who want liberation. The acarya continues, speaking on Krsna’s behalf: “ ‘O Uddhava, what is the use of asking about meditation for persons desiring liberation, since you are a pure devotee? You should ask how you can meditate on Me!’ With folded hands Uddhava points toward the Lord’s two feet. ‘This is my meditation.’”

*Texts 32-46: Krsna describes the yogic process of meditation and liberation*

*Texts 32-35: The process of meditation*

The initial elements of Uddhava’s question indicate his desire to hear about the practical methodology of meditation - how it is done. In the second part he asks Krsna to reveal the goal of meditation. Thus yogis and meditators will again hear what Krsna has already stated in the Bhagavad-gita (6.47):that to meditate on Him is the actual perfection of yoga.

His description of the yoga process here in this fourteenth chapter of the Eleventh Canto is much more abbreviated than the description He gives in the Gita's sixth chapter. Here He touches briefly on sitting places and proper asanas, then stops at pranayama, which is used to steady the mind in preparation for pratyahara, or withdrawing it from the external and focusing it within. Krsna explains that one should practice pranayama step by step, lifting the life-air until it reaches the heart, where the sacred syllable om is situated. Then one should direct the life-air and the om syllable further upward and meditate on the Lord’s form.

*Texts 36-43: The goal of meditation - the Supreme Personality of Godhead in the heart*

After discussing “the process” and “nature” of meditation, Krsna next describes the goal of meditation. The meditating yogi, his eyes focused on the tip of his nose, his vision alert but drawn within, views the Supersoul sitting on the whorl of an eight-petaled lotus in his heart. This is the form on which those who desire liberation should meditate.

On that lotus flower, one should see the transcendental form of the Supersoul, along with the sun, moon, and fire. The Lord’s form is wonderful! It is “perfectly proportioned, gentle and cheerful. He possesses four beautiful long arms, a charming, beautiful neck, a handsome forehead, a pure smile, and glowing, shark-shaped earrings suspended from two identical ears. That spiritual form is the color of a dark rain cloud and is garbed in golden-yellowish silk. The chest of that form is the abode of Srivatsa and the goddess of fortune, and that form is also decorated with a conch shell, disc, club, lotus flower, and garland of forest flowers. The two brilliant lotus feet are decorated with ankle bells and bracelets, and that form exhibits the Kaustubha gem along with an effulgent crown. The upper hips are beautified by a golden belt, and the arms are decorated with valuable bracelets. All of the limbs of that beautiful form capture the heart, and the face is beautified by merciful glancing. Pulling the senses back from the sense objects, one should be grave and self-controlled and should use the intelligence to strongly fix the mind upon all of the limbs of My transcendental body. Thus one should meditate upon that most delicate transcendental form of Mine.” (SB. 11.14.37—42)

Krsna tells Uddhava to pull back the senses and focus the consciousness within. Once this is accomplished and one is strengthened by yoga practice, especially by carefully practicing pranayama ten times at each of (he clay’s three sandhyas of sunrise, noon, and sunset, the consciousness should be emptied of thoughts of the external world and filled with the gorgeous and delicately attractive limbs of Lord Visnu.

That focus achieved, Krsna tells Uddhava about a still more focused meditation: “One should then pull the consciousness back from all the limbs of that transcendental body. At that time, one should meditate only on the wonderfully smiling face of the Lord.” (SB. 11.14.43)

The Lord’s smile is the most attractive feature of His all-attractive form: “O my Lord, the transcendental body of Krsna is very sweet, and His face is even sweeter than His body. But His soft smile, which has the fragrance of honey, is sweeter still.” (Gaitanya-caritamrta, Madhya 21.136, quoted from Krsna-karnamrta 92)

*Texts 44-46: Attaining liberation*

Krsna now recommends that the meditator give up his focus on Lord Visnu’s form: “Being established in meditation on the Lord’s face, one should then withdraw the consciousness and fix it in the sky. Then giving up such meditation, one should become established in Me and give up the process of meditation altogether.” (SB. 11.14.44)

The BBT purport to this verse explains what Krsna means: “Uddhava originally inquired about the procedure of meditation for those desiring liberation. The word labdha-padam indicates that when one fixes the mind upon the Lord’s face, one achieves full liberation… By giving up the concept of being a meditator, one casts off the last small remnant of illusory energy and sees the Lord as He actually is.”

In his comment on this text, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti states that the meditator is dependent on bhakti even for his success in achieving liberation. Without some practice of bhakti, one cannot succeed at karma and jnana: “The jiva, endowed with a particle of bhakti, realizes Brahman— One who gives up karma and jnana must not desire to give up meditation through bhakti.”

It is interesting to note that the ability to withdraw the consciousness from Krsna’s charming face is absent in the Vrajavasis, especially in the gopis, and so their experience of meditation is vastly different from that of yogis who want liberation. Krsna has already described the Vrajavasis’ attachment to Him: “Dear Uddhava, all of those nights that the gopis spent with Me, their most dearly beloved, in the land of Vrndavana seemed to them to pass in less than a moment. Bereft of My association, however, the gopis felt that those same nights dragged on forever, as if each night were equal ton Hay of Brahma.” (SB. 11.12.11)

Lord Sri Krsna goes on to describe how the meditator sees the Supreme Lord and the jiva as inseparable. The individual jiva realizes the Lord in his soul and himself in the Lord, just as “one sees the sun’s rays completely united with the sun \[jyotir jyotisi samyutam\].” (SB. 11.14.45)

The language of this text may make it sound as if liberation ends with an impersonal conclusion - a merging of sun rays with the sun - but Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura dispels this idea: “Jyotir jyotisi samyutam - light is united with light. This refers to Brahman, the complete spiritual light of the Lord and the jiva, who is a particle of that light.” Krsna concludes with a description of the samadhi that results from the focused practice He has just described: “When the yogi thus controls his mind by intensely concentrated meditation, his illusory identification with material objects, knowledge, and activities is very quickly extinguished.” (SB. 11.14.46)

Thus the interdependent illusion created by false identification with the senses, sense devatas, and sense objects is destroyed.

**Chapter 15: Lord Krsna’s Description of Mystic Yoga Perfections**

*Texts 1-9: Introduction to mystic perfections*

*Texts 1-2: Uddhava inquires further after Krsna introduces the mystic perfections attained by advanced yogis*

In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.14.31, Uddhava asked Krsna how one should meditate and on what form those desiring liberation should meditate. Krsna responded by giving a brief description of astanga-yoga and then a longer discussion of its goal: meditation on His own form - especially His smiling face - before withdrawing one’s concentration to extinguish any last illusory identification with material objects, knowledge, or activities.

One may ask at this point whether meditation on Krsna’s form will carry one automatically to Goloka Vrndavana. The answer is clear: although focusing the mind on Krsna is the purpose of yoga, the specific goal that motivates that focus will determine the results of our meditation. For example, fixing the mind on Krsna can carry a soul toward liberation (SB. 11.14.36 46), but it can also establish one in his eternal service relationship with Krsna, the Supreme Absolute Truth (SB. 11.12.12-13). Or as we shall now hear, it can give mystic perfections to those who want them: “My dear Uddhava, the mystic perfections of yoga are acquired by a yogi who has conquered his senses, steadied his mind, conquered the breathing process, and fixed his mind on Me.” (SB. 11.15.1)

A yogi must control his senses to steady his mind if he wishes to successfully practice pranayama and thus focus his consciousness on Krsna. Fixing the mind on Krsna can cause one to achieve mystic perfections, and hearing this, Uddhava asks the Lord to explain how these mystical attainments are achieved and the nature and number of these perfections. Uddhava ends his question with an acknowledgement that it is ultimately Krsna who bestows these perfections on meditating yogis.

Krsna groups the mystic perfections into two categories: the eight powerful, primary perfections that emanate directly from Krsna, and the fifteen lesser perfections born of material goodness.

The eight primary mystic perfections are listed below. The first three transform the yogi’s body:

1\. Anima, becoming smaller than the smallest.

2\. Mahima, becoming greater than the greatest.

3\. Laghima, becoming lighter than the lightest.

The other five perfections are:

4\. Prapti, acquiring whatever one desires.

5\. Prakamya, experiencing any enjoyable object, either in this world or the next (but still within the material realm).

6\. Isita, manipulating maya’s subpotencies.

7\. Vasita, becoming unimpeded by the three modes of nature.

8\. Kamavasayita, obtaining anything from anywhere, “to the highest possible limit.”

“These eight,” Krsna concludes, “are considered to be naturally existing and unexcelled within this world.” (SB. 11.15.5)

Krsna then lists an additional fifteen mystic powers born of the modes of nature: ten of greater significance (SB. 11.15.6-7) and five of lesser (SB. 11.1 5.8 9) significance:

1\. Freeing oneself from hunger and thirst and other bodily disturbances.

2\. Hearing things that are far away.

3\. Seeing things that are far away.

4\. Moving the body at the speed of the mind.

5\. Assuming any form one desires.

6\. Entering others’ bodies.

7\. Dying when one desires.

8\. Witnessing the pastimes between the demigods and the Apsaras

9\. Completely executing one’s determination.

10\. Giving orders and having them fulfilled without impediment.

The five inferior perfections are:

11\. The power to know past, present, and future.

12\. The ability to tolerate heat, cold, and other dualities.

13\. The power to know others’ minds.

14\. The power to check the influence of fire, the sun, water, poison, and so on.

15\. The power to remain unconquered.

Srila Prabhupada finds commonality between these mystic achieve- ments and the attempts of ordinary materialists: “In this material world people are engaged in different activities simply to achieve a little success in sense gratification. The karmis are engaged in performing very difficult activities, and thus they open gigantic factories, build huge cities, make big scientific discoveries, etc. In other words, they are engaged in performing very costly sacrifices in order to be promoted to the higher planetary systems. Similarly, yogis are engaged in achieving a similar goal by accepting the tedious practices of mystic yoga.... The karmis flatly state that they want sense gratification. The yogis also want sense gratification, but they want it to a higher degree, h is their desire to show some miraculous results through the practice of yoga. Thus they strive very hard to achieve success in becoming smaller than the smallest or greater than the greatest, or in creating a planet like earth or, as scientists, by inventing so many wonderful machines.” (SB. 4.21.28, purport)

As nondevotee karmis have ways to attain power, control, and influence, so too do yogis. Krsna now invites Uddhava to hear how specific yogic perfections arise from specific types of meditation.

*Texts 10-31: Specific meditations to attain specific perfections*

**Eight mystic perfections that emanate from Krsna**

The Supreme Lord now explains how one should meditate on Him in order to attain particular mystic perfections. Again, the first eight (described in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.15.10-17) emanate from the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krsna, and require that the yogi focus his mind directly on Him.

Text 10: “One who worships Me in My atomic form pervading all subtle elements, fixing his mind on that alone, obtains the mystic perfection called anima.” The BBT purport explains that perfectly fixing the mind on the Lord’s subtle atomic form allows one to “enter within even the most dense matter such as stone.”

Text 11: Focusing one’s mind on the mahat-tattva and meditating on Krsna as the Supreme Soul “of the total material existence” awards one the mystic perfection called mahima. From the BBT purport: “Once the yogi has established his realization that the material creation is not different from the Lord, he obtains the perfection called mahima-siddhi. By realizing the Lord’s presence in each individual element, the yogi also acquires the greatness of each element.”

Text 12: “I exist within everything, and I am therefore the essence of the atomic constituents of material elements. By attaching his mind to Me in this form, the yogi may achieve the perfection called laghima, by which he realizes the subtle atomic substance of time.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura states that concentrating the mind on Krsna in His form as the atoms of the elements - air, water, fire, ether, or earth - the yogi attains a form that is as light as the smallest portion of time.

Text 13: By absorbing the mind in Krsna and the subtle element, the false ego, which springs from the mode of goodness, one attains the mystic perfection of acquisition, or prapti, by which one “becomes the proprietor of the senses of all living entities.” The BBT purport quotes Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura: “\[T\]hose who pursue such perfections without fixing the mind in the Supreme Lord acquire a gross and inferior reflection of each mystic potency.”

Text 14: Krsna awards the mystic perfection known as prakamya to those who concentrate on Him as the sutra, the aspect of the mahat-tattva that is dominated by the Supreme Lord’s kriya-sakti (rather than His jnana-sakti) and which manifests the chain of fruitive activities. The BBT purport notes: “Srila Viraraghava Acarya explains that the word sutra, or thread, is used to indicate that the mahat-tattva sustains one’s fruitive activities just as a thread sustains a row of jewels.”

Text 15: Focusing one’s consciousness on Visnu, the Supersoul, the ultimate controller of the external energy, awards the yogi isita, the mystic perfection that allows the yogi to control “other conditioned souls, their bodies, and their bodily designations.”

Text 16: By focusing the mind on Krsna’s form as Narayana, the yogi becomes endowed with Krsna’s own nature, which is free from the three material modes of nature. He thus attains vasita, the mystic perfection that allows a yogi to be unaffected by the material modes.

Text 17: The yogi who fixes his pure mind on Krsna in His unmanifest aspect of the impersonal Brahman attains the greatest material happiness, or kamavasayita-siddhi, the mystic perfection by which one’s desires are completely fulfilled.

**Ten mystic perfections that emanate from the modes of nature**

In the next ten texts (SB. 11.15.18-27), Krsna delineates the ten mystic perfections that emanate from the modes of nature.

Text 18: By worshiping Lord Visnu as the master and personification of material goodness, as Svetadvipa-pati, the Lord of Svetadvipa, one attains freedom from bodily disturbances - hunger, thirst, physical decay, death, grief, and illusion, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura calls this siddhi “the absence of waves."

Text 19: A purified soul who fixes his mind on “the extraordinary sound vibrations occurring within Me as the personified sky and total life air” is able to perceive the speaking of all living entities. The BBT purport explains this siddhi: “Speech occurs by vibrating air within the sky. One who meditates on the Supreme Lord as the personified sky and air thereby acquires the ability to hear that which is vibrated at great distance.”

Text 20: “Merging one’s sight into the sun planet and then the sun planet into one’s eyes, one should meditate on Me as existing within the combination of sun and vision; thus one acquires the power to see any distant thing.”

Text 21: “The yogi who completely absorbs his mind in Me, and who then makes use of the wind that follows the mind to absorb the material body in Me, obtains through the potency of meditation on Me the mystic perfection by which his body immediately follows his mind wherever it goes.”

The BBT purport explains: “Tad-anuvayuna indicates the particular subtle air that follows the mind. When the yogi merges this air together with the body and mind in Krsna by the potency of meditation on the Lord, his gross material body, like the subtle air, can follow the mind anywhere. This perfection is called mano-javah.”

Text 22: “When the yogi, applying his mind in a certain way, desires to assume a particular form, that very form immediately appears. Such perfection is possible by absorbing the mind in the shelter of My inconceivable mystic potency, by which I assume innumerable forms.”

Text 23: Next, Krsna explains how a yogi can enter another’s body: “\[H\]e should meditate upon himself within the other body, and then, giving up his own gross body, he should enter the other’s body through the pathways of air, as easily as a bee leaves one flower and flies into another.” Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments: “This takes place by the power of concentrating on Me. The statement of the previous verse - that one attains this siddhi by concentrating on Me - applies here also. This siddhi is called para-kaya-pravesa.”

Text 24: Through yoga, the expert practitioner can lilt bis soul to the cakra at the top of his bead and depart bis body to attain a destination according to his desire. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura calls this mystic perfection svacchanda-mrtu, or “dying at one’s will.” With this power, the BBT purport adds, one can attain “the spiritual sky, the impersonal brahmajyoti, or any other destination that has attracted the yogi’s mind.”

Text 25: The yogi who desires to “enjoy in the pleasure gardens of the demigods should meditate on the purified mode of goodness, which is situated within Me, and then the heavenly women, generated from the mode of goodness, will approach him in airplanes.” This mystic perfection is called deva-krida-prapti.

Text 26: “A yogi who has faith in Me, absorbing his mind in Me and knowing that My purpose is always fulfilled, will always achieve his purpose by the very means he has determined to follow.” By absorbing one’s mind in Krsna, the fulfiller of all desires, one’s own desires are fulfilled. The BBT purport explains the power of this mystic perfection: “In this verse the word yada. (‘whenever’) indicates that by the mystic power called yatha-sankalpa-samsiddhi one will achieve one’s objective even if one pursues it at an inauspicious time. Lord Krsna is called satya-sankalpa, or He whose desire, intention, purpose, or resolve always comes to pass.”

Text 27. “A person who perfectly meditates on Me acquires My nature of being the supreme ruler and controller. His order, like Mine, can never be frustrated by any means.” Again, meditation on Krsna and His potencies can award one power.

**The lesser mystic perfections**

Text 28: Purified by his devotion to Krsna, the yogi, through meditation, can gain knowledge of past, present, and future. Therefore he can see his own births and deaths along with the births and deaths of others. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura notes that this power increases, not decreases, one’s anxiety about birth and death. In other words, it does not foster a spirit of liberation.

Text 29: As large aquatics but not other beings are safe in water, a yogi who pacifies his consciousness through devotion can remain uninjured when he comes in contact with water, air, poison, lire, etc. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura adds that the devotee attains peace through his meditation on the Lord, and then his body, “which has reached maturity through yoga," remains uninjured when contacting these elements.

Text 30: A devotee can become unconquerable by meditating on Krsna’s opulent incarnations, whose imperial paraphernalia (His flags, ornamental umbrellas, and fans) indicate His omnipotence. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura mentions that this means the yogi becomes both unconquerable and equipped with the symbols of power.

*Text 31: Krsna’s conclusion*

By listing how one attains all these mystic perfections, we see what’s common to all of them: worship of Krsna and meditation on Him. Therefore, Krsna concludes, “A learned devotee who worships Me through yoga meditation certainly obtains in all respects the mystic perfections that I have described.” (SB. 11.15.31)

The BBT purport adds, “\[E\]ach devotee obtains the particular perfection for which he has qualified himself.”

*Texts 32-35: One may achieve everything by devotional service to Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead*

*Text 32: Devotion to Krsna can award all mystic perfections*

Krsna moves toward His conclusion: “For a sage who has conquered bis senses, breathing, and mind, who is self-controlled and always absorbed in meditation on Me, what mystic perfection could possibly be difficult to achieve?” (SB. 11.15.32)

The yogi’s heroic attempts to control his senses, breathing, and mind ultimately facilitate the mind’s focus on Krsna. By concentrating on Krsna, as described throughout this chapter, one may attain all mystic perfections.

Thinking of Krsna (smaranam) is bhakti, which when practiced purely can award a far more exalted result than the perfections attained by mystics; bhakti can control the incomparably powerful Supreme Lord (SB. 11.12.1 2, 11.14.20).

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.1 5. 32 offers the comments of two acaryas. “Srila Sridhara Svami comments as follows: ‘Lord Krsna here expresses that there is no need to practice many different processes, for by completely carrying out even one of the above-mentioned procedures one controls one’s senses, becomes absorbed in Him, and thus achieves all mystic perfections.’

“Srila Jiva Gosvami notes that one must meditate on the transcendental form of the Lord, which is free from any material designation. This is the essence of advancing in the yoga system; thus one acquires all mystic perfections very easily from the personal body of the Personality of Godhead.”

Mystic perfections are attractive. They award one the ability to control matter and thereby enhance one’s capacity to enjoy. Just imagine having the power to acquire whatever you desire (prakamya), which makes whatever one finds most enjoyable in the world instantly available, or isita, the power to manipulate the subpotencies of maya. Who would not be allured? Yet all mystic potencies fall far short of the pleasure one can attain by serving the all-attractive Krsna.

In the first chapter of The Nectar of Devotion, Srila Prabhupada recites a prayer spoken originally by Prahlada Maharaja: “My dear Lord, I repeatedly pray to Your lotus feet that I may simply be stronger in devotional service. I simply pray that my Krsna consciousness may be stronger and steadier, because happiness derived from Krsna consciousness and devotional service is so powerful that with it one can have all the other perfections available through religiousness, economic development, sense gratification, and even the attainment of liberation from material existence.”

Srila Prabhupada continues: “Actually, a pure devotee does not aspire after any of these perfections, because the happiness derived from devotional service in Krsna consciousness is so transcendental and so unlimited that no other happiness can compare to it. It is said that even one drop of happiness in Krsna consciousness stands beyond comparison with an ocean of happiness derived from any other activity. Thus, any person who has developed even a little quantity of pure devotional service can very easily kick out all the other kinds of happiness derived from religiousness, economic development, sense gratification, and liberation.”

Therefore, rather than viewing these powers as valuable objects of attainment, devotees reject them as obstacles to their Krsna conscious advancement. Next, Krsna speaks this same truth to Uddhava.

*Text 33: Aspiring for and even attaining mystic perfections is an impediment*

Although Krsna can and will award a spiritual aspirant mystic siddhis, these powers still obscure actual perfection. Krsna continues: “Learned experts in devotional service state that the mystic perfections of yoga that I have mentioned are actually impediments and are a waste of time for one who is practicing the supreme yoga, by which one achieves all perfection in life directly from Me.” (SB. 11.15.33)

The root of the conditioned souls’ material existence is false ego, which creates in them a sense of separateness from Krsna. So they become independent enjoyers, with Krsna as their competitor. The attainment of siddhis tends to inflame the false ego, which is why sincere devotees don’t want them.

But is desiring these perfections for use in Krsna’s service against the principles of pure devotional service? Maharaja Pariksit asked Sukadeva Gosvami why Rsabhadeva Maharaja neglected to use his mystic powers, although he was completely pure, full in knowledge, and free from fruitive desires. Sukadeva’s reply cautions all sincere seekers of the Absolute Truth to be wary of the mind and its tendencies: “\[A\]fter capturing animals, a cunning hunter does not put faith in them, for they might run away. Similarly, those who are advanced in spiritual life do not put faith in the mind. Indeed, they always remain vigilant and watch the mind’s action. All the learned scholars have given their opinion. The mind is by nature very restless, and one should not make friends with it. If we place full confidence in the mind, it may cheat us at any moment.” (SB. 5.6.2-3)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura is strong and conclusive in his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.15.33: “These siddhis are amazing for the ignorant but not for the wise. For a person who is absorbed in attaining Me, the siddhis are a waste of time, and for those who desire these mystic perfections, day by day their wealth in the form of attaining Me decreases.”

*Text 34: Only bhakti awards the ultimate attainment*

All results available from other process may be obtained through bhakti, hut bhakti alone carries one to Krsna. The Lord continues: “Whatever mystic perfections can be achieved by good birth, herbs, austerities, and mantras can all be achieved by devotional service to Me; indeed, one cannot achieve the actual perfection of yoga by any other means.” (SB. 11.15.34)

The BBT purport notes: “By meditating exclusively on the Supreme Personality of Godhead one can achieve yoga-gad, the ultimate goal of yoga, which means living on Lord Krsna’s planet and there enjoying spiritual opulences.”

*Text 35: Krsna is the ultimate object searched for in all systems of spiritual inquiry*

Krsna now describes the relationship between Himself and every system of spiritual practice, whether it be yoga meditation, jnana, or Sankhya: “My dear Uddhava, I am the cause, the protector, and the Lord of all mystic perfections, of the yoga system, of analytic knowledge, of pure activity, and of the community of learned Vedic teachers.” (SB. 11.15.35)

Ultimately, Krsna is both the source and essence of all spiritual paths and practices. He is the source of the faith each follower experiences and is the master of and ultimate substance about which each follower inquires. From the BBT purport: “Lord Krsna is not merely the Lord of material yoga perfections, but of the highest liberated perfections as well. One can obtain Sankhya, or knowledge leading to liberation, by performing pious activities, and Lord Krsna is also the cause, protector, and Lord of such activities, as well as of the learned teachers who instruct ordinary people in the means of piety. In many different ways Lord Krsna is the real object of meditation and worship for every living entity. Lord Krsna through the expansion of His potencies is everything, and this simple understanding, called Krsna consciousness, is the supreme perfection of the yoga system.”

*Text 36: Leading to His next topic, Krsna points to Himself as the Supreme Personality of Godhead*

Krsna has just described Himself as “the cause, the protector, and the I ord of all mystic perfections, of the yoga system, of analytic knowledge, of pure activity, and of the community of learned Vedic teachers. Implied in ibis is that I le is supreme, and to further confirm His slums as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, He ends chapter 15 with a glimpse of His inconceivable opulence: “Just as the same material elements exist within and outside of all material bodies, similarly, I cannot be covered by anything else. I exist within everything as the Supersoul and outside of everything in My all-pervading feature.” (SB. 11.15.36)

Yogis may gain all kinds of mystic power, but that power is still just a drop from the ocean of Krsna’s power. Krsna is the Supersoul; He is all-pervading; He is within and without everything. Yet He is a person! This statement, which briefly reveals to Uddhava Krsna’s potency and opulence, prompts Uddhava to inquire further. Clearly, Uddhava now has a perspective on the opulences yogis may gain as well as the opulences Krsna has by virtue of His being the Supreme Lord.

**Chapter 16: The Lord’s Opulence \[Vibhuti\]**

*Texts 1-5: Uddhava’s request*

In the first text of this chapter, Uddhava lists eight exalted qualities that confirm that Krsna is the Supreme Lord. Krsna is (1) beginningless, (2) endless, (3) the Absolute Truth, (4) unlimited, (5) the protector, (6) the life-giver, (7) the destroyer, and (8) the creator of everything. Uddhava calls Krsna brahma paramam saksad, directly the Absolute Truth

But, Uddhava says, despite the fact that Krsna is within all superior and inferior creations, impious persons still can’t understand how He is present in everything that exists. Nevertheless, the brahmanas who actually know the Vedas worship Krsna in truth (whereas the impious worship Krsna’s manifestations but fail to worship Him).

Unconcerned with the impious, in two questions Uddhava asks Krsna only about the pious in two questions: “Please tell me of the perfections that great sages achieve by worshiping You with devotion. Also, kindly explain which of Your different forms they worship.” (SB. 11.16.3)

The purport to this third text in the chapter explains, “Sri Uddhava here inquires about the spiritual opulences of the Lord, which consist primarily of His visnu-tattva expansions such as Vasudeva, Sankarsana, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. By worshiping different plenary expansions of the Lord one achieves particular perfections, and Sri Uddhava wants to know about this.”

Next, Uddhava speaks about how the Supersoul, although present everywhere, remains unseen: “O my Lord, maintainer of all, although You are the Supersoul of the living entities, You remain hidden. Thus being bewildered by You, the living entities cannot see You, although You are seeing them.” (SB. 11.16.4)

Krsna is present in everyone and everything, yet no one perceives Him due to the bewildering effect of His maya. He thus remains forever unknown. As Srimati Kuntidevi says: “O Krsna, I offer my obeisances unto You because You are the original personality and are unaffected by the qualities of the material world. You are existing both within and without everything, yet You are invisible to all.” (SB. 1.8.18) But despite His being hidden from the conditioned souls, the conditioned souls are not hidden to the Supersoul: “\[T\]hey cannot see that person who is actually seeing them, and simply remain bewildered.” (SB. 11.16.4, purport)

Uddhava now asks a question that follows naturally from his state- ments in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.16.1-4: “O supremely potent Lord, please explain to me Your innumerable potencies (vibhutis), which You manifest on the earth, in heaven, in hell, and indeed in all directions. I offer my humble obeisances at Your lotus feet, which are the shelter of all holy places.” (SB. 11.16.5)

Sri Krsna just revealed Himself as existing “within everything as the Supersoul and outside of everything in My all-pervading feature.” (SB. 11.15.36) Although seeing the Supersoul is beyond any ordinary person’s ability, seeing Krsna as He manifests His opulences externally through His potencies is not. Uddhava is asking Krsna to reveal His spiritual potencies along with the opulences He manifests in this realm so that those limited to mundane vision can perceive His presence.

*Texts 6-8: Krsna begins his reply*

Krsna tells Uddhava that Arjuna asked Him the same question while i hey stood together on the Battlefield of Kuruksetra, because before ihe great battle, Arjuna had considered killing his relatives an abominable act. “Thus,” Krsna says, “Arjuna was afflicted with mundane Consciousness. At that time I enlightened Arjuna, the tiger among men.” (SB. 11.16.7-8)

*Texts 9-38: Krsna speaks of His vibhutis (opulences)*

Krsna describes His opulences, showing Himself as the active principle and powerful essence of all wonderful things in existence.He begins with a general description: “My dear Uddhava, I am the Supersoul of all living entities, and therefore I am naturally their well-wisher and supreme controller. Being the creator, maintainer, and annihilator of all entities, I am not different from them.” (SB. 11.16.9)

He then adds some specifics: “I am the ultimate goal of all those seeking progress, and I am time among those who exert control. I am the equilibrium of the modes of material nature, and I am natural virtue among the pious. Among things possessing qualities I am the primary manifestation of nature, and among great things I am the total material creation. Among subtle things I am the spirit soul, and of things that are difficult to conquer I am the mind. ”(SB. 11.16.10-11)

In the Paramatma Sandharba (anuccheda 33), Srila Jiva Gosvami speaks about what it means that the spirit soul (jiva) is the subtlest: “The jiva is the limit of smallness. It is not that he is subtle in the sense of being difficult to know.”

The Supreme Lord continues: I am Brahma, the original teacher of the Vedas. I am the three-lettered sound vibration om, and among sacred meters I am the Gayatri. “Among the demigods I am Indra, and among the Vasus I am Agni, the god of fire. I am Visnu (Vamana-deva) among the sons of Aditi, and among the Rudras I am Lord Siva.” (SB. 11.16.13) I am Narada Muni among saintly demigods (text 14) and Garuda among birds (text 15). “\[A\]mong the demoniac sons of Diti know Me to be Prahlada Maharaja, the saintly lord of the asuras. Among the stars and herbs I am their lord, Candra (the moon), and among Yaksas and Raksasas I am the lord of wealth, Kuvera.” (SB. 11.16.16) Among all things that heat and illuminate I am the sun, and among human beings I am the king (text 17). I am gold among metals and Yamaraja (death) among those who suppress and punish (text 18).

The ability of gold to attract people is the potency of Krsna. Unstoppable death is also his potency. Among animals with sharp horns and teeth He is the lion,among the social orders He is the fourth, or the renounced order of life. Among occupational divisions He is the first, the brahmanas (text 19), among sacred and flowing things He is the holy Ganges, and among steady bodies of water He is the ocean (text 20). Among residences He is Mount Sumeru, and of im- pervious places He is the Himalayas. Among trees He is the holy fig tree, and among plants He is the plants that bear grains (text 21).

The BBT purport to text 21 states: “Osadhinam here indicates those plants that fructify once and then die. Among them, those that give grains, which sustain human life, represent Krsna.”

Krsna continues, “Among sacrifices I am study of the Veda, and I am nonviolence among vows. Among all things that purify I am the wind, fire, the sun, water, and speech.” (text 23) He is samadhi, the final stage in yoga practice, and among speculative philosophers He is “diversity of perception” (SB. 11.16.24).

“Among ladies I am Satarupa, and among male personalities I am her husband, Svayambhuva Manu. I am Narayana among the sages and Sanat-kumara among brahmacaris.” (SB. 11.16.25). Among religious principles He is renunciation, and of all types of security He is consciousness of the eternal soul within. Of secrets He is pleasant speech and silence (text 26). (Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura notes that neither pleasant speech nor silence reveals a person’s mind.)

Among ages Krsna is Satya-yuga, the age of truth, and among those who divided the Vedas He is Krsna Dvaipayana Vedavyasa (text 28). Among those entitled to the name Bhagavan He is Vasudeva, “and indeed, you, Uddhava, represent Me among the devotees.” (SB. 11.16.29) From the BBT purport to text 29: “Although many great personalities are sometimes called Bhagavan, ultimately Bhagavan is the one supreme entity who possesses unlimited opulences... In the Lord’s catur-vyuha, or quadruple expansion, the first manifestation is Vasudeva, who here represents all of the Lord’s expansions in the visnu-tattva category.”

“I am Hanuman among the Kimpurusas, and among the Vidya-dharas I am Sudarsana.” (SB. 11.16.29) This is because Krsna had touched the fortunate Vidyadhara, Sudarsana, when He was in the form of a serpent, with His lotus foot.

“Among jewels I am the ruby, and among beautiful things I am the lotus cup.Among all types of grass I am the sacred kusa, and of oblations I am ghee and other ingredients obtained from the cow. Among the enterprising I am fortune, and among the cheaters I am gambling. I am the forgiveness of the tolerant and the good qualities of those in the mode of goodness. Of the powerful I am bodily and mental strength, and I am the devotional activities of My devotees. My devotees worship Me in nine different forms, among which I am the original and primary Vasudeva.” (SB. 11.16.30-32)

Srila Sridhara Svami, commenting on this text writes, “Among the nine forms used in worship by the devotees (satvatam), I am called Vasudeva. These forms are Vasudeva, Sahkarsana, Pradymuna, Aniruddha, Narayana, Hayagriva, Varaha, Nrsimha, and Brahma.” Brahma is one of the nine forms mentioned by Krsna and is worshiped as the Supreme Lord when Lord Visnu accepts the position of Brahma to perform the service usually ascribed to Brahma.

Sri Krsna continues to list His opulences: I am the steadiness of mountains and the fragrance of the earth (text 33). I am the sweet taste of water. Among brilliant things I am the sun. I am the effulgence of the sun, moon, and stars. I am the transcendental sound that vibrates in the sky (ether) (text 34).

The existence of the element earth is based on fragrance, the subtle form of the sense object (tan-matra) of the nose. Taste is the source and tan-matra of water, and sound the source and tan-matra of ether.

“Among those dedicated to brahminical culture I am Bali Maharaja, the son of Virocana, and I am Arjuna among heroes. Indeed, I am the creation, maintenance, and annihilation of all living entities. I am the functions of the five working senses - the legs, speech, anus, hands, and sex organs - as well as those of the five knowledgeacquiring senses - touch, sight, taste, hearing, and smell. I am also the potency by which each of the senses experiences its particular sense object.” (SB. 11.16.35-36)

*Texts 37-41: Krsna summarizes His opulences*

In these five texts Krsna summarizes the vastness of His uncountable opulences: the foundations of the universe as well as all extraordinary qualities are His potencies.

*Text 37: Krsna’s summary begins*

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti’s comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.16.37 says that Krsna has already given indications of His opulences by naming Himself as the best of a group or as the key element in a relationship. Now the Lord will again describe those opulences, but in a more generic way: “I am form, taste, aroma, touch, and sound; false ego; the mahat-tattva; earth, water, lire, air, and sky; the living entity; material nature; the modes of goodness, passion, and ignorance; and the transcendental Lord. All these items, along with knowledge of their individual symptoms and the steady conviction that results from this knowledge, represent Me.” (SB. 11.16.37)

Everything that exists is comprised of different combinations of Krsna’s potencies. Even the modes of nature, which inhibit our vision of Krsna, are neither separate from nor independent of Him, but are one of His potencies. Knowledge of Krsna’s energies — as well as what results from that knowledge - is also Krsna.

*Text 38: All existence rests on Krsna*

Krsna is now even more expansive in His decription of His opulence: “As the Supreme Lord I am the basis of the living entity, of the modes of nature, and of the mahat-tattva. Thus I am everything, and nothing whatsoever can exist without Me.” (SB. 11.16.38)

Krsna again reveals Himself as the basis of spiritual and material existence. What in this world can exist without the combination of living entities (jiva), the modes of nature, and the mahat-tattva, the source of matter ? The existence of all three universal foundations rests on Krsna.

*Text 39: Krsna’s opulences are uncountable*

The Supreme Personality of Godhead continues: “Even though over a period of time I might count all the atoms of the universe, I could not count all of My opulences which I manifest within innumerable universes.” (SB. 11.16.39)

The BBT purport speaks of Krsna’s unlimited opulences: “According to Srila Jiva Gosvami, kalena indicates that the Supreme Personality of Godhead is within every atom and can therefore easily calculate the total number of atoms. However, although the Lord is certainly omniscient, even He Himself cannot supply a finite number for His opulences, because they are infinite.”

In similar but more dramatic words, earlier in the Bhagavatam, Lord Brahma also expresses his - or anyone’s - inability to estimate Krsna’s qualities: “In time, learned philosophers or scientists might be able (o count all the atoms of the earth, the particles of snow, or perhaps even the shining molecules radiating from the sun, the stars, and other luminaries. But among these learned men, who could possibly count the unlimited transcendental qualities possessed by You, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who have descended onto the surface of the earth for the benefit of all living entities?” (SB. 10.14.7)

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura begins his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.16.39 with a question from Uddhava: ‘“Why are You summarizing Your opulence in a general way? As You did previously, please describe Your opulence by showing Yourself as the best within a group or as the key element in a relationship.’ Krsna replies, ‘After a great amount of time I could count all the atoms of the earth or the other elements and tell you their number. But I cannot say this about my vibhutis. When one is unable to count the number of universes that have been created, can one count the vibhutis within those universes?’”

*Text 40: Another way to think of Krsna’s opulences*

Krsna offers another way that His opulences can be categorized: “Whatever power, beauty, fame, opulence, humility, renunciation, mental pleasure, fortune, strength, tolerance, or spiritual knowledge there may be is simply an expansion of My opulence.” (SB. 11.12.40)

*Text 41: Conclusion*

“I have briefly described to you all My spiritual opulences and also the extraordinary material features of My creation, which are perceived by the mind and defined in different ways according to circumstances.” (SB. 11.16.41)

Srila Sridhara Svami notes that the Sanskrit words in this text indicate two distinct sets of opulences, spiritual and material. His spiritual opulences are His expansions, such as Vasudeva, Narayana, and the Supersoul, and His material opulences are the outstanding features of the material creation.

Srila Jiva Gosvami differentiates between the two. Krsna’s spiritual manifestations are eternal and beyond the perception of the material senses, and His material opulences can be perceived by conditioned souls. Both emanate from the Lord and both are His opulent energies (vibhutis), but they are not equal. Sri Jiva explains further: “\[T\]he paraphernalia and intimate associates of a king are all considered to be part and parcel of the king and are therefore granted royal status. Similarly, the opulent features of material creation are reflected expansions of the Lord’s personal opulences and thus may he considered nondifferent from Him. One should not, however, wrongly assume that such insignificant material opulences occupy the same status as the Lord’s plenary features as the Personality of Godhead, which are qualitatively and quantitatively equal to the Lord.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura also comments on this text. He explains that Krsna uses the Sanskrit words mano-vikara to indicate that conditioned souls perceive Krsna’s material opulences according to the transformations and sentiments of their own mind. If everything in existence is Krsna, then everything we see in this world is Krsna and only Krsna. But if we fail to note a thing’s connection to Krsna, what we see remains on the mental platform - incomplete and not helpful for our spiritual growth: “But vibhutis well known among people are identified through transformations of mind like affection and hatred. Those are not My vibhutis. Out of affection (a transformation of the mind) someone will designate another as ‘This is my son’ or ‘This is my father’ or ‘This is my uncle,’ ‘my nephew,’ ‘my friend.’ These are not vibhutis of the Lord. Where there is hatred (another transformation of the mind) one says, ‘This person is offensive to me,’ ‘This person should be offended,’ ‘This person hates me,’ ‘This person should be hated,’ ‘This person kills,’ ‘This person should be killed.’ These are not vibhutis of the Lord. Thus, although Indra is my vibhuti, if Saci says, ‘This is my husband,’ or if Aditi says, ‘This is my son,’ if Jayanta says, ‘This is my father,’ or Brhaspati says, ‘This is my disciple,’ if the demons say, ‘This is our enemy,’ those also are not vibhutis of the Lord.”

On the other hand, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti explains, “My devotees, without possessiveness, can say for all things, ‘This is the Lord’s opulence (vibhuti).’ However, the spiritual vibhutis may be thought of as son, brother, etc., without harm. One can treat in this way the avataras and devotees listed among the Lord’s opulent potencies, His vibhutis.”

*Texts 42-44: Krsna’s recommendations for the practical application of His words in this chapter*

*Text 42: Krsna’s words of instruction*

“Therefore, control your speaking, subdue the mind, conquer the life air, regulate the senses, and through purified intelligence bring your rational faculties under control. In this way you will never again fall onto the path of material existence.”

One who is self-controlled and devoted can surrender to Krsna and fulfill his life’s true purpose. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura tells us that everything in existence is manifest from the Lord and thus worthy of respect: “Since all objects (and persons) are My vibhutis, you should respect them all with your words, mind, and body and not belittle them.”

*Text 43: Krsna cautions the transcendentalists*

Krsna now gives more power to His previous words by stating them in the negative, or as a statement of warning about what happens when His words are not heeded: “A transcendentalist who does not completely control his words and mind by superior intelligence will find that his spiritual vows, austerities, and charity flow away just as water flows out of an unbaked clay pot.” (SB. 11.16.43)

*Text 44: Krsna emphasizes bhakti as He concludes*

What does Krsna want Uddhava and all the other souls to do once they’ve brought their purified speech, life air, senses, and intelligence under their control? They should surrender to Him and serve Him with devotion. Thus the Lord concludes chapter 16: “Being surrendered to Me, one should control the speech, mind, and life air, and then through loving devotional intelligence one will completely fulfill the mission of life.” (SB. 11.16.44)

**Chapter 17: Lord Krsna’s Description of the Varnasrama System**

*Texts 1-7: Uddhava asks about something already discussed - varnasrama-dharma*

*Texts 1-2: Uddhava’s first question - please explain the process of advancement for those whose tendency is to perform their prescribed duties*

In chapter 10 of the Eleventh Canto, Krsna briefly explained the purpose of the varnasrama system and how to practice it properly dutifully, with detachment, and to gain knowledge (SB. 11.10.1-13). In that same tenth chapter (texts 14—34), Krsna strongly criticized Jab mini Rsi’s followers, who maintain that the goal of following Vedic processes is unending material enjoyment. To counter Jaimini Rsi and his followers, Krsna ended His discussion of varnasrama by describing its goal: knowledge (SB. 11.10.11-13). Since then, Uddhava has heard of the practices and glorious purpose of juana-yoga (11.13.38-40), bhakti-yoga (11.12.10-13 and 11.14.1-29), and astanga-yoga (11.15.32-36). Now his attention returns to the topic of varnasrama-dharma, because he wants to hear how those inclined to execute their prescribed duties can advance toward Krsna’s lotus feet (tvayi bhaktir nrnam bhavet) (11.17.1-2).

*Texts 3-4: Uddava expresses a fear*

But there is a problem. Uddhava says, “My dear Lord, O mighty-armed one, previously in Your form of Lord Hamsa You spoke to Lord Brahma those religious principles that bring supreme happiness to the practitioner. My dear Madhava, now much time has passed, and that which You previously instructed will soon practically cease to exist, O subduer of the enemy.” (SB. 11.17.3-4)

Previously (in the thirteenth chapter of the Eleventh Canto) Lord Krsna as the Hamsa-avatara explained to Brahma and the Kumaras that one can only accurately understand an object when one sees it in relation to the Absolute Truth. Seeing everything connected to the Absolute Truth allows a meditator to discern the Absolute Truth even when the mind turns to sense objects. It is only by developing this exalted consciousness that one can end the disturbingly hard work of trying to separate the mind from its sense objects, the requirement for peaceful, focused meditation.

In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.13.38, the Hamsa-avatara stated that understanding this explanation of Sankhya and yoga would carry one to his or her actual religious duty, which the Kumaras defined as bhakti. It is this understanding of bhakti as the highest religious duty that awards one the highest happiness (dharmam paramakam) that Uddhava, in texts 11.1 7.3—4, fears will be lost when Krsna abandons the earth and returns to the spiritual world. After all, Krsna’s presence stalls Kali-yuga’s onslaught, which is characterized “by increasing avarice, falsehood, cheating and violence throughout the capital, state, home, and among individuals.” (SB. 1.15.37)

*Texts 5-7: Is it possible to realize the highest religious duty in Kaluyuga?*

Kali-yuga is filled with passion and ignorance. At best, passion impels people to endless hours of hard work. How, then, will they find time to cultivate goodness, practice austerity, or meditate, which are prerequisites to realizing the knowledge taught by the Hamsa-avatara? Krsna and Uddhava are speaking at the dawn of Kali-yuga. As the years pass, who will have the purity, sincerity, and goodness to approach the goal of spiritual life through an intellectual path based on renunciation and meditation? Both the path and its goal, bhakti, will soon disappear, Uddhava says, so please again teach us how one can practice bhakti by following varnasrama-dharma so that ordinary persons inclined to karma can learn this supreme religious principle.

“Thus, my dear Lord Madhusudana,” Uddhava says, “when You, who are the very creator, protector and speaker of spiritual knowledge, abandon the earth, who will again speak this lost knowledge? Therefore, my Lord, since You are the knower of all religious principles, please describe to me the human beings who may execute the path of loving service to You \[dharmas tvad-bhakti-laksanah\] and how such service is to be rendered.” (SB. 11.17.6-7)

*Texts 8-15: History of the varnasrama system*

Krsna begins His response by enumerating the eternal religious principles (dharman aha sanatanan, SB. 11.17.8) of varnasrama-dharma, but first He tells Uddhava the history of varnasrama-dharma.

*Texts 10-11: Varnasrama in Satya-yuga*

“In the beginning, in Satya-yuga, there is only one social class, called hamsa, to which all human beings belong. In that age all people are unalloyed devotees of the Lord from birth, and thus learned scholars call this first age Krta-yuga, or the age in which all religious duties are perfectly fulfilled.” (SB. 11.17.10) During this time, it is not necessary to practice secondary religious principles that lead up to pure devotional service. Rather, “In Satya-yuga the undivided Veda is expressed by the syllable mil, and I am the only object of mental activities. I become manifest as the four-legged bull of religion, and thus the inhabitants of Satya-yuga, fixed in austerity and free from all sins, worship Me as Lord Hamsa.” (SB. 11.17.11)

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.17.11 states: “Sri Vyasa- deva divided the one Veda into four - the Rg, Yajur, Sama, and Atharva Vedas - at the end of Dvapara-yuga, hut in Satya-yuga the whole of Vedic knowledge is easily understood by everyone simply by vibrating the syllable om. In this age there are no ritualistic or pious activities such as sacrifice, since everyone is sinless, austere, and fully engaged in worshiping the Personality of Godhead, Lord Hamsa, through the process of meditation.”

*Texts 12—15: Vedic knowledge and varnasrama-dharma manifest in Treta-yuga*

Krsna continues, “O greatly fortunate one, at the beginning of Treta-yuga Vedic knowledge appeared from My heart, which is the abode of the air of life, in three divisions - as Rg, Sama, and Yajur. Then from that knowledge I appeared as threefold sacrifice. In Treta-yuga the four social orders were manifested from the universal form of the Personality of Godhead.” (SB. 11.17.12-13)

The brahmanas appeared from the Lord’s face, the ksatriyas from His arms, the vaisyas from His thighs, and the sudras from His legs. Each social division was recognized by its particular duties and behaviors. The married order of life appeared from the loins of the Lord’s universal form, and the celibate students from His heart. The forest-dwelling retired order, vanaprasthas, appeared from His chest, and the sannyasis irom the head of His universal form.“The various occupational and social divisions of human society appeared according to inferior and superior natures manifest in the situation of the individual’s birth.” (SB. 11.17.15)

*Texts 16-22: Duties of each occupational category (vama)*

Quite similar to Krsna’s words to Arjuna in Bhagavad-gita 18.42-44, the Supreme Lord continues describing varnasrama to Uddhava. As in the Bhagavad-gita, Krsna’s descriptions of the duties of each varna address the qualities and character repaired for a person to take up a specific role in society. Clearly, the divisions are not “caste” hardened according to ones birth. Rather, to properly assume the role of any one of these varnas, one requires the requisite qualities. This is an obvious point. Does my father’s skill at neurosurgery automatically offer me the credentials to perform surgery? Qualities, training, and certification are required, and these supersede any opportunities my birth as his son may afford me.

Srila Prabhupada often spoke on this point. Here is one instance, from a lecture on the Bhagavad-gita (3.17-20), given in New York on May 27, 1966:

Formerly, according to varnasrama-dharma, it is not that “Because I am a brahmana’s son, therefore I am a brahmana,” just as the practice is going on now in India - caste system. Oh, that was not the system. The system was different... But according to sastra, scripture, such persons are not called brahmanas. They are called dvija-bandhu, “a friend of a brahmana." So just like “I am the son of a high-court judge.” That does not mean I am also high-court judge. I must be qualified to become a high-court judge. But if I go on, that “Because my father is high-court judge, therefore I am also high-court judge....” So these things are going on now in India. Because his forefather was a brahmana, or his father was a brahmana - and although he has no qualification of a brahmana, he also claims to be a brahmana. But the scripture, the Vedic scripture - that does not allow. They will call, “No, you are not a brahmana. You are brahmana’s son. That’s all. We can admit so far. There is no harm admitting you, that you are the son of a brahmana, but we cannot admit you a brahmana.” That is quite reasonable.

*Text 16: The qualities of brahmanas*

“Peacefulness, self-control, austerity, cleanliness, satisfaction, tolerance, simple straightforwardness, devotion to Me, mercy, and truthfulness are the natural qualities of the brahmanas.” (SB. 11.17.16)

*Text 17: The qualities of ksatriyas*

“Dynamic power, bodily strength, determination, heroism, tolerance, generosity, great endeavor, steadiness, devotion to the brahmanas, and leadership are the natural qualities of the ksatriyas.” (SB. 11.17.17)

*Text 18: The qualities of vaisyas*

“Faith in Vedic civilization, dedication to charity, freedom from hypocrisy, service to the brahmanas, and perpetually desiring to accumulate more money are the natural qualities of the vaisyas.” (SB. 11.17.18)

The BBT purport notes that the vaisyas have faith in the Vedic civilization and therefore desire to accumulate piety, which guarantees their future wealth. Thus the culture gradually translates their greed for future earnings into a freedom from hypocrisy and a dedication to charity in the present.

*Texts 19: The qualities of sudras*

Service without duplicity to the brahmanas, cows, demigods, and other worshipable personalities, and complete satisfaction with whatever income is obtained in such service, are the natural qualities of sudras.” (SB. 11.17.19)

The generosity of brahmanas, ksatriyas, and vaisyas is both natural and prescribed to insure that others in society are well cared for, regardless of their social status.

*Texts 20—21: The qualities of those outside and the general qualities of those inside the Vedic social order*

Those with the following qualities were given facility to live outside the Vedic society proper: “Dirtiness, dishonesty, thievery, faithlessness, useless quarrel, lust, anger, and hankering constitute the nature of those in the lowest position outside the varnasrama system.” (SB. 11.17.20)

General piety, however, was recommended for everyone — those who were members of the varnasrama system and those who were not. The next text (text 21) defines those pious qualities: “Nonviolence, truthfulness, honesty, desire for the happiness and welfare of all others, and freedom from lust, anger, and greed constitute duties for all members in Vedic society.” (SB. 11.17.21)

These pious qualities are foundational for individual and collective peace and jire generally conducive to spiritual advancement. In the gurukula, the traditional Vedic educational institution, children were placed in the association of learned and pure brahmanas to be trained in these qualities, the Vedic scriptures, and how to apply both qualities and scriptures in day-to-day life.

Although in this and the following chapter Krsna will describe the varnasrama system, it must be acknowledged that this system as it appears in the Vedic culture, with its stringent rules and regulations, cannot be rigidly imposed on the citizens of today’s world. Srila Prabhupada noted this in a lecture he gave on the Bhagavad-gita in London on July 17, 1973: “Not like at the present moment, a brahmana is working, \[like\] a servant, a sudra, and he is brahmana. No. This is called asuric varnasrama. Varnasrama is very good institution. But still, varnasrama, perfect varnasrama, cannot be possible in this age.”

Yet society should be efficiently structured, and varnasrama provides a structure that guides members of society to act according to roles that match their qualities and training. The details, of course, have to be adjusted to today’s world.

Srila Prabhupada also addressed this need for structure in a lecture on the Bhagavad-gita given in Ahmedabad on December 11, 1972: “Daiva-varnasrama-dharma - there must be the four divisions. Just like we have got four divisions in our body: the head division, the arm division, the belly division, and the leg division. The leg division is the sudra, the belly division is the vaisya, and the arm division is the ksatriya, and the head division is the brahmana. So these divisions are now lost. Actually, there is no ksatriya, no brahmana. Maybe there are some vaisyas and sudras. So suppose if your whole body - there is only belly and leg. Then what is the body? If you have no head and no arm, then how it is? What kind of body it is? So therefore, in the social order of the present day, there is no brahmana, no ksatriya. Only there are some few vaisyas and sudras. So therefore there is chaos all over the world.”

Srila Prabhupada wanted to establish rural, agrarian, self-sufficient varnasrama communities to set an example of an ideal and organized devotional lifestyle. These communities would be based on the principles of varnasrama-dharma and focused on simple living and high thinking.I have summarized in six points Srila Prabhupada’s basic teachings on varnasrama-dharma:

1\. A spiritually oriented society has an innate, systematic organization known as varnasrama-dharma, where the members of the society fit into two sets of four overlapping divisions. When the members of such a society learn to serve the Lord according to these natural divisions, society runs efficiently and brings happiness to the participating individuals.

*varnasramdcara-vata,*

*purusena parah puman*

*visnur aradhyate pantha*

*nanyat tat-tosa-karanam*

“The Supreme Personality of Godhead, Lord Visnu, is worshiped by the proper execution of prescribed duties in the system of varna and asrama. There is no other way to satisfy the Supreme Personality of Godhead. One must be situated in the institution of the four varnas and asramas.” (Caitanya-caritamrta, Madhya 8.58)
