2\. The essential purpose of the varnasrama system is to provide protection and shelter, allowing individuals to live peacefully and to make progress in their spiritual lives. Varnasrama society is compared to a body, with the head, arms, belly, and legs working harmoniously to fulfill the common interests of all parts, especially their interest in attaining spiritual perfection.

3\. Individuals’ places in a varnasrama sociey should be decided according to their qualities and inclinations, not simply their birth. The misapplication of varnasrama in contemporary India is called casteism. Casteism forces individuals into occupational functions strictly according to birth, regardless of their qualification or inclinations. Allowing persons to position themselves in society according to their guna and karma resolves the main objection to varnasrama - that it is an imposed injustice - and remedies its flawed application.

4\. In Kali-yuga, it’s almost impossible for people to follow all the prescribed Vedic injunctions in relation to the various varnasrama divisions. Yet it is possible to understand the basic form and function of varnasrama, and to apply it intelligently in order to reap the system’s benefits and help Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s sahkirtana movement take shape.

5\. All four asramas are meant for spiritual development. One should situate oneself in the asrama most suitable for oneself according to one’s age, circumstances, and level of detachment. One must be committed to the spiritual essence of one’s asrama while following the rules and regulations given for that asrama by sastra and adjusted according to time, place, and circumstances by Srila Prabhupada and other acaryas.

6\. The heart of the asramas: the essence of brahmacarya is celibacy, study, and service to the guru. The essence of grhastha life is to restrict sense enjoyment and to give in charity. One should engage one’s family and use one’s occupation for the pleasure of the guru and the Supreme Lord. Brahmacari householders should be esteemed by all. The essence of the vanaprastha-asrama is austerity. Vanaprasthas may remain celibate and either live near one’s wife or on their own. Male vanaprasthas may use their time in this asrama to prepare for sannyasa. And the essence of the sannyasa-asrama is celibacy, detachment, preaching, and dependence on Krsna.

Krsna now begins a more detailed description of the rigorous prescribed duties of the four asramas and will continue to describe these until the topic ends in chapter 18. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura notes in his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.17.22 that Lord Krsna particularly intends to describe the duties of the householder asrama, for by that “the duties of the varnas are naturally revealed.” Toward this end, Krsna lists, in nine texts, the duties of those in the brahmacari-asrama.

*Texts 23-38: The brahmacaruasrama*

*Texts 23-26: The basic practice of students is brahmacarya*

A brahmacari should live simply and peacefully. He should not decorate or care for his body in such a way that his body becomes appealing or attractive. He should control his mind and remain free from any type of sexual indulgence. Celibacy is essential for a brahmacari if he wishes his mind to remain peaceful and alert. He should control his speech, keeping silent at appropriate times. He should refrain from cutting his nails and hair, sit on simple seats rather than luxurious ones, and offer respect and worship to others, as appropriate.

*Text 27: Krsna defines the acarya*

*acaryarh mam vijaniyan*

*navamanyeta karhicit*

*na martya-buddhyasuyeta*

*sarva-deva-mayo guruh*

“One should know the acarya as Myself and never disrespect him in any way. One should not envy him, thinking him an ordinary man, for he is the representative of all the demigods.” (SB. 11.17.27)

Krsna tells Uddhava that the teacher should be seen as above material estimations. In the bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 211), Srila Jiva Gosvami quotes Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.17.27 to show the necessity of accepting a guru even for those on the karma path.

*Texts 28-31: The dynamic between teacher (guru) and brahmacari student*

Teachers naturally pass on their knowledge to students who maintain a mood of service: “In the morning and evening one should collect foodstuffs and other articles and deliver them to the spiritual master. Then, being self-controlled, one should accept for oneself that which is allotted by the acarya. While engaged in serving the spiritual master, one should remain as a humble servant, and thus when the guru is walking the servant should humbly walk behind. When the guru lies down to sleep, the servant should also lie down nearby, and when the guru has awakened, the servant should sit near him, massaging his lotus feet and rendering other, similar services. When the guru is sitting down on his asana, the servant should stand nearby with folded hands, awaiting the guru’s order. In this way one should always worship the spiritual master. Until the student has completed his Vedic education, he should remain engaged in the asrama of the spiritual master, should remain completely free of material sense gratification, and should not break his vow of celibacy \[brahmacarya\].” (SB. 11.17.28-30)

Today, few people attend a gurukula, and serving one’s teacher may seem to have nothing to do with the quality of education one receives. Serving one’s teacher may even seem counterproductive - even dangerous in the face of modern educational realities. How will being submissive prepare one to face life’s si niggles? And won’t being submissive possibly make one vulnerable to some sort of abuse? Shouldn’t com- petition, high achievement, and technological expertise be the rubric to guarantee success?

To understand the purpose behind submitting to one’s teacher requires one to understand the goal of the Vedic educational system. Character training was foremost, and strong, self-disciplined individuals its product. Students would graduate as self-controlled members of society. Learning to control oneself when young and impressionable can save students incalculable suffering in their lives.

In addition, as Srila Prabhupada mentioned in Melbourne in 1974, the mind becomes “fertile” for spiritual life when one remains celibate between the ages of sixteen and twenty-one.

Toward this end, both sastra and the Vedic culture dictated that a gurukula student practice submission to his teacher. It is natural for young children to obey adults, so to learn submission to authority from an early age helps develop a willingness to subordinate the mind, along with its unlimited desires, to higher authority. Step by step, as the young student matures, the guru trains him to transfer his submission to external authority to submission to his own internal authority, his matured intelligence, which the guru has trained to have proper discrimination based on sastra. Thus a student graduates with the best chance at a successful life, because he has determination, focus and, especially, strength of character.

The full submission to authority a student gives his teacher allows the teacher to mold the student’s character, something largely absent in contemporary teacher-student relationships. In gurukula, students begin young, studying under a venerable teacher, someone learned, pure, and kind. The culture outside the gurukula was also supportive of such teacher-student relationships. Naturally, few students rebelled against their teachers in that system. Much of the difficulty one would encounter today if one were to try to impose the gurukula system on children would have been absent during Vedic times.

Veneration of teachers - and seniors in general - is natural to the human psyche, but it runs contrary to the mood of contemporary life, which is based on a model of social Darwinism - that is, the unspoken duty of the young to surpass their elders, who are, by definition, less evolved.

What underpins Vedic society (and most more natural civilizations) is that wisdom is passed from the old to the young, along with time-honored practices and cultural expressions. We can understand, with this frame of reference, the importance of students learning to defer to their teachers.

*Texts 32-36: Practices for the brahmacaris who choose not to marry*

Krsna now instructs those who want to achieve the higher realms of the material universe. For such people, it is necessary to maintain life-long celibacy and to study under the guidance of an acarya. Krsna first describes how a brahmacan dedicated to lifelong celibacy and with suitable qualifications will worship the Supreme Absolute Truth: “Thus enlightened in Vedic knowledge by service to the spiritual master, freed from all sins and duality, one should worship Me as the Super- soul, as I appear within fire, the spiritual master, one’s own self, and all living entities.” (SB. 11.17.32)

To achieve such a vow of sustained celibacy, brahmacaris (and other celibates in the varnasrama framework) were restricted from freely mingling with the opposite sex. “Those who are not married - sannyasis, vanaprasthas, and brahmacaris - should never associate with women by glancing, touching, conversing, joking, or sporting. Neither should they ever associate with any living entity engaged in sexual activities.” (SB. 11.17.33)

*Texts 34-35: Basic principles for everyone*

Finally, Krsna offers the basic principles required for brahmacaris but recommended for all members of Vedic society. Those who follow these principles are guaranteed success, and when society as a whole adheres lo them, there is peaceful interaction between all society’s members. “My dear Uddhava, general cleanliness, washing the hands, bathing, performing religious services at sunrise, noon, and sunset, worshiping Me, visiting holy places, chanting japa, avoiding that which is untouchable, uneatable, or not to be discussed, and remembering My existence within all living entities as the Supersoul - these principles should be followed by all members of society through regulation of the mind, words, and body.” (SB. 11.17.34-35)

Text 36: Bhakti - the result of proper following

And what is the fruit of cultivating this tree of Vedic brahmacan life? “A brahmana observing the great vow of celibacy becomes brilliant like fire and by serious austerity burns to ashes the propensity to perform material activities. Free from the contamination of material desire, he becomes My devotee \[mat-bhaktah\].” (SB. 11.17.36)

The true goal of Vedic education, therefore, with its methodology of submission, service, sense and mind control, and celibacy has now been named: to become Krsna’s bhakta.

*Texts 37-38: The brahmacari completes his education*

*Text 37: Practices for brahmacaris who plan to become householders*

“A brahmacari who has completed his Vedic education and desires to enter household life should offer proper remuneration to the spiritual master, bathe, cut his hair, put on proper clothes, and so on. Then, taking permission from the guru, he should go back to his home.” (SB. 11.17.37)

Krsna Himself went through these steps, as described in the forty-fifth chapter of the Tenth Canto. Here is Srila Prabhuapda’s summary from the Krsna book:

Lord Krsna and Balarama, the reservoir of all knowledge, exhibited Their perfect understanding of all the arts and sciences mentioned above. Then They offered to serve Their teacher by awarding him anything he desired. This offering by the student to the teacher or spiritual master is called guru-daksina. It is essential that a student satisfy the teacher in return for any learning received, either material or spiritual. When Krsna and Balarama offered Their service in this way, the teacher, Sandipani Muni, thought it wise to ask Them for something extraordinary, something no common student could offer. He therefore consulted with his wife about what to ask from Them. He and his wife had already seen the extraordinary potencies of Krsna and Balarama and could understand that the two boys were the Supreme Personality of Godhead. They decided to ask for the return of their son, who had drowned in the ocean near the shore at Prabhasa-ksetra.

Krsna accomplished this mission for his guru and returned the boy to Sandipani Muni. “The brothers asked if Their teacher had anything more to ask from Them, but he replied, ‘My dear sons, You have done enough for me. I am now completely satisfied. What further want can there be for a man who has disciples like You? My dear boys, You may now go home. These glorious acts of Yours will always be renowned all over the world. You are above all blessing, yet it is my duty to bless You. I therefore give You the benediction that whatever You speak will remain as eternally fresh as the instructions of the Vedas. Your teachings will be honored not only within this universe or in this millennium but in all places and ages and will remain increasingly new and important.’ Due to this benediction from His teacher, Lord Krsna’s Bhagavad-gita is ever increasingly fresh and is renowned not only within this universe but in other planets and other universes also.”

*Text 38: Moving on from the brahmacari-asrama*

Depending on their desire and inclination, after leaving their spiritual master’s asrama, students may marry or else live at home with their families. They are also free to accept the vanaprastha order, or if brahmanas, to take sannyasa. Krsna’s description of changing one’s asrama ends with these words: “One who is not surrendered to Me should move progressively from one asrama to another, never acting otherwise.” (SB. 11.17.38)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on this text creates both interest and surprise: “One enters an asrama according to one’s qualification. If he has desires, he becomes a householder. If he has no desires due to having a purified heart, he becomes a vanaprastha. If he is a brahmana and is without desire, he becomes a sannyasi. Some persons desire to go through all the asramas - brahmacari, grhastha, vanaprastha, and finally sannyasa. One should not enter the asramas in a reverse order, and one should not live without an asrama - unless one is Krsna’s devotee. If one is a devotee, then one does not have to follow the rules of asrama. ... If a devotee enters asramas in a different order or has no asrama, there is no fault.”

*Texts 39-44: The householder asrama*

*Text 39: Choosing a wife*

“One .who desires to establish family life should marry a wife of his own caste \|sadrsim\|, who is beyond reproach, and younger in age. If one desires to accept many wives he must marry them after the first marriage, and each wife should be of a successively lower caste.” (SB. 11.17.39)

Maintaining peace and congenial dealings among family members is essential for both progressive family life and a progressive society. To help establish peace, the Vedic society recommends marriage between those of similar qualities, mentalities, and habits (sadrsim). It also ere- ates an authority structure within a family by recommending that subsequent wives be of lower castes than the first wife. This is to minimize the inevitable struggle between false egos.

*Text 40: Prescribed duties of householders*

“All twice-born men - brahmanas, ksatriyas, and vaisyas - must perform sacrifice, study the Vedic literature, and give charity. Only the brahmanas, however, accept charity, teach the Vedic knowledge, and perform sacrifice on behalf of others.” (SB. 11.17.40)

Sri Krsna gave this same principle to Arjuna: “Acts of sacrifice, charity, and penance are not to be given up; they must be performed. Indeed, sacrifice, charity, and penance purify even the great souls.” (Bhagavad-gita 18.5)

*Texts 41-43: How householder brahmanas achieve perfection*

“A brahmana who considers that accepting charity from others will destroy his austerity, spiritual influence, and fame should maintain himself by the other two brahminical occupations, namely teaching Vedic knowledge and performing sacrifice. If the brahmana considers that those two occupations also compromise his spiritual position, then he should collect rejected grains in agricultural fields and live without any dependence on others.” (SB. 11.17.41)

Knowing that in the future he will reap the results of his spiritual attainments and austerities helps a brahmana maintain his spiritual focus. By being tolerant and focusing on the future his present piety will grant him, he avoids having to continually circumvent the material inconveniences that so characterize modern life. The brahmana practices being self-satisfied in all circumstances and faithfully cultivates the exalted quality of trusting Krsna’s promise to protect Hjs devotees.

He may even practice the great austerity of making no endeavour for his own maintenance and remain fully dependent on God. In this way, a householder brahmana may live at home with minimal attachment. Even so, he may practice generosity. How can an impoverished person he generous? As his primary religious principle, a highly qualified brahmana may distribute whatever he gains through his study, austerity, and performance of sacrifice. And by absorbing his consciousness in Krsna, he will advance. Krsna says about the consciousness of such great souls: With his mind dedicated to Me (mayy arpitatma), he attains liberation (SB. 11.17.43).

*Text 44: Krsna’s reciprocation with those who help His impoverished brahmana devotees*

Brahmanas who practice these principles may become extremely poor. Sudama Brahmana provides an example of this type of brahmana. Krsna expresses His dedication to these brahmanas by offering great rewards to those who care for and protect such austere souls: “Just as a ship rescues those who have fallen into the ocean, similarly, I very quickly rescue from all calamities those persons who uplift brahmanas and devotees suffering in a poverty-stricken condition.” (SB. 11.17.44)

The BBT purport adds: “The Lord has described how brahmanas and devotees achieve the perfection of life, and now a similar perfection is offered to those who utilize their materialistic wealth to relieve the poverty-stricken condition of devotees and brahmanas… Just as a boat saves hopeless people who have fallen into the ocean, similarly, the Lord uplifts persons who have hopelessly fallen into the ocean of material attachment if they have been charitable to the brahmanas and devotees.” Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on the same text is important: “The result of serving brahmanas with devotion by giving diem wealth is described. The Lord saves not only persons who save devotee brahmanas, but He also saves those who save any devotee.” Next, Krsna will describe the duties of ksatriya householders.

*Texts 45-46: Prescribed duties for ksatriya kings*

“Just as the chief hull elephant protects all other elephants in his herd and defends himself as well, similarly, a fearless king, just like a lather, must save all of the citizens from difficulty and also protect himself. An earthly king who protects himself and all citizens by removing all sins from his kingdom will certainly enjoy with Lord Indra in airplanes as brilliant as the sun.” (SB. 11.17.45-46)

A ksatriya protects his citizens from physical harm just as a father protects his children. While protecting their bodies, he simultaneously protects them from the harm that comes from living a sinful life.

*Texts 47-49: Varnasrama duties and emergency times*

For a social system to be effective, it cannot be overly rigid; it must be flexible when times are difficult, such as during periods of extreme poverty, which might come about - for example, during a famine. Clearly, a system like varnasrama has to be practical. Krsna will now describe how to adjust the principles of varnasrama during trying circumstances.

A brahmana who is poverty-stricken can buy and sell items, acting like a merchant. If he is unable to alleviate his condition through the work of a vaisya, he can take sword in hand (khadgena) and behave like a ksatriya. But he cannot accept employment like a sudra. Similarly, a ksatriya who is in difficulty may take on the work of a vaisya. He may also hunt or even teach others like a brahmana. “But he cannot in any circumstances become like a dog, accepting an ordinary master.” (SB. 11.17.47) Although a ksatriya is more highly placed than a vaisya in the varn- asrama system, Krsna nevertheless first recommends that a brahmana in financial difficulty take on the work of a vaisya. Why? Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura answers this question: “One may think that taking up ksatriya duties would be superior to vaisya duties, but according to the Lord, the vaisya occupation is superior to the ksatriya occupation for a brahmana because ksatriya duties often necessitate violence.” And why shouldn’t a brahmana accept employment as a sudra does? “One should not maintain oneself by serving low persons.”

Similarly, Krsna explains, in emergency times, ksatriyas may act as vaisyas, live by hunting, or, like brahmaitas, live by teaching Vedic knowledge to others. But under no circumstances should they adopt the profession of a sudra.

The psychology behind this is simple. Working for others as an employee tends to make one want to please one’s employer. Working for an employer of low character would therefore tend to degrade one. For this reason, the main protectors of society the brahmanas and the ksatriyas are prohibited from demeaning themselves by accepting employment. In addition, working for others tends to crush one s integrity and sense of independence, both of which are necessary for social leaders on whom others depend to set an example of strong moral principles.

Krsna concludes the topic of duties during exceptional circumstances with instructions for the vaisyas and sudras: “A vaisya, or mercantile man, who cannot maintain himself may adopt the occupation of a sudra, and a sudra who cannot find a master can engage in simple activities like making baskets and mats of straw.” (SB. 11.17.49)

Although Krsna validates here the necessity to somehow or other survive, He also validates the need to maintain an ordered society by adding a universally applicable caveat to these instructions for emergency times: “However, all members of society who have adopted inferior occupations in emergency situations must give up those substitute occupations when the difficulties have passed.” (SB. 11.17.49)

So Krsna has given instructions that are flexible when strict following is too difficult and yet supportive of the overall social structure.

*Texts 50-58: A householder’s worship of Krsna through prescribed duties*

*Texts 50-51: Further instructions for householders*

**Householders serving Krsna by worshiping specific items**

A householder should worship (1) the sages by studying sastra, (2) the forefathers and demigods by offering them appropriate mantras, (3) all living beings by offering them a share of their meals, and (4) humans by offering them grains and water.

Sri Krsna continues: “Thus considering the demigods, sages, fore-fathers, living entities and human beings to be manifestations of My potency, one should daily perform these five sacrifices.” (SB. 11.17.50)

**Optional Duties**

A householder “should comfortably maintain his dependents either with money that comes of its own accord or with that gathered by hones! execution ol one’s duties. According to one’s means, one should perform sacrifices and other religious ceremonies.” (SB. 11.17.51)

A householder’s tendency to be selfish and accumulate too much is counterbalanced by nurturing a charitable attitude. In addition to using his money to comfortably maintain his dependents, a householder should support others along with maintaining his own practice of spiritual life.

*Texts 52—54: A householder should remain mindful that all material relationships are temporary*

Krsna offers sober words to the householders: “A householder taking care of many dependent family members should not become materially attached to them, nor should he become mentally unbalanced, considering himself to be the lord. An intelligent householder should see that all possible future happiness, just like that which he has already experienced, is temporary. The association of children, wife, relatives, and friends is just like the brief meeting of travelers. With each change of body one is separated from all such associates, just as one loses the objects one possesses in a dream when the dream is over. Deeply considering the actual situation, a liberated soul should live at home just like a guest, without any sense of proprietorship or false ego. In this way he will not be bound or entangled by domestic affairs.” (SB. 11.17.52-54)

Here Krsna’s weighty instructions on varnasrama-dharma are unsentimental. They may make us uncomfortable, but they are meant to protect us from the misery of attachment to the temporary, to those things that will sink in the stormy waves of time. From the BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.17.52: “A family man often acts like a lord, protecting his wife, ordering his children, maintaining servants, grandchildren, domestic animals, and so forth… one should remember that all material enjoyment, either here or in the next life, is temporary and ultimately useless. A responsible householder should guide his family members and other dependents back home, back to Godhead, for an eternal life of bliss and knowledge. One should not become a false and puffed-up lord for a brief span of time, for then one will remain bound up, along with his family members, in the cycle of repeated birth and death.”

And from the BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.17.53: “An intelligent person realizes there is no actual pleasure or satisfaction for the soul on either this planet or any other material planet. Therefore, like a weary traveler exhausted from his journey, he should go back home, back to Godhead, for eternal peace as the faithful servant of Lord Sri Krsna.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments on text 52, saying that these verses are primarly aimed at householder jnanis who are detached from their material activities (karmas): “Although detached, he should not be inattentive or mentally imbalanced, but should focus on hearing and remembering the Lord. He should see that his family is perishable. He sees that a future birth in heaven is as temporary as is his present life, and he gives up the desire for both.”

*Text 55: Three alternatives for householders who are about to die*

“A householder devotee who worships Me by execution of his family duties may remain at home, go to a holy place, or, if he has a responsible son, take sannyasa.” (SB. 11.17.55)

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments that a “householder desiring jnana can choose his asrama. A devotee leaving his family members may also choose his asrama in order to take the opportunity to practice bhakti."

*Texts 56-58: Faults in material attachment*

Krsna now condemns householders who remain attached to hearth and home, for such attachment brings greatly unfortunate results: “But a householder whose mind is attached to his home and who is thus disturbed by ardent desires to enjoy his money and children, who is lusty after women, who is possessed of a miserly mentality, and who unintelligently thinks, ‘Everything is mine and I am everything,’ is certainly bound in illusion. ‘O my poor elderly parents, and my wife with a mere infant in her arms, and my other young children! Without me they have absolutely no one to protect them and will suffer unbearably. How can my poor relatives possibly live without me?’ Thus, because of his foolish mentality, a householder whose heart is overwhelmed by family attachment is never satisfied. Constantly meditating on his relatives, he dies and enters into the darkness of ignorance.” (SB. 11.17.56-58)

Members of the Vedic culture considered it the purpose of life to awaken the eternal soul’s relationship with the Absolute Truth. Parallel. to that, Vedic culture provided a lens, formed from scistra, through which one could live aware of the fleeting relationship between the soul and the mundane. Whatever nourishes these realizations is condoned; whatever inhibits them is condemned. Here, varnasrama culture, by the nature of its structure and knowledge-filled practices, nurtures material detachment and dependence on Krsna.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura further describes the faulty mentality Krsna just mentioned in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.17.57. His comments are meant to be both dramatic and confronting: “I have a one-month-old baby! Without me, the baby cannot survive! He will be attacked by enemies! I have a two-year-old. Without me - without a protector - how can my child live?”

**Chapter 18: Description of Varnasrama-dharma**

*Texts 1-11: Going to the forest - the vanaprastha order*

*Texts 1-9 Austerities of the vanaprasthas*

Like everyone in every asrama, householders get old, with time stealing their youth and mercilessly walking them toward death. In old age, therefore, the Vedic culture encourages one to prepare for the next life by increasing detachment from family comforts, which he will soon be forced to leave behind, by adopting the vanaprastha order and entering the forest to perform austerities.

So having spoken about brahmacaris and householders, Krsna now begins to describe the vanaprasthis. “The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: One who desires to adopt the third order of life, vanaprastha, should enter the forest with a peaceful mind, leaving his wife with his mature sons, or else taking her along with him.” (SB. 11.18.1)

Vanaprasthis should simplify their eating and dress by gathering both food and clothing from whatever is available in the forest. They may eat bulbs, roots, and fruits and dress themselves in cloth made of tree bark, grass, leaves, or the skins of animals that have died a natural death. They should sleep on the ground and bathe thrice daily, immersing themselves in water without scrubbing their bodies. They should not groom themselves; they should care for the body in the simplest fashion. In this way, vanaprasthis will strengthen the mind and increase their detachment.

Vanaprasthis can learn to become more tolerant by sitting in the center of a circle of fires during the heat of summer, standing outside in the pouring monsoon rains, and submerging themselves in chilly water in the freezing winter. Wherever practical, they should refrain from stocking provisions for the future. The vanaprasthis should offer the appropriate Vedic ritual fire sacrifices, such as the agnihotra, darsa, or paurnamasa, and perform the caturmasya vow. But they should never offer sacrifices of animals or eat meat (texts 1-8).

The essence of the vanaprastha life is to help a householder transition from material comfort to material detachment as a preparation for inevitable death. Extreme austerities are half the recommended vehicle to attain this. In the Bhagavad-gita (2.59) Krsna emphasizes the second half of the vehicle: the cultivation of a higher spiritual taste. There, He tells Arjuna, “The embodied soul may be restricted from sense enjoyment, though the taste for sense objects remains. But, ceasing such engagements by experiencing a higher taste, he is fixed in consciousness.”

*Texts 9-10: The results of a vanaprasthi’s austerities*

As vanaprasthis accept only the bare necessities of life, they may become so thin that their veins are visible under their skin. Yet their severe penances, offered in worship of Krsna (Krsna says in SB. 11.18.9, mam tapo-mayam aradhya: “worshiping Me through severe penances”) carry the vanaprasthis first to Maharloka (if they are not yet fully Krsna conscious) and then directly to Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. One who performs these difficult penances to fulfill material desires is the greatest fool (text 10).

*Text 11: An old and frail vanaprastha*

“If the vanaprastha is overtaken by old age and because of his trembling body is no longer able to execute his prescribed duties, he should place the sacrificial fire within his heart by meditation. Then, fixing his mind on Me, he should enter into the fire and give up his body.” (SB. 11.18.11)

Clearly, the goal of those in the vanaprastha order is to realize that the eternal soul lives forever while the body is temporary. The BBT purport adds a practical note: “Although ibis may not be possible in the modern age, we can appreciate the absolute seriousness of going back home, back to Godhead, as evidenced in this verse.”

*Texts 12-41: Sannyasa*

Sri Krsna now describes the sannyasa-asrama, the topmost asrama in the varnasrama structure.

It is interesting to note the number of texts the Supreme Lord devotes to each of the four asramas. Earlier, in chapter 17, Sri Krsna spoke of the vanaprastha order in eleven texts. Now, in chapter 18, He will speak thirty texts about the sannyasa-asrama, from Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.18.12-41. In the previous chapter, chapter 17, Krsna first introduced varnasrama-dharma and spoke of its history. He then described the brahmacari-asrama in fifteen texts, from Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.17.23-38. In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.17.39-43, Krsna described the basic duties of householders. In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.17.44-49, He delineated those duties of householders further, focusing on living within one or another of each of the four varnas. Krsna then again spoke about householders in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.17.50-58. So in total, Krsna described the brahmacari-asrama in fifteen texts, the householder asrama in twenty texts, the vanaprastha-asrama in eleven texts - all far less than the thirty texts He devotes to describing the sannyasa-asrama. Clearly, Krsna is emphasizing the importance of sannyasis in a varnasrama society.

*Texts 12-29: The stages of sannyasa*

In chapter 18, Krsna describes the sannyasa-asrama to Uddhava in five successive sections: entering the sannyasa-asrama from the vanaprastha-asrama (texts 12-14), guidance for sannyasis (texts 15-27), the actions of perfected sannyasis (texts 28-37), instructions for sannyasis advancing toward perfection (38-39), and condemnation of sannyasis who have poor character (texts 40-41).

*Texts 12-14: Entering the sannyasa-asrama from the vanaprastha-asrama*

The detached vanaprasthis who have truly realized the inherent misery in every material situation, from the topmost to the lowest, are qualified to accept sannyasa. Such rare souls should worship Krsna according to scriptural injunctions (istva yathopadesam mam), renounce all possessions, and, with a fully detached mind, enter the sannyasa order of life (texts 12-13).

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.18.13 offers wise words of caution to sannyasis: “Any material desire will gradually prove to he a stumbling block in the prosecution of renounced life. Therefore, a liberated sannyasi must vigilantly remain free from the weeds of material desires, which surface principally in the form of attachment to women, money, and reputation.”

It is rare that anyone can become this detached. Sri Krsna explains why this is so: “ ‘This man taking sannyasa is going to surpass us and go back home, back to Godhead.’ Thus thinking, the demigods create stumbling blocks on the path of the sannyasi by appearing before him in the shape of his former wife or other women and attractive objects. But the sannyasi should pay the demigods and their manifestations no heed.” (SB. 11.18.14)

To this text the BBT purport adds: “Lord Krsna here encourages all sannyasis by telling them, ‘Pay no attention to such illusory manifestations. Continue your duties and go back home, back to Godhead.’ ”

*Texts 15-27: Guidance for sannyasis*

*Text: 15: Possessions*

Because material attachment stultifies a sannyasi’s desire for advancement, his dress and possessions are regulated: “If the sannyasi desires to wear something besides a mere kaupina, he may use another cloth around his waist and hips to cover the kaupina. Otherwise, if there is no emergency, he should not accept anything besides his danda and waterpot.” (SB. 11.18.15)

Text 16: Purity

To help a sannyasi practice ahimsa, even while walking, to ensure that impure water does not contaminate his consciousness and to help him remain pure in thoughts and speech, Sri Krsna offers specific prescriptions to protect him: “A saintly person should step or place his foot on the ground only after verifying with his eyes that there are no living creatures, such as insects, who might he injured by his foot. He should drink water only after filtering it through a portion of his cloth, and he should speak only words that possess the purity of truth. Similarly, he should perform only those activities his mind has carefully ascertained to be pure.” (SB. 11.18.16)

*Text 17: Internal disciplines*

Integrity in the sannyasa order is maintained by three internal disciplines: “avoiding useless speech, avoiding useless activities, and controlling the life air.” A sannyasi who neglects these three disciplines is “never considered a sannyasi merely because of his carrying bamboo rods.”

*Texts 18-19: Prescriptions for eating*

“Rejecting those houses that are polluted and untouchable, one should approach without previous calculation seven houses and be satisfied with that which is obtained there by begging. According to necessity, one may approach each of the four occupational orders of society.” (SB. 11.18.18) One should then eat in a secluded place, while still offering charity of the begged food to anyone who may need food. The sannyasi should leave no remnants nor save food for eating later.

Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura is quoted in the BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.18.18 about three ways to beg alms: “Madhukara is the process of imitating the bee, who collects a tiny amount of nectar from each flower. In this way, the saintly person accepts a very small amount from each person, avoiding social conflict. The process mentioned here is asanklpta, by which one indiscriminately approaches seven houses, being satisfied with whatever may be obtained. Prakpranita is that process by which one establishes regular donors and collects one’s maintenance from them.”

The purport to text 19 also quotes Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura: “\[A\] saintly person should not argue or quarrel with materialistic persons who may request or demand part of his foodstuff. ... \[O\]ne should give something to such persons to avoid disturbance, and then, offering the remnants to Lord Visnu, one should eat everything on one’s plate, without saving food for the future.... \[O\]ne should not eat in a public place ... one should eat silently, meditating upon the Lord’s mercy.”

*Texts 20-21: Prescriptions for sannyasis who travel and for those who live in one place*

The sannyasi should be free of material attachment, and with controlled senses, enthusiasm, and satisfaction in his realization of the Lord, he should travel the world alone, fixed in the equal vision born of the spiritual platform. His dwelling place should be safe and solitary, and his thinking purified by constant meditation on the Supreme Lord. His attention should be concentrated on the soul and its relationship with the Supreme.

Srila Jiva Gosvami comments on text 21 in the bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 227) that this text describes bhakti mixed with the processes of jnana (jnana-misra-bhakti). Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments that meditating on the jiva as nondifferent from the Paramatma is for those who want undifferentiated oneness with the Lord, or sayujya-mukti. (In other words, this instruction is not for devotees.)

*Texts 22—23: Discriminatory thinking*

Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.18.22—23 offers sannyasis both knowledge and prescriptions to carry them from bondage to liberation. Sannyasis should know what causes bondage and what causes liberation: “Bondage occurs when the senses are deviated to sense gratification, and complete control of the senses constitutes liberation.” (SB. 11.18.22) They should therefore control their “five senses and the mind by Krsna consciousness,” and “having experienced spiritual bliss within the self... live detached from insignificant material sense gratification.” (SB. 11.18.23)

*Texts 24-25: Instructions for sannyasis who travel*

Krsna prescribes travel, detachment, solitary living, freedom from illusion, begging, humility, and purification: “The sage should travel in sanctified places, by flowing rivers and within the solitude of mountains and forests. He should enter the cities, towns, and pasturing grounds and approach ordinary working men only to beg his bare sustenance.” (SB. 11.18.24) He should practice taking charity from others, and thereby become free of illusion. Obtaining one’s eatables in this humble manner purifies a sannyasi’s existence.

*Texts 26-27: Detachment through discrimination*

One should never see as ultimate reality those material things which will perish. With consciousness free from attachment to this world and the next, he should withdraw from all activities meant for material progress. “One should logically consider the universe, which is situated within the Lord, and one’s own material body, which is composed of mind, speech, and life air, to be ultimately products of the Lord’s illusory energy. Thus situated in the self, one should give up one’s faith in these things and should never again make them the object of one’s meditation.” (SB. 11.18.27)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura writes, in relation to text 26: “How can one give up sweets and develop an inclination for coarse grains collected from the field ? One should not see things like food as substantial, since they are temporary and will be destroyed. Being unattached to this world and the next, one should become disinterested in activities to obtain such things.”

*Texts 28-37: The actions of a perfected sannyasi*

The paramahamsa'sannyasi, who has reached perfection either through jnana or bhakti, no longer needs to follow the rules and regulations of varnasrama-dharma. Still, he conceals his exalted position because he hopes to avoid the adulation the general public naturally offers advanced souls. Sri Krsna suggests an appropriate cloak: “Although most wise, the paramahamsa should enjoy life like a child, oblivious to honor and dishonor; although most expert, he should behave like a stunted, incompetent person; although most learned, he should speak like an insane person; and although a scholar learned in Vedic regulations, he should behave in an unrestricted manner.” (SB. 11.18.29)

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura extracts practical guidelines from text 28: “Complete indifference to things is impossible for a devotee who has not developed prema. Thus the devotee who has developed prema can give up his asrama along with the all signs of his asrama (such as his stick and water pot), but one who has not developed love for Krsna gives up the actions of the asramas hut not its external signs.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti quotes Srimad-Bhagavatam 11,20.9 to indicate the purpose of sastric rules and regulations and why they should not be prematurely renounced: “As long as one is not satiated by fruitive activity and has not awakened his taste for devotional service by sravanam kirtanam visnoh, one has to act according to the regulative principles of the Vedic injunctions.”

Only one who has already fulfilled the exalted purpose of the varnasrama rules and regulations has the right to give them up. From the BBT purport to text 29: “Although neglecting ordinary rules and regulations, a paramahamsa does not ever become sinful or immoral, but rather neglects ritualistic aspects of religious custom, such as dressing in a particular way, performing certain ceremonies, or executing specific penances and austerities.”

Sri Krsna next adds caveats to His advice on how to keep one’s exalted status hidden: Yet he should not conceal his exalted nature to the degree that he participates in Vedic karma-kanda fruitive rituals, becomes atheistic, acts or speaks in opposition to the Vedas, speaks like a mere logician or skeptic, or takes any side in a useless argument. These activities are so detrimental to spiritual life that they shouldn’t even he done for show. He should neither become frightened nor disturbed, nor should he frighten or disturb others. He should create no hostility with others for the sake of his body. He should see the Supersoul in all bodies. Viewing all bodies as composed of the Lord’s energy, he should be respectful and careful in his dealings with all creatures, regardless of their insignificance. Fixed in the understanding that his life is fully under God’s control, he should neither become joyful nor depressed by the quality of food he receives. Still, “one should endeavor to get sufficient foodstuffs, because it is always necessary and proper to maintain one’s health. When the senses, mind, and life air are lit, one can contemplate spiritual truth, and by understanding the truth one is liberated. A sage should accept the food, clothing, and bedding — be they of excellent or inferior quality — that come of their own accord.” (SB. 11.18.34-35)

The BBT purport to text 34 tells us how to make this ideal of total detachment practical: “If foodstuffs do not come automatically or by token begging, then one should endeavor to keep body and soul together so that one’s spiritual practices will not be disturbed.” Sincere devotees protect their life for service, and therefore they keep Krsna’s pleasure central in everything they do.

It is difficult to follow these injunctions, hut Krsna Himself freely adheres to them despite 11 is position as the all-powerful cynosure of existence. Therefore, as Krsna orders in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.18.36, even a mature sage should follow these regulations, not by force, but just as He does.

The BBT purport to text 36 explains the perfected jnani-sannyasi’s mood: “A self-realized soul is a servant of Lord Krsna and not of rules and regulations. Nevertheless, a transcendentalist strictly complies with regular duties for the pleasure of the Supreme Lord... Lord Krsna is discussing the paramahamsa stage of life, and those who are attached to the material body have nothing to do with this paramahamsa stage, nor should they exploit its unique privileges and status.”

Krsna completes His instructions about how perfected sannyasis should act by describing the results that await them: “A realized soul no longer sees anything as separate from Me, for his realized knowledge of Me has destroyed such illusory perception. Since the material body and mind were previously accustomed to this kind of perception, it may sometimes appear to recur; but at the time of death the self-realized soul achieves opulences equal to Mine.” (SB. 11.18.37)

*Texts 38-39: Instructions for sannyasis advancing toward perfection*

Krsna now instructs those sincere sannyasis who have not yet attained perfection but who desire to advance further: “One who is detached from sense gratification, knowing its result to be miserable, and who desires spiritual perfection, but who has not seriously analyzed the process for obtaining Me, should approach a bona fide and learned spiritual master. Until a devotee has clearly realized spiritual knowledge, he should continue with great faith and respect and without envy to render personal service to the guru, who is nondifferent from Me.” (SB. 11.18.38-39)

*Texts 40-41: Krsna criticizes sannyasis of poor character*

The purport to text 41 states that Krsna concludes his discussion on sannyasis with a condemnation “of bogus personalities who adopt the sannyasa order of life for sense gratification while still maintaining all of the symptoms of gross illusion.” “One who has not controlled the six forms of illusion \[lust, anger, greed, excitement, false pride, and intoxication\], whose intelligence, the leader of the senses, is extremely attached to material things, who is bereft of knowledge and detachment, who adopts the sannyasa order of life to make a living, who denies the worshipable demigods, his own self, and the Supreme Lord within himself, thus ruining all religious principles, and who is still infected by material contamination, is deviated and lost both in this life and the next.” (SB. 11.18.40-41)

*Texts 42-43: The essential duty of each asrama, and the ultimate goal of each asrama*

Having completed His detailed description of the many stringent regulations required for those in each of the four asramas, in text 42 Krsna summarizes the essential duty of each asrama:

1\. “The main religious duties of a sannyasi are equanimity and nonviolence ...”

2\. “... for the vanaprastha austerity and philosophical understanding of the difference between the body and soul are prominent.”

3\. “The main duties of a householder are to give shelter to all living entities and perform sacrifices ...”

4\. “... \[T\]he brahmacari is mainly engaged in serving the spiritual master.” (SB. 11.18.42)

The Lord’s final instructions for householders (given in text 43) is this: despite the householders’ tendency to remain absorbed in family affairs until the moment of death, they should use their life as a vehicle for spiritual progress: “A householder may approach his wife for sex only at the time prescribed for begetting children. Otherwise, the householder should practice celibacy, austerity, cleanliness of mind and body, satisfaction in his natural position, and friendship toward all living entities.” (SB. 11.18.43)

If both husband and wife follow these principles, they can be said to be living in an asrama, a position that allows them to make spiritual advancement.

This topic almost complete, Krsna next tells Uddhava that the duty common to each asrama is sarvesam mad-upasanam: “Worship of Me is to be practiced by all human beings, regardless of social or occupational divisions.” (SB. 11.18.43)

Krsna indicates that worshiping Him - bhakti - is both the essence and goal of karma. He has already pointed to bhakti as the goal of jnana and yoga, and now the Supreme Lord has done the same for karma. The essence of karma is born of prescribed duties in the Vedic social system, varnasrama.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on text 43 discusses both the householder asrama and the essence of every asrama: “The method of the householder’s brahmacarya is described: he should approach his wife only while she is fertile. However, everyone must worship Me, since I give life to all of varnas and asramas. Without that worship, all varnas and asramas are useless.”

*Texts 44-48: Transforming prescribed varnasrama duties (karma) into devotional service (bhakti)*

Expanding on the point He just made, Krsna now speaks of the true purpose of karma and practicing varnasrama-dharma: one should transform one’s duties under varnasrama into bhakti. “One who worships Me by his prescribed duty, having no other object of worship, and who remains conscious of Me as present in all living entities, achieves unflinching devotional service unto Me.” (SB. 11.18.44)

The BBT purport to this text translates it into a summary of Krsna’s instructions on varnasrama: “It is clearly explained in this verse that loving devotional service unto Lord Krsna is the ultimate goal of the entire varnasrama system, which the Lord has been elaborately explaining. In any social or occupational division of human society one must be a devotee of the Supreme Personality of Godhead and worship Him alone.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments: “By this method, since everyone must worship Me (in the varnasrama system), when one understands that worshiping Me is the superior process and so worships Me through his occupational duties, with exclusive devotion to that worship, he attains bhakti in santa-rasa." But, he notes, the duties prescribed by the Vedas for one’s varna or asrama may require that one worship the demigods. Does worshiping the demigods stand in the way of one’s performance of pure bhakti? His reply to this question points again to Krsna’s words in the text: “One should see the Supreme Lord as present in all living entities as Paramatma.”

Srila Prabhupada summarized the entire varnasrama system and its purpose in a lecture on the Bhagavad-gita in Delhi on November 3, 1973:

Atah pumbhir dvija-srestha varnasrama-vibhagasah. There are divisions. In the human society there should be divisions of work. The activities for the most intellectual person - that should be a division. That is called brahmana division. The activities of the politicians and administrators — that is called ksatriya division. The activities of the mercantile people - that is called vaisya division. And ordinary worker - they get some salary for serving the master, they are called sudras. So in this way everybody has got his duty. The brahmana has got his duty, the ksatriya has got his duty, the vaisya has got his duty, and the sudras also, they have got also duty. Similarly, brahmacan, he has got his duty. And the grhastha, householder, they have got their duties. And vanaprastha, retired life, they have got their duties, and the sannyasi, renounced order of life, they have got their duties. The first division \[is\] called varna: brahmana, ksatriya, vaisya, sudra. And the second division is called asrama. So Vedic civilization means varna and dsrama, the human society divided into varnas and asramas. So everyone has got his particular duty.

Therefore Suta Gosvami \[says\] atah pumbhir dvija-sresthah: “O the best of the brahmanas.” Varnasrama-vibhagasah. Every varna, caste or division of the society, social division. And dsrama means spiritual division. Varnasrama-vibhagasah. As there are divisions so ... svanusthitasya dharmasya. Everyone has got his duty to do something particular. But whether he is perfect in discharging that duty, that may be considered when, svanusthitasya dharmasya samsiddhih, perfection. What is that? Hari-tosatiam. Whether you have satisfied the Supreme Personality of Godhead by your duty... after doing something, the activities should be tested, whether by such activities, the Supreme Lord is satisfied.

*Text 45: Knowledge about Krsna supports bhakti*

And why should the entire society he organized to satisfy Krsna? As He has done many times during His instructions to Uddhava, Krsna describes I Its postion as the unlimitedly powerful Supreme Personality of Godhead: ‘My dear Uddhava, I am the Supreme Lord of all worlds, and I create and destroy this universe, being its ultimate cause. I am thus the Absolute Truth, and one who worships Me with unfailing devotional service comes to Me.” (SB. 11.18.45)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura illuminates the principle of Krsna’s reciprocating with each soul according to his desire: “By that bhakti, some also attain Me. As the Lord of all planets. I, the giver of power equal to my own, give him liberation in the form of sarsti \[the attainment of opulences similar to Krsna’s\]. Some attain Me as the cause of all creation and destruction. I create for them the bliss of the jnana- and yoga-siddhis that they desire, and I destroy samsara for them. Some attain me as Brahman. I give these persons impersonal liberation.”

The BBT purport summarizes the point - that Krsna reciprocates with each soul according to that soul’s desire: “Lord Krsna absorbs the impersonal philosophers into the rays of His body, appears before the perfect yogis as the Lord of the heart, and ultimately brings His pure devotees back to His own abode for an eternal life of bliss and knowledge.”

*Texts 46-48: Krsna’s summary*

*Text 46: Achieving Krsna through performance of varnasrama duties*

Jnanis attain their desired goals through their laboriously acquired knowledge, renunciation, and austerity. Devotees, on the other hand, may quickly attain Krsna simply by performing their duties. Krsna summarizes this section with these words: “Thus, one who has purified his existence by execution of his prescribed duties, who fully understands My supreme position, and who is endowed with scriptural and realized knowledge, very soon achieves Me.” (SB. 11.18.46)

*Text 47: The results of varnasrama when dedicated to Krsna*

“Those who are followers of this varnasrama system accept religious principles according to authorized traditions of proper conduct. When such varnasrama duties are dedicated to Me in loving service, they award the supreme perfection of life.” (SB. 11.18.47)

Krsna stressed the principle of serving Him through one’s prescribed duties throughout the Bhagavad-gita for example, in Bhagavad-gita 18.45-46. Srila Prabhupada’s purport to this Gita text is clear: “Everyone should think that he is engaged in a particular type of occupation by Hrsikesa, the master of the senses. And by the result of the work in which one is engaged, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Sri Krsna, should be worshiped. If one thinks always in this way, in full Krsna consciousness, then, by the grace of the Lord, he becomes fully aware of everything. That is the perfection of life. The Lord says in Bhagavad-gita (12.7), tesam aham samuddharta. The Supreme Lord Himself takes charge of delivering such a devotee. That is the highest perfection of life. In whatever occupation one may be engaged, if he serves the Supreme Lord he will achieve the highest perfection.”

In the Bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 224), Srila Jiva Gosvami notes two ways one can offer his work to the Lord. The first is to perform the work for His pleasure, and the second is to offer Krsna the results of the work once it is completed. Sri Jiva then cites the Kurma Purana: “May the Supreme Personality of Godhead always be pleased with this work. One who always thinks in this way offers his work to the Supreme. Or one may also offer the results of one’s work to the Supreme Personality of Godhead. The sages say that this is also a peerless offering to the Supreme.”

*Text 48: Krsna has answered Uddhava’s question*

My dear saintly Uddhava, I have now described to you, just as you inquired, the means by which My devotee, perfectly engaged in his prescribed duty, can come back to Me, the Supreme Personality of Godhead.” (SB. 11.18.48)

Krsna concludes His instructions on varnasrama-dharma, in chapters 17 and 18, by referring back to Uddhava’s original question, asked in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.17.1-2: My dear lotus-eyed Lord, now please explain to me how all human beings can achieve loving service unto You by the execution of their prescribed duties.”

As the Lord previously describedfollowing prescribed duties for material pleasure, He has now established the best alternative, revealing to Uddhava that the execution of prescribed duties may also lead to worshiping Krsna with devotion. Krsna has definitively answered 1 Jddhava s question in chapters 17 and 18. He will now again return to l he topic of jnana.

**Chapter 19: The Perfection of Spiritual Knowledge**

*Texts 1-7: Give up knowledge and the processes to attain it*

In the previous two chapters, Krsna described varnasrama-dharma and illuminated its goal. Now the Supreme Lord turns again to the path of knowledge, for the Lord wishes to point out that a sincere soul who has realized the falsity of the material world and the reality of the eternal soul should nevertheless move forward in his spiritual life to the path of devotional service. “The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: A self-realized person who has cultivated scriptural knowledge up to the point of enlightenment and who is free from impersonal speculation, understanding the material universe to be simply illusion, should surrender unto Me both that knowledge and the means by which he achieved it.” (SB. 11.19.1)

The knowledge and processes Krsna instructs sages to renounce pertain to liberation from the world of maya. Moving forward from that, Krsna wants the jnani to become His devotee, just as He wants astanga-yogis and karma-yogis to adopt the devotional path. In his comment on this first text of chapter 19, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura stresses that jnana practices should be neglected once their purpose has been fulfilled: “Understanding that the universe arises from ignorance through false identity with his body and related objects, or understanding that this world is temporary, he renounces both jnana and jnana-sadhana in order to attain Me.”

The BBT purport adds: “\[O\]nce one is situated on the transcendental platform, both knowledge of illusion and the process of acquiring such knowledge have no further practical application. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura gives the example that a man may be haunted by the ghost of a snake or a tiger. As long as the man is possessed and thinks, ‘I am a snake’ or ‘I am a tiger,’ attempts will be made to counteract the ghostly influence by application of jewels, mantras, and herbs. But when the man is freed from being possessed by the ghost, he again thinks, ‘I am Mr. So-and-so, the son of Mr. So-and-so,’ and returns to his original nature. At that time the jewels, mantras, and herbs have no further immediate application.”

*Text 2: Will bhakti also one day he renounced?*

One may wonder, If I am now required to renounce the goal and processes of jnana, will I one day be asked to also renounce bhakti! Krsna replies: “For learned, self-realized philosophers I am the only object of worship, the desired goal of life, the means for achieving that goal, and the settled conclusion of all knowledge. Indeed, because I am the cause of their happiness and their freedom from unhappiness, such learned souls have no effective purpose or dear object in life except Me.” (SB. 11.19.2)

So Krsna’s response is a resounding “No!” Krsna Himself is the object of worship, the goal, the means, the definitive conclusion of all processes, as well as the dearest object in life. Neither He nor bhakti, the means to attain Him, will ever be something to be renounced.

When Krsna declares that He is “the means” (hetuh), it indicates that the processes that stimulate one’s advancement in bhakti, such as sravanam, kirtanam, and smaranam, are Krsna Himself. This is far different from the processes of jnana, yoga, and karma, where there the means and the end are different.

From the BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.19.2: “Material attachments are certainly problems for the living entities, since they are diseases of the spirit soul... Since material desire is a disease of the soul, one must acquire knowledge to treat this disease and eliminate it. Such therapeutic knowledge is essential as long as one is diseased, but when one is fully healthy, such technical medical knowledge is no longer interesting to the healthy person... After giving up constant meditation on such problems, one can then become a lover of God.”

*Text 3: The object of perfect knowledge*

A jnani’s path is to obtain knowledge, which leads to the goal of liberation. Krsna instructed jnanis to give up both their process and their goal. Now He instead points these exalted souls to the loftiest, most perfect goal: “Those who have achieved complete perfection through philosophical and realized knowledge recognize My lotus feet to be the supreme transcendental object. Thus the learned transcendentalist is most dear to Me, and by his perfect knowledge he maintains Me in happiness.” (SB. 11.19.3)

The greatest of jnanis, the Four Kumaras, were entranced and then transformed when they focused their pure attention on Krsna’s lotus feet “When the breeze carrying the aroma of tulasi leaves from the toes of the lotus feet of the Personality of Godhead entered the nostrils of those sages, they experienced a change both in body and in mind, even though they were attached to the impersonal Brahman understanding.” (SB. 3.15.43) Thus they became devotees of the Supreme Lord and very dear to Him.

*Text 4: Comparing this perfection to other attainments*

Krsna continues, “That perfection which is produced by a small fraction of spiritual knowledge cannot be duplicated by performing austerities, visiting holy places, chanting silent prayers, giving in charity, or engaging in other pious activities.” (SB. 11.19.4)

Clearly, the all-knowing, all-powerful Supreme Personality of Godhead considers the attainment of His own lotus feet the supreme goal.This is not a declaration born of false pride on Krsna’s part; rather, it is something He discloses to His dear devotee Uddhava as a revelation of absolute truth by the Absolute Truth. In the Bhagavad-gita (10.12-14), Arjuna evokes the authority of great sages while speaking the same conclusion: “You are the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the ultimate abode, the purest, the Absolute Truth. You are the eternal, transcendental, original person, the unborn, the greatest. All the great sages such as Narada, Asita, Devala, and Vyasa confirm this truth about You, and now You Yourself are declaring it to me. O Krsna, I totally accept as truth all that You have told me. Neither the demigods nor the demons, O Lord, can understand Your personality.”

*Texts 5-6: Krsna’s conclusion and its confirmation*

Krsna now summarizes His instructions to the jnanis: “Therefore, My dear Uddhava, through knowledge you should understand your actual self. Then, advancing by clear realization of Vedic knowledge, you should worship Me in the mood of loving devotion \[bhaja mam bhakti-bhavatah\].” (SB. 11.19.5) This is how the great sages in the past attained perfection, for they too knew Me as the Supersoul and the Supreme Lord of sacrifices.

So Krsna is emphasizing the shift from the development of discriminative knowledge, jnana, to the deepest realization of the soul’s relationship with Krsna, or bhaja mam bhakti-bhavatah - worship of Krsna “in the mood of loving devotion.” Srila Sridhara Svami states that text 5 indicates that all other processes should be given up.

In the Bhagavat Sandarbha (anuccheda 90), Srila Jiva Gosvami notes that the Kumaras and Sukadeva Gosvami are examples of self-satisfied, self-realized souls (atmaramas) that have progressed from jnana to bhakti.

*Text 7: Foundational spiritual truth*

Krsna s words now climb down from the topmost secret of bhakti to a lower, more basic rung, where He discusses knowledge: “My dear Uddhava, the material body and mind, composed of the three modes of material nature, attach themselves to you, but they are actually illusion, since they appear only at the present, having no original or ultimate existence.” (SB. 11.19.7)

The body and its workings, both subtle and gross, are the interactions of the modes of nature. They are unreal. Unlike the soul, who is the person inhabiting the body, they are ephemeral. After His words establish this basic spiritual truth, Krsna takes Uddhava - and through him, us - to the next logical step: the temporary body and the eternal soul are independent of each other. How is it possible, He says, for the various stages a body goes through - birth, growth, reproduction, maintenance, dwindling, and death - to have any relationship with the eternal self? These phases of life relate only to the material body, which has no original existence” (it appeared somewhere in the stream of time, but not at the souls point of origin) and “no ultimate existence” (it will disappear somewhere in the stream of time). The body exists merely in the present.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains why Krsna is speaking these basic spiritual truths after already having established more exalted understandings: “The jnani endowed with knowledge and realization then worships Me as the highest goal. But I am a distant goal. So first, he should rise above ignorance, knowing he is an eternal soul. As if directing his words to Uddhava, the Supreme Lord addresses people in general in this verse.”

*Texts 8—10: Uddhava inquires further*

Having just heard of the need to renounce both the process and product of the path of jnana, and having heard Krsna speak of the need to “worship Me in the mood of loving devotion” (SB. 11.19.5), Uddhava asks Krsna to speak further about serving Him with devotion. Uddhava first glorifies Krsna as the Lord anti the form of the universe (visvesvara, visva-murti), and then asks Him to explain not jnana or karma but the process of knowledge that:

1\. automatically brings detachment

2\. automatically gives direct perception of the truth

3\. is transcendental

4\. is traditionally understood by great spiritual philosophers

5\. is sought after by elevated personalities

Uddhava qualifies the knowledge he wants to hear still further as describing “loving devotional service unto Your Lordship” (tvad-bhakti-yogam).

In his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.19.8, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura notes that the specific names by which Uddhava has addressed Krsna - visvesvara (Lord of the universe) and visva-murti (form of the universe) - indicate Uddhava’s negation of the Mayavada philosophical conclusions. Mayavadis contend that the universe is illusory and false. Would Uddhava’s calling Krsna Visvesvara and Visvamurti feel true to a Mayavadi? Clearly, calling out to Krsna as the Lord and controller of something that has only an imagined existence would sound, even to a Mayavadi, absurd or even insulting.

According to Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti, the jnana Uddhava now wishes Krsna to speak is superior to the knowledge about the existence of the eternal soul he has just heard; Uddhava wishes to hear about Brahman, God. Ultimately, however, Uddhava wants to hear the most extraordinary jnana, knowledge of the service of Krsna’s divine lotus feet. Krsna has just named His lotus feet as the loftiest goal and the supreme, transcendental, shelter-giving object (padam srestham vidur mama, SB. 11.19.3), and Sri Uddhava wants to hear more about those lotus feet: “My dear Lord, for one who is being tormented on the terrible path of birth and death and is constantly overwhelmed by the threefold miseries, I do not see any possible shelter other than Your two lotus feet, which are just like a refreshing umbrella that pours down showers of delicious nectar.” (SB. 11.19.9)

In Kali-yuga, people require shelter from the harsh storms and intense suffering so common in this age. But the umbrella of the Lord’s lotus feet do more than simply protect. Uddhava’s prayer to Krsna paints a far more extraordinary picture. This umbrella not only protects us from external suffering but simultaneously showers with nectar those who have achieved its shelter.

The BBT purport comments: “Lord Krsna, recognizing Uddhava’s highly intellectual nature, has repeatedly recommended to him that one should achieve perfection by cultivation of transcendental knowledge. But the Lord has also clearly demonstrated that such knowledge must bring one to the point of loving devotional service to Him, for otherwise it is useless. In this verse Uddhava corroborates Lord Krsna’s statements that actual happiness is obtained by surrendering to His lotus feet.”

Uddhava humbly concludes his request with a prayer for instruction: “O almighty Lord, please be merciful and uplift this hopeless living entity who has fallen into the dark hole of material existence, where the snake of time has bitten him. In spite of such abominable conditions, this poor living entity has tremendous desire to relish the most insignificant material happiness. Please save me, my Lord, by pouring down the nectar of Your instructions, which awaken one to spiritual freedom.” (SB. 11.19.10)

Uddhava is equating Krsna’s instructions with the protection an umbrella offers from a heavy rain, but makes us think of the nectar-rain (hat falls from under the shelter of the umbrella itself. Both the protection and the nectar shower help a soul awaken to its eternal life. The BBT purport comments: “Sri Uddhava... appeals to the Lord to be kind to... poor fallen souls, humbly represented by his own self. If one receives t lie Lord’s mercy, then even without any further qualification one can go back home, back to Godhead; and without the mercy of Lord Krsna, i lie most learned, austere, powerful, wealthy, or beautiful man will be pathetically crushed by the material world’s machinery of illusion.... The Lord’s mercy is manifest in the form of His nectarean instructions such as die Bhagavad-gita and the Uddhava-gita, being spoken here.”

Although he actually wants to hear about bhakti, Uddhava again asks about jnana. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains why in bis comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.19.10: ‘“Why ask about puma if pure bhakti can award success?’ Uddhava answers with Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.19.10. Pure bhakti does not arise by human effort, since it can only be attained by the mercy of great devotees. Jnana-yoga can easily be attained by niskama-karma, working without attachment to the results, be cause that leads to knowledge of the self. Therefore, jnana- yoga can be attained by human effort. Those who do not attain pure bhakti easly be delivered by jnana. For ibis reason I have asked You about jnana. Please sprinkle me with the sweetness of Your words, which bestow liberation. The nectar of jnana coming from Your moonlike mouth will produce liberation.”

*Texts 11-18: Krsna speaks about jnana (knowledge), vijnana (self-realization), and vairagya (detachment)*

*Texts 11-13: Krsna repeats the words of Bhismadeva*

Krsna tells Uddhava He will repeat what Bhismadeva told Yudhisthira about the path of liberation: “I will now speak unto you those religious principles of Vedic knowledge \[jnana\], detachment \[vairagya\], self-realization \[vijnana\], faith \[sraddha\], and devotional service \[bhakti\] that were heard directly from the mouth of Bhismadeva.” (SB. 11.19.13)

Texts 14-16: Krsna speaks about jnana and vijnana

“I personally approve of that knowledge by which one sees the combination of nine, eleven, five, and three elements in all living entities, and ultimately one element within those twenty-eight.” (SB. 11.19.14)

Next, Krsna defines self-realization (vijnana) as seeing behind the twenty-eight elements their one ultimate cause. That one element is the Paramatma, the Supersoul. In his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.19.15, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura differentiates between jnana and vijnana. Jnana he defines as knowing that everything in existence arises from the Supersoul, who is the cause of all effects, without seeing the Supersoul Himself. Vijnana, on the other hand, is the direct experience of Paramatma. In such an understanding one does not see the temporary material effects the Paramatma has caused “because the bliss of realizing the Paramatma” leaves one with “no opportunity to see His products.” This, Visvanatha Cakravarti writes, “is a realization of oneness.”

Next, in text 16, Krsna defines that one eternal, the Paramatma, as He who accompanies all matter as it transforms through its three phases of creation, maintenance, and dissolution yet remains alone both prior to matter and after matter is annihilated. In this way the Paramatma is the lone, uncaused cause of everything. He alone possesses absolute existence, is the cause of all causes, and is the ultimate entity.

In his comment on this text 16, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura points out that knowing that everything in existence and the Paramatma are one, is the realization of those on the level of jnana. “There is only one entity, the Paramatma. This is again stated. That which exists during creation and, after transformation, during destruction - that which continues as the shelter while effect after effect is produced, and which remains after the final destruction - is the real and eternal cause... At the stage of jnana, one should see the non-duality of the Paramatma.”

*Texts 17-18: Vairagya*

Krsna next explains vairagya, detachment, by indicating that all four forms of evidence (mentioned in text 17, below) point to the wisdom of detaching oneself from the relentless shifting of matter as it appears, transforms, and vanishes in the flux of its temporary existence. Detachment, therefore, is the natural product of true knowledge and wisdom. Krsna says: “From the four types of evidence - Vedic knowledge, direct experience, traditional wisdom, and logical induction - one can understand the temporary, insubstantial situation of the material world, by which one becomes detached from the duality of this world. An intelligent person should see that any material activity is subject to constant transformation and that even on the planet of Lord Brahma there is thus simply unhappiness. Indeed, a wise man can understand that just as all that he has seen is temporary, similarly, all things within the universe have a beginning and an end.” (SB. 11.19.17-18)

*Texts 19-26: Krsna speaks about bhakti*

In chapters 12 and 14, Krsna told Uddhava about pure bhakti. Several texts ago, in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.19.8, Uddhava asked Krsna to speak about jnana, vairagya, and vijnana, but he also asked Him to speak again about the great path, bhakti - the knowledge that “describes loving devotional service unto Your Lordship.” Having spoken about the first three topics, Krsna will now speak about bhakti: “O sinless Uddhava, because you love Me, I previously explained to you the process of devotional service. Now I will again explain the supreme \[param\] process \[karanam\] for achieving loving service unto Me \[mad-bhakteh\].” (SB. 11.19.19)

*Texts 20-24: Fifteen elements ofbhakti*

Krsna lists fifteen powerful elements that form the means (karanam) to achieve the supreme (param) quality, devotional service to Him (mad-bhakteh). Here is the Sanskrit to texts 20-24. I have broken the translation up element by element and added in relevant points from Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura, or the BBT purport. I have also occasionally made my own comments:

*sraddhamrta-kathayam me*

*sasvan mad-anukirtanam*

*parinistha ca pujayam*

*stutibhih stavanam mama*

*adarah paricaryayam*

*sarvangair abhivandanam*

*mad-bhakta-pujabhyadhika*

*sarva-bhutesu man-matih*

*mad-arthesv anga-cesta ca*

*vacasa mad-guneranam*

*mayy arpanam ca manasah*

*sarva-kama-vivarjanam*

*mad-arthe ’rtha-parityago*

*bhogasya ca sukhasya ca*

*istam dattam hutam japtam*

*mad-artham yad vratam tapah*

*evam dharmair manusyanam*

*uddhavatma-nivedinam*

*mayi sanjayate bhaktih*

*ko ’nyo 'rtho’syavasisyate*

1\. sraddhamrta-kathayam me: firm faith in the blissful narration of My pastimes.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura: “One should have intense faith in the topics, which are nectar. Although everything about the Lord is sweet, one should have faith in the very sweet narrations of the Lord’s pastimes, such as the narration of His rasa-lila.”

2\. sasvan mad-anukirtanam: constant chanting of My glories.

3\. parinistha. ca pujayam: unwavering attachment to My ceremonial worship.

4\. stutibhih stavanam mama: praise of Me through beautiful hymns.

5\. adarah paricaryayam: great respect for My devotional service.

6\. sarvangair abhivandanam: the offering of obeisances with the entire body.

7\. mad-bhakta-pujabhyadhika: the performance of first-class worship of My devotees.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura: “One should worship the devotees extensively, since one understands that this is more pleasing than worshiping Me.”

BBT purport: “The words mad-bhakta-pujabhyadhika are significant in this verse.
