Thus they attain their ultimate benefit by transferring themselves to His abode, Vaikuntha.”

**Chapter 21: Lord Krsna’s Explanation of the Vedic Path**

In this chapter Krsna continues His explanation of good and evil, pious and impious, pure and impure. In doing so He will sum up, at the end of i he chapter (in texts 42- 43), the purpose of the entire Vedic path, which, the l.ord asserts, no one but He knows. That purpose is to know Him.

*Texts 1-7: Oneness, good and bad, and the Vedic purpose behind these distinctions*

According to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.20.6, Lord Krsna accepts three paths for spiritual advancement - karma, jnana, and bhakti, along with the Vedic scriptures strictly prescribed and regulated actions for each of these paths. But what of those who neglect these paths? Will Krsna (and the laws of nature) consider such persons - as Krsna considers His devotees - beyond being judged as good or bad, pious or impious? Will they be exempt from reactions to their actions? What results will they reap?

Krsna’s opening words in chapter 21 answer these questions. Those who forsake His three paths, He says, and who instead cultivate sense gratification, “certainly undergo the continual cycle of material existence.” (SB. 11.21.1)

Clearly, Krsna views spiritual progress as the purpose of human life, and He wants all His parts and parcels to fulfill that purpose. Toward that end, the Vedas prescribe duties appropriate for and specific to one’s current position on the spiritual path, and if we follow these prescriptions, we are guaranteed an upward path from karma, through jnana, to bhakti, and finally to pure love for Krsna.

This is why in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.21.2 Krsna again defines “good” and “bad” relative to one’s fixedness in his prescribed duties: “Steadiness in one’s own position is declared to be actual piety, whereas deviation from one’s position is considered impiety. In this way the two are definitely ascertained.”

From the BBT purport: “Here the Lord emphasizes that a conditioned soul should not artificially disrupt the natural evolution of his Krsna consciousness by deviating from those duties prescribed by the Lord Himself.”

Whether one’s duties appear higher or lower than those of others, one should still steadfastly maintain one’s own duties.The propriety or impropriety of an action, therefore, can only be evaluated in the context of one’s duties, for that which degrades one conditioned soul, such as the sacrifice of an animal, may be a step forward for an indiscriminate consumer of meat. In ordinary dealings, therefore, and even for one’s physical survival, good and bad, auspicious and inauspicious, must be ascertained according to one’s position.

In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.19.45, the Lord rejected such discriminations, hut now He gives a frame of reference for them: they are meant “for those bearing the burden of mundane religious principles.” (SB. 11.21.4)

In texts 7-15 Krsna will offer specific prescriptions within the realm of duality.But first He asserts the transcendental principle that unites them before describing the frame of reference in which they can be usefully applied for spiritual advancement: “Earth, water, fire, air, and ether are the five basic elements that constitute the bodies of all conditioned souls, from Lord Brahma himself down to the nonmoving creatures. These elements all emanate from the one Personality of Godhead.” (SB. 11.21.5) Although all human bodies, regardless of what they look like, are composed of the same elements and in that sense are equal, the Vedic literatures has categorized them to assist each person’s advancement toward his or her goal of life. This categorization, with its individualized prescription of duties, is called varnasrama-dharma, and its purpose is the gradual elevation of souls to Krsna consciousness. Krsna Himself is the source of these distinctions and is the detached and unifying transcendental principle that supports them.

Krsna once told Arjuna: “According to the three modes of material nature and the work associated with them, the four divisions of human society are created by Me. And although I am the creator of this system, you should know that I am yet the nondoer, being unchangeable.” (Bhagavad-gita 4-13 )

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.21.6 explains the purpose of varnasrama-dharma: knowledge of Krsna. It is to help us achieve this goal that the Vedic scriptures define the relative dualities (favorable and unfavorable, pious and impious, good and bad) of everyday, mundane actions: “Although this knowledge is the real basis of the Vedic literature, mundane piety is enjoined and sin is prohibited so that one can gradually come to the platform of material goodness, whereupon spiritual knowledge becomes visible.”

In the next text, Krsna explains His reasoning behind how He distinguishes between good and bad, favorable and unfavorable, and auspicious and inauspicious: “O saintly Uddhava, in order to restrict \[niyamartham\] materialistic activities, I have established that which is proper and improper among all material things, including time, space, and all physical objects.” (SB. 11.21.7)

That is, by creating sastric regulations and restrictions, Krsna wants lo pull conditioned souls away from fleeting pleasures and aim them inward 11ic-it own eternal good.

*Texts 8-15: How to recognize piety and choose piety over impiety*

Krsna starts by distinguishing pure from impure places (text 8) and pure from impure times (text 9). He then speaks about ways to purify substances (text 10) as well as the contaminating reactions from impure acts (text 11). He describes other aspects of purity and impurity (texts 12-13), including what purifies those persons or things that purify others, such as the brahmanas (text 14), mantras, and work (text 15)Krsna concludes this topic in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.21.15 with a summary: “Thus by purification of the place, time, substance, doer, mantras, and work, one becomes religious, and by negligence of these six items one is considered irreligious.”

Here are some points from the BBT purports to these texts, as well as excerpts from Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comments on them.

*Text 8: Purity of places of residence*

From the BBT purport: “Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura explains that previously the provinces of Bihar and Bengal were bereft of devotional service to the Lord and were considered impure. Then great Vaisnavas such as Jayadeva appeared in these territories, converting them into holy places— Even in such provinces, however, any place where saintly persons gather is considered to be holy.... Srila Madhvacarya quotes from the Skanda Purana as follows: ‘Religious persons should reside within an eight-mile radius of rivers, oceans, mountains, hermitages, forests, spiritual cities, or places where the salagrama-sila is found. All other places should be considered kikata, or contaminated. But if even in such contaminated places black and spotted antelopes are found, one may reside there as long as sinful persons are not also present. Even if sinful persons are present, if the civil power rests with respectable authorities, one may remain. Similarly, one may dwell wherever the Deity of Visnu is duly installed and worshiped.’”

*Text 9: Purity of times*

From the BBT purport: “Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura explains that the most auspicious of all times is the moment one achieves the mercy of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, II one neglects the loving service of the Lord, being carried away by sense gratification, he is certainly living in most inauspicious times.”

*Text 10: Purification of substances*

“An object’s purity or impurity is established by application of another object, by words, by rituals, by the effects of time, or according to relative magnitude.” (SB. 11.21.10) Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura writes: “\[An example of objects made pure or impure by another object:\] Plates are purified by water and made impure by urine or other impure items; \[made pure or impure by words\] when there is doubt, if a brahmana says an object is pure, it is pure, and if he says it is impure, it is impure; \[by ritual\] objects are purified by cleaning and sprinkling with water \[not by washing, but by a ritual sprinkling with water, such a dcamana\]. This is how flowers are purified; flowers are made impure by smelling their fragrance. \[An example of being made pure or impure by time:\] New rain water becomes purified by keeping it for ten days.”

*Text 11: Discriminations about the contaminating reactions from the impure*

From the BBT purport: “Concerning opulence (samrddhi), worn-out, dirty clothing or a messy residence are considered impure for a rich man but acceptable for one who is poor. The word desa indicates that in a safe and peaceful place one is obligated to strictly perform religious rituals, whereas in a dangerous or chaotic situation one may be excused for occasional negligence of secondary principles. One who is physically healthy must offer obeisances to the Deities, attend religious functions, and execute his prescribed duties, but a young child or sickly person may be excused from such activities, as indicated by the word avastha."

*Text 12: More on the purification of substances*

From Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura: “Grains, wood, ivory, cloth, liquids like oil and ghee, precious metals, skins, and earthen objects like pots and bricks become pure in time, or through wind, fire, earth, and water, according to scriptural rules. These purifying agents may be used in combination or singly. Metals are purified by earth, water, and fire. Wool is purified by air alone.”

*Texts 13: Purifing substances*

From Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura: “If a seat, cloth, or vessel is contaminated by an impure item, it gives up the contamination and smell through the use of water, earth, acids, soap, and by scraping. It is then restored to its original nature. That is its purity. One should measure the purification from the extent by which the smell of the contamination is removed by scraping or other means.”

*Text 14: Purifying the Purifier*

From the BBT purport: “As stated in the Garuda Purana, ‘Whether one is pure or contaminated, and regardless of one’s external situation, simply by remembering the lotus-eyed Personality of Godhead one can internally and externally cleanse one’s existence.’ Lord Caitanya recommended that we constantly remember the Supreme Lord by chanting His holy names, Hare Krsna, Hare Krsna, Krsna Krsna, Hare Hare/ Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. This sublime process is essential for every human actually desirous of purifying his existence.”

From Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura: “Now purification of the person who purifies objects is described. Purification of the performer \[is accomplished\] by bathing, offering charity, practicing austerity, old age, conducting oneself according to one’s capability, samskaras like the upanayana, and rites such as sandhya worship.”

*Text 15: Purification of mantras and work*

From Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura: “Suitable knowledge from the mouth of the pure guru purifies a mantra. Action is purified by offering it to the Lord. If it is not offered, it is impure. By the purity of these six items one should conduct oneself in life.”

**Krsna summarizes religiousness**

Krsna offers a summary of (dharma) religiousness: “Thus by purification of the place, time, substance, doer, mantras, and work, one becomes religious, and by negligence of these six items one is considered irreligious.” (SB. 11.21.15)

*Texts 16-17: Principles of purity and impurity*

Next, the Supreme Lord explains the relative nature of sin and piety, especially how they are dictated and defined by the specifics of time and circumstances. Krsna doesn’t want to simply relativize ethics; rather, He wants to point out the fine discriminations that are sometimes required to differentiate between piety and impiety. The surgeon who uses his knife to cut skin to save a life is pious, and the dacoit who uses his knife to slash a throat is impious. Arjuna’s killing of his kinsmen during the Battle of Kuruksetra was the perfection of piety, whereas the indiscriminate killing of relatives is depravity.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains the relative nature of “good” and “bad” in his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.21.16: “This division of good and bad is not always fixed. During calamity, hoarding is a good quality, but during normal times hoarding is a bad quality and is forbidden. Although giving up one’s family is a fault, it is a good quality if done while following the rules for detachment… The rule that says it is wrong to give up one’s family also negates the fault should it be done by a particular, qualified person, since it is a good quality for a jnani to give up his family. The rule that says it is good to give up one’s family also negates it as a good act for a karmi, since it is wrong for a karmi to abandon his family. Thus good and bad are not universally fixed but are determined according to particular circumstances.”

The BBT purport to text 16 adds: “According to Srila Madhvacarya, persons above the age of fourteen are considered capable of distinguishing between good and bad and are thus responsible for their pious and sinful activities. Animals, on the other hand, being merged in ignorance, cannot be blamed for their offenses or praised for their so-called good qualities, which all arise ultimately from ignorance.”

In text 17, Krsna takes the subtleties of piety and impiety still further, explaining that an “improper” act degrades one person but may not degrade another: “The same activities that would degrade an elevated person do not cause falldown for those who are already fallen. Indeed, one who is lying on the ground cannot possibly fall further. The material association that is dictated by one’s own nature is considered a good quality.” (SB. 11.21.17)

*Texts 18-22: Freedom from bondage to impious acts*

Renunciation can help release one from material bondage: “By refraining from a particular sinful or materialistic activity, one becomes freed from its bondage. Such renunciation is the basis of religious and auspicious life for human beings and drives away all suffering, illusion, and fear.” (SB. 11.21.18)

But it takes the power of the positive to make one steadfast in renunciation, something Krsna pointed out to Arjuna in Bhagavad-gita 2.59: “The embodied soul may be restricted from sense enjoyment, though the taste for sense objects remains. But, ceasing such engagements by experiencing a higher taste, he is fixed in consciousness.”

**The miserable results of material attachment**

Those who experience the higher taste of Krsna consciousness will obviously be spiritually self-motivated, but what about those who do not yet possess such a wealth of spiritual experience? What would entice them to undergo the austerities of spiritual life just so that they could become free from material “bondage”? After all, millions of jivas consider “bondage” the only reality, and some consider it a heavenly condition. Comparing one’s own experiences with the words Krsna now speaks to Uddhava helps us understand why spiritualists always condemn materialism: “One who accepts material sense objects as desirable certainly becomes attached to them. From such attachment lust arises, and this lust creates quarrel among men. From quarrel arises intolerable anger, followed by the darkness of ignorance. This ignorance quickly overtakes a man’s broad intelligence. (SB. 11.21.19—20)

The BBT purport to text 20 states: “The desire for material association arises from one’s propensity to deny that everything is God’s energy. Falsely imagining material sense objects to be separate from the Supreme Lord, one desires to enjoy them; such desire gives rise to conflict and quarrel in human society. This conflict inevitably gives rise to great anger, which makes human beings become foolish and destructive. Thus the actual goal of human life is quickly forgotten.”

**Make use of your human life**

The Supreme Personality of Godhead concludes: “O saintly Uddhava, a person bereft of real intelligence is considered lo have lost everything. Deviated from the actual purpose of his life, he becomes dull, just like a dead person. Because of absorption in sense gratification, one cannot recognize himself or others. Living uselessly in ignorance like a tree, one is merely breathing just like a bellows.” (SB. 11.21.21-22 )

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s strong comments add to the imagery of the text: “\[Such a person\] maintains his life like a tree, which takes only water. In this way he is like a person who has fainted. He breathes like a bellows. In this way he is similar to a dead man.”

From the BBT purport to text 22: “Just as trees, having no means of defending themselves, are always being cut down, similarly, the conditioned souls are constantly being cut down by the cruel laws of nature… Absorbed in gratifying the senses of the external body, they spend their lives uselessly, without spiritual profit. This useless lifestyle can be transformed into a perfect life simply by chanting the holy names of God in Krsna consciousness, as recommended by Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu.”

*Texts 23-35: The flowery words of the Vedas*

Sri Krsna compares the superficial following of Vedic prescriptions to the ignorance of a child whose parents have offered him a sweet to get him to take his medicine. Materialistic tendencies are natural for t hose born in this world, yet these commonplace attachments tend to absorb the mind and defeat one’s self-interest. Absorption in the temporary is a downward path leading to darkness. Therefore it cannot be that sense gratification is the actual intention of the Vedas, despite that some of the Vedic prescriptions make it appear so. Only those ignorant of the true purpose of the Vedas think of sense gratification as i he goal of the Vedas.

Those with uncontrolled material desires (lust, anger, and greed), Krsna says, mistake the enticingly fragrant flowers offered by the Vedic system for tbe system’s fruits. “Bewildered by the glare of fire and suffocated by its smoke, they cannot recognize their own true identity.” (SB. 1 1.21.27) Because these persons are so dedicated to sense gratification, even though they follow the sense gratification prescribed by the Vedas, Sri Krsna says they “cannot understand that I am situated in everyone’s heart and that the entire universe is nondifferent from Me and emanates from Me. Indeed, they are just like persons whose eyes tire covered by log.” (SB. 11.21.28)'

Their dedication to sense gratification involves them in violence - they may slaughter innocent animals in the name of sacrifice, for example. “Such passion for violence, however, is never encouraged within the process of Vedic sacrifice.” (SB.11.21.30) These bewildered persons pursue blessings to attain dreamlike heavenly pleasures. Controlled by the three material modes, they worship demigods, but they fail to properly worship Krsna. Proud, greedy, and bewildered by the flowery words of the Vedas, they worship demigods expecting to attain pleasures in heaven and an aristocratic rebirth on their return to earth. “They are not attracted to topics about Me, the Supreme Lord.” (SB.11.21.34)

**Sri Krsna’s conclusion**

“The Vedas, divided into three divisions, ultimately reveal the living entity as pure spirit soul. The Vedic seers and mantras, however, deal in esoteric terms \[paroksa-vada\], and 1 also am pleased \[paroksam mama ca priyam\] by such confidential descriptions.” (SB. 11.21.35)

Krsna has now explained what the purpose of the Vedas is and what it is not. These same facts have been described indirectly throughout the Vedas (paroksa-vada): Krsna is pleased with indirect presentations.

Jiva Gosvami indicates, in his Bhagavat Sandarbha (anuccheda 106), that Krsna prefers that the message of the Bhagavatam be expressed indirectly because it is confidential: “Thus a valuable, rare object which should not be given everywhere is hidden from sight, or made paroksa. Muktirh dadati karhicit sma na bhakti-yogam: the Lord gives liberation, but rarely prema'bhakti (SB. 5.6.18).”

Yet in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.3.44, the merciful Supreme Lord has already directly indicated the practical results He desires by His indirect presentation: “Childish and foolish people are attached to materialistic, fruitive activities, although the actual goal of life is to become free from such activities. Therefore, the Vedic injunctions indirectly lead one to the path of ultimate liberation by first prescribing fruitive religious activities, just as a father promises his child candy so that the child will take his medicine.”

Nevertheless, one may wonder whether a forceful, direct statement of Krsna’s intentions would be clearer and thus easier to follow. The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.5.44 addresses this point: “If a father tells his child, ‘You must rake this medicine by my order,’ the child may become fearful and rebellious and reject the medicine. Therefore the father entices his child by saying, ‘I am going to give you a delicious piece of candy. But if you want this candy, first just take this little bit of medicine, and then you can have the candy.’ Such indirect persuasion is called paroksa-vadah, or an indirect description that conceals the actual purpose. The father presents his proposal to the child as if the ultimate goal were to receive the candy and only a minor condition must be fulfilled to receive it. Actually, however, the father’s goal is to administer the medicine to the child and cure him of his disease. Thus, describing the primary purpose indirectly and concealing it with a secondary proposal is called paroksa-vadah, or indirect persuasion.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura summarizes: “The Vedas are divided into three: karma-kanda, brahma-kanda, and devata-kanda. All three ultimately indicate worship of Me (brahmatma-visayah). \[To this one could respond:\] ‘Why do the mantras or the sages who revealed the mantras speak indirectly, not directly? What is their intention in only indirectly stating their purpose?’ \[Krsna replies:\] ‘Understanding that I prefer indirect speech, they speak in that way.’”

*Texts 36-41: The potency of the Vedic sound vibration*

Vedic sound is, like the ocean, deep and unfathomable. That sound manifests differently on increasingly subtle levels. “As the unlimited, unchanging, and omnipotent Personality of Godhead dwelling within all living beings, I personally establish the Vedic sound vibration in the form of omkara within all living entities. It is thus perceived subtly, just like a single strand of fiber on a lotus stalk.” (SB. 11,21.37)

In the Bhagavat Sandarbha (anuccheda 49), Srila Jiva Gosvami explains that Krsna’s name, being nondifferent from Krsna, is like the Vedas in that neither can be generated from within the senses of a human. Rather, the Lord Himself manifests both His name and the Vedas in a person’s senses. The Supreme Personality of Godhead manifests the great and limitless Vedas from His heart and creates them through the agency of His mind. He continues His description of the Vedas: “The Vedic sound branches out in thousands of directions, adorned with the different letters expanded from the syllable om.” (SB.11.21.17) Ultimately, these sounds with their different metersare again drawn by the Lord into Himself.

*Texts 42-43: Conclusion - attaining Krsna is the purpose of the Vedic path*

**Krsna alone knows the purpose of the Vedas**

The deep purpose of these unfathomable and potent Vedic sound vibrations is virtually unknown, causing the Vedas to remain mysterious and misunderstood. Sri Krsna states this directly (and not indirectly): “In the entire world no one but Me actually understands the confidential purpose of Vedic knowledge. Thus people do not know what the Vedas are actually prescribing in the ritualistic injunctions of karma-kanda, or what object is actually being indicated in the formulas of worship found in the upasana-kanda, or that which is elaborately discussed through various hypotheses in the jnana-kanda section of the Vedas.” (SB. 11.21.42)

**What, then, is the purpose of the Vedas?**

By all the Vedas Krsna is to be known.The Supreme Lord says: “I am the ritualistic sacrifice enjoined by the Vedas, and I am the worshipable Deity. It is I who am presented as various philosophical hypotheses, and it is I alone who am then refuted by philosophical analysis. The transcendental sound vibration thus establishes Me as the essential meaning of all Vedic knowledge. The Vedas, elaborately analyzing all material duality as nothing but My illusory potency, ultimately completely negate this duality and achieve their own satisfaction.” (SB. 11.21.43)

Srila Jiva Gosvami quotes Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.21.42 in the Krsna Sandarbha (anuccheda 29): “What alternatives do the Vedas raise? No one except Me or My dear devotee knows the intended meaning of the Vedas… I have proposed and rejected karma and jnana, and by negating these, the conclusion is reached that I, Krsna, am the final truth.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments: “‘What is the purpose of the Vedasl Please tell me the answer.’ Sri Krsna replies: ‘Yes, certainly I will tell you. That the Vedas prescribe Me means that bhakti is not different from my svarupa, My intrinsic nature. Thus the Vedas enjoin that one should perform bhakti to Me. This means that the injunctions of scripture, like performing sacrifice, etc., produce bhakti for Me. I have said dharmo mad-bhakti-krt prokto: actual religious principles are stated to be those that lead one to My devotional service (SB. 11.19.27). I am the meaning of all the Vedas.’”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura then reiterates Krsna’s purpose in having presented karma, jnana, and bhakti one after another in the previous chapters. Krsna says, “My dear Uddhava, because I desire that human beings may achieve perfection, I have presented three paths of advancement - the path of knowledge, the path of work, and the path of devotion. Besides these three there is absolutely no other means of elevation.” (SB. 11.20.6) Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti writes: “In the three kandas, karma, jnana, and bhakti are presented as alternatives. First I say, ‘Do karma.’ Then I say, ‘Practice jnana.’ Then I say ‘Perform bhakti.’ They are presented one by one and then rejected. First sakama-karma is rejected in favor of niskama-karma. Then when one rises to jnana, niskama-karma is rejected. When jnana is perfected, jnana should be rejected in order to attain Me: jnanam ca mayi sannyaset (SB. 11.19.1). But no scripture ever says that at any time one should reject bhakti.”

In conclusion, it is Krsna who is established by the Vedic sound vibrations. It is Krsna whom Vedic worshipers are led to worship, and He is the ultimate result discovered by Vedic philosophers.Thus the Vedic path followed to its end leads solely to knowing and devotedly serving Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

In the Bhagavat Sandarbha (anuccheda 108), Srila Jiva Gosvami gives a number of sastric references in order to reach the same conclusion: “Thus all the Vedas conclude that Bhagavan is supreme.” In his own comment on the Bhagavat Sandarbha, Sri Jiva notes that the Vedic arts and skills (such as war, diplomacy, architecture, and music) are useless without Krsna and only reach their perfection in His service. In addition, Sri Jiva explains, by understanding these arts one may realize the sweetness of the Lord’s pastimes.

The Supreme Personality of Godhead, Sri Krsna, began this dialogue we call the Uddhava-gita with a discourse on yoga (SB. 11.14-15), His opulences (SB.11.16), and the varnasrama system for social organization (SB. 11.17-18). While describing varnasrama, He described the prescribed duties for each person in society and simultaneously explained i lie goal of these duties - not the attainment of temporary, heavenly delights, as Jaimani Rsi and his followers propose (SB. 11.10), but knowledge of Him (SB. 11.18—19). Now, in chapter 21, the final chapter of this dialogue, alter journeying through karma, jnana, and yoga, Krsna brought us to a clear conclusion.

Throughout these chapters, Krsna has wanted to establish His position as the Supreme Lord and natural object of worship. He also wanted to establish bhakti as the supreme process for attaining Him. The Supreme Lord has now achieved both purposes.

## Dialogue 6. Bhakti: the Uddhava-gita’s conclusion

*Canto eleven: chapters 22-29*

**Chapter 22: Enumeration of the Elements of Material Creation**

*Texts 1-25: Enumerating the universal elements*

*Texts 1-3: Uddhava’s first question - why did the sages calculate the number of elements in the universe?*

Like a crescendo heralding the end of a symphonic movement, Krsna has just spoken of Himself as the essential meaning and goal of all Vedic knowledge (SB. 11.21.43). Uddhava now begins a new episode in the Uddhava-gita by asking four questions. In answering Uddhava’s first question (SB. 11.22.1-3), in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.4-25, Krsna will define the Supreme Lord’s spiritual energy (purusa) as distinct from the material manifestation (prakrti). Answering Uddhava’s second question (SB. 11.22.26-28), in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.29-34, Krsna will parse the purusa category into two - the Supreme Lord and the individual jiva both of which are fully spiritual and eternally distinct. In His response in Uddhava’s third question (SB. 11.22.35-36), in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.17 59, Krsna will detail the reason behind the eternal jiva’s transmigration through countless bodies. And Uddhava’s fourth question, asked in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.60-61, creates the bridge to Krsna’s response in chapter 24.

In Uddhava’s first question, the great devotee recalls a previous theme of the Uddhava-gita and asks Krsna to explain why different sages have reached different totals when calculating the number of elements in the universe. Krsna said, “Earth, water, fire, air, and ether are the five basic elements that constitute the bodies of all conditioned souls, from Lord Brahma himself down to the nonmoving creatures.” (SB. 11.21.5) Uddhava has also heard Krsna use twenty-eight as the number of elements (God, the jiva, the mahai-tattva, false ego, the five gross elements, the ten senses, the mind, the five subtle objects of perception, and the three modes of nature).But Uddhava also knows that great sages have theorized the number of elements in various ways - as 26, 25, 7, 9, 6, 4, 11, 17, 16, and 13.He therefore inquires, “What did each of these sages have in mind when he calculated the creative elements in such different ways? O supreme eternal, kindly explain this to me.” (SB. 11.22.1-3)

Clearly, Uddhava is asking for a conclusive answer from Krsna, the supreme authority. The BBT purport classifies Uddhava’s question in the category of “intermediate questions that must be answered so the path of liberation will be clear.” Having heard from Krsna the conclusive truth about varnasrama and the path of karma, Uddhava is now asking about the path of knowledge, jnana.

*Texts: 4-25: Sri Krsna’s reply*

Lord Krsna begins: “Because all material elements are present everywhere \[santi sarvatra\], it is reasonable that different learned brahmanas have analyzed them in different ways. All such philosophers spoke under the shelter of My mystic potency \[maya\], and thus they could say anything without contradicting the truth.” (SB. 11.22.4) Ultimately, Krsna says, His impenetrable potencies are the cause of the sages’ differing viewpoints.

Each element contains within it the next element, which it causes.Ether contains air, air contains fire, fire contains water, and water contains earth. This means that the element ether contains the subtle forms of all the other elements, air contains everything but ether, fire contains everything but ether and air, etc. In other words, the elements caused by an earlier element are also subtly contained within their cause.The BBT purport comments: “The words santi sarvatra in this verse indicate that all material elements are found within each other in gross and subtle forms. In this way there are innumerable ways to categorically describe them.”

Also from the BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.4: “Srila Jiva Gosvami states that the word maya in this verse does not refer to mahci- maya, or the potency of ignorance, but to the Lord’s inconceivable mystic power, which shelters the learned followers of Vedic knowledge. Each of the philosophers mentioned here reveals a particular aspect of truth, and their theories are not contradictory, since they are simply describing the same phenomena with different categorical systems.”

What, then, causes disagreements - often heated - over differing intellectual points of view? Krsna explains: “When philosophers argue, ‘I don’t choose to analyze this particular case in the same way that you have,’ it is simply My own insurmountable energies that are motivating their analytic disagreements.” (SB. 11.22.5)

The ultimate cause of philosophical disagreements is Krsna. He is not only the cause of all causes but the Lord in each philosopher’s heart and the master of maya. He benedicts philosophers with a partial glimpse of reality and makes them think their glimpse is comprehensive. Srimad-Bhagavatam 6.4.31 states, “Acting from within the cores of the hearts of all philosophers, who propagate various views, He caused them to forget their own souls while sometimes agreeing and sometimes disagreeing among themselves. Thus He creates within this material world a situation in which they are unable to come to a conclusion. I offer my respectful obeisances unto Him.”

Or, as stated in the Mahabharata (and quoted by Srila Prabhupada in his purport to the above Sixth Canto text): “All speculators must disagree with other speculators; otherwise, why should there be so many opposing parties concerned with ascertaining the supreme cause?” Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.4 sums up the point: “Why is there a dispute at all? Because of My maya’s bewilderment. My maya gives them the ability to ... dispute for as long as the sun and moon exist.”

Can the philosophers ever find a resolution? Krsna says yes: “By interaction of My energies different opinions arise. But for those who have fixed their intelligence on Me and controlled their senses, differences of perception disappear, and consequently the very cause for argument is removed.” (SB. 11.22.6)

*Texts 7-9: Krsna restates Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.4*

*Texts 7-8: All the elements are present in every other element*

“O best among men, because subtle and gross elements mutually enter into one another, philosophers may calculate the number of basic material elements in different ways, according to their personal desire. All subtle material elements are actually present within their gross effects; similarly, all gross elements are present within their subtle causes, since material creation takes place by progressive manifestation of elements from subtle to gross. Thus we can find all material elements within any single element.”(SB. 11.22.7-8)

*Text 9: Therefore ...*

Krsna concludes: “Therefore, no matter which of these thinkers is speaking, and regardless of whether in their calculations they include material elements within their previous subtle causes or else within their subsequent manifest products, I accept their conclusions as authoritative, because a logical explanation can always be given for each of the different theories.” (SB. 11.22.9)

*Texts 10-16: Enumerating twenty-five or twenty'Six elements*

*Text 10: The jiva and the Supreme Lord cannot be the same*

**The difference**

As He explains His method of calculating the number of elements, Krsna argues against any undifferentiated oneness between Himself and the jiva. The Supreme Lord continues: “Because a person who has been covered by ignorance since time immemorial is not capable of effecting his own self-realization, there must be some other personality who is in factual knowledge of the Absolute Truth (tattva-jna) and who can impart this knowledge to him \[jnana-da\].” (SB. 11.22.10) If the jiva and the all-knowing, all-powerful Supreme Lord were exactly the same, no jiva could be covered by illusion. Nor would the jivas require enlightenment from anyone outside themselves. Again, Krsna raises this point here because some philosophers, according to Uddhava in texts 1-3 of this chapter, claim that there are twenty-five elements instead of twenty-six or twenty-eight. Their system of enumeration is the same as other sages, but they have included the jiva and the Supreme Lord as one, undifferentiated element. Krsna speaks against this system of counting and thus against impersonalism.

From the BBT purport to text 10: “Although the Lord tolerates different methods of calculating material causes within their effects and material effects within their causes, there cannot be any speculation regarding the two spiritual elements found in this universe, namely the individual soul and the Supersoul. Lord Krsna clearly states in this verse that the living entity is incapable of effecting his own enlightenment. The Supreme Lord is tattva-jna, omniscient, and jnana-da, the spiritual master of the entire universe.”

*Text 11: Knowledge of the oneness of the jiva and the Supreme Lord is material*

Knowledge of the undifferentiated, qualitative equality of the Supreme Lord with the jiva is born of the material mode of goodness. The materialistic conclusion that there is a qualitative difference is simply speculation.

The BBT purport leads us to the balanced understanding that Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu presents: “Knowledge of the Lord’s qualitative oneness with the living entity, as described in this verse, refutes the materialistic concept of life and partially establishes the Absolute Truth. Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu described the actual situation as acintya-bhedabheda-tattva: the supreme controller and the controlled living entities are simultaneously one and different. In the material mode of goodness the oneness is perceived. As one proceeds further, to the stage of visuddha-sattva, or purified spiritual goodness, one finds spiritual variety within the qualitative oneness, completing one’s knowledge of the Absolute Truth… Any philosophical attempt to separate the living entity from the Supreme Lord and deny his eternal servitude to the Lord is thus refuted.”

*Texts 12-13: Further discriminations in the enumeration of elements*

**The jiva is nonmaterial**

Just as philosophers have inaccurately calculated the number of elements by combining as one the jiva and the Supreme Foul, others have wrongly considered as one the jiva and material nature (prakrti). Having refuted the first, Krsna now establishes the jiva as distinct from material nature: “Nature \[prakrti\] exists originally as the equilibrium of the three material modes, which pertain only to nature, not to the transcendental spirit soul. These modes - goodness, passion, and ignorance - are the effective causes of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of this universe.” (SB. 11.22.12)

**Jnana, action (sutra), ignorance, time, and svabhava are not elements**

In this section of texts Krsna explains why certain aspects of material nature should not be considered elements: “In this world the mode of goodness is recognized as knowledge, the mode of passion as fruitive work, and the mode of darkness as ignorance. Time is perceived as the agitated interaction of the material modes, and the totality of functional propensity is embodied by the primeval sutra, or mahat-tattva.” (SB. 11.22.13)

In his comment on this text, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura notes that jnana is not an element, because it arises from the mode of goodness. The qualities of action and avidly a (ignorance) are also not elements, because they arise from the two lower modes, passion and ignorance. Is time an element? No, time (kala) is the Supreme Lord’s potency, which agitates the three modes. Time is therefore included under the Supreme Lord, who is Himself counted as an element. The living entities’ innate tendencies (svabhava) are caused by their actions, and these are a specific function of the totality of the material energy (mahat-tattva) called the sutram.Therefore, Krsna concludes, all authorities agree that the number of elements should not be increased to include jnana, action (sutra), ignorance, time, or svabhava.

*Texts 14-16: Krsna enumerates 25 of the 28 elements*

Krsna has now critiqued the calculation of twenty-five elements, favoring twenty-six, because the list of twenty-six elements allows for the separation of the element of the jiva from the element of the Supreme Lord. Therefore we should take the twenty-five elements (which will be listed in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.14-16) and add one, the Supreme Lord, to come to a subtotal of twenty-six elements. Then, when we substitute three - one for each of the three modes of material nature - for the single element prakrti in the list of twenty-five, we arrive at twenty-eight elements, which in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.19.14 the Lord Himself certifies as correct. In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.14-15, Krsna describes the first twenty elements in His list of twenty-five: “I have described the nine basic elements as the enjoying soul, nature, nature’s primeval manifestation of the mahat-tattva, false ego, ether, air, fire, water, and earth. Hearing, touch, sight, smell, and taste are the five knowledge-acquiring senses, My dear Uddhava, and speech, the hands, the genitals, the anus, and the legs constitute the five working senses. The mind belongs to both these categories. (SB. 11.22.14-15)

In text 16, the Lord appears to add ten more elements, which gives a total of thirty elements, two more than the twenty-eight He previously stated was the correct number: “Sound, touch, taste, smell, and form are the objects of the knowledge-acquiring senses, and movement, speech, excretion, and manufactureare functions of the working senses.” (SB. 11.22.16)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains that the number of elements is twenty-five, and lists the functions of the working senses (movement, speech, excretion, and manufacture) not as elements but as results of the actions of the working senses. Thus the five sense objects (sound, touch, taste, smell, and form) are added to the list of elements, which makes the total Krsna presents here twenty-five.

*Text 17: Krsna answers Uddhava’s question*

In the first three texts of this chapter, Uddhava asked Krsna what the various sages had in mind when they calculated the basic elements of creation in different ways. In text 17 Krsna replies: “In the beginning of creation nature assumes, by the modes of goodness, passion, and ignorance, its form as the embodiment of all subtle causes and gross manifestations within the universe. The Supreme Personality of Godhead does not enter the interaction of material manifestation but merely glances upon nature.” (SB. 11.22.17)

Material nature (prakrti) is in continuous flux due to the actions of the three modes, goodness, passion, and ignorance. But the Supreme Lord neither interacts with material nature nor transforms nor changes it in any way. He remains the ultimate, indirect cause (nimitta-karana) and witness. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains: “Uddhava has asked the sages’ intention in describing the elements in the various ways they have. Krsna shows the conclusion of their opinions… The Lord, who is the indirect cause (nimitta) undergoes no transformation but simply acts as a witness. The Lord is different from prakrti, which undergoes transformation.”

Regardless of the differing opinions among the sages, the sages’ common purpose was to explain the Lord’s transcendental position.

*Texts 18-24: Further considerations about the elements*

*Text 18: The mahat-tattva*

Next, Krsna describes the mahat-tattva, the vast pool of material ingredients, as well as the source of its power: “As the material elements, headed by the mahat-tattva, are transformed, they receive their specific potencies from the glance of the Supreme Lord, and being amalgamated by the power of nature, they create the universal egg.” (SB. 11.22.18)

*Texts 19-24: Other conclusions regarding the categorization of elements*

Krsna has already explained His own enumeration of the elements. Now He explains the opinions of the sages Uddhava noted in the first verses of this chapter, focusing on the thinking that caused various sages to conclude a total of seven elements (text 19), six elements (text 20), four elements (text 21), seventeen elements (text 22), sixteen and thirteen elements (text 23), and eleven and nine elements (text 24).

*Text 25: Krsna’s summary - purusa and prakrti are distinct*

The Supreme Lord approves of these varied categorizations: “All of their proposals are reasonable, since they are all presented with ample logic. Indeed, such philosophical brilliance is expected of the truly learned.”

Srila Sridhara Svami explains Krsna’s mood in saying this: These theories should all be accepted as reasonable to assist in “instructing about the difference between prakrti and the purusa.”

*Texts 26-34: Both the jiva and the Supreme Lord are fully distinct from matter*

*Texts 26-28: Uddhava’s second question*

After hearing Krsna’s authoritative enumeration of the elements and especially of the clear distinction He makes between the material elements (prakrti) and Himself (purusa), Sri Uddhava asks Krsna to differentiate between the material elements and the infinitesimal jiva, who is also spiritual and also known as purusa. In answering Uddhava Krsna will also be inspired to clarify the difference between these two purusas. So Uddhava asks his next question: “Although nature and the living entity are constitutionally distinct, O Lord Krsna, there appears to be no difference between them, because they are found residing within one another. Thus the soul appears to be within nature and nature within the soul.” (SB. 11.22.26)

The existence of the body depends on the soul, and for the soul to have any practical workings in this world it needs a body. The two, therefore, appear interdependent. Noting this, and adopting the mood of an ordinary conditioned soul, Uddhava asks Krsna to explain the relationship between soul and body.

Srila Sridhara Svami writes that Uddhava’s question refers to an apparently blurry distinction between soul and body: the two seem mutually dependent because “it is never seen that the soul and material nature can avoid each other.”

Uddhava’s words are filled with affection for His Lord. He asks Him questions because he knows that only Krsna fully sees reality completely as it is: “O lotus-eyed Krsna, O omniscient Lord, kindly cut this great doubt out of my heart with Your own words, which exhibit Your great skill in reasoning. From You alone the knowledge of the living beings arises, and by Your potency that knowledge is stolen away. Indeed, no one but Yourself can understand the real nature of Your illusory potency.” (SB. 11.22.27-28)

*Texts 29-34: Sri Krsna’s reply - both the Supreme Lord and the jiva are independent of material nature*

Krsna’s answer is clear. “The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: O best among men, material nature \[prakrti\] and its enjoyer \[purusa\] are clearly distinct. This manifest creation undergoes constant transformation, being founded upon the agitation of the modes of nature.” (SB. 11.22.29)

Bhagavad-gita 13.22 and 15.17 state that both the jiva and the Supreme Lord are purusas and clearly distinct from material nature (prakrti). The modes of nature continuously transform material nature, but both purusas are eternal and nonchanging. The BBT purport highlights the distinctions between the category of purusa and that of prakrti: “The word purusa indicates the living entity and also the Supreme Lord, who is the supreme living entity. Material nature, subject to transformation, is full of duality, whereas the Lord is one and absolute. Material nature is dependent on its creator, maintained and annihilator; the Lord, however, is completely self-reliant and independent. In the same way, material nature is unconscious and dull, lacking self-awareness, whereas the Supreme Lord is self-sufficient omniscience. The individual living entity shares the eternality, bliss, and knowledge of the Personality of Godhead and is also completely distinct from material nature.”

*Texts 30-32, Point one: The Supreme Lord is independent of matter*

Next, Krsna explains from a different perspective how the Supreme Personality of Godhead is independent of matter.

**Perception requires three interdependent factors**

The three modes of nature work through the material energy to manifest the objects in the universe as well as the different levels of consciousness one needs to perceive those objects. For a living entity to be conscious of a material object, he requires three interdependent factors to work: adhyatma (the senses), adhidaiva (the presiding deities), and adhibhuta (the actual object perceived).

*Text 31: The Supreme Lord is independent, not interdependent*

These three factors must work interdependently if a jiva is to perceive anything in the material world. The sense organ of the perceiver (adhyatma), such as the eye, is a necessary component. There must also be an object with form (adhibhuta), say, an apple. And a devata (adhidaiva) is also required - someone to supply sunlight through the sun globe. If any one of these three is absent, one cannot see, which implies that all three must be present in every act of perception.

In the example of seeing an apple, we have concluded that the sun devata must be present. Yet the sun itself requires no other adhidaiva agent to make itself perceivable, because it is self-luminous. Similarly, although everything in existence depends on Krsna and cannot exist without Him, He Himself is not dependent on anything in this materially interdependent universe.

The BBT purport explains these points: “Thus the three factors - adhyatma, represented by the senses such as the eye; adhibhuta, the sense objects such as form; and adhidaiva, the influence of the controlling deities - exist in an interdependent relationship. The sun globe itself is said to be self-manifest, self-luminous, and self-experiencing; it does not share the interdependence of the senses and sense objects although facilitating their function. Similarly, the Supreme Personality of Godhead facilitates the interdependent experiences of all living entities.”

*Text 32: All three agents are required for perception through any sense*

Like sight, perception through the other senses (the ears, nose, skin, tongue), as well as the functioning of the subtle body (mind, intelligence, conditioned consciousness, and false ego) require the com- Lined actions of the three interdependent factors, adhyatma, adhidaiva, and adhibhuta.

Srila Prabhupada’s purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.10.9 clarifies Krsna’s point:

There are innumerable living entities, one dependent on the other in the relationship of the controlled and the controller. But without the medium of perception, no one can know or understand who is the controlled and who is the controller. For example, the sun controls the power of our vision, we can see the sun because the sun has its body, and the sunlight is useful only because we have eyes. Without our having eyes, the sunlight is useless, and without sunlight the eyes are useless. Thus they are interdependent, and none of them is independent. Therefore the natural question arises concerning who made them interdependent. The one who has made such a relationship of interdependence must be ultimately completely independent. As stated in the beginning of the Srimad-Bhagavatam, the ultimate source of all interdependent objectives is the complete independent subject. This ultimate source of all interdependence is the Supreme Truth or Paramatma, the Supersoul, who is not dependent on anything else. He is svasrayasrayah. He is only dependent on His self, and thus He is the supreme shelter of everything.

Statistically, it is unlikely that the components of a system, in which each part has no independent functional value, can spontaneously or randomly self-organize. Rather, common sense points to an organizer existing independent of and external to the system. Ultimately, the interdependence of the various parts of the universe’s innumerable systems naturally makes one inclined to consider the existence and nature of a creator. Is it illogical to assume that such a creator must exist outside the universe in full independence?

Thus Krsna has answered Uddhava’s question regarding the distinction between the Supreme Lord (purusa) and matter. He now turns to answering how the “little” purusa, the jiva, is also independent of matter. In doing so, Krsna will describe why the jiva misindentifies with matter.

*Texts 33-34, Point two: The jiva is also independent of matter*

**False ego causes a conditioned jiva to wrongly misperceive itself as matter**

When the primal material ingredient of pradhana (sometimes called prakrti) is agitated by the Supreme Lord’s glance, it transforms into false ego in the three phases, goodness, passion, and ignorance. It is the element of false ego that causes a jiva to perceive that he, a purusa, is non- different from his material body (prakrti).

The speculations about material existence - “Is it real?” “Is it unreal?” - are based on what Srila Prabhupada often called, “a poor fund of knowledge,” especially a lack of understanding of what Krsna has explained above. “Although such argument is useless, persons who have turned their attention away from Me, their own true Self, are unable to give it up.” (SB. 11.22.34)

*Texts 35-59: Sense gratification binds the eternal soul to samsara*

*Texts 35-36: Uddhava’s third question*

Having heard of how broad Krsna’s material energy is, in reply to his first question, and of how both the Lord and the jiva are distinct from the material energy, in reply to his second question, Uddhava now wants to understand why the conditioned soul still suffers from mis- identification of itself with the body. How does that misidentification come about, and how does it endure as the jiva transmigrates from one body to another - to countless others? He asks: “Please explain to me how such persons accept superior and inferior bodies by their materialistic activities and then give up such bodies.” (SB. 11.22.35) Uddhava already knows the answer to this question; he himself said that the jiva’s addiction to fruitive actions separates him from the Lord and causes his endless spinning on the wheel of samsara. Still, he asks, knowing that those whom illusion has cheated are unaware of the truth.

*Text 37: Causes of a soul’s transmigration*

Sri Krsna replies in almost sutra form, describing the process of transmigration in a brief way that still fully answers Uddhava’s question: “The material mind of men is shaped by the reactions of fruitive work. Along with the five senses, it travels from one material body to another. The spirit soul, although different from this mind, follows it.” (SB. 11.22.37) Let’s examine Krsna’s words sentence by sentence.

“The material mind of men is shaped by the reactions of fruitive work.” That is, a man’s actions are based on his mentality, which his previous actions have shaped and colored. (See Bhagavad-gita 8.6: “Whatever state of being one remembers when he quits his body, O son of Kunti, that state he will attain without fail.”)

“Along with the five senses, \[the mind\] travels from one material body to another.” That is, the mind, along with the subtle senses, does not perish with the body. For a human, the mind’s contents at the moment of death determine the soul’s next body. (See Bhagavad-gita 15.9: “The living entity, thus taking another gross body, obtains a certain type of ear, eye, tongue, nose and sense of touch, which are grouped about the mind. He thus enjoys a particular set of sense objects.”)

“The spirit soul, although different from his mind, nevertheless follows it.” That is, the soul follows the mind and gives life to his next body.

*Texts 38-43: The soul is different from the body*

The mind’s absorption in pleasurable objects carries the soul to his next body, which in turn causes him to forget his previous birth - he begins to identify strongly with his new body and relinquishes his focus on the old one. “Consequently, the mind appears to come into being and to suffer annihilation along with its objects of perception, and thus its ability to distinguish past and future is lost.... This total forgetfulness of one’s previous material identity, which comes about for one reason or another, is called death.... what is called birth is simply a person’s total identification with a new body.” (SB. 11.22.38-40) Accepting the body as the self is the same as accepting a dream as reality. As a person who is dreaming forgets his previous dreams, so a person taking birth in a body perceives himself as having just come into being. This is because the mind, which is the resting place of the senses, has created a false sense of identity by seeing himself as his new body. Due to this mental misidentification, the soul thinks it is experiencing both pleasures and miseries as if they were his own. “Thus the self creates external and internal duality, just as a man might give birth to a bad son.” (SB. 11.22.42)

*Texts 43: All bodies imperceptibly undergo creation and destruction*

Sri Krsna states, “My dear Uddhava, material bodies are constantly undergoing creation and destruction by the force of time, whose swiftness is imperceptible. But because of the subtle nature of time, no one sees this.” (SB. 11.22.43)

*Texts 44-46: Examples to aid our understanding*

The transformation of material bodies occurs imperceptibly, like the light from a candle’s flickering flame or a river’s constantly changing waters or how a tree hears fruit. The rays of light emanating from a candle cause us to think one continuous, steady light exists, but this is not true. A river’s current is carrying its waters ever forward, yet we don’t notice the flow but perceive the river as if it doesn’t change. As the BBT purport to text 44 notes: “The fruits of a tree gradually take birth, grow, ripen, sweeten, and eventually rot and die. Similarly, one can easily understand that one’s own body is undergoing constant transformation, and that the body is certainly subject to old age, disease, and death.” Despite its continued transformations, we falsely consider each of the body’s stages as “us,” when the actual person in the body, the soul, neither takes birth nor dies. The person in the body only appears to come into existence, just as fire appears to burst into flames suddenly from a piece of wood.

*Texts 47-50: The soul and the body’s transformations*

We identify with each stage of our body despite the fact that the body passes through one stage after the other. “Impregnation, gestation, birth, infancy, childhood, youth, middle age, old age, and death are the nine ages of the body.” (SB. 11.22.47) Due to ignorance, “one falsely identifies oneself with the superior and inferior bodily conditions. Sometimes a fortunate person is able to give up such mental concoction.” (SB. 11.22.48) That our forefathers have died predicts that we will too, and when we see our children born, we’re reminded that we too took birth. One who understands this duality properly is subject neither to birth nor death. To see the birth and death of a tree must mean one stands apart from the tree. “In the same way, the witness of the birth and death of the material body remains separate from it.” (SB. 11.22.50)

*Texts 51-56: Why the soul transmigrates*

The unintelligent (abudhah), considering his body himself, becomes bewildered and enters the cycle of birth and death (samsara). The modes of nature with which he associates then determine his next birth. “\[B\]y contact with the mode of goodness, \[he\] takes birth among the sages or demigods. By contact with the mode of passion he becomes a demon or human being, and by association with the mode of ignorance he takes birth as a ghost or in the animal kingdom.” (SB. 11.22.52) Whatever the body, the bewildered soul then imitates others with similar bodies, just as a person may imitate dancers or singers lie has seen. I bis imitation is forced, because it is not based on anything true to himself, and it works according to the qualities he has acquired from his material intelligence. The soul suffers from the im- position of the false sense of self (false ego) on the body and mind, but only that. As the movement of water in a pond imposes a false sense of quivering on the reflection of a tree, and as spinning one’s body around imposes a false sense that the earth is spinning, so “the soul’s material life, his experience of sense gratification, is actually false.” (SB. 11.22.54-55) Although there is no true connection between the soul and his material life, the soul is nevertheless pursued by that illu' sion. Why? “For one who is meditating on sense gratification, material life, although lacking factual existence, does not go away, just as the unpleasant experiences of a dream do not.” (SB. 11.22.56)

*Text 57: Krsna’s conclusion*

In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.35-36, Uddhava asked Lord Krsna what causes the misfortune of eternal souls, and the Lord’s reply, in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.37-56, was clear: the soul is distinct from matter but still suffers on the wheel of samsara, endlessly spinning his way through birth and death and birth and death. Now, in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.57, the Supreme Lord gives a summary of His answer in the form of a warning: “Therefore, O Uddhava, do not try to enjoy sense gratification with the material senses. See how illusion based on material dualities prevents one from realizing the self.”

Clearly, the eternal soul’s spirited attempts to enjoy the world of matter trap and encage him in the cycle of birth and death. Krsna also states this in Bhagavad-gita 13.22: “The living entity in material nature thus follows the ways of life, enjoying the three modes of nature. This is due to his association with that material nature. Thus he meets with good and evil among various species.”

*Texts 58-59: Separating oneself from material identification through the intelligence*

The illusion that the body and self are one is deeply rooted in a conditioned soul’s consciousness. Can this illusion be cracked? Can one actually dissociate himself from his body enough to end his spirit of enjoyment? Krsna tells Uddhava that yes, such detached dissociation is possible, even on the subtle, mental level: “Even though neglected, insulted, ridiculed, or envied by bad men, or even though repeatedly agitated by being beaten, tied up, or deprived of one’s occupation, spat upon or polluted with urine by ignorant people, one who desires the highest goal in life should in spite of all these difficulties use his intelligence to keep himself safe on the spiritual platform.” (SB. 11.22.58-59)

*Texts 60-61: Uddhava asks a fourth question*

Hearing this, Uddhava asks how to attain this amazing state of detachment - and tolerance - and then immediately answers his own question by saying that such extreme detachment from the body and mind, which is the perfection of jnana-yoga, is possible only for those who are fixed in devotional service: “O soul of the universe, the conditioning of one’s personality in material life is very strong, and therefore it is very difficult even for learned men to tolerate the offenses committed against them by ignorant people. Only Your devotees, who are fixed in Your loving service and who have achieved peace by residing at Your lotus feet \[rte tvad-dharma-niratan santams te caranalayan\], are able to tolerate such offenses.” (SB. 11.22.61)

**Chapter 23: The Song of the AvantI Brahmana**

Sri Krsna explained the reasoning behind His calculation of the number of material elements in answer to Uddhava’s first question, asked in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.1-3. In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.17, He told Uddhava that the Supreme Lord is nonmaterial. Then He answered Uddhava’s second question, asked in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.26-28, clarifing the distinction between the Supreme Lord and the material energy and certifying that the Lord is the only fully independent living entity. That was in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.31-32. Krsna said that the individual soul is distinct from matter in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.33-34.

This statement prompted Uddhava’s third question, about why the pure jwa suffers continued rebirths in successive bodies (SB. 11.22.35-36). Krsna replies that although the eternal soul’s experience of sense gratification is false, its attachment to fruitive activities and sense gratification causes it to suffer transmigration from body to body (SB. 11.22.54-56). He also said, in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.58-59, that devotional service is the means to fully separate the soul from its identification with both the gross and subtle body. Uddhava’s fourth question, asked in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.22.60-61, acknowledges the power of devotional service to effect detachment. Uddhava then asks the Lord to tell him more about how to achieve complete detachment. The Lord’s answers have taken jnana to its perfection, because jnana born only of the material mode of goodness differentiates between matter and spirit but has no vision of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

*Texts 1-5: Introduction - the ultimate level of tolerance*

Krsna’s reply to Uddhava’s fourth question begins with a realistic, if dour, observation: “O disciple of Brhaspati, there is virtually no saintly man in this world capable of resettling his own mind after it has been disturbed by the insulting words of uncivilized men.” (SB. 11.23.2) Krsna then makes a point worth noting: “Sharp arrows which pierce one’s chest and reach the heart do not cause as much suffering as the arrows of harsh, insulting words that become lodged within the heart when spoken by uncivilized men.” (SB. 11.23.3)

Yet, Krsna tells Uddhava, please hear with attention the pious and purifying story of a sannyasi who was insulted by impious men but who transcended these insults completely. How did he survive words that pierced him like an arrow? “\[W\]ith determination he remembered that he was suffering the fruit of his own previous karma.” (SB. 11.23.5)

The BBT purport to text 5 adds some weighty advice as an introduction to the story of the Avanti brahmana: “Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura comments as follows: ‘Often those who give up the materialistic path and devote themselves to renunciation are attacked by impious persons. This analysis, however, is superficial, since the punishment is actually the cumulative result of one’s past karma. Some renunciants show lack of tolerance when presented with the remnants of their previous sins and thus are forced to enter again onto the path of impious life. Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu therefore instructs that one should become as tolerant as a tree.’ ”

Next, Sri Krsna will tell Uddhava about the disaster that hurled the brahmana from a wealthy but miserly life to the land of renunciation and deep spiritual realizations.

*Texts 6-13: Loss may lead to renunciation*

There once was a wealthy but parsimonious brahmana who allowed suffering to purify and transform his consciousness: “In the country of Avantithere once lived a certain brahmana who was very rich and gifted with all opulences, and who was engaged in the occupation of commerce. But he was a miserly person — lusty, greedy, and very prone to anger.” (SB. 11.23.6)

Sri Krsna then describes the brahmana’s shameful qualities and the effect they had on him and his family: “In his home, devoid of religiosity and lawful sense gratification, the family members and guests were never properly respected, even with words. He would not even allow sufficient gratification for his own body at the suitable times. Since he was so hardhearted and miserly, his sons, in-laws, wife, daughters and servants began to feel inimical toward him. Becoming disgusted, they would never treat him with affection. In this way the presiding deities of the five family sacrifices became angry at the brahmana, who, being niggardly, guarded his wealth like a Yaksa, who had no good destination either in this world or the next, and who was totally deprived of religiosity and sense enjoyment.” (SB. 11.23.7-9)

Due to his impiety and his disrespect of the demigods, the brahmana lost all the money, gold, and jewels he was hoarding. Factually, however, the little bit of wealth that was truly his remained intact. The BBT purport to text 10 quotes Srila Jiva Gosvami: “\[T\]he brahmana had a trace of piety directed at the Supreme Lord with hopes of liberation. That pure portion of the branch of his piety remained unwithered, eventually giving the fruit of knowledge.”

Sri Krsna continues: “Some of the wealth of this so-called brahmana was taken away by his relatives, My dear Uddhava, some by thieves, some by the whims of providence, some by the effects of time, some by ordinary men, and some by government authorities.” (SB. 11.23.11)

The BBT purport notes: “\[A\]ccording to Srila Sridhara Svami, providence here refers to fires in the home and other types of occasional misfortune. Effects of rime here refers to the destruction of agricultural crops through seasonal irregularities and other such occurrences.”

I laving lost all bis wealth, the brahmana felt an unbearable misery and shed tears. In his pain he cries, in text 14, “How could this misfortune have befallen me?” But then “a powerful feeling of renunciation came over him.” (SB. 11.23.13)

Suffering in itself is insufficient to evoke bhakti to the Supreme Lord. In Srila Sridhara Svami’s comments on Pingala’s words in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.8.34, he points to the association of devotees as the cause of Pingala’s bhakti, not her disappointment. That the AvantI brahmana developed bhakti indicates that he must have at some point had the association of devotees. In the Bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 179), Srila Jiva Gosvami writes that becoming a devotee without apparent association with Vaisnavas indicates that there must have been some association with Vaisnavas in this or a past life. In his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.23.13, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura writes that the brahmana’s suffering of the results of his offenses to others “completed their effects,” and that “an old impression then arose within him and he became detached.”

*Texts 14-30: The use and misuse of human life*

*Texts 14-16: Miserliness and greed condemned*

At this point, the brahmana speaks deeply considered words of self- condemnation: Alas! What great misfortune! I have uselessly tormented myself, struggling to attain money that was intended neither for religious pursuits nor material enjoyment. A miser’s wealth affords him no happiness, because it torments him while he’s alive and delivers him to hell at death. “Whatever pure fame is possessed by the famous and whatever praiseworthy qualities are found in the virtuous are destroyed by even a small amount of greed, just as one’s attractive physical beauty is ruined by a trace of white leprosy.” (SB. 11.23.16)

*Texts 17-21: The self-centered accumulation of wealth condemned*

The miserable, now poverty-stricken brahmana next condemns greed itself: All men have to work hard to first earn wealth and then increase it. Protecting wealth, spending it, losing it, and enjoying it - all give rise to experiences of fear, anxiety, and delusion. “Theft, violence, speaking lies, duplicity, lust, anger, perplexity, pride, quarreling, enmity, faithlessness, envy, and the dangers caused by women, gambling, and intoxication are the fifteen undesirable qualities that contaminate men because of greed for wealth. Although these qualities are undesirable, men falsely ascribe value to them. One desiring to achieve the real benefit of life should therefore remain aloof from undesirable material wealth.” (SB. 11.23.18-19)

The brahmana is speaking from experience, and his suffering has forced him to be introspective, to examine the desires and expectations that have driven his life and compare them to what he has actually achieved. His stark realizations lay bare material reality. This reality is likely at odds with what ever-hopeful accumulators imagine it to be. “Even a man’s brothers, wife, parents, and friends united with him in love will immediately break off their affectionate relationships and become enemies over a single coin. For even a small amount of money these relatives and friends become very agitated and their anger is inflamed. Acting as rivals, they quickly give up all sentiments of good will and will reject one at a moment’s notice, even to the point of committing murder.” (SB. 11.23.20-21)

*Texts 22-23: The proper use of human life*

The brahmana next proposes an alternative goal for his life, one based on what only humans can achieve. Human life is rare, he says, and those who have achieved it have the innate ability to attain heaven or liberation. Those who ignore the opportunity a human birth affords fail to act in their own self-interest and so experience only misfortune. Who would misuse his life simply so he can gather some worthless material property?

From the BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.23.22: “Srila Bhakti-siddhanta Sarasvati Thakura comments as follows: ‘Human birth is better than that of the demigods, ghosts, spirits, animals, trees, lifeless stones, and so forth, because the demigods simply enjoy celestial pleasures, and in other forms of life there is excessive suffering. It is only in human life that one deeply considers one’s ultimate benefit.”’

Narada Muni, Rsabhadeva, and Prahlada Maharaja reached similar conclusions about the wise use of human life. Sri Narada said: “Persons who are actually intelligent and philosophically inclined should endeavor only for that purposeful end which is not obtainable even by wandering from the topmost planet \[Brahmaloka\] down to the lowest planet \[Patala\|. As far as happiness derived from sense enjoyment is concerned, it can be obtained automatically in course of time, just as in course of time we obtain miseries even though we do not desire them.” (SB. 1.5.18)

Rsabhadeva instructed his sons: “My dear boys, of all the living enti- ties who have accepted material bodies in this world, one who has been awarded this human form should not work hard day and night simply for sense gratification, which is available even for dogs and hogs that eat stool. One should engage in penance and austerity to attain the divine position of devotional service. By such activity, one’s heart is purified, and when one attains this position, he attains eternal, blissful life, which is transcendental to material happiness and which continues forever.” (SB. 5.5.1)

And from Sri Prahlada: “My dear friends born of demoniac families, the happiness perceived with reference to the sense objects by contact with the body can be obtained in any form of life, according to one’s past fruitive activities. Such happiness is automatically obtained without endeavor, just as we obtain distress.” (SB. 7.6.3)

*Texts 24-25: The brahmana’s lamentation continues*

The Avanti brahmana’s lamentation and his understanding of his own faults, which have caused his misery, lead him to ponder a weighty subject: wealth should not be hoarded. Rather, it should be properly used and redistributed. An intelligent person will use his wealth, youth, and strength to gain perfection. But I have no intelligence! I feverishly squandered all three as I pursued money. Now I am old. What can I possibly accomplish in the remaining years of my life?

Maharaja Pariksit asked this same question when he was confronted with his own imminent death: “O trustworthy brahmanas, I now ask you about my immediate duty. Please, after proper deliberation, tell me of the unalloyed duty of everyone in all circumstances, and specifically of those who are just about to die.” (SB. 1.19.24)

*Texts 26-27: Progress through questions*

**Whose illusory potency causes even the intelligent to pursue wealth?**

The brahmana again questions and laments the ways be lias misspent bis life. His conclusion is intriguing: “Why does even an intelligent man suffer by his constant vain efforts to get wealth? Indeed, this whole world is most bewildered by someone’s illusory potency.” (SB. 11.23.26)

Struggling mightily to get something that will offer no lasting satisfaction is foolish. That people are still willing to struggle even after they have seen that the pleasure they obtain from the objects they covet is ephemeral is proof to the brahmana that some powerful force of illusion must be at work. That illusion covers so many people, thought the brahmana, indicates the presence of an extremely potent bewilderer.

**Why perform activities that cause future suffering?**

“For one who is in the grips of death, what is the use of wealth or those who offer it, sense gratification or those who offer it, or, for that matter, any type of fruitive activity, which simply causes one to again take birth in the material world?” (SB. 11.23.27)

As the brahmana’s realizations thicken, he abstracts a general principle fundamental to spiritual life: no material situation can satisfy someone who remains wrapped in death’s tight embrace. Krsna said the same thing to Arjuna: “From the highest planet in the material world down to the lowest, all are places of misery wherein repeated birth and death take place.” (Bhagavad-gita 8.16)

*Texts 28-30: Seeing Krsna’s mercy*

**The glory of detachment from matter**

The brahmana now concludes that his troubles are Krsna’s gift: “The Supreme Personality of Godhead, Lord Hari, who contains within Himself all the demigods, must be satisfied with me.” Can one truly view misfortune as the grace of God? The brahmana continues: “Indeed, He has brought me to this suffering condition and forced me to experience detachment, which is the boat to carry me over this ocean of material life.” (SB. 11.23.28)

Only an exalted and fortunate soul can experience this realization deeply; theoretical understandings of Krsna’s mercy tend to pale in the face of personal disaster.

The Avanti brahmana was financially ruined and he lost his family. If we were to go through something similarly dire, would we remain faithfully and affectionately focused on Krsna’s lotus feet? When someone we love is threatened with cancer or our own health fails, can we maintain our focus on Krsna’s kindness toward us? Yet seeing Krsna’s mercy in every circumstance qualifies us for life in the spiritual realm: “My dear Lord, one who earnestly waits for You to bestow Your causeless mercy upon him, all the while patiently suffering the reactions of his past misdeeds and offering You respectful obeisances with his heart, words, and body, is surely eligible for liberation, for it has become his rightful claim.” (SB. 10.14.8)

So by the mercy of Krsna and the power of previous spiritual advancement, the brahmana came to see his loss as his greatest gain.
