Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments on the words the brahmana speaks in text 28: “Gaining intelligence, the brahmana became joyful, and he expresses his joy in three verses \[SB. 11.23.28-30\]. ‘Because of the Lord’s satisfaction, I have attained this condition. And through His satisfaction with Me, I have become indifferent to material life, which is a boat to cross the ocean of birth and death (samsara).’”

**Recouping lost time: the brahmana’s path of detached action**

The brahmana wants to transform his realizations into immediate action: “If there is any time remaining in my life, I will perform austerities and force my body to subsist on the bare necessities. Without further confusion I shall pursue that which constitutes my entire self-interest in life, and I shall remain satisfied within the self.” (SB. 11.23.29)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments on the brahmana’s mood: “I will wither my body, for I had with great effort previously supplied it with so much enjoyment. I shall be attentive in my goal of meditating on the lotus feet of the Lord. If my life ends in this manner, I will be satisfied.”

His detachment from matter has become detachment from living in his current body. Rather than this being an example of clinical depression or narcissism, the brahmana had entered the universe of true humility. Walking through that door, he had surrendered himself as a servant to His Lord. His focus had reached its perfection, shifting from the arrogant accumulation of wealth to a meditative, internal focus on the Lord’s lotus feet and service to I lim.

**The brahmana’s desire and hope**

The brahmana remains hopeful that he will be able to attain his lofty desire at this late stage of his life. He seeks mercy and gains strength from the life of a hero he read about in sastra: “Thus may the presiding demigods of these three worlds kindly show their mercy upon me. Indeed, Maharaja Khatvangawas able to achieve the spiritual world in a single moment.” (SB. 11.23.30)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura adds: “May the devatas like Indra be merciful! May they not present me with obstacles! ‘Will you possibly be able to reach perfection in such a short time?’ Khatvanga achieved perfection in a moment!”

*Texts 31-41: Remaining fixed in the Lord’s service while meeting one’s fate*

*Texts 31-33: The Avanti brahmana depended on Krsna as he wandered about*

Detached and now fully determined to achieve his goal, the Avanti brahmana cut the knots of attachment in his heart (hrdaya-granthin) and assumed the role of a peaceful and silent sannyasi (bhiksu). Alone and unrecognized, he begged humbly for his maintenance. Regardless of what conditions he met as he wandered, he kept his intelligence, senses, and life-air fixed. He also took full shelter of the Lord and became a glorious devotee. Overtly, his life was troublesome and austere he had been dishonored and insulted, because uncultured people considered him an old, dirty beggar and couldn’t see him for who he actually was.

*Texts 34-39: The Avanti brahmana’s experience*

Read the following descriptions carefully. We can appreciate the depth of the Avanti brahmana’s surrender to Krsna’s mercy in all sorts of circumstances by soberly hearing the insults and behavior to which he was subjected: “Some of these persons would take away his sannyasi rod, and some the water pot which he was using as a begging bowl. Some look his deerskin seat, some his chanting beads, and some would steal his torn, ragged clothing. Displaying these things before him, they would pretend to offer them back but would then hide them again. When he was sitting on the bank of a river about to partake of the food that he had collected by his begging, such sinful rascals would come and pass urine on it, and they would dare to spit on his head. Although he had taken a vow of silence, they would try to make him speak, and if he did not speak they would beat him with sticks. Others would chastise him, saying, ‘This man is just a thief.’ And others would bind him up with rope, shouting, ‘Tie him up! Tie him up!’ They would criticize and insult him, saying, ‘This man is just a hypocrite and a cheat. He makes a business of religion simply because he lost all his wealth and his family threw him out.’ Some would ridicule him by saying, ‘Just see this greatly powerful sage! He is as steadfast as the Himalaya Mountains. By practice of silence he strives for his goal with great determination, just like a duck.’ Other persons would pass foul air upon him, and sometimes others would bind this twice-born brahmana in chains and keep him captive like a pet animal.” (SB. 11.23.34-39)

*Texts 40-41: The Avanti brahmana remains fixed*

The extreme harassment the Avanti brahmana experienced left him unshakahly peaceful. What shelter and stability he had attained! Krsna Himself reveals the secret of the brahmana’s strength to Uddhava: “The brahmana understood that all his suffering - from other living beings, from the higher forces of nature, and from his own body - was unavoidable, being allotted to him by providence \[distam\].” (SB. 11.23.40)

Srila Sridhara Svami’s comment on text 40 categorizes the disturbances tolerated by the brahmana. “Due to other physical entities,” the dcarya writes, means “those instigated by rascals and others.” “Due to his own body” means “based on suffering fever, and so on.” “Due to divine forces” means “by the influence of heat, cold, and so on.” Distam refers to that which is awarded by fate.

The brahmana’s profound ability to accept his fate blessed him with an undisturbed consciousness: “Even while being insulted by these low-class men who were trying to effect his downfall, he remained steady in his spiritual duties \[sva-dharma\].” (SB. 11.23.41)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura’s comment on text 40 directs us to how we ourselves can achieve the level of surrender attained by the Avanti brahmana: “One who sees things in a material way fails to realize the true self and will therefore lack any quality of tolerance. But one can attain peace from the threefold material sufferings by taking shelter of the lotus feet of Sri Nityananda, the older brother and very image of the most magnanimous Sri Gaurasundara, who is no different from Lord Krsna, Vrajendranandana Himself. The jwas who have given up all unwanted qualities are never shaken by the words and activities of atheists, who have no devotion for Lord Visnu. Rather, they understand that the ridiculous antics of those without devotion for the Lord are natural for persons inimical to the devotees. The devotees are prone to be very merciful to such persons.”

Indeed, the level of tolerance and acceptance a Vaisnava exhibits astounded even Mother Parvatl. She observed such tolerance in Maharaja Citraketu before hearing about the glories of Vaisnavas from Lord Siva: “Devotees solely engaged in the devotional service of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Narayana, never fear any condition of life. For them the heavenly planets, liberation, and the hellish planets are all the same, for such devotees are interested only in the service of the Lord.” (SB. 6.17.28)

In his purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 6.17.27, Srila Prabhupada writes: “As stated by Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu, taror api sahisnuna. Just like a tree, a devotee can tolerate all kinds of curses and reversals in life. This is the excellence of a devotee.”

Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu teaches (as quoted above, Siksastakam 3) that trees and blades of grass exhibit the complete level of tolerance required for properly focused, continuous chanting of Krsna’s names. Otherwise, the disturbed mind will again and again break the chanter’s focus and determination.

*Texts 41-57: The song of the Avanti brahmana (Bhiksu-gita)*

Sri Krsna already described the Avanti brahmana’s thoughts, and now i he song the brahmana himself will sing reveals in more detail just how exulted those thoughts are: “These people are not the cause of my happiness and distress. Neither are the demigods, my own body, the planets, my past work, or time. Rather, it is the mind alone that causes \[manah pa rath karanam\] happiness and distress and perpetuates the rotation of material life \[samsara-cakram parivartayed yat\].” (SB. 11.23.42)

In this first verse of his song, the brahmana names the six categories of items we tend to blame for our suffering: other people, the demigods, one’s own body, the planets, one’s past karma (work), and time. Later, in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.23.50-55, the Avanti brahmana will refute each of these so-called causes one by one, because he has already identified the lone culprit, his mind.

*Texts 43-49: The mind - and the importance of keeping it under control*

The brahmana begins with a brief analysis of the relationship between the mind, the Supersoul, and the soul wandering from birth to death to rebirth.

*Texts 43-44: The central role of the mind*

According to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.23.43, the mind’s tendencies activate the modes of nature that control us. From these tendencies, which are specific combinations of goodness, passion, and ignorance, the activities that determine one’s position in life are generated.

The Supersoul is present in the body along with the individual soul, who is the life beneath the coverings of the inert body and mind. The brahmana now describes the relationship between the Supersoul, himself (the soul), and the mind: “Acting as my friend, He simply witnesses from His transcendental position. I, the infinitesimal spirit soul, on the other hand, have embraced this mind, which is the mirror reflecting the image of the material world. Thus I have become engaged in enjoying objects of desire and am entangled due to contact with the modes of nature.” (SB. 11.23.44)

By showing the soul’s relationship with the mind, the brahmana has disclosed the mind’s central role in material life. When the soul embraces the mind as the self, he is forced to also embrace whatever desires and thoughts fill the mind. These desires and thoughts are determined by one’s karma - the specific configuration of the three modes of nature that encase each soul.

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura writes in his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.23.44: “As my friend, the Supersoul observes from a level of superior knowledge without being affected \[by the modes of nature\]... Accepting the mind, or subtle hotly, as itself, the jiva becomes bound up, engaging in... actions produced by the qualities in the mind. The experience of repeated birth and death (samsara) arises for the jiva from this imposition of the mind.”

*Texts 45-49: The importance of controlling the mind*

**The purpose of religiosity and piety**

Next, the brahmana explains the relationship between pious acts and Vedic practices, and controlling the mind. The goal of focusing the mind is to fix it on the Supreme Lord: “Charity, prescribed duties, observance of major and minor regulative principles, hearing from scripture, pious works, and purifying vows all have as their final aim the subduing of the mind. Indeed, concentration of the mind on the Supreme is the highest yoga.” (SB. 11.23.45)

Then he reiterates the same truth in a different way: “If one’s mind is perfectly fixed and pacified, then tell me what need does one have to perform ritualistic charity and other pious rituals? And if one’s mind remains uncontrolled, lost in ignorance, then of what use are these engagements for him?” (SB. 11.23.46)

Controlling the mind is central to all spiritual success, because the mind is either an exalted friend or a deadly enemy. The brahmana speaks this realization with power: “All the senses have been under the control of the mind since time immemorial, and the mind himself never comes under the sway of any other. He is stronger than the strongest, and his godlike power is fearsome. Therefore, anyone who can bring the mind under control becomes the master of all the senses.” (SB. 11.23.47)

**The primary effect of an uncontrolled mind**

The uncontrolled mind as the director of one’s life increasingly defines modern civilization, for moral, religious, and social restraints appear to lessen day by day: “Failing to conquer this irrepressible enemy, the mi nil, whose urges are intolerable and who torments the heart, many people are completely bewildered and create useless quarrel with others. I bus they conclude that other people are either their friends, their enemies, or parties indifferent to them.” (SB. 11.23.48)

**The horrific result of identifying with the uncontrolled mind**

“Persons who identify with this body, which is simply the product of the material mind, are blinded in their intelligence, thinking in terms of ‘I’ and ‘mine.’ Because of their illusion of ‘this is I, but that is someone else,’ they wander in endless darkness.” (SB. 11.23.49)

Acting on one’s mental impulses is dangerous, as Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura states: “Accepting the body produced by the mind, they think, ‘This is my body and this is my son.’ In this way they wander in samsara.”

*Texts 50-57: False and true causes of happiness and distress*

The soul’s identification with the mind’s desires and attachments is the sole cause of its continued embodiments in the material world. Real- izing this, the Avanti brahmana was unwilling to blame anything or anyone else for what had befallen him. Rather, he remained peaceful, thinking, “At whom should I become angry?” In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.23.50-55, the brahmana rejects all the usual persons and things that become targets for our anger.

*Text 50: So, true or false? - other people cause my unhappiness. False.*

If other people cause our happiness and distress, “then where is the place of the soul in such a conception?” The soul has no place, because material happiness and distress are related not to the soul but to the interaction between one material body and another.

If you bite your tongue with your own teeth, who is to blame? Taking full responsibility for everything that occurred to him, yet not allowing any occurrence to affect his inner, deep shelter, which was beyond the shifting experiences of his mind, the brahmana reasoned, “If someone bites his tongue with his own teeth, at whom can he become angry in his suffering?”

The BBT purport adds: “Although the brahmana was receiving kind offerings of charity from some people and being harassed and beaten by others, he denied that these people were the ultimate cause of his happiness and distress, for he was fixed on the platform of self-realizat ion beyond the material hotly and mind.”

*Text 51: The demigods cause my unhappiness. False*

Can a demigod who controls a specific sense cause an eternal soul to suffer? The demigod (adhidaivika deity) is simply interacting with the sense he controls. What does this have to do with the soul? At whom can one become angry when one limb of the body attacks another limb of the same body?

*Text 52: The soul (jiva) causes its own unhappiness. False*

“If the soul himself were the cause of happiness and distress, then we could not blame others, since happiness and distress would be simply the nature of the soul. According to this theory, nothing except the soul actually exists, and if we were to perceive something besides the soul, that would be illusion. Therefore, since happiness and distress do not actually exist in this concept, why become angry at oneself or others?”

From the BBT purport: “Because a dead body does not feel pleasure or pain, our happiness and distress are due to our own consciousness, which is the nature of the soul. It is not, however, the original function of the soul to enjoy material happiness and suffer material distress. These are produced by ignorant material affection and enmity based on ialse ego. Our involvement in sense gratification drags our consciousness into the material body, where it is shocked by the inevitable bodily pains and problems.”

Sri Madhvacarya also comments on this text: “Because the jiva is by his very nature happy, we cannot ascribe unhappiness to him. Therefore he has become unhappy only by falsely identifying with his mind.”

*Text 53: The planets (my astrological chart) cause my suffering. False*

The planets have no relationship with the eternal soul, for the planets affect only things that have taken birth. The planets cause pain only lo one another as they fight, and since the living entity is distinct both bom the planets and his own body, how can he blame the planets for his sufferings?

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment separates the actions of planets on bodies from their noneffect on the actual person, the soul: “The planets relate to bodies that are born. Depending on the ascendant at birth, the planets situated in the twelve zodiac signs cause suffering, as they do when they are placed in the eighth house, for example. Astrologers also say that the planets afflict one another by aspecting one another, and this is the cause of suffering. They do not afflict the person. The affliction from planets arises from the Jiva’s identity with the body, which is born on the ascendant.”

*Text 54: My karma causes my unhappiness. False*

Thinking that the reactions to my previous fruitive activities are causing my suffering, the AvantI brahmana says, neglects my identity as an eternal soul. Fruitive actions require both a material body, which is unconscious, and a soul, which is eternal, spiritual, and ultimately aloof from the body. Therefore neither can receive the karmic fruits of action.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura indicates that neither the soul, being eternal, nor the body, being unconscious, can experience karma: “Since pure consciousness cannot amalgamate with the dead material body any more than pure light can combine with darkness, at whom should one become angry? Karma, therefore, is not at the root of happiness or distress.”

*Text 55: The movement of time causes my misery. False*

Time cannot cause the soul happiness or distress, since both time and the soul are manifest from the Lord’s spiritual potencies. Can a fire burn its own flames? Can cold harm a snowflake or a hailstone? The “spirit soul is transcendental and beyond the experience of material happiness and distress. At whom, therefore, should one become angry?

Srila Sridhara Svami illuminates the text: “Fire does not cause its own flames to become burned or destroyed. If someone objects, ‘But there is the burning and destruction of the wood, which is the covering designation of that fire,’ another example is spoken: the coldness of snow does not affect the destruction of its snowflakes. And further, when accepting that the soul is part of the whole and is therefore transcendental, no such duality of happiness and distress exists for one who is transcendental.”

*Text 56: The false ego is causing my suffering. True*

The brahmana concludes: “The false ego gives shape to illusory material existence and thus experiences material happiness and distress. The spirit soul, however, is transcendental to material nature; he can never actually be affected by material happiness and distress in any place, under any circumstance, or by the agency of any person. A person who understands this has nothing whatsoever to fear from the material creation.”

Neither these six previously named agents (texts 50-55) nor an object to be named later is the cause of suffering. Earlier, in text 42 of this chapter, the brahmana named the actual culprit, the mind. Now he points to the mind’s co-conspirator, the false ego. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura summarizes texts 50-56: “What indeed causes the spirit soul, who is transcendental to maya, to experience suffering? The answer is given that the cause of suffering is the false ego, which is in the subtle body predominated by the mind. There is no other cause. The nature of false ego is to create the bondage of material life .... That the mind is alone the cause of suffering is the basic meaning of this whole section of verses. When the soul is covered by the bodily conception (due to false ego), he forgets his pure nature. Only then do these six causes of suffering, following in the footsteps of the soul’s becoming covered, bring their effects. This is the meaning.”

*Text 57: Crossing the ocean of material suffering - the Avanti brahmana prescribes the cure*

Now the Avanti brahmana prescribes the cure for suffering, which he himself has taken: “I shall cross over the insurmountable ocean of nescience by being firmly fixed \[paratma-nistham\] in the service of the lotus feet of Krsna \[mukundarighri\]. This was approved by (he previous acaryas, who were fixed in firm devotion to the Lord, Paramatma, the Supreme Personality of Godhead.”

Thus the Avanti brahmana establishes that serving Krsna purely while practicing full dependence on Him is the essence of'sannyasa and also the way to transcend the ferocious ocean of material existence. The BBT purport quotes from Srila Prabhupada’s commentary on this text, which appears in Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, Madhya 3.6: “In connection with this verse, which quotes Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.23.57, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura says that of the sixty-four items required for rendering devotional service, acceptance of the symbolic marks of sannyasa is a regulative principle. If one accepts the sannyasa order, his main business is to devote his life completely to the service of Mukunda, Krsna. If one does not completely devote his mind and body to the service of the Lord, he does not actually become a sannyasi… The dress is not sannyasa, but the attitude of service to Krsna is.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura also emphasizes the Avanti brahmana’s fixed devotion even over his spirit of renunciation. Consequent to this, the previous pure devotional service to Me, which had been checked by various obstacles, reappeared in his mind. When bhakti manifested, he rejected thoughts of renunciation and his methods of tolerating the dualities. Submerging himself in the sweet ocean of service to the Lord’s lotus feet, he danced with great boldness. Fixed in the svarupa of the Jiva, which is purified of its identification with the body, and slighting fixed on Paramatma, he will cross over samsara by service alone (eva). 'Why do you fix yourself on the Paramatma? I will do what was established by the ancient predecessors.’”

*Texts 58-60: A summary of the Avanti brahmana’s path*

In texts 58-59 Sri Krsna summarizes the life and lessons of the Avanti brahmana before describing, in text 60, the essence of that path. “Thus becoming detached upon the loss of his property, this sage gave up his moroseness. He left home, taking sannyasa, and began to travel about the earth. Even when insulted by foolish rascals he remained unswerved from his duty and chanted this song. No other force besides his own mental confusion makes the soul experience happiness and distress. His perception of friends, neutral parties and enemies, and the whole material life he builds around this perception are simply created out of ignorance.” (SB. 11.23.58-59)

Sri Krsna now points to the goal of yoga and other preliminary practices: “My dear Uddhava, fixing your intelligence on Me, you should thus completely control the mind. This is the essence of the science of yoga.” (SB. 11.23.60)

Again Krsna has concluded that all paths - in t his instance the paths of renunciation and sannyasa — end in devoted service to Him. The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.23.58 quotes Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura, where he underscores the potency of the Avanti brahmana’s song and gives a warning: “\[O\]ne not capable of listening to the song of this sannyasi will certainly remain an obedient servant of material illusion.”

In Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on text 59, he reminds us that “nothing other than bewilderment of the mind causes happiness and distress.” And to text 60 Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura adds: “Only devotional service is capable of subduing the mind. The processes of karma-yoga, hatha-yoga, juana-yoga, raja-yoga, and the yoga of being an enemy of the Supreme Lord all simply agitate the mind. Through them, one becomes attached to a particular religious process and remains a nondevotee.”

*Text 61: A benediction*

Krsna concludes with a benediction to those who enter deeply into the meaning of the Avanti brahmana’s song: “Anyone who listens to or recites to others this song of the sannyasi, which presents scientific knowledge of the Absolute, and who thus meditates upon it with full attention, will never again be overwhelmed by the dualities of material happiness and distress.” (SB. 11.23.61)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura informs us that the Avanti brahmana was not only fully detached from matter and attached to Krsna, but he was also mercifiul. He himself “meditated on and heard this song, and had others also meditate on it and hear it. Therefore, since he was endowed thus with all mercy, he awarded other living entities intelligence by disseminating his exceptional mercy to take to the path of following in the footsteps of the devotees.”

**Chapter 24: The Philosophy of Sankhya**

In the twenty-second chapter of Canto Eleven, Sri Krsna stated that i he reason the soul transmigrates is because it identifies with the mind, which is filled with material desires. Chapter 23 showed an example of someone who learned to separate himself from his desire-filled mind and offered instructions for those of us who wish to do the same. In his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.24.1, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains why Krsna follows the song of the exalted Avanti brahmana, in chapter 23, with a summary of Sankhya philosophy. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti reminds us that we learned from the Avanti brahmana that suffering is caused by the soul’s misindentification with the subtle body, which is predominated by the mind. This misidentification dissolves when one learns to discriminate between the body and the soul. Thinking in terms of Sankhya philosophy develops this discrimination. “Therefore,” Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura writes, “the Lord teaches Sankhya so that one can give up the illusion of bodily identification.”

Sridhara Svami’s comment on chapter 24, text 1: “In the twenty-fourth chapter, the confusion of the mind is stopped by Sankhya, which teaches the understanding that all things are created out of and return to the Supersoul. Having in the previous chapter stated how controlling the mind is the means for becoming free from duality for those who are devoted to His two lotus feet, Lord Krsna now speaks the philosophy of Sankhya to help aspirants be successful in controlling the mind.”

Srila Jiva Gosvami’s introductory comment to this chapter is also helpful: “The cause of the soul’s suffering is his self-identification with the subtle body, which is predominantly characterized by the mind. This we have understood from the previous chapter, the Bhiksu-gita. That same false identification of the self can be eradicated by properly discriminating between spirit and matter, and that ability to discriminate between spirit and matter is based on knowledge of Sankhya.”

*Texts 1-10: Creation, part one - Krsna is the cause of the primary creation*

**Krsna causes the creation of the universal ingredients (sarga)**

Sri Krsna introduces the Sankhya process, a yoga process using the intellect, as having been “perfectly established by ancient authorities.” Understanding the science of Sankhya, He says, will award one freedom from “the illusion of material duality.” (SB. 11.24.1)

He begins by describing His existence both during Satya-yuga, the first age after creation, and during the period before creation - the annihilation, when everything that was and will be in the future is wound up in the Lord. At this time, “the seer existed alone, non-different from the seen object.” (SB. 11.24.2) Why does Krsna tell Uddhava about this? He wishes to illustrate that everything in existence emanates from and ultimately enters into Him, the primeval Lord, the Supreme Personality of Godhead.Krsna thus establishes Himself as the ultimate object of knowledge, the Supreme Lord, and the Supersoul. From that one Lord, who is inaccessible to the intelligence of man and free of all dualities, comes His material (maya-sakti) and marginal potencies (tatastha-sakti). His material potency evolves into matter (prakrti), which embodies the principle of cause and effect; from His marginal potency emanate the conditioned living entities (Jivas), who attempt to enjoy matter.

Krsna continues: When material nature is agitated by My glance, the three material modes - goodness, passion, and ignorance - manifest so the jivas can fulfill the desires they had before they were annihilated. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura mentions in this regard that the Supreme Personality of Godhead creates the means to dull the spiritual perception of those living entities who have chosen to either enjoy or renounce matter.

From these modes arose the sutra and the mahat-tattva.From the mahat-tatlva comes false ego. The essential function of the false ego is to award jivas an experience of self that feels separate from and independent of Krsna - as if they are the material body they now inhabit. False ego manifests in three varieties, one for each of the three modes of nature: goodness, passion, and ignorance. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura comments that jivas have the tendency to become covered, as a special aspect of their infinitesimal consciousness.

False ego combines individually with each mode, which causes the other basic ingredients of creationto arise. False ego in the mode of ignorance gives rise to the subtle physical perceptions, from which the gross elements are generated. False ego in the mode of passion gives rise to the senses, and false ego in the mode of goodness gives rise to the eleven demigods (the BBT purport to text 8 tells us that these are “the deities of the directions, the wind, and the sun, Varuna, the Asvini deities, Agni, Indra, Upendra, Mitra, Brahma, and Candra”). The Lord’s potencies combine these ingredients to form an egg-shaped universe. The Lord then enters into the universe, which becomes “My excellent place of residence.” (SB. 11.24.9) According to Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura, the Lord creates this universe as “a field for enjoyment or renunciation for the jivas uninterested in devotional service.”

As the Lord floats on the causal waters in the universe, a lotus, which becomes the birthplace of Brahma, grows from His navel. Sripada Madhvacarya notes that the Lord enters the universe without relinquishing His purely transcendental body made of knowledge and ecstasy. But “from the lotus coming from His navel, the greatly powerful ascetic, four-headed Brahma, whose body pervades all universal existence, was born with a material body \[and not a transcendental one\].”

*Texts 11-15: Creadon, part Two - Krsna allots appropriate residences to the conditioned souls*

**The secondary creation (visarga) of Lord Brahma**

The Supreme Lord’s merciful empowerment coupled with Brahma’s performance of austerities allowed Brahma to create the three planetary systems and their presiding deities as residences: the demigods were given the Svar planetary system, the “ghostly spirits” the Bhuvar planetary system, the human beings and other mortal creatures the Bhur planetary system, and the demons and Nagas the regions below the earth. Seekers of liberation achieve higher, more exalted realms: “In this way the destinations of the three worlds were arranged as the corresponding reactions for different kinds of work performed within the three modes of nature. By mystic yoga, great austerities, and the renounced order of life, the pure destinations of Maharloka, Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka are attained. But by devotional yoga, one achieves My transcendental abode \[bhakti-yogasya mad-gatih\].” (SB. 11.24.13-14) Based on the reactions conditioned souls must face for the fruitive work they performed in previous births, the Supreme Lord, through His time potency, arranges the upward and downward movements that position the conditioned souls in the mighty river of the modes of nature.

Sridhara Svami writes in his comment on text 15 of this chapter that these descriptions are meant to encourage renunciation, because every destination, whether upward or downward, apart from Krsna’s abode, is temporary. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura adds that those who fail to take shelter of devotional service either drown or float in the world created of the three modes. The time potency, he explains, keeps the living entities, who are enjoying the fruits of their work, wandering within the fourteen worlds.

*Texts 16-21: Maintenance - the Supreme Personality of Godhead is both the essence and basis of material existence*

As Lord Krsna speaks Sarikhya philosophy, He reveals Himself as the Supreme Lord and the primal cause of both the ingredients and process of creation.

Sri Krsna continues: Everything in material existence is a combina- tion of material nature and the jiva’s attempt to enjoy that material nature.As the ingredient gold exists before a gold ring is cast of it, and that gold continues to exist even after the ring is made, so everything in the material world is based on its primal elements. That is, “one created object becomes the cause and basis of another created object. A particular thing may thus be called real in that it possesses the basic nature of another object that constitutes its origin and final state.” (SB. 11.24.18)

The acaryas commenting on this text claim that text 18 responds to a statement made in sruti: reality is the original cause of existence. Sruti makes this statement, Srila Sridhara Svami explains, to establish the reality of the ultimate cause, the Supreme Soul. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains that a product that is created by transforming an already existing product is just as real as the original product, even though the new product’s existence is relative to and dependent on the product that caused it. The acarya gives an example: a pot is a relative product, a transformation of earth, which is the cause of the pot. Unlike the relative or dependent product we call “pot,” the pot’s cause, earth, is absolute, since it has the character of being the ultimate cause of the pot. So even though the cause (earth) and the product (the pot) are both real, we call the cause “reality,” since this is how the Supreme Personality of Godhead designates it. This definition of “reality” and the “real” is to be accepted in accordance with the sruti statement, “Only the original earth is reality.”

In this way, it should he accepted that the foundation of the universe is not illusory but real: it is the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Thus Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura adds to his own comment, “In other explanations in this chapter, the Mayavada interpretation of reality is shown to be meaningless, since everyone understands the qualities of cause and effect.”

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura writes that the Supreme Personality of Godhead is “factual reality.” Therefore even on seeing that the various manifest creations He has produced are temporary, we should not concoct the idea that He is God, the Reality, but that everything He has produced is illusory. He adds that we should also not accept the temporary conditions of this world as eternal. Rather, we should understand that the temporary existence of the uni- verse and everything in it is vastly different from the eternal reality of Vaikuntha.

The BBT purport explains the meaning and significance of text 18: “In relation to the clay pot, clay is the beginning and final state; thus the pot is called real, for it possesses the essential characteristics of clay, which exists before and after the existence of the functioning instrument known as the pot. Similarly, earth exists before and after the clay, and thus clay may be considered real because it possesses the essential characteristics of earth, which exists before and after the existence of the clay. Similarly, earth and other elements are created from the mahat-tattva, which exists before and after the existence of the elements, which may be considered real because they possess the essential characteristics of the mahat-tattva. The mahat-tattva is ultimately the creation of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the cause of all causes, who exists after all is annihilated. The Absolute Truth is the Supreme Lord Himself, who step by step gives meaning and character to all that exists.”

Based on the above conclusion that “reality” refers both to the cause and the effect, even if the cause is eternal and the effect temporary, one may ask, “The universe is real. It springs from prakrti, or the eternal material nature, which remains after the universe is annihilated. But this conclusion doesn’t consider both the Supreme Person (purusa) and time, which combine with prakrti to form the material universe (as explained in chapter 22). Is there not a single, ultimate cause of all causes?”

In text 19, Sri Krsna continues His exposition of Sankhya philosophy, drawing Uddhava closer to understanding His own position as the Absolute Truth and Supreme Personality of Godhead: “The material universe may be considered real, having nature as its original ingredient and final state. Lord Maha-visnu is the resting place of nature, which becomes manifest by the power of time. Thus nature, the almighty Visnu, and time are not different from Me, the Supreme Absolute Truth.” (SB. 11.24.19)

Srila Sridhara Svami explains that what Krsna is saying in this text is that prakrti, the ingredient cause of this real material world, and its basis, the Supreme purusa, as well as the time factor, which causes the universe to manifest by agitating the modes of nature - all three of these are not separate but are He Himself, the original Absolute Truth. Nature is His potency, and the purusa and time are His manifestations.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura adds that although prakrti is subject to change, the Supreme Lord is not; this is because prakrti is His external energy.

It is due to the Supreme Lord’s continued glance that the material world continues to exist and manifest “the great and variegated flow of universal creation.” (SB. 11.24.20) Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura explains this further: the temporary but variegated objects of material existence, as well as time, are manifest as long as the Lord continues to glance at the material energy. “He glances in order to create objects of enjoyment for those inimical to Him.”

Krsna concludes this section by reiterating what He has already established in His exposition on Sankhya - that He is the foundation on which everything in material existence rests: “I am the basis of the universal form \[viran maya\],which displays endless variety through the repeated creation, maintenance, and destruction of the planetary systems. Originally containing within itself all planets in their dormant state, My universal form manifests the varieties of created existence by arranging the coordinated combination of the five elements.” (SB. 11.24.21)

*Texts 22-28: Destruction - the universe’s annihilation rests on Krsna*

Creation proceeds from subtle to gross; at the time of annihilation the direction is reversed — everything that has been created merges back into the state from which it emanated. Material bodies merge into food, which merges into grains, which merge back into the earth element. Earth returns to fragrance, which merges into water, which returns to taste. Taste merges back into fire, which merges back into form, which returns to touch. Touch merges into ether and ether into sound. All the senses return to their origins, their individual presiding demigods. The demigods merge into mind, which merges into false ego in the mode of goodness. Similarly sound becomes one with false ego in the mode of ignorance, and the “all-powerful false ego, the first of all the physical elements, merges into the total nature. The total material nature, the primary repository of the three basic modes, dissolves into the modes. These modes of nature then merge into the unmanifest form of nature, and that unmanifest form merges into time.” (SB. 11.24.26)

Ultimately, everything returns again to the Supreme Lord, the ultimate source and resting place of all things: “Time merges into the Supreme Lord, present in the form of the omniscient Maha-purusa, the original activator of all living beings. That origin of all life merges into Me, the unborn Supreme Soul, who remains alone, established within Himself. It is from Him that all creation and annihilation are manifested.” (SB. 11.24.27)

*Text 28: The power of this knowledge*

“Just as the rising sun removes the darkness of the sky, similarly, this scientific knowledge of cosmic annihilation removes all illusory duality from the mind of a serious student. Even if illusion somehow enters his heart, it cannot remain there.” (SB. 11.24.28)

Sridhara Svami tells us about the utility of the Sankhya knowledge Krsna has just introduced by asking how delusion based on duality can remain in the heart after one has learned to discriminate between spirit and matter through Sankhya.

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura comments that one living on the mental platform “and searching for truth” must take shelter of mundane dualities. But when such a person is able to rid himself of these dualities, then the natural function of the soul makes him eager to engage in the eternal service of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

*Text 29: Thus Krsna has spoken the knowledge of Sankhya*

Krsna has now concluded His description of Sankhya, which awards knowledge that can eradicate the illusion of considering the body and all other temporary phenomena as one’s self. Through His analysis, Krsna also established that He is the cause, maintainer, and annihilator of everything that exist in the world of matter. The Lord concludes: “Thus I, the perfect seer of everything \[paravara-drsa maya\] material and spiritual, have spoken this knowledge of Sankhya, which destroys the illusion of doubt by scientific analysis of creation and annihilation.” (SB. 1 1.24.29)

Krsna is the authority when it comes to information about the universe, its components, and its creation. He is paravarct'drsa maya, the perfect seer and knower of everything material and spiritual. In his last comments on this chapter, Srila Sridhara Svami thus offers his respects to the Supreme Lord: “I offer my obeisances unto that Lord Hari, who, by explaining the science of Sankhya, has clearly shown us the truth of the self as if it were right before our eyes.” Srila Jiva Gosvami also makes some final comments on this chapter, pointing out the devotional conclusion of Sankhya philosophy. He explains that the Personality of Godhead, who resides in Vaikuntha along with His internal energy, is the same “I” who is “the perfect seer of everything material and spiritual” (SB. 11.24.29). Thus that person has established Himself as the original Personality of Godhead, the origin of everything, and that which remains after the annihilation.

In Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura’s final comment, he calls his readers to recognize an opportunity for action: “Various modes of thought arise from the mental determination and doubting function of the living entity. These different ways of thinking generate false arguments about which path is best. But the person who has taken shelter of the lotus feet of the Supreme Personality of Godhead can view all things with a clear intelligence. By investigating the Supreme Personality of Godhead and His energies, by both positive and negative means, the conditioned soul can become liberated and devote himself to the eternal service of the Supreme Lord.”

**Chapter 25: The Three Modes of Nature and Beyond**

*Text 1: Introduction to the three modes of nature*

In speaking Sankhya philosophy, Sri Krsna philosophically separated matter from spirit and described Himself as the cause of all causes, the creator, maintainer, and destroyer. He now shifts to a peripheral topic, the three modes of nature, His potencies that control the material world: “O best among men, please listen as I describe to you how the living entity attains a particular nature by association with individual material modes.” (SB. 11.25.1)

Why does Krsna shift His focus? Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura indicates why we need to hear about the three modes: “The functions of the three frunas are described, because as long as one does not conquer the actions of the three gunas, one continues to identify the self with the body, even if one can \[philosophically\] distinguish the body from the atma with the help of Sankhya.”

By the end of this chapter, in texts 32-36, Krsna will reveal the process of becoming free from the modes’ dominance, but first, He lists the effects of each mode to warn us just how tightly we are bound.

*Texts 2-4: The effects of the modes of nature*

Krsna first describes the qualities that appear when one of the three modes is prominent. Signs of goodness: “Mind and sense control, tolerance, discrimination, sticking to one’s prescribed duty, truthfulness, mercy, careful study of the past and future, satisfaction in any condition, generosity, renunciation of sense gratification, faith in the spiritual master, being embarrassed at improper action, charity, simplicity, humbleness, and satisfaction within oneself.” (SB. 11.25.2)

Signs of passion: “Material desire, great endeavor, audacity, dissatisfaction even in gain, false pride, praying for material advancement, considering oneself different and better than others, sense gratification, rash eagerness to fight, a fondness for hearing oneself praised, the tendency to ridicule others, advertising one’s own prowess, and justifying one’s actions by one’s strength.” (SB. 11.25.3)

Signs of ignorance: “Intolerant anger, stinginess, speaking without scriptural authority, violent hatred, living as a parasite, hypocrisy, chronic fatigue, quarrel, lamentation, delusion, unhappiness, depression, sleeping too much, false expectations, fear, and laziness constitute the major qualities of the mode of ignorance.” (SB. 11.25.4)

*Texts 5-8: The three modes manifest their influence in all circumstances*

Having delineated the general characteristics of each dominant mode, Krsna now explains (in text 6) that the effects of the modes infiltrate every circumstance. They affect how jivas view objects as identical with themselves or as owned by them. They affect their endeavors, religiosity, economic development, faith, wealth, preferred sense pleasures and other types of desires, family attachments, as well as their religious and occupational duties.

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.25.6 describes that we are not affected by only one mode at a time but a mixture of the modes: “One completely absorbed in the mentality of being peaceful could not work in the material world; he would lack any impulse to perform activity. Similarly, one absorbed in lust would be blinded without at least a tinge of peacefulness or restraint. One overwhelmed with anger could not function properly in the material world without the mixture of other qualities. Thus we find that a material mode does not occur in a pure, isolated form but rather is mixed with other modes, thereby making possible normal functioning within this world.”

*Texts 9-29: More on the effect of the modes*

*Text 9: When one guna or another is predominant*

Although the modes of nature that affect a person are mixed, one of the three is generally dominant. Krsna now lists characteristics that allow us to see which guna is dominant in someone: “A person exhibiting qualities such as self-control is understood to be predominantly in the mode of goodness. Similarly, a passionate person is recognized by his lust, and one in ignorance is recognized by qualities such as anger.” (SB. 11.25.9)

*Texts 10-11: How the modes affect one’s worship*

The modes of nature affect all aspects of people’s lives, even how they worship the Supreme Lord. Sri Krsna explains: “Any person, whether man or woman, who worships Me with loving devotion, offering his or her prescribed duties unto Me without material attachment, is understood to be situated in goodness.When a person worships Me by his prescribed duties with the hope of gaining material benefit, his nature should be understood to be in passion, and one who worships Me with the desire to commit violence against others is in ignorance.” (SB. 11.25.10-11)

*Text 12: The Supreme Lord is not influenced by the gunas*

The modes of nature hind everyone, but they are unable to hind Krsna, l he ull imate cause of all causes and (he ultimate creator and controller of the modes. The modes can no more bind Krsna than a prison warden can bind the reigning monarch of his kingdom: “The three modes of material nature - goodness, passion, and ignorance - influence the living entity but not Me. Manifesting within his mind, they induce the living entity to become attached to material bodies and other created objects. In this way the living entity is bound up.” (SB. 11.25.12)

In his comment on text 12, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura stresses the difference between the conditioned soul, the jiva, and the Supreme Lord: “The jiva, attached to the body and related things, becomes bound. However I \[Krsna\] am not attached. Although I carry out creation and destruction by regulating the gunas, I am eternally free of them. This is the big difference between us.”

*Texts 13-15: The effects of a mode’s predominance*

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura offers a general comment that explains this next section of texts: “The gunas in each jiva predominate one over the other, and based on this the jiva attains his corresponding qualities. The states the jiva attains are described in three verses.”

*Text 13: Goodness*

Goodness allows one to control his mind and senses. “When the mode of goodness, which is luminous, pure, and auspicious, predominates over passion and ignorance, a man becomes endowed with happiness, virtue, knowledge, and other good qualities.” (SB. 11.25.13)

*Text 14: Passion*

“When the mode of passion, which causes attachment, separatism, and activity, conquers ignorance and goodness, a man begins to work hard to acquire prestige and fortune. Thus in the mode of passion he experiences anxiety and struggle.” (SB. 11.25.14)

*Text 15: Ignorance*

“When the mode of ignorance conquers passion and goodness, it covers one’s consciousness and makes one foolish and dull, balling into lamentation and illusion, a person in the mode of ignorance sleeps excessively, indulges in false hopes, and displays violence toward others.” (SB. 11.25.15)

*Texts 16-18: Lifting oneself above the lower gunas*

The mode of goodness affects one’s consciousness in a way that is favorable for spiritual advancement, and the practices that cultivate goodness, such as waking early and refraining from meat-eating, illicit sex, intoxicants, and gambling therefore form the foundation on which devotees build their sadhana.

*Text 16: Goodness*

“When consciousness becomes clear and the senses are detached from matter, one experiences fearlessness within the material body and detachment from the material mind. You should understand this situation to be the predominance of the mode of goodness, in which one has the opportunity to realize Me.” (SB. 11.25.16)

The specific mode of nature dominating our consciousness causes that mode to increase its influence. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments on this sequence of three texts: “\[W\]hen a particular guna increases, the other two are suppressed.”

To assist our advancement, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti then describes how to recognize goodness in one’s consciousness: “When consciousness becomes pure, the senses are without agitation and one is unattached to the mind. Goodness (sattva) then increases. In that state one performs activities to attain Me.”

*Text 17: Passion*

“You should discern the mode of passion by its symptoms - the distortion of the intelligence because of too much activity, the inability of the perceiving senses to disentangle themselves from mundane objects, an unhealthy condition of the working physical organs, and the unsteady perplexity of the mind.” (SB. 11.25.17)

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments further on the symptoms of increased passion: “When one’s consciousness deteriorates, the intelligence becoming scattered in all directions due to attraction to various sense objects, and when one does not control the mind, intelligence, or senses and instead gives in to the thirst for those sense objects, know that passion (rajas) is predominant.”

*Text 18: Ignorance*

“When one’s higher awareness fails and finally disappears and one is thus unable to concentrate his attention, his mind is ruined and manifests ignorance and depression. You should understand this situation to be the predominance of the mode of ignorance.” (SB. 11.25.18)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura expands Krsna’s description of the symptoms of ignorance: “When consciousness becomes bewildered and insensitive because of being unable to perceive objects (due to low consciousness), and when the mind fails to make decisions but becomes filled with despair, understand that ignorance (tamas) has become dominant.”

*Texts 19-29: The effects of the three modes on strength, consciousness, future births, working mentality, knowledge, one’s residence, types of workers, faith, food preferences, and happiness*

*Text 19: Increased strength with the increase of a specific mode*

“With the increase of the mode of goodness, the strength of the demigods similarly increases. When passion increases, the demoniac become strong. And with the rise of ignorance, O Uddhava, the strength of the most wicked increases.” (SB. 11.25.19)

Srila Sridhara Svami writes that the actions of one’s senses place one either in the category of a demigod (deva), demon (asura), or the truly demoniac (Raksasa) as we display renunciation, indulgence, or confusion. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura notes that the Vais- navas’ strength increases as they become more and more free from the influence of the modes of nature.

*Text 20: Three of the four states of consciousness are produced from the modes*

“It should be understood that alert wakefulness comes from the mode of goodness, sleep with dreaming from the mode of passion, and deep, dreamless sleep from the mode of ignorance. The fourth state of consciousness pervades these three and is transcendental.” (SB. 11.25.20)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments that text 20 answers the question, “Which state of consciousness arises from which mode?” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura writes that one in the fourth state, which is transcendental to the modes of nature, takes shelter of Vaikuntha, which is devoid of all material modes.

*Texts 21-22: How the three modes affect future births*

“Learned persons dedicated to Vedic culture are elevated by the mode of goodness to higher and higher positions. The mode of ignorance, on the other hand, forces one to fall headfirst into lower and lower births. And by the mode of passion one continues transmigrating through human bodies.” (SB. 11.25.21)

Sridhara Svami comments that the situation persons achieve as a result of their activities is shown in terms of which mode predominates in their lives. Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments that this text implies that by pure bhakti - devotional service performed free of the modes of nature - one goes to the Lord’s abode in the spiritual world.

Krsna next explains the consequences of dying under the dominance of one mode or another: “Those who leave this world in the mode of goodness go to the heavenly planets, those who pass away in the mode of passion remain in the world of human beings, and those dying in the mode of ignorance must go to hell. But those who are free from the influence of all modes of nature come to Me.” (SB. 11.25.22) Srila Sridhara Svami explains that devotees beyond the modes attain Krsna while still living in their material body. Srila Jiva Gosvami writes that this text explains that Krsna’s abode is attained by becoming free of the modes. He also writes that by saying “they come to Me” instead of “they go to My planet,” Krsna is asserting that He and His abode are nondifferent.

*Text 23: Work in the three modes of nature*

“Work performed as an offering to Me, without consideration of the Iruit, is considered to be in the mode of goodness. Work performed with a desire to enjoy the results is in the mode of passion. And work impelled by violence and envy is in the mode of ignorance.” (SB. I 1.25.21)

According to Srila Sridhara Svami, by this text Krsna declares that devotional service is transcendental to the modes and all other kinds of material work, even up to the point of work offered to the Supreme, is connected with the modes of nature.

The BBT purport summarizes: “Ordinary work performed as an offering to God, without desire for the result, is understood to be in the mode of goodness, whereas activities of devotion - such as chanting and hearing the glories of the Lord - are transcendental and are beyond the modes of nature.”

*Text 24: Knowledge in the three modes*

Srila Sridhara Svami’s comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.25.24 groups this text with texts 25-29. He explains that Krsna now speaks of knowledge and other items in four categories, distinguishing between items free from the modes and items influenced by the modes: “Absolute knowledge is in the mode of goodness, knowledge based on duality is in the mode of passion, and foolish, materialistic knowledge is in the mode of ignorance. Knowledge based upon Me, however, is understood to be transcendental.” (SB. 11.25.24)

The BBT purport makes clear the distinction between absolute knowledge born of goodness and knowledge of Krsna: “Srila Jiva Gosvami elaborately explains in his commentary on this verse that the material mode of goodness does not award perfect knowledge of the Absolute Truth. He quotes from Srimad-Bhagavatam (6.14.2), proving that many great demigods in the mode of goodness could not understand the transcendental personality of Lord Krsna. In the material mode of goodness, one becomes pious or religious, aware of a higher, spiritual nature. On the spiritual platform of purified goodness, however, one establishes a direct, loving relationship with the Absolute Truth, rendering service to the Lord rather than merely maintaining a connection to mundane piety.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains that knowledge of the jiva’s existence as separate from the body is in goodness; knowledge filled with doubt, such as “The existence of jiva may or may not be real” or “The jiva may or may not be eternal” is in rajas; and material knowledge concerning eating or other enjoyments is in tamas. But he concludes, “Knowledge with Me as its subject is beyond the modes of nature.”

*Text 25: Places of residence in each of the three modes*

“Residence in the forest is in the mode of goodness, residence in a town is in the mode of passion, residence in a gambling house displays the quality of ignorance, and residence in a place where I reside is transcendental.” (SB. 11.25.25)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura quotes Srila Sridhara Svami that the Lord’s residence is beyond the gunas, because the Lord is directly manifest in His abode. Srila Jiva Gosvami comments that the Lord’s abode is transcendental due to its greatness at being connected to the Lord, according to the logic of the touchstone. That is, everything surrounding a touchstone, which turns everything it touches to gold, will be gold.

In the Bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 135), Srila Jiva also comments on this text: “Living in the forest refers to a vanaprastha. Living in the town refers to a grhastha. Gambling dens are representative of many such places where sinful people reside. The abode of the Lord, where persons perform service to the Lord, is beyond the gunas.”

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura clarifies still further the effect the modes of nature have on places of residence: “Persons in the mode of goodness, freed from materialistic enjoyment, live in the forest. By the gradual path, they can eventually appreciate the beauty of Vrndavana. Persons in the mode of passion are always striving for their own prestige, discriminating between good and bad enjoyment derived from objects of pleasure. Persons in the mode of ignorance are always attached to winning, losing, and other gambling engagements. But if one becomes attached to hearing about the descriptions of the transcendental qualities of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, such a pure unalloyed devotee who has become freed from the modes becomes qualified to take up residence in the place of the Lord’s residence.”

*Text 26: Workers in the three modes*

“A worker free of attachment is in the mode of goodness, a worker blinded by personal desire is in the mode of passion, and a worker who has completely forgotten how to tell right from wrong is in the mode of ignorance. But a worker who has taken shelter of Me is understood to he transcendental to the modes of nature. ” (SB. 11.25.26)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura’s comments on this text are especially worth noting: “A person who is endowed with the mode of goodness is prone to solitude, in the sense of rejecting the association of bad persons. A man in the mode of passion is inclined toward sense gratification and thus becomes entangled in external things. Similarly, a man in the mode of ignorance loses all discrimination of what is good and what isn’t, and thus acts whimsically. But those persons who are transcendental to the modes remain pure devotees under the shelter of the Personality of Godhead. Those who give up the association of materialistic enjoyers but do not instead accept the association of the devotees of the Supreme Lord are deprived of the worship of Lord Hari in spite of their worship in solitude.”

*Text 27: Faith in the three modes*

“Faith directed toward spiritual life is in the mode of goodness, faith rooted in fruitive work is in the mode of passion, faith residing in irreligious activities is in the mode of ignorance, but faith in My devotional service is purely transcendental.” (SB. 11.25.27)

In this connection, Sripada Madhvacarya comments that even if one has not heard the evidence of Vedic scripture, one who takes exclusive shelter of Lord Vasudeva is considered by learned men to be a transcendental devotee of the Lord.

*Text 28: Food in the three modes*

“Food that is wholesome, pure, and obtained without difficulty is in the mode of goodness, food that gives immediate pleasure to the senses is in the mode of passion,and food that is unclean and causes distress is in the mode of ignorance.”

Both Srila Sridhara Svami and Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura indicate in their comments that Sri Krsna is implying that food offered to Him is free from the modes of nature.

*Text 29: Happiness in the three modes*

“Happiness derived from the self is in the mode of goodness, happiness based on sense gratification is in the mode of passion, and happiness based on delusion and degradation is in the mode of ignorance. But that happiness found within Me is transcendental.”

In the Bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 134), Srila Jiva Gosvami shows that bhakti is composed of activities like hearing about Krsna. These activities are caused by bhakti, and, having no material cause, are transcendental (nirguna). He offers Srimad-Bhagavatam 1.2.16 as sastric evidence of this point: “O twice-born sages, by serving those devotees who are completely freed from all vice, great service is done. By such service, one gains affinity for hearing the messages of Vasudeva.” Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura similarly notes that happiness arising from chanting about Krsna is transcendental, beyond the gunas.

*Texts 30—31: Summarizing the effects of the three modes of nature*

“Therefore material substance, place, result of activity, time, knowledge, work, the performer of work, faith, state of consciousness, species of life, and destination after death are all based on the three modes of material nature.” (SB. 11.25.30) Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura gravely notes that among all those things in and beyond the modes of nature, those things in the modes cause continued birth and death (samsara) for the jiva.

*Text 31: All mental and physical actions based on the enjoying spirit are subject to the modes*

“O best of human beings, all states of material being are related to the interaction of the enjoying soul and material nature. Whether seen, heard of, or only conceived within the mind, they are without exception constituted of the modes of nature.” (SB. 11.25.31)

Not only the categories of things Krsna mentions in text 30, but all the actions of a conditioned soul are impelled by the modes of nature.

*Texts 32-36: Transcending the modes*

*Text 32: Establishing the goal*

Concluding this topic by noting that the modes are all-encompassing as they hind the conditioned soul, Krsna now establishes as the goal of human life transcending the modes and developing love for Him: “O gentle Uddhava, all these different phases of conditioned life arise from work horn of the modes of material nature. The living entity who conquers these modes, manifested from the mind, can dedicate himself to Me by the process of devotional service and thus attain pure love for Me.” (SB. 11.25.32)

The BBT purport to text 32 describes the quandary of the conditioned soul and its cure: “The conditioned soul falsely imagines himself to be the enjoyer of the modes of nature, and thus a particular type of material work is generated, the reaction of which binds the conditioned soul to repeated birth and death. This fruitless process can be counteracted by loving service to the Lord, as described here.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains that a jwa conquers the modes of nature by practicing bhakti-yoga. He cites the above text along with Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.29.12 to show that the process of bhakti is beyond all three modes of material nature. He then cites Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.25.22 and 26 to show that devotees too are beyond the modes and that they therefore attain the Lord. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti adds, “The ingredients used by a bhakta in Deity worship, such as an umbrella, camara, incense, flowers, fragrance, and lamps, are also beyond the gunas. Additionally, as it has been stated in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.25.27, the devotee’s faith is beyond the gunas. Thus it can be understood from the Lord that anything related to bhakti is beyond the gunas."

*Texts 33: Striving for freedom from the modes*

“Therefore, having achieved this human form of life, which allows one to develop full knowledge, those who are intelligent should free themselves from all contamination of the modes of nature and engage exclusively in loving service to Me.” (SB. 11.25.33)

*Text 34: How to free oneself from the modes*

“A wise sage, free from all material association and unbewildered, should subdue his senses and worship Me. He should conquer the modes of passion and ignorance by engaging himself only with things in the mode of goodness.” (SB. 11.25.34)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments: “What should a person who worships You do in the beginning? This verse answers that question.” Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura continues: “One endowed with pure bhakti will conquer the three gunas by bhakti alone. That was already stated in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.25.52. If he has a predominance of bhakti with some mixture of other elements (such as jharm), another method for conquering the three gunas is herein stated: engage in goodness to conquer passion and ignorance. Krsna has already stated this principle in Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.13.6.”

*Text 35: Then, transcend even goodness*

“Then, being fixed in devotional service, the sage should also conquer the material mode of goodness by indifference toward the modes.Thus pacified within his mind, the spirit soul, freed from the modes of nature, gives up the very cause of his conditioned life and attains Me.” (SB. 11.25.35)

The BBT purport adds: “By attachment to the loving service of the Lord, which is completely transcendental, one gives up one’s interest in the modes of nature.”

*Text 36: The attainment of those who have transcended the modes*

“Freed from the subtle conditioning of the mind and from the modes of nature born of material consciousness, the living entity becomes completely satisfied by experiencing My transcendental form. Fie no longer searches for enjoyment in the external energy, nor does he contemplate or remember such enjoyment within himself.” (SB. 11.25.36)

Srila Sridhara Svami’s comment on this text is a suitable conclusion to this chapter: “Those who are intelligent should cleanse away with the transcendental nectar of devotional service the variegated manifestations of material life that follow in the wake of the development of the three modes by speaking and hearing about the most auspicious topics of the unconquerable Supreme Lord. Indeed, there is no more fortunate activity than this in the human form of life.”

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura further describes the process of transcendence: “\[W\]hen one gives up all ideas of enjoyment and renunciation, one no longer tries to take hold of the incomplete objects separate from the Lord. He is thus no longer impelled by external and internal perverted consciousness. Then, by the mercy of the Supreme Lord, the incomplete conditioned soul can give up his totally unsatisfactory enjoyment and so-called full enjoyment of matter and become engaged in the service of Sri Nama, who has a completely transcendental, personal form. When the Personality of Sri Nama manifests as His transcendental form, qualities, entourage, and various pastimes, there is no scope for one to become bound up in hankering for material enjoyment or material renunciation.”

The BBT purport to text 36 offers a precise summary of how to attain transcendence: “Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu has ordered us to take shelter of the holy name of Lord Krsna, by which process we can easily transcend the modes of nature and begin our real life of loving devotional service to Lord Krsna.”

**Chapter 26: The Aila-Gita**

*Texts 1-3: Avoid materialistic association*

Sri Krsna begins this chapter by listing two states those with advanced consciousness achieve through either bhakti or jnana. In text 1, He says that human life affords one the opportunity to practice devotional service and to attain Him, the abode of bliss and the supreme soul. In text 2, He says that those fixed in knowledge remain free from false identification and entanglement in the modes of nature. Even when surrounded by the products of the modes, those in knowledge remain aloof from them.

These two texts, explains Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, form the prelude to the theme of this chapter: one should avoid bad association and seek out good association. The quality of one’s association is important to everyone; everyone should seek out good association in all circumstances. This is true even for those who are already liberated. Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura adds, “By telling the story of Aila, Krsna will teach Uddhava that association with women causes bewilderment while association with devotees brings enlightenment.... It is said that the wise man contemplating his means of success also contemplates the obstacles to that success. Association with women is a great obstacle.”

Here, and throughout much of this chapter, Krsna will stresses the danger of men associating with women. Why? The answer is simple and obvious: association with women, for men, sparks the false ego and inflames men’s inherent tendency to enjoy the senses.

Krsna has just finished talking about the modes of material nature as the all-powerful binding and controlling forces in the world of matter. In Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.25.33—35 He instructed Uddhava to free himself “from all contamination of the modes of nature and engage exclusively in loving service to Me.” Now He brings to Uddhava’s attention the greatest obstacle people face in their attempt to free themselves from the modes: sexual desire. The material prison is powered by the material modes and constructed in such a way that conditioned souls prefer life behind bars to the free life that is natural to the soul.

The material prison’s bars are made of sex desire, a force so powerful that very few even want to escape it! Srila Prabhupada spoke mockingly of this volunteer imprisonment in a lecture given on Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.43—4, in Los Angeles in 1972:

Srila Prabhupada: Now, yesterday ... there was a cinema signboard, what is that?

Karandhara: “Is there sex after death?”

Prabhupada: Yes. (Laughter) You see? Because this material life means sex. So, they are seeking sex after death, also. (Laughter)… “Is there sex after death?” They’re inquiring. If there is sex after death, then they are not fearful of death. (Laughter) There is a story that one man was drinking. So, drinking in India is a great sin. So his friend advised that “You are drinking. You’ll go to hell.” So he said, “Oh, my father also drinks.” So he said, “Your father also will go to hell.” “Oh, my brother also drinks.” “Oh, he also will go to hell.” In this way he continued to say my father, my brother, my sister, my this, my that ... And he was replying, “Yes, he will also go to hell.” “Oh! Then hell is heaven! Because we’re all drinking here and drinking there. So what is the hell? That is heaven.”

Similarly ... this signboard is like that. “If sex is there after death, then that is not death. That is life.” (Laughter) You see? So actually, you have got sex after death. Because you’ll get into another body. Now you are having sex as human being in very nice apartment or on the street, on the beach, as you like. In the next life also, as cats and dogs, you will have sex life.

In this twenty-sixth chapter of Srimad-Bhagavatam, Krsna cuts a clear swath between the things that bind and the things that liberate. What determines whether we bind ourselves by the modes or move toward liberation is the quality of our association.

In texts 18-21, Krsna will hurl spearlike words to penetrate the illusion of thinking a woman’s body beautiful anti worth enjoying. He spoke similar words about a woman’s illusory attraction to men through the enlightened words of the prostitute Pingala.

Krsna opens His topic in text 3, where He announces half of the points He intends to make: “One should never associate with materialists, those dedicated to gratifying their genitals and bellies. By following them one falls into the deepest pit of darkness, just like a blind man who follows another blind man.”

*Texts 4-6: Introduction to the Aila-gita*

In Srimad-Bhagavatam 9.14.1-16, Sukadeva Gosvami recounts the history of the dynasty in which Maharaja Pururava was born. Texts 17-49 describe the king’s birth, along with his attraction, subsequent marriage to, and later separation from the heavenly damsel Urvasi. The BBT summary of this twenty-sixth chapter of Canto Eleven describes these events in brief: “The emperor Pururava, who was bewildered by the association of the heavenly lady Urvasi, later became renounced after being separated from her. He thus sang a song expressing his contempt for womanly connection.” For a large part of his life, Pururava was swept away by a succession of powerful emotions, all related to Urvasi. He was infatuated when he met her, completely attached to her as he enjoyed her company, and obsessed and bewildered when she left him. Pururava lamented for years. When he was finally able to see his relationship with her with dispassion, he achieved detachment.

Srimad-Bhagavatam 11.26.5 recounts Pururava’s response when Urvasi first rejected him: “\[E\]ven though he was naked he ran after her just like a madman and called out in great distress, ‘O my wife, O terrible lady! Please stop!’”

The BBT purport provides more details about Pururava’s attraction to Urvasi: “As his beloved wife was leaving him, the shocked king was crying out, ‘My dear wife, please think for a moment. Just stop! You terrible lady, can’t you stop? Why don’t we speak together for a while? Why are you killing me?’ Thus lamenting, he followed her.” The pleasures the emperor had tasted in Urvasi’s company had fermented into a bitter brew of misery. Lost in lamentation and traveling all over the universe seeking her, Pururava eventually noticed that innumerable days and nights of his life had come and gone. He wove his realization of his foolishness into an eighteen-verse song called the Aila-gita.

*Texts 7-24: The Aila-gita verses*

*Texts 7-14: One’s consciousness becomes impoverished when one tries to enjoy a woman*

Aila grieves that he, the emperor, had become a weak, powerless fool, and he erupts in an outpouring of angst: “Alas, just see the extent of my delusion! This goddess was embracing me and held my neck in her grip. My heart was so polluted by lust that I had no idea how my life was passing. That lady cheated me so much that I did not even see the rising or setting of the sun. Alas, for so many years I passed my days in vain! Alas, although I am supposed to be a mighty emperor, the crown jewel of all kings on this earth, just see how my bewilderment has rendered me a toy animal in the hands of women! Although I was a powerful lord with great opulence, that woman gave me up as if I were no more than an insignificant blade of grass. And still, naked and without shame, I followed her, crying out to her like a madman. Where are my so-called great influence, power, and sovereignty? Just like an ass being kicked in the face by his she-ass, I ran after that woman, who had already given me up. What is the use of a big education or the practice of austerities and renunciation, and what is the use of studying religious scriptures, of living in solitude and silence, if, after all that, one’s mind is stolen by a woman? To hell with me! I am such a fool that I didn’t even know what was good for me, although I arrogantly thought I was highly intelligent. Although I achieved the exalted position of a lord, I allowed myself to be conquered by women as if I were a bullock or a jackass. Even after I had served the so-called nectar of the lips of Urvasi for many years, my lusty desires kept rising again and again within my heart and were never satisfied, just like a fire that can never be extinguished by the oblations of ghee poured into its flames.” (SB. 11.26.7-14)

*Text 15: Only Krsna can save one from addiction to sense gratification*

“Who but the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who lies beyond material perception and is the Lord of self-satisfied sages, can possibly save my consciousness, which has been stolen by a prostitute?” Speaking as Aila, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura reveals Aila’s mood: “How will I be freed from the taste of her lips and develop distaste:’ No one, not even an atmarama, can free the mind of one who delights in the body.
