In the same way, intelligence, the senses, and sense perceptions have no existence separate from the supreme reality, although that Absolute Truth remains totally distinct from them.”

As a lamp, the eye that sees by the lamp’s light, and the object the eye views are all dependent on and therefore nondifferent from light, so the intelligence, the senses, and the sense objects are dependent on and caused by - and therefore nondifferent from - the Absolute Truth. Yet the Absolute Truth, like the light, has its own separate existence and is different from what it has caused.

In his Paramatma Sandarbha (anuccheda 73), Srila Jiva Gosvami cites this text to illustrate a point regarding the Paramatma: “Just as the element light is not contaminated by the faults of the lamp or eye, neither is the Paramatma contaminated by the faults of the intelligence or the senses. The Paramatma is totally distinct.”

*Text 25: Wakefulness, sleep, and deep sleep*

“The three states of intelligence are called waking consciousness, sleep, and deep sleep. But, my dear King, the variegated experiences created for the pure living entity by these different states are nothing more than illusion.”

The various experiences created within wakefulness, sleep, and deep sleep appear real, but they are only illusion. That is, the Absolute Truth is the reality which exists consistently through all three states of consciousness.

Srila Jiva Gosvami cites Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.4.25 to show the coverings over the jiva’s pure consciousness: “It was stated that intelligence, the senses, and sense perceptions were composed of the natural potencies (saktis) of Paramatma. They were also described as having faults due to the impurity of matter. Thus Paramatma, endowed with His internal energy (antaranga-sakti) and marginal energy (tatastha-sakti), is also different from the elements that are part of His external energy (bahiranga-sakti). So that one can know how to give up the covering of the senses, the sense perceptions, and the intelligence, how these three cover the pure soul is described.”

*Text 26: Clouds*

“Just as clouds in the sky come into being and are then dispersed by the amalgamation and dissolution of their constituent elements, this material universe is created and destroyed within the Absolute Truth hy the amalgamation and dissolution of its elemental, constituent parts.”

As clouds come into being and are later dispersed into their constituent elements in the sky, so everything within the universe is created and destroyed within the Absolute Truth.

Srila Jiva Gosvami cites this text in the Paramatma Sandarbha (anuccheda 75) to indicate that although matter is certainly the Lord’s energy, the Lord is nevertheless inconceivably aloof from material existence: “A cloud, which is vapor, which itself occurred as a transformation of water, heat, and wind, becomes visible in the sky before dissipating and again becoming invisible. But the clouds do not touch the sky. Similarly this universe, manifest by the glance of the Lord, becomes visible and then disappears. After disappearing, it remains in a subtle form, as the form endowed with the potency (sakti) to produce the universe remains. Thus it is said, ‘The material universe may be considered real, having nature as its original ingredient and final state. Lord Maha-visnu is the resting place of nature, which becomes manifest by the power of time. Thus nature, the almighty Visnu, and time are not different from Me (Krsna),the Supreme Absolute Truth’ (SB. 11.24.19).”

*Text 27: Threads of a cloth*

“My dear King, it is stated \[in the Vedanta-sutra\] that the ingredient cause that constitutes any manifested product in this universe can be perceived as a separate reality, just as the threads that make up a cloth can be perceived separately from their product.”

The threads that make up a cloth have a separate existence beyond the cloth of which they are a part. Each object’s ingredient causes can all be conceived of separately in a similar way. Srila Jiva Gosvami calls this philosophy sat-karya-vada, the idea that the cause of something continues to exist after it has manifested its effect - ultimately referring to the idea that the ultimate cause of the material universes, the Paramatma aspect of the Absolute Truth, continues to exist despite the fact that the universe and its constituent gross matter also exist.

*Text 28: Material cause and effect*

“Anything experienced in terms of general cause and specific effect must be an illusion, because such causes and effects exist only relative to each other. Indeed, whatever has a beginning and an end is unreal.”

That a material cause can only be recognized as a cause in relation to the effect it generatesindicates that both a cause and its effects are interdependent. Being dependent and therefore temporary, both can be considered illusory. The Absolute Truth, on the other hand, is independent; everything in existence is dependent on the Absolute Truth.

In the Paramatma Sandarbha (anuccheda 77), Srila Jiva Gosvami explains the meaning of this text as a Mayavadi might misinterpret it: “If it is said that previously, the universe did not exist in a subtle state, but only pure Brahman existed everywhere, then Brahman would have necessarily transformed into the universe… The universe would therefore be considered nonexistent or illusory, since what is produced by a cause and thereby becomes an effect must, by definition, be an illusion. Thus pure Brahman transforms into the universe by its sakti (potency) in the form of ignorance.” Sri Jiva concludes his comment by saying, “We do not agree with this view.”

*Text 29: A single atom*

“Although perceived, the transformation of even a single atom of material nature has no ultimate definition without reference to the Supreme Soul. To be accepted as factually existing, something must possess the same quality as pure spirit - eternal, unchanging existence.”

An atom only truly exists when understood in relation to its cause, the Supreme Soul, the Absolute Truth. Why? Because only pure spirit is eternal and unchanging, and only that which is eternal and unchanging can be said to truly exist.

Jiva Gosvami cites this text in the Paramatma Sandarbha (anuccheda 79), using it to philosophically describe the nature of the Paramatma. There he explains that although something may be manifested, not even the slightest transformation in the universe can accurately be called independent of the Paramatma. This is what has been called “oneness.” If something \[for example, a tree\] could exist without reference to the Paramatma, the universe would then be equal to His spiritual form - self-manifesting and eternal, like the Paramatma - but this is obviously untrue. Clearly the existence of all other things \[including a tree\] depends on other existing items \[trees depend on light, soil, air, and water for their existence!. Nothing in the material world exists independently; everything depends on the Paramatma, who Himself exists independently.

*Text 30: Air and a pot*

“There is no material duality in the Absolute Truth. The duality perceived by an ignorant person is like the difference between the sky contained in an empty pot and the sky outside the pot, or the difference between the reflection of the sun in water and the sun itself in the sky, or the difference between the vital air within one living body and that within another body.”

As no actual difference exists between the air inside a pot and the air outside it, no material duality or change exists within the eternal Absolute Truth. Srila Jiva Gosvami cites this text in the Paramatma Sandarbha (anuccheda 80) to show that no material variety or duality exists inside or outside the Paramatma: “If you think such variety exists, you are ignorant, like one seeing a difference between sky in the great sky and the sky in a pot, or seeing a difference between the light in the sky and the light in a room, or seeing a difference between the air outside the body and the air inside it.”

*Text 31: Gold*

Since nothing exists without the Paramatma (SB. 12.4.29), all words describe the Paramatma. Text 31 gives an example: “According to their different purposes, men utilize gold in various ways, and gold is therefore perceived in various forms. In the same way, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is inaccessible to material senses, is described in various terms, both ordinary and Vedic, by different types of men.”

As the one object, gold, can be perceived in different forms - in rings or bracelets, for example - as constructed by different men for their different purposes, so the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the one Absolute Truth, can similarly be described differently by different types of people with different purposes.

Srila Jiva Gosvami cites this text in anuccheda 81 of the Paramatma Sandarbha. There he explains that gold is known by many names depending on how it has been shaped (into earrings, bracelets, etc.). Similarly, all words, secular and Vedic, describe the Lord. As the Skanda Purana says, sarva-namabhidheyas ca sarva-vededitas ca sah: “the Lord is referred to by all names and is worshiped in the Vedas.”

*Texts 32-34: The ultimate annihilation (atyantika)*

Sukadeva Gosvami now uses the example of the cloud and the sun to describe the third of the four types of annihilation, the ultimate annihilation of material existence, which is caused by the soul cutting off its false ego.

*Texts 32—33: A cloud and the sun*

How can a soul become covered, for he is a part of the Supreme Lord? An example is given that illustrates that the cloud, although produced by the light-giving sun, nevertheless creates darkness as it obscures that same vision that the sun grants.” Similarly, material false ego, a particular product of the Absolute Truth made visible by the Absolute Truth, obstructs the individual soul, another partial expansion of the Absolute Truth, from realizing the Absolute Truth.” (SB. 12.4.32)

And how can a covered soul become free of bewilderment? “When the cloud originally produced from the sun is torn apart, the eye can see the actual form of the sun. Similarly, when the spirit soul destroys his material covering of false ego by inquiring into the transcendental science, he regains his original spiritual awareness.” (SB. 12.4.33)

The BBT purport to text 33 states: “Just as the sun can burn away the clouds that prevent one from seeing it, the Supreme Lord (and He alone) can remove the false ego that prevents one from seeing Him. There are some creatures, however, like owls, who are averse to seeing the sun. In the same way, those who are not interested in spiritual knowledge will never receive the privilege of seeing God.”

In his comment on this text, Srila Jiva Gosvami explains more about the example of the sun, the cloud, and one’s eyes: “\[Gjiving up of the false covering does not arise automatically, but rather by study of the Supersoul, and consequently, by the power of the Supersoul. This example is discussed in order to state this fact. Saying, ‘When the cloud originally produced from the sun is torn apart,’ it clarifies that this tearing apart is not accomplished by the eye's power but by the sun’s influence. Thus this example states that false ego is driven away \[destroyed\] by the mercy of the Supersoul.”

In the Priti Sandarbha (anuccheda 1), Sri Jiva cites text 33 to indicate the complete annihilation of material existence in the form of absolute liberation: “Realizing Paramatma, whose name is Acyuta, and remaining in that realized state is called absolute liberation. Sukadeva Gosvami expresses the same meaning in Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.10.6. muktir hitvanyatha-rupam sva-rupena vyavasthitih — that is, that liberation means giving up other forms and being situated in realization of the Lord’s form (svarupa). This is because being situated in one’s own svarupa (sva-rupena vyavasthitih) means directly contacting the Lord s svarupa.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura also comments on text 33. He says that this text shows how one realizes Brahman: \[W\]hen the cloud is destroyed, the eye sees the sun in its true form. But it is the human eye, not the eye of the owl, that can see the sun. Similarly, it is the eye of the jnani who has attained some bhakti that can perceive Brahman, not the eye of one without bhakti. Bhaktyaham ekaya grahyah: I am only achieved by bhakti (SB. 11.14.21).”

Srila Sukadeva Gosvami continues: “My dear Pariksit, when the illusory false ego that binds the soul has been cut off with the sword of discriminating knowledge and one has developed realization of Lord Acyuta, the Supreme Soul, this is called the atyantika, or ultimate, annihilation of material existence.” (SB. 12.4.34)

According to Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, this text shows that jnana mixed with bhakti (bhakti-misra-jnana) destroys ahankara. This state of being free from the false ego is the ultimate (atyantika) annihilation of material existence: “After cutting the bondage of ahankara by jnana-sastra, one remains firm in his meditation on Acyuta. Or, for the accomplished yogi, after destroying ahankara through complete realization of Brahman, one remains steady. Being fixed without false ego is called atyantika-pralaya.”

*Texts 35-37: Annihilation four - the continuing process of creation and annihilation*

The creation and annihilation of everyone and everything in existence is a natural occurrence in the material world. “Experts in the subtle workings of nature, O subduer of the enemy, have declared that there are continuous processes of creation and annihilation that all created beings, beginning with Brahma, constantly undergo.” (SB. 12.4.35) Time is the overwhelming, ever-changing, annihilating force: “All material entities undergo transformation and are constantly and swiftly eroded by the mighty currents of time. The various stages of existence that material things exhibit are the perpetual causes of their generation and annihilation.” (SB. 12.4.36)

Yet although these annihilations, shifts, and changes occur ceaselessly, one cannot directly perceive them: “These stages of existence created by beginningless and endless time, the impersonal representative of the Supreme Lord, are not visible, just as the infinitesimal momentary changes of position of the planets in the sky cannot be directly seen.” (SB. 12.4.37)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura shows that the example in this text indicates that we can only infer the process of constant annihilation, since we cannot directly observe it: “Just as we must infer that a planet is continuously moving by our noticing that it attains a different position in the sky each night, so one must also infer subtle states of change between the stages of infancy and youth, because the differences between those two stages can be perceived \[although the minute-by-minute changes cannot\]. Thus the argument is not without proof.”

The BBT purport to text 37 stresses the same transforming and destructive power of time: “Although everyone knows that the sun is constantly moving in the sky, one cannot normally see the sun moving. Similarly, no one can directly perceive his hair or nails growing, although with the passing of time we perceive the fact of growth. Time, the potency of the Lord, is very subtle and powerful and is an insurmountable barrier to fools who are trying to exploit the material creation.”

*Text 38: A summary of the chapter*

“In this way the progress of time is described in terms of the four kinds of annihilation - continuous, occasional, elemental, and final.” (SB. 12.4.38) Maharaja Pariksit’s time on earth is coming to an end. Considering that annihilation is both constant and inevitable on every material level, he should not lament his current circumstances. Rather, he should detach himself from this world and leave fully attached to Sri Krsna. I hen he should go home, hack to Godhead.

*Texts 39-40: Sukadeva Gosvami ends his instructions to Maharaja Pariksit*

Thus Sukadeva Gosvami concludes his description of the Supreme Lord’s pastimes: “O best of the Kurus, I have related to you these narrations of the pastimes of Lord Narayana, the creator of this world and the ultimate reservoir of all existence, presenting them to you only in brief summary. Even Lord Brahma himself would be incapable of describing them entirely.” (SB. 12.4.39)

**Srimad-Bhagavatam’s potency**

Hearing Srimad-Bhagavatam as Sukadeva Gosvami narrated it to King Pariksit bestows on a hearer the supreme benediction: “For a person who is suffering in the fire of countless miseries and who desires to cross the insurmountable ocean of material existence, there is no suitable boat except that of cultivating devotion to the transcendental taste \[rasa\] for the narrations of the Supreme Personality of Godhead’s pastimes.” (SB. 12.4.40)

The BBT purport briefly summarizes the benefit of boarding the boat of hearing about Krsna: “Although it is not possible to completely describe the pastimes of the Lord, even a partial appreciation can save one from the unbearable miseries of material existence. The fever of material existence can be removed only by the medicine of the holy name and pastimes of the Supreme Lord, which are perfectly narrated in Srimad-Bhagavatam."

The demigods have similarly described the glorious boat of absorption in the lotus feet of Krsna: “O lotus-eyed Lord, by concentrating one’s meditation on Your lotus feet, which are the reservoir of all existence, and by accepting those lotus feet as the boat hy which to cross the ocean of nescience, one follows in the footsteps of mahajanas. By this simple process, one can cross the ocean of nescience as easily as one steps over the hoof print of a calf. (SB. 10.2.30)

In his purport to this Tenth Canto text Srila Prabhupada invites his readers to board the boat: “Here the Lord is described as amhujaksa, or lotus-eyed. By seeing the eyes of the Lord, which are compared to lotus flowers, one becomes so satisfied that one does not want to turn his eyes to anything else. Simply hy seeing the transcendental form of the Lord, a devotee is at once fully absorbed in the Lord in his heart… The process recommended in this verse for crossing the ocean of nescience is easy not only for the devotee but also for common persons who follow the devotee.”

Returning to Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.4.40, Srila Sridhara Svami also expresses the need to hear about Krsna: “But, it may be asked, if it is not possible to list the pastimes of Lord Narayana in full, then what is the use of trying to list them at all? That question is answered in this verse. The various miseries of material existence are like a forest fire, and for the person who is distressed and tormented by this forest fire and who wishes to cross beyond it, there is no other boat by which one can cross other than serving and honoring the transcendental taste of the narrations of the pastimes of the Personality of Godhead. No other means exists. In other words, one should engage in the service of hearing the topics of the Supreme Lord to one’s fullest capacity.”

Srila Jiva Gosvami makes a similar point in his comment on text 40. He states that in Sri Sukadeva’s winding up of his instructions to Maharaja Pariksit, he references hearing, which also implies the other processes of devotional service. “\[Sukadeva\] thus glorifies narrations about the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Those who desire only devotional service as the goal of their life should listen properly to these narrations of the Lord’s pastimes. Even those who desire liberation should hear them, as stated in Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.4.40. Saying that ‘no means other than hearing is possible’ is appropriate, because all other forms of devotional service can be enacted only after the performance of hearing about the Lord.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura underlines the importance for everyone, even those desiring liberation, to hear krsna-katha: “The topics of the Lord are the life-sustaining medicine for all types of devotees, and even for those desiring liberation. Even those who desire liberation cannot achieve liberation without these topics.”

He also indicates that text 40 answers the question Maharaja Pariksit asked at the beginning of the Bhagavatam: “What should a person who is about to die do?” Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura continues to explain that other than food, nothing can satisfy an “intolerable hunger.” Similarly, no means - not karma, not jnana - provides an effective method for crossing ibe ocean of material existence. Holding up jnana as a shelter lo a dying man, is like giving a garland and sandalwood lo a person dying ol hunger.

So in text 40, Sukadeva has directly prescribed hearing krsna-katha as the only effective medicine for one who is about to die and has decried any other prescription. Yet amazingly, Sukadeva’s final words to the dying king, spoken in chapter 5, will be about jnana, winch although clearly useful for a dying man, do not describe King Pariksit’s beloved Lord. Why would Sukadeva speak such words, after extolling the benefits of hearing the Lord’s pastimes?

In his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.4.40, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura reveals the consistent mind of Sukadeva Gosvami: “You should not accept jnana, with which I am covering the great secret of bhakti, as the recommended process. Rasa in this verse means sweetness produced by the topics of the Lord’s pastimes. One should not prescribe any other medicine except this nectar for persons suffering in the great fire of material life.”

In this way, Visvanatha Cakravarti comments point us to the next chapter and Sukadeva Gosvami’s final words to Maharaja Pariksit.

*Texts 41-43: The history of Srimad-Bhagavatam and information about when it will be spoken again*

“Long ago this essential anthology of all the Puranas was spoken by the infallible Lord Nara-Narayana Rsi to Narada, who then repeated it to Krsna Dvaipayana Vedavyasa. My dear Maharaja Pariksit, that great personality Srila Vyasadeva taught me this same scripture, Srimad-Bhagavatam, which is equal in stature to the four Vedas.” (SB. 12.4.41-42)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura notes that Sukadeva Gosvami spoke this text to indicate that this literature should be studied, taught, heard, and recounted from the unbroken disciplic line of divine, pure spiritual masters. He explains that “the wise Narayana taught \[the Bhagavatam\] to Brahma, who, without a decrease in bhakti because of having no offenses, taught it to Narada.

“O best of the Kurus, the same Suta Gosvami who is sitting before us will speak this Bhagavatam to the sages assembled in the great sacrifice at Naimisaranya. This he will do when questioned by the members of the assembly, headed by Saunaka.” (SB. 12.4.43)

Both Srila Sridhara Svami and Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura say that Sukadeva Gosvami pointed into the assembly of sages surrounding him and indicated the Bhagavatam s next speaker with a That Suta!

**Chapter 5: Sukadeva Gosvami Offers Final Instructions to Maharaja Pariksit**

Maharaja Pariksit asked four final questions in Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.3.17:

1\. Please explain the different ages of universal history.

2\. Please explain the special qualities of each age.

3\. Please explain the duration of cosmic maintenance and destruction.

4\. Please explain the movement of time, which is the direct representation of the Supreme Soul, the Personality of Godhead, Lord Visnu.

The great sage Sukadeva described the four ages and their qualities in Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.3.18-52. He then described the four kinds of annihilation in Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.4.1-38. Now he will describe the movement of time. He begins where he left off in chapter 4, after glorifying Srimad-Bhagavatam. In this first text of chapter 5, the great devotee sage clearly explains that the essence of the Bhagavatam is Lord Hari Himself: “This Srimad-Bhagavatam has elaborately described in various narrations the Supreme Soul of all that be - the Personality of Godhead, Hari - from whose satisfaction Brahma is born and from whose anger Rudra takes birth.” (SB. 12.5.1)

According to the bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 86), this text shows that the main practice of bhakti is hearing the Lord’s pastimes, because such hearing has great power.

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.5.1 refers to an elaborate summary of Srimad-Bhagavatam that Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura has given in his commentary on this text: “The essence of the great deary as statement is that unconditional loving surrender to the Supreme Lord, Krsna, as described by Sukadeva Gosvami, is the highest perfection of life. The exclusive purpose of Srimad-Bhagavatam is to convince the conditioned soul to execute such surrender to the Lord and go back home, back to Godhead.”

In that summary, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti explains Sukadeva Gosvami’s mood close to the great king’s passing and why, he again teaches dial the body and soul are separate anti that liberation has value - instead of speaking directly about bhakti. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti quotes over twenty Bhagavatam texts, spoken by Sukadeva throughout the work, which reveal that the unequivocal message of Srimad-Bhagavatam is hari-bhakti. Why, then, does he hide his own message in his final words to the king?

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura writes:

Having completed the Bhagavatam, Sukadeva considered the matter within himself. Ah! It is improper that I have opened my heart and disclosed the great jewel among secrets and made it visible to all people. The Lord said in the Bhagavad-gita (9.2) that bhakti is the king of knowledge and also the king of secrets (raja-vidya raja-guhyam). In this scripture I have explicitly revealed out of great mercy to Pariksit the most secret subject (sarva-guhyatamam, Bhagavad-gita 18.64). I have shown both through negative and positive statements that bhakti awards all results… However, the Lord prefers some matters to remain secret: “The Vedas, divided into three divisions, ultimately reveal the living entity as pure spirit soul. The Vedic seers and mantras, however, deal in esoteric terms, and I also am pleased by such confidential descriptions.” (SB. 11.21.35)

Since I have revealed the Lord’s greatest secret, I have become not so dear to Him. What should I do now? I have already finished speaking Srimad-Bhagavatam. Let that be. Now at the Bhagavatam’s conclusion I will try to hide the great secret of bhakti. Someone may impetuously show off a great secret jewel to all people, and then, reconsidering, again hide it in a box or put it in his vault. He then shows off another, less valuable jewel, and praises it as more valuable \[to distract people from his secret\]. Thus I will now teach jnana to King Pariksit so that people will think, “Sukadeva is teaching Pariksit jnana.” By the influence of the Lord’s may a, they will think that jnana is ultimate and bhakti only a means to attain jnana.

When I do this I will also be able to test the development of bhakti in my disciple Pariksit. The wise should know that this test is simply to announce to the world the steadiness of Pariksit s bhakti. Ignorant people will explain that liberation is the only result of both bhakti and jnana. But one should understand that this is not my intention. I already said that, compared to liberation, bhakti is a much greater attainment: muktim dadati karhicit sma na bhakti-yogam, “The Lord gives liberation but not bhava-bhakti to those who worship him.” (SB. 5.6.18)

One should not fear that Pariksit will attain impersonal liberation by my teaching him jnana. Suta, my disciple, has understood my intentions, and will later express them: “Pariksit, the great devotee, with pure intelligence attained liberation in the form of the feet of the Lord, who possesses a flag marked with Garuda, through knowledge spoken by Sukadeva.” (SB. 1.18.16)...

Finally I will produce a work including jnana teachings, which will do for me what the Mohini avatara did for the demons: cheat them of the nectar of prema. While teaching jnana I will utter words first with one meaning and then indicate another meaning smeared with bhakti-rasa to please the devotees. In this way, I will convert all the elements of jnana unfavorable for bhakti into processes favorable for devotion. Thinking in this way, Sukadeva spoke \[Srimad-Bhagavatam, Canto Twelve, chapter 5\].

*Texts 2-9: The soul and the body are separate*

From the beginning of the Bhagavatam to the end, Maharaja Pariksit remained a fully surrendered devotee focused solely on devotional service to Krsna. He described his life’s goal in Srimad-Bhagavatam 1.19.16: “I pray that if I should again take my birth in the material world I will have complete attachment to the unlimited Lord Krsna, association with His devotees, and friendly relations with all living beings.” He was also fearless when he described how he would achieve that goal: “Let the snake-bird - or whatever magical thing the brahmana created - bite me at once. I only desire that you all continue singing the deeds of Lord Visnu.” (SB. 1.19.15)

Now we are near the end of Maharaja Pariksit’s life, and Sukadeva Gosvami is still speaking strongly to him - but especially to us. He wants to ensure that those listening, with the king, to the recitation of the Bhagavatam will become free from attachment to the body and mundane objects and thus be able to sidestep the future material births such attachments create for us. The sage says: “O King, give up the animalistic mentality of thinking, ‘I am going to die.’ Unlike the body, you have not taken birth. There was not a time in the past when you did not exist, and you are not about to he destroyed.” (SB. 12.5.2)

In the Bhakti Sandarbha (anuccheda 86), Srila Jiva Gosvami writes that Sukadeva Gosvami’s talk of jnana in chapter 5 is simply to show us that Pariksit was fixed in bhakti. This, of course, has already been stated in Srimad-Bhagavatam 1.19.5: “Maharaja Pariksit sat down firmly on the banks of the Ganges to concentrate his mind in Krsna consciousness, rejecting all other practices of self-realization, because transcendental loving service to Krsna is the greatest achievement, superseding all other methods.”

Srila Jiva Gosvami also notes that Sukadeva’s talk of jnana is not so different from the Lord offering liberation to His devotees, which they then reject in favor of His unalloyed devotional service.

Srila Sukadeva Gosvami continues: “You will not take birth again in the form of your sons and grandsons, like a sprout taking birth from a seed and then generating a new seed. Rather, you are entirely distinct from the material body and its paraphernalia, in the same way that fire is distinct from its fuel.” (SB. 12.5.3) You, the self, are fully distinct from your body. The soul is unborn and immortal. That the gross and subtle bodies perish allows the eternal living being within them to resume its spiritual identity. “The material bodies, qualities, and activities of the spirit soul are created by the material mind. That mind is itself created by the illusory potency of the Supreme Lord, and thus the soul assumes material existence.” (SB. 12.5.6) Material life is based on the soul’s identification with its body, which is made up of the workings of goodness, passion, and ignorance. The soul itself is separate from both subtle and gross bodies. It is luminous, endless, and without material comparison.

Sukadeva Gosvami now describes the way one can solidify one’s realization of the eternal self and become liberated from the ever-shifting, miserable realm of matter: “My dear King, by constantly meditating upon the Supreme Lord, Vasudeva, and by applying clear and logical intelligence, you should carefully consider your true self and how it is situated within the material body.” (SB. 12.5.9)

Srila Jiva Gosvami comments: Sukadeva Gosvami instructs Maharaja Pariksit to meditate on his inner identity as a personal associate of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, along with his identity as an individual spirit soul. “Think about this with your intelligence,” Sukadeva says, “and use logical deduction. Also, use your intelligence, which is absorbed in thoughts of Vasudeva, to meditate on attaining that Lord as your destination.”

*Texts 10-12: When the snake-bird approaches*

“The snake-bird Taksaka, sent by the curse of the brahmana, will not burn your true self. The agents of death will never burn such a master of the self as you, for you have already conquered all dangers on your path back to Godhead. You should consider, ‘I am nondifferent from the Absolute Truth, the supreme abode, and that Absolute Truth, the supreme destination, is nondifferent from me.’ Thus resigning yourself to the Supreme Soul, who is free from all material misidentifications, you will not even notice the snake-bird Taksaka when he approaches with his poison-filled fangs and bites your foot. Nor will you see your dying body or the material world around you, because you will have realized yourself to be separate from them.” (SB. 12.5.10-12)

The BBT purport to text 10 explains that Sukadeva Gosvami is congratulating the king for having developed true depth in his realization, for “as a pure devotee of Lord Krsna \[he was\] homeward bound to the spiritual sky, \[and\] far beyond the reach of death.”

In his comment on texts 11-12, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura notes the overt meaning of the texts, but then ascribes a deeply devotional meaning to Sukadeva’s words: “You will not see Taksaka biting while pressing his two lips and noisily tasting the edge of his lips with his tongues as he relishes his fire mixed with poison. You will not see your body bitten by that snake or the universe different from yourself. The other meaning is ‘You will not see all this because you will be fainting with the bliss of direct contact with the lotus feet of Krsna.’”

*Text 13: Sukadeva Gosvami’s narration about Lord Hari is complete*

“Beloved King Pariksit, I have narrated to you the topics you originally inquired about - the pastimes of Lord Hari, the Supreme Soul of the universe. Now, what more do you wish to hear?” (SB. 12.5.13)

In his comment on text 13, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura again indicates the mood in which Sukadeva Gosvami has spoken to Maharaja Pariksit in this chapter about jnana and how to gain liberation: ‘“I have spoken to you about jnana, about which you did not inquire. I have previously answered the questions you asked about the Lord’s pastimes.’ He then again asks Pariksit \[what he wishes to hear\] in order to proclaim the perfection of his disciple’s realization.” That is, whatever Maharaja Pariksit will now speak will reveal the completeness of Sukadeva Gosvami’s teachings and the fullness of Maharaja Pariksit’s realization of them.

**Chapter 6: Maharaja Pariksit Passes Away**

*Texts 1-7: A grateful Maharaja Pariksit makes a final request of his guru*

“Suta Gosvami said: After hearing all that was narrated to him by the self-realized and equipoised \[samena\] Sukadeva, the son of Vyasadeva, Maharaja Pariksit humbly approached his lotus feet. Bowing his head down upon the sage’s feet, the King, who had lived his entire life under the protection of Lord Visnu, folded his hands in supplication and spoke as follows.” (SB. 12.6.1)

Maharaja Pariksit is clearly a devotee, and when he reveals his final desire to Sukadeva Gosvami (in Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.6.6), it will become even clearer just how much of a devotee he is. So that we do not misunderstand the exchange, the BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.6.1 describes yet one more reason Sukadeva Gosvami chose to speak about jnana in the previous chapter: “According to Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, some of the sages present while Sukadeva was instructing King Pariksit were impersonalist philosophers. Thus the word samena indicates that in the previous chapter Sukadeva Gosvami had spoken the philosophy of self-realization in a way pleasing to such intellectual yogis.”

“Maharaja Pariksit said: I have now achieved the purpose of my life, because a great and merciful soul like you has shown such kindness to me. You have personally spoken to me this narration of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Hari, who is without beginning or end.” (SB. 12.6.2)

Helping a soul attain the true goal of life is the definition of kindness. Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains the reason that Maharaja Pariksit is so grateful to have heard from Sukadeva Gosvami about Lord Hari. The king had previously seen the Lord when he was still in his mother’s womb and had always been a devotee, so hearing hari-katha was exactly what Maharaja Pariksit had wanted from his association with Srila Sukadeva Gosvami: “O greatly fortunate Sukadeva Gosvami, please continue narrating Srimad-Bhagavatam so that I can place my mind upon the Supreme Soul, Lord Krsna, and, being completely freed from material qualities, thus relinquish this body.” (SB. 2.8.3)

Maharaja Pariksit says: “I do not consider it at all amazing that great souls such as yourself, whose minds are always absorbed in the infallible Personality of Godhead \[acyutatmanam\], show mercy to the foolish conditioned souls, tormented as we are by the problems of material life.” (SB. 12.6.3)

Maharaja Pariksit states his deep appreciation for the compassion of souls like Sukadeva Gosvami, whose minds are acyutatmanam, always absorbed in Acyuta.

“I have heard from you this Srimad-Bhagavatam, which is the perfect summary of all the Puranas and which perfectly describes the Supreme Lord, Uttamasloka.” (SB. 12.6.4)

According to Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, here Maharaja Pariksit describes what he has gained by hearing Srimad-Bhagavatam from Sukadeva Gosvami: he has heard descriptions of the Supreme Lord while having the main theme, devotion to the Lord, supported and nourished by whatever other topics were discussed. He states: “My lord, I now have no fear of Taksaka or any other living being, or even of repeated deaths, because I have absorbed myself in that purely spiritual Absolute Truth \[pravisto brahma nirvanam\], which you have revealed and which destroys all fear.” (SB. 12.6.5)

Clearly, Maharaja Pariksit is absorbed in the Supreme Personality of Godhead and not in the impersonal Brahman. Jiva Gosvami enhances our understanding of Maharaja Pariksit’s words: “Now I have realized what you have instructed me. The Bhagavatam has entered me and I have become absorbed in the Brahman \[Absolute Truth\] which is nirvana \[exclusive of everything material\], the very form of supreme ecstasy, the Supreme Truth of the Personality of Godhead, who is greater than all.”

In his own comment on this text, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura continues in the mood of his initial comments on this chapter:

O lord \[Sukadeva Gosvami\] who knows everything (bhagavan)! Knowing that my heart was fixed in bhakti, why did you teach me jnana I do not fear Taksaka or other deaths in other births. But entering into the impersonal Brahman, which destroys fear-which you have just taught me that I fear. This is similar to making a statement like, “I am not afraid of misfortunes that may come while I am at home, but going to the forest - that I fear.” The phrase “that I fear” is understood, not spoken, and therefore “I will not enter the forest” is also understood. I have a much greater fear of the impersonal Brahman you have described than of many deaths at the hands of Taksaka. Impersonal liberation is intolerable for devotees like me, who have renounced everything and given everything to the Lord, and whose real desires were revealed by the great devotee Siva in his statement:

*narayana-parah sarve na kutascana bibhyatih*

*svargapavarga-narakesv api tulyartha-darsinah*

“Devotees solely engaged in the devotional service of Narayana never fear any condition of life. For them the heavenly planets, liberation, and the hellish planets are all the same.” (SB. 6.17.28) Although I have previously vowed devotion to the Supreme Lord -

*punas ca bhuyad bhagavaty anante*

*ratih prasangas ca tad-asrayesu*

*mahatsu yam yam upayami srstirh*

*maitry astu sarvatra namo dvijebhyah*

“On the other hand, in whatever birth I receive, may I have rati for the unlimited Lord, excellent association with his devotees who take shelter of Him, and friendship with all living beings! I offer respects to the brahmanas .’’(SB 1.19.16) - you now teach me about Brahman!

There is a hint of anger in his words. By that, Sukadeva, who was testing the firmness of Maharaja Pariksit’s bhakti, became happy. Similarly, at the beginning of the rasa dance, the gopis, having disobeyed the orders of their elders, became angry with Krsna and rebuked Him by this indirect expression… The devotees do not accept another meaning of the present text, such as “I have entered the Brahman, which destroys all fear,” since the Bhagavatam presents two alternative meanings for persons of different qualifications.

“O brahmana, please give me permission to resign my speech and the functions of all my senses unto Lord Adhoksaja. Allow me to absorb my mind, purified of lusty desires, within Him and to thus give up my life.” (SB. 12.6.6)

Sukadeva Gosvami asked King Pariksit at the end of chapter 5 what more he wished to hear. The king has now replied that he needs no further instructions: he is ready to leave his body and the world and enter the spiritual world of the Supreme Lord. By speaking about Lord Hari, Sukadeva Gosvami has fulfilled Maharaja Pariksit’s desires (expressed in Srimad-Bhagavatam 1.19.15), and the king has perfectly understood the Srimad-Bhagavatam exactly as Sukadeva Gosvami intended. He is ready, without further discussion, to withdraw his consciousness from the world and focus it fully on the Lord. He is now prepared to journey back home, back to Godhead.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on this text is simple and to the point: “O brahmana! Give me the order, by your mercy, and \[at this time give me\] nothing unfavorable. Give me permission to leave my body, having concentrated my mind, free of material desires and impressions, on Lord Adhoksaja, Sri Krsna.”

What is the king’s meditation? “You have revealed to me that which is most auspicious, the supreme personal feature of the Lord \[param bhagavatah padam\]. I am now fixed in knowledge and self-realization, and my ignorance has been eradicated.” (SB. 12.6.7)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s notes that padam refers to the Lord’s personal form, His lotus feet, and His abode. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti reveals more of Maharaja Pariksit’s thinking: By knowing about the Lord and realizing His sweetness (madhurya) and powers (aisvarya), my ignorance has been destroyed. How did this occur? You have shown me the supreme form, abode, and lotus feet of the Lord!”

*Texts 8-10: Maharaja Pariksit focuses his consciousness and departs*

“Suta Gosvami said: Thus requested, the saintly son of Srila Vyasadeva gave his permission to King Pariksit. Then, after being worshiped by the King and all the sages present, Sukadeva departed from that place.” (SB. 12.6.8)

Amazingly, Sukadeva Gosvami, himself detached and inspired by Kpsim, leaves Maharaja Pariksit’s side only moments before the king’s death. “Maharaja Pariksit then sat down on the bank of the Ganges, upon a seat made of darbha grass with the tips of its stalks facing east, anil turned himself toward the north. Having attained the perfection of yoga, he experienced full self-realization and was free of material attachment and doubt. The saintly King settled his mind within his spiritual self by pure intelligence and proceeded to meditate upon the Supreme Absolute Truth \[param\]. His life air ceased to move, and he became as stationary as a tree.” (SB. 12.6.9-10)

Srila Jiva Gosvami explains that Maharaja Pariksit meditated on param, the transcendental Lord named Sri Krsna. The king was filled with the existence of Krsna, the Supreme Brahman, because he was fully absorbed in pure love for Him. This is along the lines of Narada Muni’s statements to Maharaja Yudhisthira, which contain the phrase gudham param brahma manusyadihgam, in praise of the dying king’s forefathers, the Pandavas: “My dear Maharaja Yudhisthira, all of you \[the Pandavas\] are extremely fortunate, for the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krsna, lives in your palace just like a human being \[gudham param brahma manusya-lingam\]. Great saintly persons know this very well, and therefore they constantly visit this house.” (SB. 7.10.48) “My dear Maharaja Yudhisthira, you Pandavas are so very fortunate in this world that many, many great saints, who can purify all the planets of the universe, come to your house just like ordinary visitors. Furthermore, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krsna, is living confidentially with you in your house, just like your brother \[gudham param brahma manusya-lingam\].” (SB. 7.15.75)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura tells us that as the king sat on the kusa grass, with its tips facing east, he withdrew his consciousness and life airs into himself and surpassed the three gunas. Through his intelligence, he then intensely concentrated his mind on Krsna and left this world.

*Texts 11-15: The pastime continues - Taksaka bites Maharaja Pariksit*

“O learned brahmanas, the snake-bird Taksaka, who had been sent by the angry son of a brahmana, was going toward the King to kill him when he saw Kasyapa Muni on the path. Taksaka flattered Kasyapa by presenting him with valuable offerings and thereby stopped the sage, who was expert in counteracting poison, from protecting Maharaja Pariksit. Then the snake-bird, who could assume any form he wished, disguised himself as a brahmana, approached the King, and bit him. While living beings all over the universe looked on, the body of the great self-realized saint among kings was immediately burned to ashes by the fire of the snake’s poison.” (SB. 12.6.11-13)

In his comment on these texts, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura describes that Taksaka disguised himself as a brahmana in his attempt to approach Maharaja Pariksit. Kasyapa Muni was nearby and was gathering materials to create a remedy for Taksaka’s poison. Kasyapa had demonstrated his ability to counteract poison when he grew a banyan tree from a sprout after it had been turned to ashes by Taksaka’s poison. But Taksaka satisfied Kasyapa with objects the sage favored and thus waylaying him, stopped him from protecting the king.

But Taksaka’s diversion was fruitless; Maharaja Pariksit had already focused his consciousness on the Supreme Lord’s lotus feet and left both his body and the world. Therefore, as Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura assures us, Taksaka’s attack was useless; Maharaja Pariksit was already in the spiritual world. The poison caused Maharaja Pariksit’s body to ignite into flames, but this was only like the funeral rites performed by a son for his father.

“There arose a terrible cry of lamentation in all directions on the earth and in the heavens, and all the demigods, demons, human beings, and other creatures were astonished. Kettledrums sounded in the regions of the demigods, and the celestial Gandharvas and Apsaras sang. The demigods showered flowers and spoke words of praise.” (SB. 12.6.14-15)

The BBT’s short purport to text 15 ends the Srimad-Bhagavatam’s telling of Maharaja Pariksit’s glorious death: “Although lamenting at first, all learned persons, including the demigods, soon realized that a great soul had gone back home, back to Godhead. This was certainly a cause for celebration.”

*Texts 16-28: Maharaja Janamejaya performs a sacrifice to rid the world of snakes*

*Texts 16-22: The sacrifice to destroy all snakes begins*

Maharaja Pariksit’s son, Maharaja Janamejaya, was furious to learn that his father had been fatally bitten by the snake-bird, so he decided to enlist some brahmanas in performing a sacrifice to rid the world of snakes. Seeing even the most powerful snakes being destroyed in Maharaja Janamejaya’s sacrificial fire, Taksaka took shelter of Lord India. When King Janamejaya understood that Indra was protecting Taksaka, the immediate culprit in his father’s death, he further instructed the powerful brahmanas to make Taksaka fall into the fire along with his protector. As a result, Indra’s airplane was pulled from its position and drawn along with Taksaka toward the sacrificial fire.

*Texts 23—28: Brhaspati ends the sacrifice*

Seeing this, Brhaspati approached King Janamejaya and pleaded for In- dra’s life along with the life of Taksaka, the king of snakes, because killing both these persons was inappropriate. After all, Brhaspati explained, even those who cause us harm are mere instruments of our own fate: “The life and death of an embodied soul and his destination in the next life are all caused by himself through his own activity. Therefore, O King, no other agent is actually responsible for creating one’s happiness and distress. When a conditioned soul is killed by snakes, thieves, fire, lightning, hunger, disease, or anything else, he is experiencing the reaction to his own past work.” (SB. 12.6.25-26)Please, Brhaspati says, end this sacrifice, for it is meant simply to harm others. Although it appears that the snakes who have already been killed were innocent, they too must be suffering unforeseen consequences for their past actions. But don’t kill any more of them.”

In Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.6.26, he writes about Brhaspati’s philosophy - that the acts a living being performs determine whether he goes to heaven or hell at death. But this principle defines the arrangements for ordinary living beings, according to Brhaspati, and not for a soul like Maharaja Pariksit. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti continues: “Your father’s living, dying, and attaining the Supreme Lord’s abode were enacted by the Lord’s arrangement. With His own hand the Lord protected your father from Asvatthama’s weapon and arranged for him to die by the curse of the sage. The Lord also arranged that your father hear from his beloved Sukadeva to aid his \[Pariksit’s\] attainment of His own spiritual abode. The Lord Himself arranged all these events. It only appears that Taksaka caused your father’s death. Due to being under the control of their own karma, persons of this world die through events such as a snakebite, hut not your father, for he was the king of devotees.”

“Suta Gosvami continued: Advised in this manner, Maharaja Janamejaya replied, ‘So be it.’ Honoring the words of the great sage, he desisted from performing the snake sacrifice and worshiped Brhaspati, the most eloquent of sages.” (SB. 12.6.28)

*Texts 29-35: Suta Gosvami speaks about how to remain forever free of the grip of illusion*

When Maharaja Pariksit was cursed to die, he responded with acceptance and humility. How could the king’s son and follower, the great and qualified devotee Janamejaya Maharaja, have acted so vengefully, so contrary to his father’s mood? In reply to this question, Suta Gosvami ascribes to the Lord’s subtle, potent, maya the ability to place everyone, even the great Maharaja Janamejaya, into an illusory identification with his body: “This is indeed the Supreme Lord Visnu’s illusory energy, which is unstoppable and difficult to perceive. Although the individual spirit souls are part and parcel of the Lord, through the influence of this illusory energy they are bewildered by their identification with various material bodies.” (SB. 12.6.29)

The BBT purport to text 29 offers a balancing comment: “The illusory energy of Lord Visnu is so powerful that even the illustrious son of King Pariksit was temporarily misdirected. Because he was a devotee of Lord Krsna, however, his bewilderment was quickly rectified.”

Suta Gosvami continues: But beyond the conditioned souls dominated by maya are the souls who are free from deceit and who live in the supreme reality: “In that supreme reality there is no manifestation of the material mind, which functions in terms of alternating decision and doubt. Created material products, their subtle causes, and the goals of enjoyment attained by their utilization do not exist there. Furthermore, in that supreme reality there is no conditioned spirit, covered by false ego and the three modes of nature. That reality excludes everything limited or limiting. One who is wise should therefore stop the waves of material life and enjoy within that Supreme Truth.” (SB. 12.6.30-31)

That realm is the abode of the Personality of Godhead. Illusion cannot function there, since Maya herself is shy to stand in Krsna’s presence, just as darkness does not stand in the presence of light. As Lord Brahma states in Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.5.13, Maya is ashamed to stand face to face with the Supreme Lord.

In his comment on text 30, Srtla Sridhara Svami explains how one can stop maya ami its effects. I he great commentator says that the basic idea of the entire Srimad-Bhagavatam answers this question: the way to stop everything undesirable is to discover Sri Visnu and worship Him. This is the point, Srila Sridhara Svami notes, that is being discussed in this and subsequent texts (SB. 12.6.30-34).

In text 32, Suta Gosvami describes how to attain the land of freedom, far from maya’s grip: “Those who desire to give up all that is not essentially real move systematically, by negative discrimination of the extraneous \[yan neti netity atad-utsisrksavah\], to the supreme position of Lord Visnu \[param padam vaisnavam\]. Giving up petty materialism, they offer their love exclusively \[ananya-sauhrdam\] to the Absolute Truth within their hearts and embrace that highest truth in fixed meditation.”

The BBT purport to this text defines “negative discrimination” of the extraneous as well as the positive process of attainment: “The words yan neti netity atad-utsisrksavah indicate the process of negative discrimination, by which one engaged in the search for essential and absolute truth systematically rejects all that is superfluous, superficial, and relative… Those who actually desire perfect knowledge must not only reject the nonessential but must also ultimately understand the essential spiritual reality called param padam vaisnavam: the supreme destination, the abode of Lord Visnu. Padam indicates ... the abode of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, which can be understood only by those who give up petty materialism and adopt the position of ananya-sauhrdam, exclusive love for the Lord.”

Again, detached from the petty, such souls do not remain empty- handed: “Such devotees come to understand the supreme transcendental situation of the Personality of Godhead, Lord Visnu, because they are no longer polluted by the concepts of ‘I’ and ‘my,’ which are based on body and home.” (SB. 12.6.33)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura provides some essential details hidden in Sri Suta’s guidance: “The devotees concentrate by continual remembrance on the form of Visnu. They give up the evil tendency to think in terms of ‘I’ and ‘mine.’ They discriminate, understanding that ‘this is not favorable’ or ‘that is not favorable.’ They desire to give up everything unrelated to the Lord, such as body, house, sons, and wife, which are objects of possessiveness, because they have friendship with the fully dedicated devotees. The Lord’s form can be understood by devotees who have a fully concentrated focus and not by others.”

Free from meditation on matter, and one’s consciousness instead filled with the Lord’s form, a sincere soul will attain the spiritual world through this practice of pure devotional service. Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura offers other sastric texts to support these words:

For those who worship Me, giving up all their activities unto Me and being devoted to Me without deviation, engaged in devotional service and always meditating upon Me, having fixed their minds upon Me, O son of Prtha - for them I am the swift deliverer from the ocean of birth and death. (Bhagavad-gita 12.6-7)

It is the Personality of Godhead Sri Krsna who gives liberation. By thinking of His lotus feet at every second, following in the footsteps of authorities, the devotee in trance can see the Absolute Truth.

The learned mental speculators, however, think of Him according to their whims. May the Lord be pleased with me.” (SB. 2.4-21)

Full determination to attain transcendental love for the Supreme Personality of Godhead allows one to walk through this world without envy and free from enmity: “One should tolerate all insults and never fail to show proper respect to any person. Avoiding identification with the material body, one should not create enmity with anyone.” (SB. 12.6.34)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura emphasizes Suta Gosvami’s meaningful words: “If a person commits offenses, the form of Visnu will disappear. The method of avoiding offenses is now taught. One should tolerate sharp words; one should not answer with equally harsh words.” Suta concludes this topic by offering his respects to his worshipable Lord, Sri Krsna, whom he has understood as the Supreme Personality of Godhead due to his having heard from the lotus mouth of Sukadeva Gosvami:

*namo bhagavate tasmai*

*krsnayakuntha-medhase*

*yat-padamburuha-dhyanat*

*sarhhitdm adhyagam imam*

“I offer my obeisances to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the invincible Lord Sri Krsna. Simply by meditating upon His lotus feet I have been able to study and appreciate this great literature.” (SB. 12.6.35)

Srila Jiva Gosvami comments on Suta Gosvami’s obeisances: “With the idea that reality can be understood from Srimad-Bhagavatam, Suta Gosvami offers obeisances to his own instructor in the verse beginning namah. Although his actual instructor was Sri Sukadeva, nevertheless, he is offering his obeisances to Sri Krsna Dvaipayana Vyasa.This is because Suta Gosvami is acknowledging that even the instructions given by Sukadeva were received by the mercy of Vyasadeva.”

Thus the narration of Maharaja Pariksit’s birth and activities, his being cursed, his meeting Srila Sukadeva Gosvami, his hearing from Sukadeva the entire Srimad-Bhagavatam, as well as his departure from this world, have now been concluded. Sukadeva Gosvami has spoken his final words to Maharaja Pariksit:

*etat te kathitam tata*

*yad atma prstavan nrpa*

*harer visvatmanas cestam*

*kim bhuyah srotum icchasi*

“Beloved King Pariksit, I have narrated to you the topics you originally inquired about - the pastimes of Lord Hari, the Supreme Soul of the universe. Now, what more do you wish to hear?” (SB. 12.5.13)

Soon after speaking these words, and minutes before Maharaja Pariksit’s departure, Srila Sukadeva Gosvami stands and walks away, back to his wandering through the world and his absorption in service to the Supreme Absolute Truth, Sri Krsna.

When the narration of the Srimad-Bhagavatam resumes, Sri Suta Gosvami will again be answering the questions of the sages at Naimisaranya, headed by Saunaka Rsi.

## Dialogue 9. Concluding the Srimad-Bhagavatam

*Canto twelve: chapters 6-13*

**Chapter 6**

*Texts 36-80: The Vedic literature*

As already mentioned, Sukadeva Gosvami finished speaking the Bhagavatam to Maharaja Pariksit and resumed his mendicant wandering. Fortunate Maharaja Pariksit is also gone, his consciousness, like Sukadeva’s, absorbed in Krsna. Now Sri Suta Gosvami, who was listening to the sacred conversation between the sage and the king, continues as the next-generation speaker. He is, of course, addressing the sages at Naimisaranya. So that overlay of storyline introduced in the First Canto will continue until the end of the Twelfth Canto.

In his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.5.1, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura asks why the parts of the story that don’t involve Maharaja Pariksit - the words of Suta Gosvami, for example, which include all of Canto One as well as Canto Twelve, chapters 6-13 - are also considered “the Bhagavatam.” Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura answers this question with examples: “Just as the preliminary and concluding portions of a sacrifice are also called ‘the sacrifice,’ and the introduction to a drama and the blessings at the end are part of ‘the drama,’ so the beginning and concluding parts of the Bhagavatam are part of the Bhagavatam. Consider the following statement from the fourth verse of the Gita-mahatmya: ‘One should recite the Gita. What is the necessity of any other scripture, when the C ala emanates from the lotus mouth of the Supreme Lord?’ Although not every word of the Gita’s eighteen chapters was spoken by the Lord, each is said to have been spoken by Him in this statement. Similarly, ah though the last part of the Twelfth Canto was not spoken by Sukadeva, it is also said to have been spoken by him. This is the conclusion.”

In Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.6.35, Suta Gosvami offered his respectful obeisances to invincible Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, because meditation on Krsna’s lotus feet is what makes it possible for him to study and appreciate Srimad-Bhagavatam.

Saunaka Rsi, chief of the 88,000 sages at Naimisaranya, now asks Suta Gosvami another question.

*Text 36: Saunaka Rsi’s question*

Saunaka Rsi, who already accepts the Srimad-Bhagavatam as the essence of all Vedic literature, wants to hear how the Srimad-Bhagavatam was developed from its Vedic sources: “\[P\]lease narrate to us how Paila and the other greatly intelligent disciples of Srila Vyasadeva, who are known as the standard authorities of Vedic wisdom, spoke and edited the Vedas.” (SB. 12.6.36)

*Text 37-61: The early history of the Vedic literature*

*Text 37: The primordial sound*

Suta Gosvami begins at the point when a subtle sound vibrated from Brahma’s heart: “O brahmana, first the subtle vibration of transcendental sound appeared from the sky of the heart of the most elevated Lord Brahma, whose mind was perfectly fixed in spiritual realization. One can perceive this subtle vibration when one stops all external hearing.” (SB. 12.6.37)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains that the subtle yet transcendental sound (called nada) appeared from the ether in Brahma’s heart.

*Text 38: The results of worshiping the subtle form of the Vedas*

“By worship of this subtle form of the Vedas, O brahmana, mystic- sages cleanse their hearts of all contamination caused by impurity of substance, activity, and doer, and thus they attain freedom from repeated birth and death.”

*Texts 39-43: Orhkara, the seed of all Vedic hymns, arises from nada*

“From that transcendental subtle vibration arose the omkara composed of three sounds. The omkara has unseen potencies and manifests automatically within a purified heart. It is the representation of the Absolute Truth in all three of His phases - the Supreme Personality, the Supreme Soul, and the supreme impersonal truth.” (SB. 12.6.39)

Srila Jiva Gosvami comments on text 39 in the Bhagavata Sandarbha (anuccheda 110): “Tattva (the Absolute Truth) appears in two forms: Bhagavan and Brahman. The cit-sakti (Krsna’s knowledge-awarding potency) also has two forms: the form of bhakti dedicated to His personal svayam-prakasa forms, and the form of knowledge about Brahman. The srutis dedicated to bhakti deal with Bhagavan, and the srutis dedicated to jnana deal with Brahman. This is the general conclusion.”

Suta Gosvami then gives more detail about the omkara: “This omkara, ultimately nonmaterial and imperceptible, is heard by the Supersoul without His possessing material ears or any other material senses. The entire expanse of Vedic sound is elaborated from omkara, which appears from the soul, within the sky of the heart. It is the direct designation of the self-originating Absolute Truth, the Supersoul, and is the secret essence and eternal seed of all Vedic hymns.” (SB. 12.6.40-41)

In his comment on text 40, Srila Jiva Gosvami notes that the Bhagavatam’s statement that it is the Supersoul who is the true hearer of the nada sound is meant to counter the argument that ordinary shouts can be heard when the ears are stopped up and that awake or asleep, the deaf are unable to hear. That is, the Supersoul’s hearing is independent of the jiva’s ability to perceive sound. Further, Sri Jiva adds, a living being can only hear the transcendental omkara through worship and mercy.

*Text 42: Omkara is the sustainer*

Described next, Srila Sridhara Svami explains, is the process by which the entire material creation is generated from omkara.

Srila Suta Gosvami: “Omkara exhibited the three original sounds of the alphabet - A, U, and M. These three, O most eminent descendant of Bhrgu, sustain all the different threefold aspects of material existence, including the three modes of nature, the names of the Kg, Yajur, and Santa Vedas, the goals known as the Bliur, Bhuvar, and Svar planetary systems, and the three functional platforms called waking consciousness, sleep, and deep sleep.”

*Text 43: The Vedas to arise from omkara*

“From that omkara Lord Brahma created all the sounds of the alphabet - the vowels, consonants, semivowels, sibilants, and others - distinguished by such features as long and short measure.”

In Teachings of Lord Caitanya, chapter 31, Srila Prabhupada describes how Brahma was infused with Vedic knowledge and how the Vedas were subsequently manifest:

In the Brahnasamhita (5.27-28) a nice description of the sound of Krsna’s flute is given: “When Krsna began to play on His flute, the sound vibration entered into the ear of Brahma as the Vedic mantra om.” This om is composed of three letters - A, U, and M - and it describes our relationship with the Supreme Lord, our activities by which we can achieve the highest perfection of love and the actual position of love on the spiritual platform. When the sound vibration of Krsna’s flute is expressed through the mouth of Brahma, it becomes Gayatri. Thus by being influenced by the sound vibration of Krsna’s flute, Brahma, the supreme creature and first living entity of this material world, was initiated as a brahmana. That Brahma was initiated as a brahmana by the flute of Krsna is confirmed by Srila Jiva Gosvami. When Brahma was enlightened by the Gayatri mantra through Krsna’s flute, he attained all Vedic knowledge. Acknowledging the benediction offered to him by Krsna, he became the original spiritual master of all living entities.

*Text 44: The Vedas emanate from Brahma*

“All-powerful Brahma made use of this collection of sounds to produce from his four faces the four Vedas, which appeared together with the sacred omkara and the seven vyahrti invocations. His intention was to propagate the process of Vedic sacrifice according to the different functions performed by the priests of each of the four Vedas.” Thus by these groups of sounds produced from his four faces, Lord Brahma created the four Vedas.

*Texts 45-61: The earliest teachers of Vedic knowledge*

“Brahma taught these Vedas to his sons, who were great sages among the brahmanas and experts in the art of Vedic recitation. They in turn took the role of acaryas and imparted the Vedas to their own sons.” (SB. 12.6.45) Thus through each cycle of four ages, generation after generation, the Vedas were passed from qualified teacher to qualified student, who then later became the next generation of teachers.

Inspired by Krsna from within their hearts (hrdi-sthacyuta-coditah), sages systematically edited (vyastah) and divided the Vedas to make them easier to understand. They did this at the end of each Dvapara-yuga, for they saw that time was diminishing people’s lifespans, intelligence, and strength.

The editing of the Vedic literature, according to Srila Sridhara Svami, means that the literature was divided into parts. To overcome the objection that the division of the Vedas was a product of human intelligence and therefore need not be respected, Srila Sridhara Svami notes that Srila Suta Gosvami ends Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.6.47 with the words hrdi-sthacyuta-coditah, proving that the division was inspired (coditah) by Lord Acyuta, who was sitting in the sages’ hearts.

Srila Suta Gosvami continues: The dividing of one Veda into four distinct parts - the Rg, Atharva, Yajur, and Sama - at the end of this Dvapara-yuga was completed by a divine spark of a portion of the Lord’s plenary portion, Krsna Dvaipayana Vyasa. The original, undivided Veda is generally accepted as the Atharva Veda, but sometimes it is said that it is the Yajur Veda.

The Rg Veda then became the Veda for mantras that point practitioners to the Supreme Lord through worship of the devatas; the Sama Veda explains the science of musically chanting those mantras as hymns; the Yajur Veda uses those mantras and hymns to prescribe methods of performing rituals and sacrifices; and the Atharva Veda gives mystical incantations for dealing with the practical elements of this world, such as health, wealth, weather, marriage, business, and enemies.

After dividing the Vedas into four, “the most powerful and intelligent Vyasadeva called four of his disciples, O brahmana, and entrusted to each of them one of these four samhitas \[collections of mantras and hymns\].” (SB. 12.6.51) To ease the assimilation of these divisions, Vyasa’s disciples further divided the Vedic texts entrusted to them and taught these pieces to their own disciples. These disciples further divided the parts of the Vedas entrusted to them into paramparas, or disciplic successions.

*Texts 62-74: Yajhavalkya’s contribution to the Vedic literature - even the Vedas not yet revealed have Krsna as their source and object*

Srila Vyasadeva entrusted his disciple Sri Vaisampayana with the Yajur Veda mantras. Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains in his comments on Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.6.61-62 that some of Vaisampayana’s disciples were priests expert in performing Yajur Veda rituals, and they performed vows on behalf of their guru to destroy the sinful reactions he had incurred after killing a brahmana.While they were doing this, another disciple, Yajnavalkya, proudly said to his guru, “What is the use of the atonements these weak disciples can enact? Let them take their ease and be happy. I alone am able to perform proper austerity.”

“Addressed thus, the spiritual master Vaisampayana became angry and said: Go away from here! Enough of you, O disciple who insults brahmanas! Furthermore, you must immediately give back everything I have taught you.” (SB. 12.6.63)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura describes Vaisampayana’s reaction and his rejection of Yajnavalkya: “You deride humble brahmanas as being weak and worthless! Go away! What use is a disciple like you? Yajnavalkya replied, ‘Yes, I will go,’ and while he was leaving the guru said, ‘Give back the knowledge I have taught you.’ ”

Suta Gosvami continues: “Yajnavalkya, the son of Devarata, then vomited the mantras of the Yajur Veda and went away from there. The assembled disciples, looking greedily upon these yajur hymns, assumed the form of partridges and picked them all up. These divisions of the Yajur Veda therefore became known as the most beautiful Taittiriya-samhita, the hymns collected by partridges \[tittirah\].” (SB. 12.6.64)

The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.6.64 illuminates this unique occurrence: “According to Srila Sridhara Svami, it is improper for a brahmana to collect what has been vomited, and so the powerful brahmana disciples of Vaisampayana assumed the form of tittiras, partridges, and collected the valuable mantras."

*Texts 67-72: The prayers of Yajnavalkya*

After being rejected, Yajnavalkya decides to try to gain Yajur mantras unknown even to his spiritual master, so the powerful brahmana worshiped the all-powerful Supreme Lord through the sun god, whose unending fire and scorching rays are caused by the Lord’s potent energies. In Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.6.67-72, Yajnavalkya prays to the sun in order to attain his purpose: “I offer my respectful obeisances \[om namah\] to the Supreme Personality of Godhead \[bhagavate\] appearing as the sun. You are present as the controller of the four kinds of living entities, beginning from Brahma and extending down to the blades of grass. Just as the sky is present both inside and outside every living being, you exist both within the hearts \[antar- hrdayesu\] of all as the Supersoul \[atma-svarupena\] and externally in the form of time. Just as the sky cannot be covered by the clouds present within it, you are never covered by any false material designation. By the flow of years, which are made up of the tiny fragments of time called ksanas, lavas, and nimesas, you alone maintain this world, drying up the waters and giving them back as rain.” (SB. 12.6.67)

The BBT purport explains: “This prayer is not offered to the sun god as an independent or autonomous entity but rather to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, represented by His powerful expansion the solar deity.”

In his comment on this text, Srila Jiva Gosvami identifies the deity to whom Yajnavalkya offered his prayers. He states that whatever praise is offered to the sun god in the prose texts beginning om namah is given while envisioning the sun god as representing the Supreme Lord, the Supersoul, not with the faulty perception that the sun god is independent of Him.

Clearly, Yajnavalkya respects the source of the sun’s energy. Free from material coverings, that ultimate Source is the ultimate support of life in the universe. That same Lord, appearing as the sun, controls all living entities and exists both in everyone’s heart as the Supersoul and externally as unstoppable time. He is never covered by matter and maintains all beings through His time potency, which brings rain in its season to nourish crops.

Yajhavalkya’s method of worshiping the Supreme Lord, his worshipaide Deity, through the sun is proper. Krsna equates Himself with the sun in the Bhagavad-gita (10.21): jyotisdrh ravir amsumdn, “of lights I am the radiant sun.” Srila Prabhupada writes in his purport to this Gita verse: “\[I\]n the Brahrna-samhitd the sun is accepted as the glowing eye of the Supreme Lord.” In the Bhagavad-gita (15.12), Krsna also states, “The splendor of the sun, which dissipates the darkness of this whole world, comes from Me.” Srila Prabhupada’s purport explains why this view is helpful to a spiritual aspirant: “One should simply try to understand that the splendor of the sun ... \[is\] coming from the Supreme Personality of Godhead. In such a conception of life, the beginning of Krsna consciousness, lies a great deal of advancement for the conditioned soul in this material world.”

Srila Sridhara Svami notes that Srnnad-Bhagavatam 12.6.67 explains why the Lord is praised as varenya, most worshipable, as stated in the the Gayatri mantra. Srila Sridhara Svami ascribes further explanations of Gayatri to subsequent texts spoken by Yajnavalkya.

Yajnavalkya describes the sun’s glory: “O glowing one, O powerful lord of the sun, you are the chief of all the demigods. I meditate with careful attention on your fiery globe, because for those who offer prayers to you three times daily according to the Vedic method passed down through authorized disciplic succession, you burn away all sinful activities, all consequent suffering and even the original seed of desire \[bija\].” (SB. 12.6.68)

Worshiping the sun as Yajnavalkya describes burns away all sinful activities, all the suffering that results from sinful activities, and even the original cause (bija) of all sinful activities, material desires. The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.6.70 states: “According to Vedic culture, the three higher classes of society (the intellectual, political, and mercantile sections) are formally connected with the spiritual master by initiation and receive the Gayatri mantra. This purifying mantra is chanted three times daily - at sunrise, noon, and sunset. Auspicious moments for the performance of spiritual duties are calculated according to the sun’s path in the sky, and this systematic scheduling of spiritual duties is here attributed to the sun as the representative of God.”

Yajnavalkya prays: “You are personally present as the indwelling lord \[bhagavate\] in the hearts \[antar-hrdayesu\] of all moving and nonmoving beings, who depend completely on your shelter. Indeed, you animate their material minds, senses, and vital airs to act.” (SB. 12.6.69)

Here, Yajnavalkya recognizes the Lord as the shelter-giving Super-soul in the hearts of all moving and nonmoving beings - as He who gives them life and causes them to act. It is through the sun’s actions, such as the daily sunrise, that the Lord awakens all beings, setting into motion their unconscious minds and senses.Srila Sridhara Svami considers this and the next text as a comment on the words in the Gayatri mantra: savitur varenyam bhtirgo devasya.

Yajnavalkya’s prayers describing how the Lord functions as the sun continue: “The world has been seized and swallowed by the python of darkness in its horrible mouth and has become unconscious, as if dead. But mercifully glancing upon the sleeping people of the world, you raise them up with the gift of sight. Thus you are most magnanimous. At the three sacred junctures of each day, you engage the pious in the path of ultimate good, inducing them to perform religious duties that situate them in their spiritual position.” (SB. 12.6.70)

The reason the Lord acts through the sun to awaken the living beings is to engage those who are asleep in the dark in reclaiming their spiritual position. Nearing his conclusion, Yajnavalkya prays: “Just like an earthly king, you travel about everywhere spreading fear among the unholy as the powerful deities of the directions offer you in their folded palms lotus flowers and other respectful presentations.” (SB. 12.6.71)

After comparing the sun to a king whose daily travels cause fear in the unholy while the pious, including the deities of the directions, respect him with folded hands, Yajnavalkya now reveals the reason for his prayer: “Therefore, my lord, I am prayerfully approaching your lotus feet, which are honored by the spiritual masters of the three worlds, because I hope to receive from you mantras of the Yajur Veda unknown to anyone else.” (SB. 12.6.72)

*Texts 73-75: The sun god awards Yajnavalkya previously unknown Vedic mantras*

The sun god became satisfied with the sage and, appearing in the form of a horse, awarded him esoteric Yajur Veda mantras. “From these countless hundreds of mantras of the Yajur Veda, the powerful sage \[Yajnavalkya\] compiled fifteen new branches of Vedic literature. These became known as the Vajasaneyi-samhita, because they were produced from the hairs of the horse’s mane.” (SB. 12.6.74)

That Yajnavalkya’s prayers are directed to the sun but ultimately meant for the Supersoul indirectly indicates that it is from Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, that both the revealed and the unrevealed Vedas spring. The Vedas we know announce His supreme position: vedais ca sarvair aham eva vedyo, “By all the Vedas, I am to be known.” (Bhagavad-gita 15.15). Thus both the Vedas we don’t know and the Vedas we have been given emanate from Krsna and can bring us directly or indirectly to His lotus feet.

*Texts 76-80: Jaimini Rsi and his followers disseminate and increase the collections of Sama Veda hymns*

Jaimini Rsi, the authority of the Sama Veda, spoke parts of this Veda to his different disciples and sons. Sukarma, one of those disciples and a great scholar in his own right, divided the Sama Veda into one thousand samhitas.
