His own disciples later took charge of the Sama Veda, and their disciples became famous as they sang these sacred hymns in the east and the west. Still other disciples received additional collections of Sama Veda hymns.

**Chapter 7: The Puranic Literature**

*Texts 1-4: The dissemination of the Atharva Veda*

The immeasurably brilliant sage Sumantu Rsi, after receiving the Atharva Veda from Srila Vyasadeva, gave it to his disciples, who in turn divided it and passed it on to their disciples. In this way, many great souls became authorities and teachers of this great sastra.

*Texts 5-25: The Puranas*

*Texts 5-8: The Puranic knowledge is disseminated*

Sri Suta Gosvami continues: Wanting the masses to imbibe the Vedic teachings, Vedavyasa wrote the essence of the Vedas into the Puranas (“old” histories) and ltihasas (histories such as the Mahabharata and Ramayana).The six masters of the Puranas, Suta Gosvami explains, all studied their individual sacred anthologies (samhitas, which are collections of different Puranas) under Srila Vyasadeva’s disciple Romaharsana, Suta Gosvami’s father. Suta Gosvami then became a disciple of these six authorities and learned all the Puranic wisdom from them. Thereafter, Romaharsana further divided the Puranic literature into four parts and taught those parts to four individuals. One of those four was Suta Gosvami.

*Texts 9-25: The Puranic literature*

*Texts 9—21: Ten topics of a Purana*

Sota Gosvami now tells Saunaka Rsi the ten topics that make up a Purana: “O brahmana, authorities on the matter understand a Purana to contain ten characteristic topics: the creation of this universe, the subsequent creation of worlds and beings, the maintenance of all living beings, their sustenance, the rule of various Manus, the dynasties of great kings, the activities of such kings, annihilation, motivation, and the supreme shelter. Other scholars state that the great Puranas deal with these ten topics, while lesser Puranas may deal with five. (SB. 12.7.9-10)

The BBT purport to text 9-10 cites Jiva Gosvami: “The ten principal topics of Srimad-Bhagavatam are found within each of the twelve cantos. One should not try to assign each of the ten topics to a particular canto. Nor should the Srimad-Bhagavatam be artificially interpreted to show that it deals with the topics successively. The simple fact is that all aspects of knowledge important to human beings, summarized in the ten categories mentioned above, are described with various degrees of emphasis and analysis throughout the Srimad-Bhagavatam.”

In the Tattva Sandarbha, texts 61.3—5, Srila Jiva Gosvami writes that each canto contains a number of topics, and that no one topic is exclusively covered in any one canto. Srila Sridhara Svami, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, and Srila Prabhupada have taken a different approach while describing the contents of the individual Bhagavatam cantos. These acaryas - Srila Sridhara Svami and Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura in their introductions to every canto, and Srila Prabhupada on the cover of each of his Srimad-Bhagavatam volumes as well as his initial chapter summary of Canto Six - say that specific topics are extensively covered in particular cantos, topics that correspond to the ten topics mentioned in Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.10.1 and Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.7.9. All the acaryas are in accord when they conclude that regardless of any one canto’s emphasis, a number of topics are discussed in each canto.

*Texts 11-21: The ten topics*

Text 11, Sarga: The Supreme Lord’s primary creation - the creation of the ingredients required for the universal creation. The word sarga is also used in Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.10.1.

Text 12, Visarga: The secondary creation, by Brahma, using the primary ingredients (sarga). The term visarga is also used in Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.10.1. A second characteristic mentioned in Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.10.1, uti, the creative impetus, is included in visarga.

Text 13, Vrtti: “The process of sustenance,” which for a human specifically means to maintain oneself according to one s nature, either in pursuit of selfish desire or in accordance with the law of God. The word sthanam, sustenance, is used in Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.10.1, and since the earth and other planets sustain all who live on them, the translation given for sthanam in the synonyms of Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.10.1 is “the planetary systems.”

Text 14, Raksa: Protection. The Lord incarnates in various species and protects the universe. In the course of offering protection He kills the enemies of Vedic culture. Even protecting Ajamila from fear in the Sixth Canto falls under raksa. In Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.10.1, the word posanam is used for “protection.’

Text 15, Antarani: The Manus’ reigns. “In each reign of Manu, six types of personalities appear as manifestations of Lord Hari: the ruling Manu, the chief demigods, the sons of Manu, Indra, the great sages, and the partial incarnations of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.” (SB. 12.7.15) Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments that a manvantara is the period of time in which the above six types of persons perform their designated duties. In Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.10.1 the word manvantara is used to indicate the lifespan of a Manu. Srila Prabhupada speaks of manvantaras in his purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 4.28.31: “There are fourteen Manus in one day of Brahma. A manvantara, the lifespan of one Manu, is given as 71 multiplied by 4,320,000 years. After one such Manu passes on, another Manu begins his lifespan. In this way the life cycle of the universe is going on.”

Text 16, Vamsa and vamsanucaritam: The dynasties of great kings and narrations of their activities. The line of kings arising from Brahma is called vamsa, and the activities of the famous among those kings, such as Priyavrata, Dhruva, and Prthu, is called vamsanucaritam. These two topics take the place of isanukatha, the “science of God” from Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.10.1. Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.10.5 states: “The science of God describes the incarnations of the Personality of Godhead and His different activities together with the activities of His great devotees.”

Text 17, Samstha: The four types of cosmic annihilation. Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.7.17 calls samstha dissolution. Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.10.1 refers to it as nirodha, going back to Godhead. In Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.10.6 Sukadeva Gosvami explains the specific frame of reference in which this term is used, calling it “the winding up of the cosmic manifestation,” in which the living entity, along with his conditioned tendencies, merges “with the mystic lying down of the Maha-visnu.”

Text 18, Hetu: The cosmos is caused by the desires of the conditioned souls; those desires impel the Lord to create, maintain, and destroy the universes to facilitate the living entities’ dreams of enjoyment. When conditioned soul use their senses and intelligence to serve the Lord instead of seeking mundane pleasure, they gain freedom from material bondage. Thus hetu may also refer to mukti, liberation, as it does in Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.10.1.

Text 19, Apasraya: Apasraya refers to the the Supreme Shelter, who is also the shelter and source of all the other nine topics mentioned in the Bhagavatam. The Supreme Absolute Truth is present in all phases of consciousness - waking, sleep, and deep sleep - as He manifests, through His illusory energy, the sense objects and the consciousness to perceive them. But “He also exists separate from all these. Thus situated in His own transcendence, He is the ultimate and unique shelter.” (SB. 12.7.19) In Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.10.1, the apasraya is known as asraya, the summum honum, the Supreme Fountainhead, the Supreme Absolute Truth.

*Text 20: An example that describes the apasraya*

“Although a material object may assume various forms and names, its essential ingredient is always present as the basis of its existence. Similarly, both conjointly and separately, the Supreme Absolute Truth is always present with the created material body throughout its phases of existence, beginning with conception and ending with death.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura makes the point easily understandable: “Here the previous text \[SB. 12.7.19\] is explained with an example. Earth is present in an object like a pot, but earth also exists separately from the pot.... In all states of the body, from conception to death, that which is present as the controller and witness but also separate from the body and its states is called apasraya.

*Text 21: The conclusion*

The Bhagavatams first nine topics are meant to impart knowledge of the final topic, the apasraya. “Either automatically or because of one’s regulated spiritual practice, one’s mind may stop functioning on the material platform of waking consciousness, sleep, and deep sleep. Then one understands the Supreme Soul and withdraws from material endeavor.” (SB. 12.7.21)

By knowing that the apasraya is the Supreme Absolute Truth, the shelter of everything, one can withdraw one s consciousness from everything that appears as if it is separate from Him and become conscious only of Him. One will then exist in his pure, spiritual identity as His servant. The BBT purport notes: As stated in Srimad-Bhagavatam (3.25.33), jarayaty asu yd kosam nigirnam analo yatha: ‘Bhakti, devotional service, dissolves the subtle body of the living entity without separate endeavor, just as fire in the stomach digests all that we eat.

Thus Suta Gosvami has now stated the purpose of the entire Vedic literature: to focus one’s full consciousness on the Absolute Truth. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura notes how the Absolute Truth, as He has just been described, will be perceived differently according to how one approaches Him. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti makes his own preference clear: “Giving up the three states of material consciousness by pure bhakti, which consists of hearing and chanting, the mind spontaneously becomes detached from the modes of nature. Or, the mind spontaneously takes great joy in the lotus feet of the Lord. Or, by astanga-yoga the mind reaches nirvana - freedom from the material qualities. At that time the mind realizes Paramatma and becomes detached from material desires.”

*Texts 22-24: Three groups of six Puranas*

“Sages expert in ancient histories have declared that the Puranas, according to their various characteristics, can be divided into eighteen major Puranas and eighteen secondary Puranas. The eighteen major Puranas are the Brahma, Padma, Visnu, Siva, Linga, Garuda, Narada, Bhagavata, Agni, Skanda, Bhavisya, Brahma-vaivarta, Markandeya, Vamana, Varaha, Matsya, Kurma, and Brahmanda Puranas.” (SB. 12.7.22-24)

According to Gopiparanadhana Prabhu’s commentary on Tattva Sandarbha 17.4, the eighteen major Puranas were spoken by Suta Gosvami at Naimisaranya and accepted by the sages as authentic. At the same time, he notes, the Puranas are meant for three fundamentally different audiences, defined according to how each audience is influenced by the three modes of nature. He cites the forty-third chapter of the Padma Parana, Uttara-khanda (236.18-21) as his source: “The Visnu, Narada, Bhagavata, Garuda, Padma, and Varaha Puranas are in the mode of goodness. The Brahmanda, Brahma-vaivarta, Markandeya, Bhavisya, Vamana, and Brahma Puranas are in the mode of passion. And the Matsya, Kurma, Linga, Siva, Skanda, and Agni Puranas are in the mode of ignorance.”

In the Tattva Sandarbha (21.1-2), Srila Jiva Gosvami establishes the Bhagavata Purana (Srimad-Bhagavatam) in a class of its own, even among the Puranas in the mode of goodness. He shows that the Srimad-Bhagavatam is the natural commentary on the Vedanta-sutra. In his comment on Tattva Sandarbha 20.5, Gopiparanadhana Prabhu states, while explicating Jiva Gosvami’s points, that the Srimad-Bhagavatam is nondifferent from Krsna,and quotes Srimad-Bhagavatam 1.3.43, proving that the Srimad-Bhagavatam is Krsna Himself, who appears after the Lord’s departure, as His representative, to enlighten the unfortunate souls of Kali-yuga:

*krsne sva-dhamopagate*

*dharma-jnanadibhih saha*

*kalau nasta-drsam esa*

*puranarko ’dhunoditah*

“This Bhagavata Purana is as brilliant as the sun, and it has arisen just after the departure of Lord Krsna to His own abode, accompanied by religion, knowledge, etc. Persons who have lost their vision due to the dense darkness of ignorance in the Age of Kali shall get light from this Purana.” (SB. 1.3.43)

Thus in answering Saunaka Rsi’s question about the evolution of the Vedic literature, we understand Suta Gosvami’s conclusion through the discerning words of Srila Jiva Gosvami: The Srimad-Bhagavatam contains the potent essence of the Vedas, and the Srimad-Bhagavatam is especially meant to purify and carry to the spiritual world the fallen, disturbed souls living in the Age of Kali. Srila Jiva’s conclusion will be reconfirmed in the final two chapters of Srimad-Bhagavatam, when Suta Gosvami summarizes the Srimad-Bhagavatam and recites its glories.

*Text 25: Phala-sruti*

Suta Gosvami now offers a benediction to those who have heard his history: “I have thoroughly described to you, O brahmana, the expansion of the branches of the Vedas by the great sage Vyasadeva, his disciples and the disciples of his disciples. One who listens to this narration will increase in spiritual strength.” (SB. 12.7.25)

**Chapters 8-10: The Pastimes of Markandeya Rsi**

**Chapter 8: Markandeya’s Prayers to Nara-Narayana Rsi**

*Texts 1-14: Saunaka Rsi hears about Markandeya Rsi from Suta Gosvami*

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura notes that the Markandeya Purana was mentioned in text 24 of the last chapter. That mention reminded Saunaka of the story of Markandeya Rsi, which he decides to tell in chapters 8-10 of the Twelfth Canto. The BBT purport offers a comment from Srila Jiva Gosvami: “\[T\]he sages saw that Suta Gosvami was about to end his narration of Srimad-Bhagavatam, and thus they urged him to first tell the story of Markandeya Rsi.”

Markandeya Rsi was the son of the sage Mrkandu, a great devotee of Lord Siva. Mrkandu and his wife were unable to have children, so the sage performed tremendous austerities to please Lord Siva, hoping to be blessed with a son. Lord Siva was pleased and offered him a choice: he could have an impious, unintelligent foolish son who was long-lived, or he could father a pious, pure, and devoted son who would live for only sixteen years. Mrkandu Rsi chose the latter. When his son was born, the sage named him Markandeya.

Markandeya proved bright, obedient, and devoted to Lord Hari, and as he grew he studied the Vedas and other sastras. But despite this, his parents’ worry increased by the day, for they knew that each day brought their beloved son closer to his sixteenth birthday, the year predicted for his death. Markandeya saw his parent’s sadness. Finally, he inquired about this from his father and Mrkandu Rsi explained Lord Siva’s benediction, which now felt like a curse.

The boy sought permission from his parents to go to the forest, and there he performed austerities and worshiped a linga to please Lord Siva, Lord Hari’s greatest devotee.

Finally, on the boy’s sixteenth birthday, Yamaraja, with noose in hand, approached Markandeya while the boy was ardently worshiping Lord Siva. Seeing Yamaraja, Markandeya threw his arms around the linga, embracing it so tightly that when Yamaraja threw his noose over the boy, it also looped around the linga. Yamaraja pulled to rip Markandeya’s soul from his body, and the linga ruptured, causing Lord Siva to appear to protect his devotee. Yamaraja, death himself, was then “killed” by Lord Siva, although later, by the prayers of the demigods, his life was restored. Lord Siva then blessed Markandeya to remain sixteen forever.

Markandeya Rsi was the great jewel of Saunaka Rsi’s dynasty, so wishing to hear of him, Saunaka asks Suta Gosvami: “ Authorities say that Markandeya Rsi, the son of Mrkandu, was an exceptionally long-lived sage who was the only survivor at the end of Brahma’s day, when the entire universe was merged in the flood of annihilation. But this same Markandeya Rsi, the foremost descendant of Bhrgu, took birth in my own family during the current day of Brahma, and we have not yet seen any total annihilation in this day of Brahma. Also, it is well known that Markandeya, while wandering helplessly in the great ocean of annihilation, saw in those fearful waters a wonderful personality - an infant boy lying alone within the fold of a banyan leaf. O Suta, I am most bewildered and curious about this great sage, Markandeya Rsi. O great yogi, you are universally accepted as the authority on all the Puranas. Therefore kindly dispel my confusion.” (SB. 12.8.2-5)

Suta Gosvami replies that hearing about Markandeya “will help remove everyone’s illusion, for it leads to the topics of Lord Narayana, which cleanse away the contamination of this Kali age.” (SB. 12.8.6) Suta begins: Markandeya Rsi worshiped the Supreme Lord (aradha- yan hrsikesam) as he led his perfect student’s life, maintaining his lifelong vow of celibacy (brhad-vrata-dharah). “Lord Brahma, Bhrgu Muni, Lord Siva, Prajapati Daksa, the great sons of Brahma, and many others among the human beings, demigods, forefathers, and ghostly spirits - all were astonished by the achievement of Markandeya Rsi. In this way the mystic Markandeya maintained rigid celibacy through penance, study of the Vedas, and self-discipline. With his mind thus free of all disturbances, he turned it inward and meditated on the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who lies beyond the material senses. While the mystic sage thus concentrated his mind by powerful yoga practice, the tremendous period of six lifetimes of Manu passed by.” (SB. 12.8.12-14)

*Texts 15-31: Indra’s attempt - “Make Markandeya Rsi fall”*

“O brahmana, during the seventh reign of Manu, the current age, Lord Indra came to know of Markandeya’s austerities and became fearful of his growing mystic potency. Thus he tried to impede the sage’s penance. To ruin the sage’s spiritual practice, Lord Indra sent Cupid, beautiful celestial singers, dancing girls, the season of spring, and the sandalwood-scented breeze from the Malaya Hills, along with greed and intoxication personified.... The springtime breeze sent by Lord Indra entered there, carrying cooling drops of spray from nearby waterfalls. Fragrant from the embrace of forest flowers, that breeze entered the hermitage and began evoking the lusty spirit of Cupid.” (SB. 12.8.15-16, 20)

In his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.8.20, Sridhara Svami describes the breeze, which acted like an intoxicant as it passed through the sage’s asrama: “Entering that hermitage, the breeze from the Malaya Hills blew about. Because of passing through the trees, the wind became mild. Because of picking up the cold drops of water from the waterfalls, it became cool, and because of embracing the flowers, it became fragrant.”

Suta Gosvami continues: “While the son of passion \[greed personified\], spring, and the other servants of Indra all tried to agitate Markandeya’s mind, Cupid drew his five-headed arrowand fixed it upon his bow. The Apsara Punjikasthali made a show of playing with a number of toy balls. Her waist seemed weighed down by her heavy breasts, and the wreath of flowers in her hair became disheveled. As she ran about after the balls, glancing here and there, the belt of her thin garment loosened, and suddenly the wind blew her clothes away. Cupid, thinking he had conquered the sage, then shot his arrow. But all these attempts to seduce Markandeya proved futile, just like the useless endeavors of an atheist.” (SB. 12.8.25-27)

Cupid and his followers, however, felt themselves being burned alive by the sage’s potency, for Markandeya did not succumb to any influence born of false ego. Thus Cupid and his followers stopped their mischief “just like children who have aroused a sleeping snake.” (SB. 12.8.29)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains that the beings Indra sent became frightened, thinking, “We do not know what will happen now.” The example of the snake, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti explains, is meant to reveal that when Markandeya Rsi was attacked by Cupid, a little lust was aroused, but the sage became angry before controlling both lust and anger. Seeing this, Cupid and his servants stopped their mischief and withdrew. Indra was astonished to see Cupid powerless in the sage’s presence.

*Texts 32-39: Nara-Narayana Rsi appears before Markandeya Rsi*

“Desiring to bestow His mercy upon the saintly Markandeya, who had perfectly fixed his mind in self-realization through penance, Vedic study, and observance of regulative principles, the Supreme Personality of Godhead personally appeared before the sage in the forms of Nara and Narayana.” (SB. 12.8.32) One of the twins was blackish and the other whitish, and Their eyes resembled the petals of a lotus flower. They held mendicants’ water pots, straight bamboo staffs, and lotus-seed prayer beads. Their hands carried the Vedas in a symbolic form as bundles of darbha grass. They were tall and effulgent, and looked like austerity personified. The foremost of the demigods performed Their worship.

Markandeya Rsi saw them and felt ecstacy. He quickly stood up, but immediately fell to the ground like a stick. Fully satisfied but still overwhelmed, his eyes filled with tears. “Standing with his hands folded in supplication and his head bowed in humility, Markandeya felt such eagerness that he imagined he was embracing the two Lords. In a voice choked with ecstasy, he repeatedly said, ‘I offer You my humble obeisances.’” (SB. 12.8.37) The sage washed Nara-Narayana’s feet and offered Them auspicious items. Again bowing down, He offered prayerful words of welcome.

*Texts 40-49: Markandeya Rsi glorifies Nara-Narayana Rsi*

In ten texts, this greatest of sages, who had assimilated all the Vedic conclusions, speaks his praise of Sri Nara-Narayana Rsi. To help us imbibe the flow of Markandeya Rsi’s words, I will first give a brief overview of his realizations.

Text 40: The Lord is the source of our abilities, but we cannot know Him through those abilities or any of our endeavors. Still, He mercifully becomes the intimate friend of those who worship Him.

Text 41: That same Lord who creates, maintains, and controls all worlds kindly descends to this world in a multitude of forms to offer us the greatest benefit.

Text 42: All those who take shelter of Him remain free of the miseries of material existence. It is not only those who are suffering who take shelter of Him; those who know the essence of Vedic truth also long for His association.

Text 43, part one: Actually, all living entities, regardless of their qualification, need His shelter, because all beings fear the unstoppable, crushing time.

Text 43, part two: His lotus feet alone are in fact the only remedy for material existence.

Text 44: Understanding all this, Markandeya Rsi rejects all other shelters and worships the Lord’s lotus feet.

Texts 45-46: To successfully worship the Lord, one must act in the mode of goodness and avoid passion anti ignorance.

Text 47: Markandeya Rsi bows to Lord Nara-Narayana Rsi and offers his obeisances ...

Text 48: ... accepting that He can only be known through the Vedic literature.

Text 49: Even then, Markandeya explains, the Lord is known only with difficulty, because maya covers, conditions, and controls the pure soul.

**Markandeya Rsi’s Prayers to Lord Nara-Narayana Rsi**

*Text 40: It is impossible to fully glorify the Lord*

Sri Markandeya thinks himself incapable of adequately describing his Lord, for the one who stood before him was He from whom Markan- deya’s power to speak has emanated. Nevertheless, Markandeya Rsi prays: “O Almighty Lord, how can I possibly describe You? You awaken the vital air, which then impels the mind, senses, and power of speech to act. This is true for all ordinary conditioned souls and even for great demigods like Brahma and Siva… Nevertheless, You be come the intimate friend of those who worship You.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura brings out the remarkably loving characteristics of the Supreme Lord embedded in Markandeya Rsi’s descriptive words: “You enliven the senses not only of ordinary beings like me but also of Brahma and Siva. Like a friend, You are controlled by the love of those who worship You. Yet although You alone enable them to worship You by enlivening their minds and senses, You nevertheless feel unable to repay the debt of their worship and become indebted to and controlled by their love. That is most astonishing. That is the greatness of Your mercy.”

*Text 41: The Lord creates, maintains, and destroys the three worlds*

The sage continues: “O Supreme Personality of Godhead, these two personal forms of Yours have appeared to bestow the ultimate benefit for the three worlds — the cessation of material misery and the conquest of death. My Lord, although You create this universe and then assume many transcendental forms to protect it, You also swallow it up, just like a spider who spins and later withdraws its web.” (SB. 12.8.41)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura adds to Markandeya Rsi’s words: “You appear in this world to allow us to worship You and to let Yourself be controlled by the prema of Your mature bhaktas. But this is not the only reason You appear. You also come to protect the universe... Just as you assume various other forms, such as Matsya and Kurma, You have now appeared in these two forms \[of Nara-Narayana Rsi\].”

*Text 42, Part one: Achieving His shelter is fortunate*

The sage continues: “Because You are the protector and the supreme controller of all moving and nonmoving beings, anyone who takes shelter of Your lotus feet can never be touched by the contamination of material work, material qualities, or time.”

In his comment on text 42, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura discusses the unique potency of the shelter of Krsna’s lotus feet: “The contamination of bad conduct arising from karma, the gunas, and time do not touch the devotees who are situated at Your feet. This expresses the greatness of bhakti. Actions, pious or sinful, recent or ancient, do not touch such devotees, just as water does not touch the leaf of a lotus.”

Will only the ignorant and weak turn to the Lord for shelter to free themselves from the contaminations of their previous karma, qualities, and time? No, the sage insists, even the most scholarly, accomplished sages need the Lord’s shelter, because the material energy is ferociously powerful - far beyond the ability of any soul, regardless of his or her qualification, to overcome.

*Text 42, Part two: The Lord is the object of prayer for those who know the essence of the Vedas*

“Great sages who have assimilated the essential meaning of the Vedas offer their prayers to You.” (SB. 12.8.42)

The Vedic literature, with its various texts, different schools, and points of view, ultimately calls one to pray and surrender to the Supreme Personality of Godhead and to beg for His shelter. That act of prayerful surrender to the Lord is the essence of the Vedic teachings. After attaining shelter, what do the great sages desire?Dialogue Nine: Concluding the Srimad-Bhagavatam 509

*Text 42, Part three: The knowers of the Vedas long to attain His association*

Powerful Markandeya Rsi continues: “To gain Your association, they bow down to You at every opportunity and constantly worship You and meditate upon You.” (SB. 12.8.42)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments that the devotees, who are always silent and who know the conclusion of the Vedas, meditate on the Lord to attain Him. Thus the greatest of sages engage in the processes of bhakti with no purpose other than to remain in the Supreme Lord’s association.

In his comment on text 42, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura speaks of the potent prayers offered hy those who have assimilated the Vedic message: “When mundane perception holds sway over the contaminated mind of an individual, even if he is a so-called self- controlled sage, he cannot claim to have knowledge of the Vedas. But when one transcends the identity of being a mundane knower, it becomes possible on the platform of transcendental knowledge for him to engage in offering praise to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, bowing down to Him, worshiping Him, and meditating on Him. At that time the devotee gains intimacy with the Absolute Truth and is no longer subject to the disturbances of material propensities or the modes of nature. Nor do the material qualities of being shaken by time and temporality touch him.”

*Text 43, Part one: Material existence is dangerous*

Markandeya continues to describe material existence, which he knows is filled with fear: what to speak of ordinary conditioned souls, even the extraordinary Lord Brahma fears the passage of time. Every conditioned soul encounters “fearful dangers at every step of their lives.”

*Text 43, Part two: The Lord’s feet are the only remedy for material existence*

He then prescribes the only remedy: “I do not know of any relief from this fear except shelter at Your lotus feet, which are the very form of liberation.”

In his comment Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura underscores the sole cause of fearlessness: “Apart from the attainment of the lotus feet of the Personality of Godhead, all other things are incapable of bestowing auspiciousness. Lord Brahma’s entire life is spent at the lotus feet of the Personality of Godhead. Who can doubt, then, that all the created 1 iv- ing beings subordinate to Brahma are always fearful on account of the force of time? Apart from remembrance of Your lotus feet, there is no other means for them to gain fearlessness.”

*Text 44, Part one: The rsi worships the Lord’s feet, recognizing Them as his shelter*

Understanding this, Markandeya Rsi expresses his clear path of action: “Therefore I worship Your lotus feet, having renounced my identification with the material body and everything else that covers my true self.” He thus rejects the insubstantial shelters maya offers and accepts the full shelter of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the all-inclusive Absolute Truth. Serving Him is the only way to fully satisfy the soul.

*Text 44, Part two: The rsi rejects all shelters other than the Lord*

“These useless, insubstantial, and temporary coverings are merely presumed to be separate from You, whose intelligence encompasses all truth. By attaining You - the Supreme Godhead and the master of the soul - one attains everything desirable.”

*Text 45: The mode of goodness is acceptable for those who desire liberation*

Markandeya next describes the processes of bondage, liberation, and ultimate attainment: although the Lord accepts the three modes of nature for the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world, He uses goodness to liberate souls. The lower modes simply bring suffering and fear.

*Text 46: But the truly intelligent worship the Lord’s form in pure, transcendental goodness*

Although goodness is glorified for its ability to award liberation, the sage Markandeya Rsi further glorifies a state of goodness that is purer and still more transcendental: “O Lord, because fearlessness, spiritual happiness, and the kingdom of God are all achieved through the mode of pure goodness, Your devotees consider this mode, but never passion and ignorance, to be a direct manifestation of You, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Intelligent persons thus worship Your beloved transcendental form, composed of pure goodness, along with the spiritual forms of Your pure devotees.” (SB. 12.8.46)

Earlier in the Bhagavatam (2.9.10), Sukadeva Gosvami describes pure goodness in a similar way when he speaks of the nonmaterial nature of Vaikuntha: “In that personal abode of the Lord, the material modes of ignorance and passion do not prevail, nor is there any of their influence in goodness. There is no predominance of the influence of time, so what to speak of the illusory, external energy; it cannot enter that region. Without discrimination, both the demigods and the demons worship the Lord as devotees.”

Only pure, spiritual goodness is suitable for worshiping the Lord. This mode is superior to the material mode of goodness, which is easily mixed with passion and ignorance. One in pure goodness attains fearless, spiritual happiness, and the kingdom of God. Pure goodness is directly manifest from the Lord. The Lord’s form, which is nonmaterial, is composed of it. Therefore intelligent souls worship His form as well as the forms of His pure devotees.

*Text 47: Markandeya Rsi offers obeisances to the Lord*

Markandeya Rsi, the greatest of sages, prostrates himself in obeisance before Lord Nara-Narayana Rsi, who is “the all-pervading and all-inclusive form of the universe, as well as its spiritual master.” The sage continues: “I bow down to Lord Narayana, the supremely worshipable Deity appearing as a sage, and also to the saintly Nara, the best of human beings, who is fixed in perfect goodness, fully in control of his speech, and the propagator of the Vedic literatures.”

*Texts 48-49: The Lord can be known only through Vedic knowledge, and even then only with difficulty*

Can an ordinary person understand what this great sage has realized? Markandeya admits that materialists cannot recognize the Lord; rather, I Ic can only he known through the knowledge presented in the Vedic literature. We cannot understand or reach Him through speculation, because He is beyond anything that can be approached empirically through the mundane senses. This longest-living of sages now con- eludes his prayers with vande maha-purusam atma-nigudha-bodham: I offer homage to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who “is hidden by the bodily designations covering a conditioned soul’s spiritual identity.” (SB. 12.8.49)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains that although the Lord may be known through the Vedic scriptures, He is nevertheless difficult to understand. Even those who study the Vedas - even the best of such students, Lord Brahma - are bewildered by the Lord’s nature. Why? Because the Vedas speak indirectly, and Vedic scholars fail to fathom the Lord’s deep nature, although He is the only object of knowledge.

Why are they bewildered? Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura answers this question in his final comment on this chapter: “The Vedic literature reveals the personal identity (svarupa) of the Supreme Lord, which is very difficult to understand. In the matter of this revelation, the great scholars headed by Brahma, even after making great endeavor, remain unable to see the Lord’s original form. The reason for this is that they are bewildered by empirical thought processes. But persons whose intelligence has entered perfectly into the subject matter of the self understand how He is to be perceived and engage in offering homage to the Supreme Lord, the maha-purusa. Persons attached to the ideas of the atheistic philosophical doctrines of Sankhya, and so on, are unable to perceive the maha-purusa, whose transcendental nature is contrary to their conceptions of duality. Falsely identifying oneself as the performer of the various activities born of the material nature by her three modes subjects the spirit soul to bewilderment. He then encounters confusion, and the mistaken ideas he gets about the manifestation and non-manifestation of the Lord of Vaikuntha turn him into a nirvisesavadi, an impersonalist.”

**Chapter 9: Markandeya Rsi Experiences the Lord’s Illusory Potency**

In his prayers, Markandeya Rsi spoke about fear and the cause of fear, inevitable, relentless time, and the necessity of surrender. He also spoke of what we can conclude after poring through the entire Vedic literature. Now Nara-Narayana Rsi responds.

*Text 1-3: Nara-Narayana Rsi asks Markandeya Rsi to choose a benediction*

Intelligent Markandeya’s sweet words satisfied Nara-Narayana Rsi, who praised the sage as the best of learned brahmanas. Sri Nara-Narayana Rsi recognized that Markandeya Rsi was fixed in meditation on the Supreme Lord, with his consciousness focused on Him in devotional service and without distraction. Markandeya Rsi was also austere, studious in his approach to the Vedic literature, and firm in his adherence to the regulative principles that govern spiritual life.

After acknowledging Markandeya’s exalted qualifications, Nara- Narayana Rsi said: “We are perfectly satisfied with your practice of lifelong celibacy. Please choose whatever benediction you desire, since I can grant your wish. May you enjoy all good fortune.” (SB. 12.9.3)

The BBT purport refers to Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on this text: “\[T\]he Lord used the plural form in the beginning of this verse - ‘We are satisfied’ - because He was referring to Himself along with Siva and Uma, who Markandeya will later glorify. The Lord then used the singular - ‘I am the bestower of benedictions’ - because ultimately only Lord Narayana (Krsna) can award the highest perfection of life, eternal Krsna consciousness.”

*Texts 4-7: Markandeya makes a unique request*

In his reply, Markandeya first glorifies Nara-Narayana Rsi: “O Lord of lords, all glories to You! O Lord Acyuta, You remove all distress for the devotees who surrender unto You. That you have allowed me to see You is all the benediction I want.” (SB. 12.9.4)

He also acknowledges the fortune the Lord has already bestowed on him: “Such demigods as Lord Brahma achieved their exalted positions simply by seeing Your beautiful lotus feet after their minds had become mature in yoga practice. And now, my Lord, You have personally appeared before me.” (SB. 12.9.5)

Markandeya Rsi appreciates that the Lord’s appearance before him is a superior blessing even to the blessing He offered Lord Brahma. Yet this longest-living sage has retained a desire, which now blossoms from bis mouth in the form of a request: “O lotus-eyed Lord, O crest jewel of renowned personalities, although I am satisfied simply by seeing You, I do wish to see Your illusory potency, by whose influence the entire world, together with its ruling demigods, considers reality to be materially variegated.” (SB. 12.9.6)

The BBT purport to text 6 explains the root of Markandeya’s curiosity: “Markandeya Rsi is curious to witness the exact process by which maya, the Lord’s bewildering potency, casts living beings into illusion.” The Supreme Lord will satisfy Him. He smiles and utters, “Tatheti,” “So be it,” and leaves for His hermitage at Badarikasrama.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura speaks deeply about this text as he explains the mysterious reason for the Lord’s smile as He grants Markandeya Rsi’s request. “\[Nara-Narayana Rsi thought:\] Seeing maya can only cause grief. But if you want it, I will fulfill your desire. You yourself must realize that you do not like the experience of maya. Otherwise your desire for it will not go away. Therefore by experiencing its suffering you will give it up. It is like a father who permits his son to perform some action the stubborn son insists on performing. The father knows the act will cause his child to suffer, but the only way to get the child to give up his desire is to allow him to experience the pain that comes with it. Similarly, the Lord permits His devotee Markandeya Rsi to suffer. But later, to award him bliss, the Lord will also show the sage His form as a baby. This is the reason the Lord smiled.”

*Texts 8-19: Markandeya Rsi’s experience of the Lord’s maya*

As the great devotee Markandeya Rsi waited in his asrama for his desire to be fulfilled, he continued his constant meditation “upon the Lord within fire, the sun, the moon, water, the earth, air, lightning, and his own heart and worshiping Him with paraphernalia conceived in his mind. But sometimes, overwhelmed by waves of love for the Lord, Markandeya would forget to perform his regular worship.” (SB. 12.9.8-9)

One day, as the sage was performing his evening worship on the bank of the river, a powerful wind arose. “That wind created a terrible sound and brought in its wake fearsome clouds that were accompanied by lightning and roaring thunder and that poured down on all sides torrents of rain as heavy as wagon wheels. Then the four great oceans appeared on all sides, swallowing up the surface of the earth with their wind-tossed waves. In these oceans were terrible sea monsters, fearful whirlpools, and ominous rumblings. The sage saw all the inhabitants of the universe, including himself, tormented within and without by the harsh winds, the bolts of lightning, and the great waves rising beyond the sky. As the whole earth flooded, he grew perplexed and fearful.” (SB. 12.9.11-13)

The rains continued and the ocean, its “waters violently whipped into terrifying waves by hurricanes, covered up all the earth’s islands, mountains, and continents. The water inundated the earth, outer space, heaven, and the celestial region. Indeed, the entire expanse of the universe was flooded in all directions, and out of all its inhabitants only Markandeya remained. His matted hair scattered, the great sage wandered about alone in the water as if dumb and blind.” (SB. 12.9.14-15)

Suffering, tired, tortured, hungry, attacked by monsters, and tormented by thirst, Markandeya Rsi remained alone, aimlessly adrift in the infinite darkness of these turbulent waters. “As he grew increasingly exhausted, he lost all sense of direction and could not tell the sky from the earth.... Sometimes he felt lamentation, bewilderment, misery, happiness, or fear, and at other times he experienced such terrible illness and pain that he felt himself dying. Countless millions of years passed as Markandeya wandered about in that deluge, his mind bewildered by the illusory energy of Lord Visnu, the Supreme Personality of Godhead.” (SB. 12.9.16, 18-19)

*Texts 20-34: Markandeya Rsi sees Krsna as a small child*

As the rsi was wandering lost on the unending waters, he at last saw a small island on which a young banyan tree stood, its limbs filled with flowers and fruits. On that tree’s northeast portion, the Supreme Personality of Godhead lay upon a leaf. His effulgence swallowed the darkness.

*Texts 22-25: The Lord’s beauty*

“The infant’s dark-blue complexion was the color of a flawless emerald, His lotus face shone with a wealth of beauty, and His throat bore marks like the lines on a conch shell. He had a broad chest, a finely shaped nose, beautiful eyebrows, and lovely ears that resembled pomegranate flowers and that had inner folds like a conch shell’s spirals. The corners of His eyes were reddish like the whorl of a lotus, and the effulgence of His coral-like lips slightly reddened the nectarean, enchanting smile on His face. As He breathed, His splendid hair trembled and His deep navel became distorted by the moving folds of skin on His abdomen, which resembled a banyan leaf. The exalted brahmana watched with amazement as the infant took hold of one of His lotus feet with His graceful fingers, placed a toe within His mouth, and began to suck.” (SB. 12.9.22-25)

In his descriptive comments on these texts, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura notes that the baby had pomegranate flowers decorating His ears, whose folds were as beautiful as conches.

*Texts 27-34: Markandeya Rsi approaches the Lord in His form as a baby*

“As Markandeya beheld the child, all his weariness vanished. Indeed, so great was his pleasure that the lotus of his heart, along with his lotus eyes, fully blossomed and the hairs on his body stood on end.” (SB. 12.9.26) The sage approached this extraordinarily wonderful infant to learn who He was, but the child inhaled and the sage was drawn into Him as if he were a mosquito. Inside the child, Markandeya Rsi saw the entire universe - with skies and heavens, the earth, mountains, oceans, forests, rivers, mines, and villages, the Himalaya Mountains and his own hermitage, and the basic elements of creation as well as time itself. They looked real, just as they had before the dissolution. This astonished and perplexed Markandeya. And then the baby exhaled and the sage was thrown from His body and again cast into the ocean of dissolution.

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments on Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.9.33-34: “Again thrown into the ocean, the sage wandered about and experienced hardships for millions of years. Then he again saw the child on the banyan leaf on the upraised portion of the earth, and the child glanced on the sage with a smile endowed with nectarlike prema. Markandeya Rsi then again entered the Lord’s body when He inhaled… Within an instant, seven dissolutions (kalpas) were contracted by the Lord’s inconceivable energy.”

Kalpas later, when Markandeya Rsi again saw the banyan tree growing on the tiny island, with the baby boy lying on a leaf, “the child glanced at him from the corner of His eyes with a smile imbued with the nectar of love, and Markandeya took Him into his heart through his eyes. Greatly agitated, the sage ran to embrace the transcendental Personality of Godhead.” (SB. 12.9.31-32)

But just as the sage rushed forward, Krsna, who is hidden in every- one’s heart, became invisible. The banyan tree, the great water, and everything that signalled the dissolution of the universe suddenly vanished and Markandeya instantly found himself back in his own hermitage, as he had been before.

**Chapter 10: Lord Siva and Uma Glorify Markandeya Rsi**

*Texts 1-2: Markandeya Rsi takes shelter of the Lord*

Suta Gosvami describes Markandeya Rsi’s response to the torture of having experienced the Supreme Lord’s illusory potency: “The Supreme Lord Narayana had arranged this opulent display of His bewildering potency. Markandeya Rsi, having experienced it, took shelter of the Lord.” (SB. 12.10.1)

Writing on this first text of chapter 10, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura compares the function of Krsna’s internal energy, yoga-maya, with His external energy, the unsurpassable maha-maya: “The maya that is separated from the Personality of Godhead is simply the externally expanded potency of yoga-maya, which is created by the Lord Himself. Yoga-maya gives engagements to living entities favorable to serving the Lord, whereas maha-maya, by her powers of throwing and covering, bewilders the living entities who are averse to such service. When maha-maya, the external opulence of yoga-maya, holds sway in the heart of the conditioned soul, it remains impossible for that soul to surrender to the Personality of Godhead. Moreover, Mayadevi manipulates the nonspiritual energy in such a way that she binds up the conditioned soul and makes it impossible for him to take to the process of surrender, which is the first step in becoming the Lord’s servant.”

In Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.10.2, Markandeya expresses the depth of his realization: “O Lord Hari, I take shelter of the soles of Your lotus feet, which bestow fearlessness upon all who surrender to them. Even the great demigods are bewildered by Your illusory energy, which appears to them in the guise of knowledge.”

Great as his own powers were, Markandeya felt completely insignificant when in the grip of the Supreme Lord’s illusory energy, the supreme governess of the prison house of the material realm. Thus the Rsi sought the Supreme Lord’s shelter. Reentering a yogic trance, he meditated on the Personality of Godhead.

*Texts 3—17: Uma and Lord Siva want to give Markandeya Rsi a benediction*

*Texts 3-13: Uma and Lord Siva award Markandeya Rsi their darsana*

Uma and Lord Siva then appeared before Markandeya Rsi to pacify the sage, who was weary after his encounter with the Lord’s illusory potency. Srila Sridhara Svami mentions that it was Lord Narayana Himself who came to the sage in the form of Lord Siva. Lord Siva wanted to bless the sage, but he wondered what was left for the sage to desire after such an ordeal.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura answers this. The sage had no desire, he said - not for the mystic perfections such as anima, and not for liberation. “So,” Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura writes, speaking as Uma, “give him bhakti.” But Lord Siva replies to this: “He has already attained bhakti." And so the two exalted persons descended before Markandeya Rsi to gain his association. “After all,” Lord Siva thinks, “association with saintly devotees is the highest achievement.”

When Uma and her husband arrived, Markandeya Rsi was absorbed in trance and unaware of the presence of such exalted guests. Lord Siva noticed that the sage’s meditation was so profound that he had no awareness of himself or of the external world. Then, by his mystic power, Lord Siva entered Markandeya’s heart. Suddenly, the amazed rsi saw Lord Siva, that same great person who had saved him from death on his sixteenth birthday. Lord Siva’s golden hair resembled lightning, and he “had three eyes, ten arms, and a tall body that shone like the rising sun. He wore a tiger skin, and he carried a trident, a bow, arrows, a sword, and a shield, along with prayer beads, a damaru drum, a skull, and an ax. Astonished, the sage came out of his trance and thought, ‘Who is this, and where has he come from?’” (SB. 12.10.11-13)

*Texts 14—17: Markandeya Rsi welcomes Rudra, Uma, and Rudra’s followers*

“Opening his eyes, the sage saw Lord Rudra, the spiritual master of the three worlds, together with Uma and Rudra’s followers. Markandeya then offered his respectful obeisances by bowing his head.’’ He offered them “words of welcome, sitting places, water for washing their feet, scented drinking water, fragrant oils, flower garlands, and arati lamps.” Overjoyed, the rsi said: “O mighty lord, what can I possibly do for you, who are fully satisfied by your own ecstasy? Indeed, by your mercy you satisfy this entire world. Again and again I offer my obeisances unto you, O all-auspicious transcendental personality. As the lord of goodness you give pleasure, in contact with the mode of passion you appear most fearful, and you also associate with the mode of ignorance.” (SB. 12.10.14-17)

*Texts 18—27: Lord Siva replies — the glory of pure souls*

*Texts 18-19: “Please ask me for a benediction”*

The sage’s heartfelt greeting satisfied Lord Siva, the foremost demigod and the shelter of saintly devotees. In reply Lord Siva spoke of the purifying effect of simply seeing a brahmana like Markandeya. Lord Siva’s sweet words erased the suffering the sage was feeling after his trial in the waters of devastation. Finally, Lord Siva asked Markandeya Rsi to ask of him anything he desired: “Please ask me for some benediction, since among all givers of benedictions, we three - Brahma, Visnu, and I - are the best. Seeing us never goes in vain, because simply by seeing us a mortal achieves immortality.” (SB. 12.10.19)

*Texts 20-22: The glory of the saintly*

Lord Siva goes on to glorify the saintly brahmanas: “The inhabitants and ruling demigods of all planets, along with Lord Brahma, the Supreme Lord Hari, and I, glorify, worship, and assist those brahmanas who are saintly, always peaceful, free of material attachment, compassionate to all living beings, purely devoted to us, devoid of hatred, and endowed with equal vision.” (SB. 12.10.20-21)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura speaks on behalf of Lord Siva of the respect Siva and the other devatas have for those who are pure, like Markandeya Rsi: “The devatas worship those brahmanas who purely worship us - and not only the devatas worship such brahmanas, but I worship those brahmanas too.”

Lord Siva next speaks of the sage’s exalted vision, which is beyond material duality. Such consciousness, Lord Siva says, makes him worshipahle, for he sees Visnu, Brahma, Siva, himself, and all others in relation to the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

*Texts 23-25: The purifying power of the saintly*

Lord Siva then speaks of the immense purifying potency possessed by pure souls: “Mere bodies of water do not constitute holy places, nor are lifeless statues of the demigods actual worshipable deities. Because external vision fails to appreciate the higher essence of the holy rivers and the demigods, these purify only after a considerable time. But devotees like you purify immediately, just by being seen.” (SB. 12.10.23)

Srila Narottama dasa Thakura expands on Lord Siva’s words as he too reverently glorifies saintly Vaisnavas: “O Vaisnava Gosvami, please be merciful to me now. There is no one except you who can purify the fallen souls. Where can anyone find such a merciful personality, whose mere audience sends all sins far away? One becomes purified after bathing in the waters of the sacred Ganges many times, but just the sight of you purifies the fallen souls. This is your great power. The holy name delivers one who has offended Lord Hari, but deliverance is impossible if one offends you. Your heart is always the resting place of Lord Govinda, and Lord Govinda says, ‘The Vaisnavas are in My heart.’ I desire to have the dust of your holy feet in every birth I may take. Please consider Narottama yours, and be kind to him.”

Why do brahmanas have such tremendous purity? Lord Siva answers in Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.10.24: because brahmanas hold the three Vedas within themselves - and it is their willingness to practice austerity and lead a regulated life, as well as their study of the Vedas, that allows them to carry the essence of the Vedas within themselves. All-auspicious Lord Siva therefore offers these pure brahmanas his obeisances and then sums up the power of their brahminical purity: “Even the worst sinners and social outcastes are purified just by hearing about or seeing personalities like you. Imagine, then, how purified they become by directly speaking with you.” (SB. 12.10.25)

Lord Krsna also spoke this truth (SB. 10.84.11, 13) when He saw the powerful brahmana sages at Kuruksetra:

Mere bodies of water are not the real sacred places of pilgrimage, nor are mere images of earth and stone the true worshipable deities. These purify one only after a long time, but saintly sages purify one immediately upon being seen… One who identifies his self as the inert body composed of mucus, bile, and air, who assumes his wife and family are permanently his own, who thinks an earthen image or the land of his birth is worshipable, or who sees a place of pilgrimage as merely the water there, but who never identifies himself with, feels kinship with, worships, or even visits those who are wise in spiritual truth - such a person is no better than a cow or an ass.

*Texts 26-34: Markandeya Rsi’s requests*

*Texts 26-32: The Rsi’s amazement*

Suta Gosvami describes the deep satisfaction Markandeya Rsi felt on hearing Lord Siva’s sweet words. But Markandeya also expresses puzzlement. He says that the actions of the universal controllers are difficult to understand, because an object of his own worship, Lord Siva, was bowing down to him and praising the very being he rules. Why would such an exalted being exhibit this behavior?

Markandeya Rsi answers his own question in Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.10.29. Generally, he says, the behavior of great souls is meant to induce “embodied souls to accept religious principles... the authorized teachers of religion exhibit ideal behavior while encouraging and praising the proper behavior of others.” This exhibition of humility by the Supreme Lord and His associates, the sage continues, is therefore simply their mercy. Such behavior lessens neither their position nor their power “any more than a magician’s powers are diminished by his exhibition of tricks.” (SB. 12.10.30)

In commenting on Lord Siva’s respecting someone under his control, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura’s words are both sobering and thought-provoking: “When the various controllers of the universe offer obeisances and praise to the controlled individuals who are in the role of their disciples, this is those controllers’ pastimes. Ordinary persons cannot understand such topics. Normally, foolish persons who hanker after the position of guru and presume to be themselves great controllers give themselves the title ‘spiritual master,’ and taking their disciples to be their servants, falsely think of themselves as the enjoyers. But the mentality of enjoyment can never overtake either a properly learned guru or the real controllers of this universe. Ordinary conditioned souls, devoted to their belly anti genitals, cannot understand any of this. Living beings who are actually meant to be controlled and subservient to the spiritual master’s orders think themselves guru, or isvara. Because of this they can never achieve liberation from material life, and it becomes impossible for such persons to enter into the pastimes \[of the real gurus and isvaras\].”

Next, Markandeya Rsi speaks of the unparalleled position of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. He begins by offering his obeisances to that Lord, who creates the universe and maintains it as the Supersoul. He creates the world through the modes of nature, yet remains pure, aloof, and unequaled. “He is the supreme spiritual master of all, the original personal form of the Absolute Truth.” (SB. 12.10.32)

*Texts 33-34: Markandeya Rsi’s request*

Recalling that Lord Siva invited him to ask for a benediction (SB. 12.10.19), the sage answers in the same way he replied to Nara-Narayana Rsi (SB. 12.9.4-5): “O all-pervading lord, since I have received the benediction of seeing you, what other benediction can I ask for? Simply by seeing you, a person fulfills all his desires and can achieve anything imaginable.” (SB. 12.10.33)

“But,” the sage continues, and after his fateful words in reply to Nara-Narayana Rsi in Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.9.6,we almost hold our breath to hear what will follow: “I do request one benediction from you, who are full of all perfection and able to shower down the fulfillment of all desires. I ask to have unfailing devotion for the Supreme Personality of Godhead and for His dedicated devotees, especially you.” (SB. 12.10.33-34)

His curiosity already satisfied about the vastness of the material energy, he instead asks Lord Siva for unfailing devotion to the Supreme Personality of Godhead and unfailing devotion to the Lord’s devotees.

This is similar to what Maharaja Pariksit asked after he was cursed. Although he could have chosen any blessing from the sages who assembled with him on the bank of the river, including to be saved from the snake-bird’s bite, he humbly asked for something that would award him eternal benefit: “Again, offering obeisances unto all you brahmanas, I pray that if I should again take my birth in the material world I will have complete attachment to the unlimited Lord Krsna, association with His devotees, and friendly relations with all living beings.” (SB. 1.19.16) The king didn’t even ask the brahmana sages for freedom from material existence. Rather, if he was to take birth again, he prayed to have complete attachment to the unlimited Lord Krsna, association with His devotees, and friendly relationships with all living beings.

A third example from sastra makes the presentation of what is to be most desired conclusive. When Krsna entered Mathura, the garland-maker Sudama satisfied the Lord with his sincere offering of especially beautiful and fragrant flower garlands. In response, Krsna offered him any blessing he desired. Sudama asked for “unshakable devotion for Krsna, the Supreme Soul of all existence, friendship with His devotees, and transcendental compassion for all living beings.” (SB. 10.41.51)

Had Markandeya Rsi not been such a recluse, he too may have added the third and parallel request: compassion for all living beings. So whether one has seven days to live like Maharaja Pariksit or countless eons like Markandeya Rsi, or even if the Supreme Personality of Godhead comes and stands directly before us as He did before Sudama, we can follow these three great devotees who demonstrated with remarkable consistency the most excellent blessings a devotee can cherish if his or her prayers are to be fulfilled. From these special aspirations - fixed devotion to Krsna, association with devotees, and compassion for all souls - all further spiritual development naturally and spontaneously develops.

This wisdom of the most long-lived and worshipable Markandeya Rsi, spoken both at the beginning of the Bhagavatam by Maharaja Pariksit and at its end by Markandeya Rsi, are the essential desires readers of Srimad-Bhagavatam should imbibe.

*Texts 35-37: Lord Siva offers the sage his desired benediction*

Lord Siva, encouraged by Goddess Uma, granted Markandeya Rsi’s request. Because you are a devout bhakta of Lord Adhoksaja, he said, all your desires will be fulfilled. Lord Siva then added further blessings: “Until the very end of this creation cycle, you will enjoy pious fame and freedom from old age and death.” And “may you have perfect knowledge of past, present, and future, along with transcendental realization of the Supreme, enriched by renunciation. You have the brilliance of an ideal brahmana, and thus may you achieve the post of spiritual master of the Puranas.” (SB. 12.10.36, 37)

*Texts 38-41: The end of the pastime*

“Suta Gosvami said: Having thus granted Markandeya Rsi benedictions, Lord Siva went on his way, continuing to describe to goddess Devi the accomplishments of the sage and the direct exhibition of the Lord’s illusory power that he had experienced.” (SB. 12.10.38)

Markandeya Rsi, glorious and perfect in mystic yoga, still travels this world, a pure devotee absorbed in the devotional service of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Suta Gosvami has now completed narrating the pastimes of the highly intelligent Markandeya Rsi and his experience of the Supreme Lord’s illusory energy.

In his comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.10.41, Srila Jiva Gosvami notes that the maya Markandeya Rsi experienced was a creation of the Supreme Soul, the Personality of Godhead, and was merely an expansion of illusion created in response to the sage’s request.

How inescapably powerful is the Supreme Lord’s illusory energy! The BBT purport to text 41 speaks of the need to accept Markandeya Rsi’s unique experience as something that actually happened and not as an allegorical event: “Markandeya’s being drawn into the Lord’s body by His inhalation and expelled again by His exhalation should not be considered a symbolic description of the perennial cycles of material creation and annihilation. This portion of the Srimad-Bhagavatam describes a real, historical event experienced by a great devotee of the Lord.”

*Text 42: Phala-sruti*

Suta Gosvami summarizes: This pastime illustrates “the transcendental potency of the Supreme Lord.” The great sage then offers a blessing: “Anyone who properly narrates or hears it will never again undergo material existence, which is based on the desire to perform fruitive activities.” (SB. 12.10.42)

Hearing of Markandeya Rsi’s torturous experience of the Lord’s illusory energy will char a conditioned soul’s tendency to see the material existence in a romantic way: as a field in which to gather for his own enjoyment the colorful flowers grown in the soil of his own fruitive acts.

**Markandeya Rsi and Yajnavalkya’s conclusion**

The summary of the evolution of the Vedic literature included prayers spoken by Yajnavalkya (SB.12.6.67-72). These prayers expressed our dependence on the sun for our existence and indicated that Krsna is the ultimate source of the sun’s power. We too are dependent on the sun for our existence and are therefore also dependent on Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Thus Yajnavalkya’s prayers at the beginning of this dialogue establish the Supersoul as the Lord on whom all beings depend. Markandeya Rsi develops this concept by expressing his desire to forever remain devoted to the Lord’s service. Throughout its pages, the Srimad-Bhagavatam has expressed and developed this core message, and it is also the essential message of the Vedic literature. This same message will especially be emphasized in the Srimad-Bhagavatam’s final chapters.

**Chapter 11: Summary Description of the maha-purusa**

*Texts 1-3: Saunaka Rsi inquires further about the Vedic literature*

Continuing the theme of establishing the conclusions churned from the vast ocean of the Vedic literature, Saunaka Rsi now asks Suta Gosvami about the tantric scriptures, which are usually linked to the Atharva Veda and contain mystical prescriptions for performing ritualistic worship. Through his inquiry, we will hear of the perfection of the tantric path.

In addition, the sage asks about the “the process of kriya-yoga practiced through regulated worship of the transcendental Lord, the husband of the goddess of fortune. Please also explain how the Lord’s devotees conceive of His limbs, associates, weapons, and ornaments in terms of particular material representations. By expertly worshiping the Supreme Lord, a mortal can attain immortality.’’ (SB. 12.11.2-3)

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura tells us in his comments on texts 1 through 3 that Markandeya Rsi was expert in tantrika worship and had seen the Lord through this worship. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti also indicates that followers of the tantrika path think of the limbs of Visnu and Laksmi as they view the Lord’s opulences in the material world. Thus, the acarya explains, Suta Gosvami will describe the tantrika process of worshiping the maha-purusa, the opulence of the Lord’s major limbs (His feet and so on) and minor limbs (Garuda and others), along with an enumeration of the sun’s different explanations.

*Texts 4-26: The maha-purusa*

*Texts 4-22: Suta Gosvami describes the viraprupa*

Suta Gosvami begins by offering his obeisances to his spiritual master, for he wishes Sukadeva Gosvami to bless him with the ability to correctly understand the meaning of what he has heard. He then describes how the Supreme Lord’s universal form (virat) is generated. This description includes the transformation of the elements of creation, beginning from the unmanifest. When this form becomes conscious, one can see the three planetary systems within it.In a description similar to one given in the first chapter of the Second Canto, Suta Gosvami describes seventeen objects in the universe - those that can be observed (for example, the earth, sky, sun, and moon) and those that can be noticed (for example, greed, delusion, shame, and death), and how they are related to the Supreme Lord’s universal form - moonshine is His teeth and delusion His smile, for example.

The Lord’s universal form is not His actual, eternal form; rather, it is a subtle material form composed of His external energy. The manifestation of the universal form is also described in chapters 5 and 6 of the Second Canto, and again in chapters 5 and 6 of the Third Canto. The BBT purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.11.6-8 notes that the various aspects of material creation, such as the earth, sun, trees, etc., rest on and are sustained by the Lord’s universal body. By comparing aspects of the universe to the Lord’s form, even a materialist can see everything that exists within the planetary systems and know something about God.

But we are so near the end of Srimad-Bhagavatam, and it is neither Saunaka Rsi’s nor Suta Gosvami’s desire to train those who are listening to their narration to see the Lord in matter. Rather, they want to serve the Vedic literature, and, like Sukadeva Gosvami in the Second Canto, carry their listeners from matter to Vaikunthanatha, Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Ultimately, they want to take us to Vraja-Krsna, the beautiful son of Yasoda Mata and Nanda Maharaja. To achieve this end, in this chapter so close to the Bhagavatam’s concluding texts, Suta Gosvami describes the Lord’s universal form while explaining prominent aspects of the creation in relationship to the Lord’s Vrndavana form and its exquisite features and opulences (vibhutis).

His descriptions of these thirty-eight opulences are poetic. I will list some of them here.

Text 10, opulences 1 and 2: The Kaustubha gem on the Lord’s chest represents the pure spirit soul. His Srivatsa mark is the “direct manifestation of this gem’s expansive effulgence.”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains that the effulgence of the Kaustubha, which spreads everywhere, is Srivatsa, a fine curl of white hair whorled clockwise on the Lord’s right upper chest. This supports His opulence known as dharma. Although not mentioned, on the left side of His chest is the LaksmI-rekha, a golden line similar to the line made on a gold-testing stone when real gold is rubbed on it. This supports His opulence of royalty.

Texts 11-12, opulences 3 through 7: His flower garland is His material energy, comprising the various combinations of the modes of nature. His yellow garment is the Vedic meters and His sacred thread the syllable orh, composed of three sounds. The Lord wears the processes of Sarikhya and yoga as His two shark-shaped earrings. The supreme position of Brahmaloka is His crown, which bestows fearlessness on the inhabitants of all worlds.

In this way, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains, these aspects of the Lord’s decoration correlate with His opulences in this world.

Text 13, opulences 8 and 9: Ananta, the Lord’s sitting place, is the un- manifest phase of material nature. The Lord’s lotus throne is the mode of goodness, which is endowed with religion and knowledge.

Texts 14-15, opulences 10 through 16: The Lord’s club is the chief element, prana, which awards sensory, mental, and physical strength. His excellent conch shell is the element water. His Sudarsana disc is the element fire. His sword, pure as the sky, is the element ether. His shield embodies the mode of ignorance. His bow, Sarriga, embodies time. His arrow-filled quiver embodies the working sensory organs.

Text 16, opulences 17-20: His arrows are said to be the senses. His chariot is the active, forceful mind. His external appearance is the subtle objects of perception. The gestures of His hands are the essence of all purposeful activity.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains that the hand gestures (mudras) He uses to give benedictions and bestow fearlessness support His purposeful actions. The BBT purport presents the essence of “purposeful activities”: “All activity is ultimately aimed at the supreme perfection of life, and this perfection is awarded by the merciful hands of the Lord. The gestures of the Lord remove all fear from the heart of a devotee and elevate him to the Lord’s own association in the spiritual sky.”

Text 17, opulences 21 through 23: The sun is the place in which the Supreme Lord is worshiped.Spiritual initiation purifies the soul, and rendering Him service in devotion eradicates all sins, so both are His opulences.

Text 18, opulences 24 and 25: The Lord playfully carries a lotus, which represents the various opulences designated by the word bhaga. The Supreme Lord accepts service from a pair of camara fans, which represent the opulences of religion and fame.

Text 19, opulences 26 and 27: The Lord’s umbrella is His spiritual abode, Vaikuntha, where there is no fear. According to Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, “Whatever small amount of fearlessness one sees in this world is the opulence of the Lord’s umbrella.”

Garuda, who carries the Lord of sacrifice on his back, is the threefold Veda. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains that Garuda is “the performance of sacrifice explained in the three Vedas - Rg, Yajur, and Sama.”

Text 20, opulences 28 through 30: The goddess of fortune, Sri, who never leaves the Lord’s side, appears with Him in this world and represents His internal potency (hladinTsakti). In his comment on text 20, Srila Jiva Gosvami provides us with a vision that connects the material energy to Sri, the goddess of fortune: “That internal energy of the Lord, who has unlimited functions, appears personified in this world as Laksmi, who is present on the left side of the Lord’s body \[chest\]. In other words, one should think that opulence, the goddess of fortune, who is directly the supreme internal energy of the Lord Himself, is herself also present as the opulence of this world.”

Srila Jiva also cites the Visnu Purana (1.9.140) to illustrate the fully transcendental nature of the goddess of fortune, who is forever by Lord Visnu’s side: “Thus in the same way as the Lord of the universe, the God of gods, Janardana, descends into this world, so does His consort, the goddess of fortune. That she is purely spiritual is described in the Skanda Purana: ‘The inferior infallible entity is that nature who manifests as the material world. The goddess of fortune, on the other hand, is of the superior nature, is pure consciousness, and is under the direct shelter of Lord Visnu. She is said to be the superior infallible. The infallible who is superior even to the superior is Lord Hari Himself, the original possessor of all transcendental qualities.’”

Text 20 continues with opulences 29 and 30: Visvaksena, the chief among the Lord’s personal associates, is known to be the personification of the Pancaratra and other tantras. The Lord’s eight doorkeepers, headed by Nanda, are His mystic perfections, beginning with anima.

Texts 21—22, opulences 31 through 38: Vasudeva, Sankarsana, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are the names of the direct personal expansions of the Supreme Godhead. One can also conceive of Him in four divisions of consciousness: wakefulness, sleep, deep sleep, and pure knowledge.

In texts 21-22, Suta Gosvami first lists the Lord’s expansions followed by Their manifestation of the four states of existence. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura connects the specific elements of both: Vasudeva represents the waking state, Sankarsana dreaming, Pradyumna deep sleep, and Aniruddha the fourth state, knowledge.

*Texts 23—26: The maha-purusa — nearing the conclusion*

It is the Supreme Lord, the master of all four states of conciousness, appearing with His fully transcendental features, weapons, and ornaments, who removes the suffering of all who worship Him. Suta Gosvami has now listed the Lord’s opulences in connection with the features of the material world just to inspire us to worship Him, for our own benefit and to remove the suffering all conditioned souls experience. “He alone is the self-luminous, original source of the Vedas, perfect and complete in His own glory. By His material energy He creates, destroys, and maintains this entire universe. Because He is the performer of various material functions, He is sometimes described as materially divided, yet He always remains transcendentally situated in pure knowledge. Those who are dedicated to Him in devotion can realize Him to be their true Soul.” (SB. 12.11.24)

Suta Gosvami recognizes the Lord’s manifestions in matter as “divided,” but the Lord Himself is one complete whole and a person. The BBT purport quotes Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura to guide us through a sweet and meaningful meditation based on Suta Gosvami’s words. The acarya recommends “that we become humble by practicing the following meditation, which empowers one with both humility and success: ‘The earth, which is always visible to me, is the expansion of the lotus feet of my Lord, who is always to be meditated upon. All moving and nonmoving living beings have taken shelter of the earth and are thus sheltered at the lotus feet of my Lord. For this reason I should respect every living being and not envy anyone. In fact, all living entities constitute the Kaustubha gem on my Lord’s chest. Therefore I should never envy or deride any living entity.’ By practicing this meditation one can achieve success in life.”

Now, in Srimad-Bhagavatam 12.11.25, in a wonderful prayer, Suta Gosvami points directly to the topmost Supreme Person, Krsna, who is ultimately to be seen when viewing both His material manifestation as well as His Vaikuntha (Narayana) expansions: “O Krsna, O friend of Arjuna, O chief among the descendants of Vrsni, You are the destroyer of those political parties that are disturbing elements on this earth. Your prowess never deteriorates. You are the proprietor of the transcendental abode, and Your most sacred glories, which are sung by Vrndavana’s cowherd men and women and their servants, bestow all auspiciousness just by being heard. O Lord, please protect Your devotees.”

Thus Suta has carried those who have journeyed on the boat of his words to Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Srila Prabhupada’s purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.3.24 explains the progression of Sukadeva Gosvami’s thought in the first three chapters of the Second Canto. In doing so, Srila Prabhupada also explains the conceptual progression we have just heard here in the Twelfth Canto:

We should note with profit that in the first three chapters of the Second Canto a gradual process of development of devotional service is being presented. In the first chapter the first step in devotional service for God consciousness by the process of hearing and chanting has been stressed, and a gross conception of the Personality of Godhead in His universal form for the beginners is recommended. By such a gross conception of God through the material manifestations of His energy, one is enabled to spiritualize the mind and the senses and gradually concentrate the mind upon Lord Visnu, the Supreme, who is present as the Supersoul in every heart and everywhere, in every atom of the material universe.... but in the third chapter further development is prescribed after one has actually reached the stage of Visnu worship, or pure devotional service, and the mature stage of Visnu worship is suggested herein in relation to the change of heart. The whole process of spiritual culture is aimed at changing the heart of the living being in the matter of his eternal relation with the Supreme Lord as subordinate servant, which is his eternal constitutional position.

As Suta Gosvami says, Krsna’s glorious lotus feet are the supreme object of worship.

*Text 26: Suta Gosvami offers a phala-sruti*

“Anyone who rises early in the morning and, with a purified mind fixed upon the maha-purusa, quietly chants this description of His characteristics will realize Him as the Supreme Absolute Truth residing within the heart.” (SB. 12.11.26)

Krsna is the Supreme Absolute Truth, the maha-purusa, the Supersoul, the Lord of Vaikuntha, and the object of love for all the residents of Vrndavana. In what form will souls who have accepted themselves as His servants realize Him? Lord Brahma explains:

*tvam bhakti-yoga-paribhdvita-hrt-saroja*

*asse sruteksita-patho nanu natha pumsam*

*yad-yad-dhiya ta urugaya vibhavayanti*

*tat-tad-vapuh pranayase sad-anugrahaya*

“O my Lord, Your devotees can see You through the ears by the process of bona fide hearing, and thus their hearts become cleansed, and You take Your seat there. You are so merciful to Your devotees that You manifest Yourself in the particular eternal form of transcendence in which they always think of You.” (SB. 3.9,11)

Once a devotee’s heart is cleansed by hearing, the Lord mercifully sits in that pure heart in the exact eternal form in which His devotee has always thought of Him. In his purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 3.9.11, Srila Prabhupada describes Krsna’s subordination to His devotee and how the Lord appears before His devotee because of the devotee’s intense desire to serve a specific form:

The sruteksita path is to hear from bona fide devotees who are conversant with Vedic wisdom, free from mundane sentiment.
