Intelligent Uddhava intuits that Krsna is going to conclude His earthly pastimes. Although Krsna could have counteracted the brahmanas’ curse, He does not do so. Uddhava places his head on the Lord’s lotus feet and, distressed, begs his beloved friend to take him hack to Godhead with Him. Uddhava tells Krsna that the essence of his life has been to serve Him constantly. Having Krsna’s continual association and seeing His sweet pastimes — Uddhava cannot even contemplate his separation from the Lord (40—45). Uddhava adds that the darkness of maya can be easily overcome when one remembers and glorifies Krsna’s sweet pastimes in the association of His devotees (46-49).

**Chapter 7: Lord Krsna Instructs Uddhava**

Lord Krsna instructs Uddhava to remain on earth and to coni inue serving as His representative after His departure. I he Lord tells Uddhava to wander the earth with full knowledge and detachment, free from the duality of seeing some things as good and others as bad. Rather, Uddhava should see His form in everything. In this way Uddhava will be able to constantly feel His presence and his feelings of separation will subside.

Uddhava doubts his ability to renounce all material attachments and asks the Lord to instruct him further. Krsna explains that one can gain both knowledge and detachment by analyzing the world with one’s intelligence. To illustrate this, the Lord narrates a conversation between Maharaja Yadu and an avadhuta. The avadhuta reveals how he became enlightened by observing the world, and then names twenty-four spiritual masters from whom he has learned. Realizations drawn from the earth, air, sky, water, fire, moon, sun, and a foolish pigeon are included in this chapter.

**Summary**

Lord Krsna confirms Uddhava’s suspicion and acknowledges that He plans to depart after withdrawing the Yadu dynasty. He predicts that all the Yadus will perish by fighting among themselves and that the ocean will cover Dvaraka. When He leaves, He tells Uddhava, Kali-yuga will begin (1-4).

Although Uddhava begs to accompany the Lord, Krsna tells him to remain on earth for the moment. Uddhava is a great devotee, He says, and others will follow him. Through Uddhava, Krsna wants to both give important instructions and to satisfy the sages of Badarikasrama, who did not have the opportunity to meet him personally.

Kali-yuga degrades one’s consciousness, so the Lord tells Uddhava not to stay in a fixed place but to wander, detached, as a sannyasi, seeing Him everywhere. He should he realized, equally disposed to all, and free from duality (5-12).

Uddhava accepts Krsna’s supreme position hut doubts he will be able to renounce all material attachments. Yet he surrenders to the Lord and asks Him to instruct hgmim further (13-18).

Sri Krsna begins by explaining that one can analyze the world with one’s intelligence in order to gain spiritual insights and detachment - that is, one can use one’s life experience as well as one’s observation of others to understand truth. Krsna then trains Uddhava to see His personal form in every experience (19-23). Krsna tells Uddhava this because learning to see Him everywhere will help ease his separation after the Lord departs. To help Uddhava, Krsna relates a conversation that took place between Maharaja Yadu and an avadhuta, a spiritually exalted person not bound by cultural norms. This avadhuta wandered fearlessly and felt a deep, internal satisfaction. Maharaja Yadu asks how the avadhuta became so enlightened without performing any apparent religious or material activities (24-31).

The avadhuta replies that he has used his intelligence to take shelter of twenty-four spiritual masters: (1) the earth (as well as the mountain and the tree), (2) the air, (3) the sky, (4) water, (5) fire, (6) the moon, (7) the sun, (8) the pigeon, \[the discussion of gurus and lessons is contin- ued in the eighth chapter\], (9) the python, (10) the sea, (11) the moth, (12) the honeybee, (13) the elephant, (14) the honey thief, (15) the deer, (16) the fish, (17) the prostitute Pingala (the discussion is continued in the eighth chapter) (18) the kurara bird, (19) the child, (20) the young girl, (21) the arrow maker, (22) the serpent, (23) the spider, (24) the wasp. Thus the avadhuta indicates that he gained his realizations through intelligent observation of the world around him and not from other persons (32-36).

Lessons from these gurus are as follows:

1\. Earth - tolerance and steadfastness; mountain - to serve others; the tree - to dedicate one’s life to benefiting others (37-38).

2\. Air - detachment when contacting favorable and unpleasant things (39-41).

3\. Sky - the soul is always separate from matter (42-43).

4\. Water - remain pure and gentle. Saints are like pure water in that they transparently manifest Krsna in their hearts (44).

5\. Fire - detachment; sometimes be visible and sometimes concealed. Saints are like fire when they act as spiritual masters and burn their disciples’ reactions to ashes (45-47, 49).

6\. Moon - the soul remains the same regardless of the body it inhabits as the moon remains the same regardless of its phase (48).

7\. Sun — acceptance of material objects, to be returned to the correct person at the correct time without becoming entangled with them. Although reflected in many objects, the sun remains unchanged. Similarly the soul remains unchanged regardless of the body it inhabits (50-51).

8\. Foolish pigeon - never indulge in excessive affection or concern for anyone or anything (52-74).

**Chapter 8: The Story of Pingala**

Krsna continues to relate the conversation between the avadhuta and Maharaja Yadu, describing the instructions the avadhuta received from nine more spiritual masters: the python, the sea, the moth, the bee, the elephant, the honey thief, the deer, the fish, and Pingala.

**Summary**

Lord Krsna continues to relate the conversation between Maharaja Yadu and the avadhuta brahmana. The avadhuta describes the lessons learned from nine more of his gurus:

9\. Python - avoid endeavoring for material goals; remain spiritually alert; accept whatever food comes by destiny (1-4).

10\. Sea - remain deep and undisturbed; do not rejoice when wealthy nor feel bereft when poor (5-6).

11\. Moth - avoid attachment to women and sex and avoid the fire of one’s own destruction (7-8).

12\. Bee - collect a little from each flower; don’t become a burden on the generous; unlike the bee that collects honey to store in its hive, don’t collect too much (9-12).

13\. Elephant - avoid trying to exploit the bodies of women for enjoyment (13-14).

14\. Honey thief - one’s wealth can be stolen at any moment, so there is no point in working too hard to accumulate it; like beekeepers who take honey from the bees, mendicants are entitled to a portion of a householder’s property (15-16).

15\. Deer - do not listen to mundane songs, which can lure you to your death (17-18).

16\. Fish - don’t be “hooked” by an uncontrolled tongue (19-21).

17\. Pingala - material disappointment is the Lord’s mercy, so let it lead you toward detachment; sense gratification steals one’s intelligence, while sobriety and detachment allow one to become happy; turn your affection away from the men and women of the material world and toward the Lord, who is the real source of love and happiness (22-44).

**Chapter 9: Detachment from All that Is Material**

The avadhuta describes the seven remaining spiritual masters: the hawk, the child, the young girl, the arrow maker, the snake, the spider, and the wasp. He then describes an additional guru, his own body.

**Summary**

The avadhuta describes what he has learned from the last seven gurus:

18\. Hawk - material attachment leads to suffering, while renouncing desire produces happiness (1-2).

19\. Child - be anxiety-free, detached from family and public opinion, and satisfied in the self (3-4).

20\. Girl with bracelets - living alone leaves one free of prajalpa and conflict. Devotees do not live alone, however, because they associate with other Vaisnavas in order to glorify and serve the Lord (5-10).

21\. Arrow maker - make one’s consciousness steady, detached, free of the modes, and completely fixed on the Absolute Truth (11-13).

22\. Serpent - don’t associate with ordinary materialists; avoid having a fixed residence; wander unnoticed (14-15).

23\. Spider — the Lord, without assistance, creates the universe from His own energy and winds it up again within Himself (16-21).

24\. Insect that assumed the same form as the wasp - the jiva under the sway of affection, hate, and fear attains the identity of the object upon which it meditates (22-23).

25\. One’s body - detachment, because the body always comes to a painful end; each sense pulls the mind in a different direction, destroying one’s peace; actions to maintain the body manifest as the seeds of one’s next material life (24-27).

A human birth is valuable; it should be used to perceive the Absolute Truth and not for sense gratification, which can be obtained in any species of life (28-29).

The avadhuta concludes that by learning from many gurus he has become materially detached and free from false ego (30-31).

The avadhuta brahmana \[who was actually Dattatreya Rsi\] then accepts Maharaja Yadu’s obeisances and leaves. By Krsna’s arrangement, King Yadu thus becomes fixed on the spiritual platform and free from material attachment (32-33).

**Chapter 10: The Nature of Fruitive Activity**

Sri Krsna instructs Uddhava on varnasrama-dharma, the practical means by which one can develop the exalted qualities described in previous chapters. By taking shelter of the Lord and performing one’s duties in the Vedic social and occupational system, without attachment to the result, one’s material desires are gradually diminished. When sincere practitioners find genuine gurus and serve them with love and devotion, they gain transcendental knowledge and establish their connection with Krsna.

Krsna then refutes Jaimini Rsi’s Karma-mimamsa philosophy, which claims that the goal of the living entity is to get as much sense pleasure as possible. Jaimini Rsi proposes that sense gratification is obtained by executing rituals prescribed in scripture. Krsna concludes that those who dedicate themselves to performing rituals aimed at material gain suffer in the end. Instead of trying to get sense gratification by using the Vedas to manipulate the laws of karma, one should strive for liberation.

Uddhava asks Krsna bow a soul can be bound by the modes and how ii can become liberated while still embodied. He also asks for a description of the nuture and symptoms of both bound and liberated souls.

**Summary**

In previous chapters, Krsna described the qualities of saints: material detachment and absorption in the Supersoul. Now Krsna teaches Uddhava about varnasrama-dharma, the practical means by which one can gradually develop that consciousness.

Krsna offers three basic principles, applicable to everyone: (1) take full shelter of Him in devotional service; (2) practice the Vedic social and occupational system; (3) act without fruitive desires. One should give up sense gratification, which is temporary and does not lead one to real happiness. Instead, one should perform activities that lead to spiritual advancement according to regulative principles. By comparing sense gratification to one’s spiritual goal and understanding that sense gratification brings adverse results, one’s material desires are gradually driven from the heart (1-5).

To advance spiritually, Krsna recommends that one accept and serve a spiritual master. The guru should have knowledge about the Lord and represent him as His servant. Disciples should free themselves from pride, material possessiveness, and mundane social connections and dedicate themselves to the spiritual master’s service in a spirit of affection and friendship. When disciples are sincere and spiritual masters realized and pure, disciples become detached from matter and come to know themselves as souls different from the body. They also feel an increasing relationship with Krsna and recognize that the material world is not independent of Krsna. By submissive hearing, disciples develop pure knowledge, which bums ignorance to ashes. As they become more firmly situated in transcendence, “this pure knowledge itself ceases, just as fire ceases when the stock of fuel has been consumed” (6-13).

Krsna says that one should perform one’s Vedic duties with knowledge and detachment while fixing the mind on Him as the only shelter and goal in life. However, there are those that claim the Vedic injunctions have a different purpose. Ultimately, He says, happiness and distress are the result of one’s work and have no other controlling factor. Since the world is eternal, there’s no need of a creator. Since knowledge and consciousness change constantly, there is no absolute truth. Krsna notes that unending happiness in material consciousness is not possible, as every jiva still faces birth, death, disease, and old age (14-16).

Krsna gives five arguments against Karma-mimamsa: (1) No one is fully happy in this world, although the desire for happiness exists. This means one cannot control one’s destiny even by executing prescribed rituals. One’s destiny is under the control of superior forces. (2) No one can escape death. Material objects aren’t pleasurable when one is about to die. (3) Even happiness in the heavenly realm has obstacles, such as envy, jealousy, and fear. (4) Material actions ultimately lead to suffering. If the actions are impious they cause one to contemplate low-class material desires; if the actions are pious, time still crushes any happiness achieved. (5) Under Krsna’s time factor all souls experience the results of their actions, and these reactions cannot be misery-free. Krsna concludes that illusioned living beings see the world as separate from the Supreme and therefore experience their karmic reactions as lamentation and grief (17-34).

Krsna clarifies that the goal of Vedic culture is liberation, not sense gratification: Uddhava asks what liberation means - for example, how can a soul be liberated while performing bodily activities that are under the modes of nature? If the soul never mixes with the body, how can a nonmaterial soul be controlled by the material modes? How can one distinguish liberated from bound souls, especially when their external activities appear similar (35-37)?

**Chapter 11: The Symptoms of Conditioned and Liberated Living Entities**

Krsna answers Uddhava’s questions about conditioned and liberated souls and reveals devotional service as the perfection of jnana and as the pure and perfect process. The goal of the Vedic path is absorption in Krsna’s glories. Bhakti is rare and can be attained only by associating with Krsna’s devotees.

Uddhava asks Krsna to define a true devotee along with the practices of devotional service. Krsna emphasizes taking shelter of Him as the prime quality of a devotee, and then enumerates twenty-seven secondary qualities. He also presents practices that purify and bring about attachment to Him. By worshiping the Lord as a person, one develops realized knowledge and devotional service.

**Summary**

In reply to Uddhava’s question about bound and liberated living beings, Krsna offers Uddhava the analogy of a dream to describe how the living being is always spiritual and has no connection to the material energy. When living beings are in ignorance ihey identify with the body; when they are in knowledge they try to free themselves from the modes. Neither state of awareness is the true nature of the soul, which is always spiritual (1-4).

There are two distinct and conscious entities in the body, the jiva and the Supersoul. The jiva generally enjoys and suffers the fruits of karma produced by the body. The jiva is covered by ignorance, so is called “conditioned.” The Supersoul has no interest in the fruits of karma; He is ever satisfied, full of knowledge, and eternally liberated. Krsna then defines what it means to be a liberated or conditioned soul and describes the characteristics of each (5-17).

Next, Krsna establishes bhakti as the ultimate process and the perfection of knowledge. The Vedic path elevates the soul through knowledge. Its goal is to absorb the consciousness in the glories of Krsna. Therefore knowledge that does not end in fixing one’s mind on Krsna’s pastimes is useless. Krsna particularly teaches that one should fix the mind with love on His childhood pastimes and in that way attain Him. If one is unable to do this, one should perform all one’s activities as an offering to Krsna. By associating with Krsna’s devotees and performing the pure processes of bhakti, such as hearing, glorifying, and remembering Krsna’s activities, one attains devotional service and returns to the Lord’s abode (18-25).

Uddhava asks Krsna whom He considers a true devotee and what type of devotional service He accepts. Uddhava then defines the Lord’s ultimate principle: He is controlled by His devotees’ love. Krsna appears in various forms to facilitate His pastimes with them (26-28).

Krsna lists for Uddhava twenty-eight devotional qualities. The prime quality is to see Krsna as one’s only shelter. The other twenty-seven qualities, such as mercy, lack of envy, well-wishing friendship toward all, and sense control, are secondary and relative. If devotees have the prime quality of surrender, they should be considered saintly. Krsna concludes that one should understand that pure bhakti is superior to all other processes and therefore renounce all ordinary religious duties. He then presents the perfect stage of devotional service: the best devotees simply love and worship Him in a personal relationship with Him. He is then bound by their love (29-33).

In answer to Uddhava’s second question, Krsna offers devotional practices that purify material contamination and bring about attachment to Him. These practices include serving and worshiping the Deify and the Lord’s pure devotees, hearing and glorifying the Lord’s transcendental qualities and activities, offering the Lord valuable possessions, giving oneself completely to the Lord, participating in festivals and ceremonies related to the Lord, observing religious vows, taking initiation, and building and supporting temples (34-41).

Krsna then lists appropriate places and methods for His worship. By such worship, one understands the Lord’s all-pervading feature and engages all material and spiritual elements in His service. Thus one attains devotional service to, and realized knowledge of, the Lord. But one can only attain such devotional service by associating with Krsna’s devotees. If one does not engage in devotional service to Krsna, there is no way to escape material existence (42-49).

**Chapter 12: Beyond Renunciation and Knowledge**

Krsna glorifies Vaisnava association and then opens His heart to Uddhava to reveal the intense love He and the residents of Vrndavana feel for one another. Krsna remembers the gopis’ exclusive attachment to Him. He then instructs Uddhava to abandon the Vedic injunctions and simply take shelter of Him as the Vrajavasis have done.

Uddhava is bewildered by the many instructions the Lord had previously given him and by the description of the gopis and their intense love for Him, so he asks Krsna for further instructions. Krsna replies that both material existence and Vedic sound are His manifestations, and that the purpose of the Vedas is to understand this underlying principle. He then tells Uddhava to remove the soul’s material covering and engage in bhakti.

**Summary**

Krsna continues to glorify Vaisnava association as the source of bhakti. This association leads to a loving relationship with Krsna and detachment from matter. No process other than associating with Vaisnavas can bring Krsna under control. To demonstrate the power of Vaisnava association, Krsna gives more than thirty examples of persons who associated with devotees and attained pure bhakti. On His list are the Vraja gopis, Banasura, and the wives of the yajnic brahmanas. None of these persons needed to study the Vedas or perform austerities or any other process to attain Krsna. Vaisnava association was sufficient (17).

Krsna then reveals to Uddhava the innermost core of His heart. He remembers the residents of Vrndavana and the deep love they feel for Him. Such love is the only means to attain Krsna. Even after Krsna left Vrndavana for Mathura, the gopis remained fully attached to Him and had no other source of happiness. Their separation from Krsna seemed longer to them than a day of Brahma, while their union with Him seemed to pass in less than a moment. They were fully absorbed in fulfilling Krsna’s desires and unaware of anything else. The gopis’ love for Krsna was so intense that it covered their awareness that He was God. They simply loved Him as their most charming lover and thus attained Him. Therefore, Krsna tells Uddhava, one should ultimately abandon the Vedic injunctions and with all one’s heart fearlessly take shelter of Him (8-15).

Uddhava is still uncertain which path is best for him personally, as Krsna has described varnasrama, jnana, and bhakti. Furthermore, Krsna’s description of the gopis’ love bewilders Uddhava. Thus he again asks Krsna to further instruct him. Krsna replies that His instructions were not meant specifically for Uddhava; they were to guide all living beings in their different circumstances. Krsna then explains that He manifests as Vedic sound, as everything the senses can perceive, as the universe, and as the tree of material existence. The purpose of the Vedas, He says, is to understand this underlying principle. Krsna tells Uddhava to cut the subtle material covering away from the soul and to develop bhakti (16-24).

**Chapter 13: The Hamsa-avatara Answers the Questions of the Sons of Brahma**

Krsna instructs Uddhava how to become free of subtle material coverings and be fully self-realized as pure spirit soul. To do this, he should cultivate the mode of goodness, beginning with identifying how the modes influence the mind and intelligence, and then fully absorb his consciousness in the Supreme. Krsna first speaks directly to Uddhava, then gives the same teaching through the discussion between the Hamsa-avatara and the Four Kumaras.

**Summary**

Krsna instructs Uddhava in how to separate the soul from its subtle material coverings. First, he should elevate himself to the mode of goodness and get free of passion and ignorance. Although ultimately Uddhava will need to be in transcendental goodness, material goodness allows one to have clear vision and real knowledge. As such it is the stepping- stone to transcendence. If one cultivates goodness in his environment and interactions, goodness continues to increase in one’s consciousness. Therefore the sages recommend the mode of goodness. The modes create the gross and subtle coverings over the soul. When one uses the gross and subtle bodies to cultivate goodness and knowledge, they can destroy the modes’ influence on oneself - an influence that caused one to take a material body (1-7).

Uddhava asks Krsna why people act in passion and ignorance even when they know it is harmful. Krsna describes how the soul becomes entangled in the material energy. First, the soul is covered by false ego, and then by the subtle mind. The mind is contaminated by the mode of passion in the form of unending material desires. These desires cause a particular gross body to develop. Bewildered by passion, one then performs activities that eventually cause one harm. Krsna then describes how to overcome the modes’ influence by identifying which thoughts and feelings are caused by the lower modes, observing them with detachment, from a distance, and understanding that they are external to the self. One should then carefully and determinedly bring the mind back under control and absorb it in Krsna as much as one is able. This is the yoga system taught by Sanaka-kumara and other devotees (8-14).

Uddhava asks Krsna to describe Sanaka-kumara’s teachings, and so Krsna tells how the Four Kumaras’ asked Brahma questions, leading to the appearance of the Hamsa-avatara. The Kumaras’ primary spiritual practice is meditation, and so they want to know how to cut the mutual relationship the sense objects have with the mind so that they can focus the mind only on the Supreme. Brahma contemplates this question but cannot answer it since he is attached to creation in the mode of passion. So he fixes his mind on the Supreme Lord and, to remove His devotees’ bewilderment, the Lord incarnates as a beautiful swan. Brahma and his four sons worship the Hamsa-avatara, and then the Kumaras ask Him who He is (15-21).

The Hamsa-avatara first removes the Kumaras’ misconceptions about the Absolute Truth. If He is considered a jiva without individuality or is composed merely of matter, the Kumaras’ question is meaningless. That they ask their question at all implies I le is neither. But even if I le is the Supreme, their question is inappropriate as nothing in existence is separate from Him (22-24).

The Haiiisa-avatara then states that the sense objects and the mind interact constantly, but because both are material, they should both be given up. This may be difficult, but it’s possible by engaging the mind and senses to achieve Krsna’s pleasure. Sense gratification enhances the unwanted interaction between sense objects and mind and so is detrimental to spiritual life (25-26).

To help detach the mind from sense objects, the Hamsa-avatara recommends observing one’s thoughts from a distance without identifying with them. Such a practice - which is in the mode of goodness - overcomes the influences of passion and ignorance and increases one’s awareness that the soul is different from the mind and intelligence, both of which are born from the material modes. Instead of remaining absorbed in sense objects, one should absorb one’s consciousness in the Supreme and realize that there is nothing separate from Him. By fixing the mind on Krsna one wakens from the dream of material existence. Two methods helpful to achieving this are to break the identification with the three states of consciousness by observing how one’s identity continues throughout them, and to understand that one’s perceptions of the material world are only temporary, illusory constructs of the mind. One is actually the spirit soul, eternal and pure (27-35).

Self-realized persons who have become perfect by practicing this jnana process continue to live in their bodies as long as their karma keeps them alive, but they no longer think or experience the body to be themselves (36-37).

The Hamsa-avatara now answers the Kumaras’ question about His identity. He is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Visnu, the shelter of all religious processes and the reservoir of all transcendental qualities (38-40).

The Kumaras, fully understanding the Hamsa-avatara’s teachings, worship Him with devotion, and then the Lord returns to His abode (41-42).

**Chapter 14: Lord Krsna Explains the Yoga System to Sri Uddhava**

Uddhava asks Krsna which spiritual practice is the most excellent. Krsna rejects the Vedic processes influenced by the material modes and instead recommends fixing the mind on Him. Krsna then glorifies bhakti along with its purifying power and the unparalleled results it can bring.

In response to Uddhava’s question about meditation, Krsna presents a brief description of the external practices of yoga and then describes the goal: fix the mind on the enchanting form of the Lord in the heart and unite with Him.

**Summary**

Uddhava asks Krsna to clarify His recommendations for the different processes of self-realization. Some processes are directly connected with the Lord and award the highest perfection while others support self- realization but are in themselves insufficient to achieve it. Uddhava wants to ensure that the supreme position of bhakti is clearly understood (1-2).

Krsna first describes how He gave pure knowledge to Brahma, who then passed it down through the generations. The various descendants who received it were conditioned in their own ways by the modes, and so the Vedic path was divided to suit their individual natures. Actually, the Vedic purpose is one. The large number of Vedic processes only indicates the varieties of material illusion. Material contamination causes various theistic and atheistic philosophies and views to arise, which results in ignorance and unhappiness (3-11).

Krsna next recommends bhakti as the supreme process. Fixing the consciousness on Krsna without material desires awards a degree of happiness that cannot be otherwise achieved. This is because Krsna is inclined to give Himself only to His devotees. To the bhaktas He reveals Himself in all His sweetness, minimizing the value of all other attainments. The devotees offer themselves fully to Krsna and see Him as their only shelter, while He loves them with all His heart and always thinks of them and their exalted qualities (12-16).

Bhakti is glorious. It awards material detachment and unparalleled happiness. It has an immense purifying power - sinful reactions are eradicated and material desires uprooted from the heart. If practiced with full faith, without selfishness, and with Krsna as the only goal, bhakti can completely purify the consciousness. In addition, a mature devotee has an unlimited capacity to help and purify others. Bhakti is so potent that even the Lord allows Himself to come under its control. Through chanting and hearing about the Lord the devotee regains the ability to see Him in His spiritual form and to serve Him in the spiritual world. One should thus reject all other processes for advancement and completely absorb the mind in Krsna (17-28).

Krsna then cautions Uddhava not to act as an enjoyer, a tendency that becomes prominent in the association of the opposite sex. His point is that careless actions may cause one to suffer material bondage despite the purifying power of bhakti (29-30).

Uddhava asks Krsna about the process and goal of meditation (31).

Krsna briefly describes the external methods of meditation, from sitting places and asanas through breath control to the withdrawal of the mind from external sense objects. When the sacred syllable om is chanted and the life air controlled, real meditation can begin (32-35).

Krsna then explains the goal of meditation: yogis can actually see the Supersoul sitting on the lotus of the heart. The Supersoul has the form of Lord Visnu and is wonderful, effulgent, and captivating to the mind. The meditation should first be focused on the Lord’s delicate limbs and then on His sweet smiling face (36-43).

Those who desire impersonal liberation should stop meditating on the Lord’s form and fix the consciousness in the sky. Thus by the power of bhakti they will attain Brahman realization and destroy their identification with material objects (44-46).

**Chapter 15: Lord Krsna’s Description of Mystic Yoga Perfections**

Krsna explains that through yoga meditation one can achieve mystic perfections, and then describes the varieties and natures of these perfections and how to acquire each of them. To achieve any mystic perfection, however, yogis must worship the Lord and meditate on His form.

Krsna then stresses the superiority of devotional service to Him. Through bhakti one can achieve all the mystic perfections and much more. These perfections are actually obstructions for devotees because they can increase the enjoying tendency. The Lord concludes by describing Himself as the basis and goal of all the systems of spiritual advancement, and the Supreme Personality of Godhead with unlimited potencies.

**Summary**

Krsna described meditation in the previous chapter and how to use it to achieve liberation. He now explains that another result of meditation is the acquisition of mystic perfections. Uddhava asks Krsna to explain the varieties and natures of these perfections and how to acquire them (1-2).

Krsna divides the mystic perfections into two categories: the eight primary perfections that emanate directly from Him and the ten secondary perfections that are born of material goodness. (There are another five perfections with less power.) The primary perfections are: transforming the body into the smallest, the greatest, or the lightest, acquiring whatever one desires, experiencing any enjoyable object, manipulating the subpotencies of maya, remaining unimpeded by the modes, and obtaining anything from anywhere.

The ten secondary perfections are: freeing oneself from hunger and thirst, hearing and seeing things that are far away, moving the body at the speed of the mind, assuming any form one desires, entering the bodies of others, dying when one desires, witnessing the pastimes between the demigods and the celestial Apsaras, executing one’s determination completely, and giving orders that are fulfilled without impediment.

The other five perfections are: the power to know past, present, and future, the ability to tolerate heat and cold, knowing the minds of others, checking the influence of fire, sun, water, and poison, and remaining unconquered (3-9).

The Supreme Lord next lists the ways to meditate on Him in order to receive the perfections - for example, meditating on Him as within each atom awards the perfection of becoming the smallest, and focusing on Him as the Supreme Soul of material existence awards the perfection of becoming the greatest. The element common to all meditations is focus on and worship of Krsna (10-31).

Krsna concludes His description of the mystic perfections by describing the superiority of devotional service. Those who meditate on Krsna with devotion have no trouble achieving mystic perfections. Each process culminates in meditation on the Lord, so one may practice any of these forms of meditation and follow it to its final goal. The happiness one derives from devotional service is higher than the happiness attained by mystic perfections, and so devotees don’t seek to achieve them. All results available from other processes can be obtained through bhakti. Krsna explains that He is the cause, protector, and goal of all systems of spiritual advancement, and restates His position as the Supreme Personality of Godhead with unlimited potencies. He exists within everything as the Supersoul anti outside of everything in His all pervading feature (32-36).

**Chapter 16: The Lord’s Opulence**

Uddhava asks Krsna to reveal His material and spiritual opulences so that those with mundane vision may perceive Him. Krsna describes more than a hundred of His opulences, showing Himself to be the active principle and powerful essence of everything wonderful in existence. Krsna’s opulences are unlimited. He is the foundation of the material and spiritual worlds, and nothing can exist without Him. Krsna then recommends surrendering to Him and serving Him with loving devotion.

**Summary**

In the previous chapter Krsna pointed at Himself as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, with unlimited potencies. Here, Uddhava confirms Krsna’s position as the Absolute Truth. Krsna is present in everything that exists, but ordinary people cannot see Him. Therefore Uddhava asks Krsna to reveal His opulences so that those limited by mundane vision may perceive His presence (1-5).

Krsna recalls that Arjuna asked the same question on the battlefield of Kuruksetra (6-8). The Lord then describes His opulences, showing Himself as the active principle and powerful essence of all things wonderful. He lists more than a hundred opulences: among those seeking progress, He is the ultimate goal; among the pious He is natural virtue; among great things He is the total material creation; among the demigods He is Indra; among sacrifices He is study of the Vedas, etc. (9-36).

Krsna’s opulences are unlimited, uncountable, and everything in existence is made up of different combinations of them. There are two distinct sets of opulences, the material and the spiritual. His spiritual opulences are His expansions, such as Vasudeva and Narayana, and His material opulences are the outstanding features of the material creation. His expansions are eternal and unseen by conditioned souls, while His material opulences can be perceived. Krsna is the foundation of the material and spiritual worlds and nothing can exist without Him (37-41).

Krsna concludes by recommending devotional service. One should control one’s speech, mind, life air, and senses, and then surrender to Krsna and serve Him with loving devotion (42- 44).

**Chapter 17: Lord Krsna’s Description of the Varnasrama System**

Uddhava asks Krsna to describe the path to bhakti through varnasrama- dharma. Krsna speaks about the history of varnasrama and then describes the duties of the different social orders. He then describes in detail the religious practices of brahmacaris and grhasthas. Brahmacaris should maintain celibacy, study the Vedas, and serve the spiritual master. Grhasthas should restrict sense enjoyment, perform sacrifices, live at home without material attachment, and give charity.

Krsna explains the prescribed duties for brahmanas and ksatriyas and presents the flexibility of the varnasrama system, which allows for a limited change of occupation during emergencies. The culmination of brahmacari and grhastha life is to become a devotee of Krsna.

**Summary**

In chapters 12-15 Uddhava heard about the practices and goals of jnana-yoga, bhakti-yoga, and astanga-yoga. In chapter ten Krsna briefly explained the purpose of varnasrama and how to follow it. Uddhava now wishes to hear in detail how those inclined to the execution of prescribed duties can advance toward Krsna’s lotus feet. Uddhava fears that in Kali-yuga people will not be able to use meditation to see how everything is connected to Krsna, and so the process of bhakti will become lost. Uddhava asks Krsna to again teach how one should practice bhakti, this time through varnasrama-dharma (1-7).

Krsna begins by describing the history of varnasrama. In Satya-yuga, all human beings were devotees who meditated on the Lord; there was no need for secondary religious activities. Vedic knowledge, sacrifice, and the division of society into social and spiritual orders appeared at the beginning of Treta-yuga (8-15). Krsna then explains the duties of brahmanas, ksatriyas, vaisyas, and sudras and the qualities of those outside a varnasrama society. He then highlights the general principles of piety for all members of society (16-22).

Next, Krsna describes in more detail the four spiritual orders, starting with ihe brahmacaris. A brahmacari should live simply, control his mind, maintain celibacy, study the Vedas, and offer others respect. He should serve and worship the spiritual master and thus be trained as a self-control led member of society who is determined, focused, and of strong character. Brahmacaris should worship the Lord as Supersoul and, like other celibates, avoid association with women. They should be clean, perform religious services, visit holy places, and chant japa. The final fruit of brahmacari practice is to become devoted to Krsna. Those brahmacaris who wish to marry should offer guru-daksind, then take their guru’s permission and go home. On leaving the asrama, brahmacaris can become householders, accept vanaprastha, or take sannyasa (23-38).

Householders should build a successful family structure based on sacrifice, Vedic study, and giving charity. Householder brahmanas are especially instructed to live simply at home without attachment. They should depend on the Lord for their maintenance and always think of Him. Ksatriya householders are instructed to protect their citizens as if they were their own children (39-46).

The varnasrama structure is both supportive and flexible. In times of emergency, members of a social order may accept a different occupation, with some restrictions. Brahmanas and ksatriyas should not accept a master, as serving low persons is contaminating. A vaisya may work as a sudra, and a sudra may engage in simple activities like making baskets and mats. All members of society must give up these occupations when the difficulty has passed (47-49).

Householders should serve Krsna by performing five sacrifices a day. To counteract selfishness, they should maintain their dependents and support others. They should understand that all material relationships are temporary and should live at home without attachment, as if they are guests in their own homes. To prepare for death, Vaisnava householders may remain at home, go to a holy place, or take sannyasa. Krsna condemns householders who remain attached to their homes with the hope only to enjoy money and family. Such miserliness leaves one meditating on the temporary and so inhibits spiritual realization (50-58).

**Chapter 18: Description of Varnasrama-dharma**

Krsna describes the religious practices and duties of vanaprasthas and sannyasis and explains that the ultimate purpose of varnasrama is to develop bhakti. Householders can prepare for the next life by detaching themselves from family comforts and moving to the forest, where they perform austerities. If such a vanaprastha develops complete detachment from the fruits of material activities, he can take sannyasa. Krsna then offers a practical guide for sannyasis, describing the actions and consciousness of those who have perfected their sannyasa. He also instructs sannyasis who wish to advance toward perfection and condemns sannyasis of poor character. Finally, Krsna explains each asrama’s essential duty and defines the ultimate purpose of all asramas as developing devotional service to Him. Worshiping Krsna with loving devotion by one’s occupation awards the supreme perfection of life.

**Summary**

After describing the religious practices of brahmacaris and grhasthas (in the previous chapter), Krsna explains in detail the duties of vanaprasthas and sannyasis.

When householders become old, they should prepare for the next life by detaching themselves from family comforts. To do this, they should adopt the vanaprastha order and enter the forest to perform austerities. Vanaprasthas should eat and dress simply, using only what is available in the forest. They should care for the body in the simplest way and become tolerant by exposing themselves to heat and cold and refraining from stocking provisions. They should perform Vedic sacrifices and observe the Caturmasya vow. Successful vanaprasthas achieve Maharloka or go directly to Krsna. If they cannot perform their vanaprastha duties because of old age, they should fix the mind on the Lord and give up the body (1-11).

A fully detached vanaprastha, who has truly realized the inherent misery in all material situations, is qualified to accept sannyasa. Such men should renounce their possessions and worship Krsna according to scriptural injunctions. He should be vigilant that no material desires enter the heart to create obstacles on his spiritual path (12-14).

The Lord’s practical guidance for sannyasis includes regulations about dress and possessions. He encourages them to not commit violence and to be pure in mind and speech. They should cultivate self-discipline, maintain themselves by begging, and travel and live alone. Sannyasis should remain free from material attachment, meditate constantly on the Lord, discriminate between the actions and thoughts that cause bondage and those that bring liberation, and understand the illusory, temporal nature of material objects (15-27).

A perfected sannyasi develops love for Krsna. Such a person no longer needs to follow the ritualistic aspects of bis asrama as he has already achieved their purpose, lit order to avoid adulation and too much respect from the general public, a spiritually advanced sannyasi should conceal his true position. He should not, however, act sinfully, propagate atheistic views, or behave in any way detrimental to his spiritual life. He may follow regulative duties as service to the Lord and to instruct others. Krsna describes the inner mood of the paramahamsa: he is not afraid, feels no hostility toward others, respects everyone, and sees himself as fully under the Lord’s shelter. He accepts whatever comes of its own accord for his maintenance, but if necessary, protects his service by collecting sufficient food. At the time of death he achieves opulences equal to the Lord’s (28-37). Sannyasis who have yet to attain perfection should continue serving their guru with great faith and respect (38-39).

Krsna concludes his description of sannyasa by condemning the sannyasis who ruin religious principles, use their position to make a living, or are still engaged in sense gratification, their consciousness full of material desires (40-41).

The Lord next explains the essential duty of each asrama and advises grhasthas to use their lives as vehicles for spiritual progress and not for sense gratification (42-43).

Krsna concludes that the purpose of all prescribed duties performed in the varnasrama system is to develop bhakti. Thus the ultimate goal of karma, jnana, and yoga is bhakti. Because Krsna is the Absolute Truth, one should worship Him with loving devotion according to one’s occupation and thus come to Him. This is the supreme perfection of life. Offering one’s work to Krsna can be done by performing the work for His pleasure or by offering Him the work’s results (44-48).

**Chapter 19: The Perfection of Spiritual Knowledge**

Krsna develops His arguments about jnana, saying that both knowledge and the process of attaining knowledge should be renounced in order to achieve Him, the ultimate goal. Uddhava asks about the process of transcendental knowledge that automatically brings detachment and direct perception of truth, but which is also traditionally studied among jnanis. This knowledge, Uddhava says, describes loving devotional service to Krsna. Krsna then defines knowledge, self-realization, and detachment in connection with Himself. He then describes fifteen elements that form the means to achieve devotional service to Him. Uddhava then asks Krsna to describe the different disciplinary regulations and daily duties, as well as to define a number of religious and cultural qualities and terms. Krsna briefly defines them and then rejects them in order to emphasize the transcendental process of bhakti.

**Summary**

Krsna wishes to elevate to the path of bhakti those jnanis who have realized the falsity of matter and the reality of spirit. Such jnanis have already disentangled themselves from maya and no longer need the methods and realizations they acquired to gain liberation. Therefore Krsna instructs them to renounce their knowledge along with the process they used to obtain it and to worship Him instead. Bhakti, however, in which the means and end are the same, should never be renounced. Elevated jnanis see Krsna as the absolute conclusion, the ultimate goal, and the means of advancement. They have no effective purpose or dear object in life other than Him. Thus they are dear to Him. As spiritual knowledge is superior to pious activities, one should use such knowledge to understand oneself as soul and then worship Krsna in loving devotion. To do so, one should first understand the coverings of the self and how to dismantle them (1-7).

Uddhava asks Krsna to explain knowledge, detachment, and self- realization in a way that they ultimately award bhakti. Krsna’s lotus feet and His instructions are the only shelter Uddhava desires (8-10). In response Krsna repeats Bhismadeva’s words when Yudhisthira inquired from him about liberation. Knowledge (jnana) is the realization that everything in material existence arises from the Supersoul. Self-realization (vijnana) is the direct experience of the Supersoul within everything without perceiving the material coverings. Krsna as the Supersoul is therefore the cause of everything and the ultimate entity. Detachment (vairagya) arises when one understands the temporary, insubstantial nature of the material world (11-18).

Krsna then speaks about bhakti, listing fifteen powerful elements by which one can achieve devotional service. These are: firm faith in the narration of His pastimes, constant chanting of His glories, attachment to the ceremonial worship of His Deity form, praising Him through beautiful hymns, respect for His devotional service, offering obeisances, first-class worship of His devotees, being conscious that He is present in all living entities, offering bodily activities in His devotional service, describing His qualities, offering Him one’s mind, rejecting all material desires, giving one’s wealth in order to serve Him, renouncing sense gratification, and performing activities favorable to His service. Krsna declares that these fifteen items constitute the actual religious princb pies (dharma) by which loving devotion to Him automatically develops (19-24).

Performing devotional service in the mode of goodness, with the mind fixed on Krsna, yields religiosity, knowledge, detachment, and opulence. On the other hand, fixing the mind on objects of sense gratification, in the mode of passion, causes one to focus on the temporary and become entangled in sense gratification. Krsna next defines the goal of Vedic practices in connection with Him and service to Him (25-27).

Uddhava then asks Krsna to describe different disciplinary regulations and daily duties, as well as to define a number of religious and cultural qualities and terms - self-control, tolerance, charity, reality, sacrifice, education, humility, beauty, and happiness - and Krsna gives concise definitions of each, and then rejects both the good and bad qualities in order to emphasize devotional service, which is transcendental (28-45).

**Chapter 20: Pure Devotional Service Surpasses Knowledge and Detachment**

Krsna describes how the Vedic system leads one through detached karma to acting on the platform of knowledge and ultimately to devotional service. He encourages Uddhava to take advantage of his human birth in order to make spiritual advancement and presents useful methods for controlling the mind and focusing it on Him. Krsna establishes pure devotional service as the supreme process and goal. bhakti can cleanse the heart completely from material contamination, award all attainments, and purify all sinful reactions. Serving the Lord in a loving relationship is transcendental, free from the influence of material piety and sin, and the only actual good.

**Summary**

At the end of the chapter 19, Krsna rejected as insubstantial tbe good and bad qualities and the regulations that result in material piety or sin. Without understanding the Vedas through the frame of reference of bhakti, one could become confused, seeing that the Vedas both distinguish between pious and sinful acts and nullify that distinction. Uddhava asks Krsna for clarification (1-5).

Krsna tells Uddhava that there are only three paths for spiritual advancement: karma, jnana, and bhakti. The qualification to practice jnana-yoga is disgust at and detachment from material life. To be qualb fied to practice karma-yoga, one has to have material attachment and desires. To be qualified to practice bhakti-yoga, one needs faith in hearing and chanting Krsna’s glories (6-8).

Those with fruitive desires should act according to the Vedic injunctions in order to obtain them, but should also gradually become detached from the results of their work. Thus they will be cleansed of material contamination and attain transcendental knowledge (9-11).

Krsna encourages Uddhava to take advantage of his human birth, which offers a unique opportunity to achieve transcendental knowledge and love of God. Knowing one’s days are numbered, one should use the human body wisely, accepting the help of a spiritual master and the Lord’s instructions to cross the ocean of material existence (12-17).

Controlling the mind and fixing it on the spiritual platform is vital for those wishing to practice spiritual life, so Krsna presents methodologies suitable for jnanis and bhaktas. Whenever the mind deviates from the spiritual, one should use the intelligence strengthened by the mode of goodness to bring it back under control. One should also preach to the mind about the nonpermanent nature of this world and its pleasures and eventually completely focus the mind on the Supreme (18-24).

In case of accidental falldown, jnanis and bhaktas should continue performing their prescribed duties and be purified. Krsna defines piety as adherence to one’s prescribed duty and sin as neglecting it. Thus jnanis and bhaktas can subdue materialistic activities (25-26).

Krsna next glorifies pure devotional service. Those who are beginners in bhakti have four characteristics: faith in the narrations of Krsna’s glories, disgust with material activities, the inability to completely renounce sense enjoyment, and determination to serve the Lord. When advanced, bhaktas are completely focused on serving Krsna. The Lord from within the heart then cleanses His devotees of all material desires and destroys their false ego (27-30).

Devotees have no need to perform anything other than bhakti in order to attain perfection. All attainments can he achieved through bhakti, making bhakti superior to all other process (31-33). A pure devotee of Krsna desires nothing but to serve Him with love. This level of consciousness can be developed simply by taking shelter of and trying to serve the Lord (34-35).

Desiring to please Krsna and give Him pleasure is transcendental, and so pure devotees are on the spiritual platform, free from the influence of material piety and sin. Material good and bad fall under the modes of nature and are therefore relative and false. By following Krsna’s instructions, they become free from all contamination, attain the spiritual world, and fully realize the Absolute Truth (36-37).

**Chapter 21: Lord Krsna’s Explanation of the Vedic Path**

Krsna explains that the Vedas prescribe duties and define piety and sin in order to uplift those who are not performing devotional service. To distinguish between piety and sin, Krsna describes the purity or impurity of various places, times, and objects. Following one’s duty according to one’s current position on the spiritual path guarantees that one progresses from karma to jnana to bhakti.

The Vedic injunctions indirectly lead one to worshiping Krsna by starting with prescriptions for fruitive religious activities. Materialists follow these injunctions to achieve sense gratification but are thus gradually cured of their material disease. No one but Krsna knows the purpose of the Vedas, which are subtle and unlimitedly deep. That purpose is to know Him and to develop bhakti.

**Summary**

In previous chapters, Krsna named the three paths to spiritual advancement: karma, jnana, and bhakti. Those who neglect these three in order to enjoy their senses degrade their consciousness and remain on the material platform. Although when looked at from the reference point of devotional service, good and bad material qualities are relative and false; the only good is pleasing Krsna. But to direct conditioned souls upward in their spiritual progress, the Vedas prescribe duties appropriate to these souls’ current positions. Adherence to such duties is called piety because such adherence restricts sense gratification and increases spiritual knowledge. Deviation from them is sin. An individual’s specific duties are determined by his or her placement in the varnasrama system and conditioning by the modes. To make advancement from varnasrama duties, one should discriminate between good and bad, favorable and unfavorable, and auspicious and inauspicious in terms of time, place, and particular objects (1-7).

The Lord next details how to discern the purity or impurity of places, times, substances, mantras, work, and performers of activities. Objects are made impure when they come in contact with impure items and can be purified by time, wind, fire, water, and earth. Work is purified by offering it to the Lord (8-15).

What is piety and what is sin depends heavily on the time and the circumstance. What is good and what is bad are not relative judgments. (One sometimes needs fine discrimination to understand whether an act is pious or sinful.) The same act that can elevate a degraded person can degrade one with higher consciousness, for example (16-17).

Impious acts are the result of the enjoying tendency, which causes bondage, lust, quarrel, anger, and ignorance. Giving into these makes one lose one’s intelligence, and one’s life becomes conditioned and dull, devoid of spiritual value (18-22).

Krsna explains that the Vedic inj unctions indirectly lead one to His worship by first prescribing fruitive religious activities, which serve as the candy coating on medicine. Materialistic people perform such activities in order to increase their sense gratification and do not understand the true purpose of the Vedas. Such persons tend to be proud, greedy, and bewildered. They do not want to worship Krsna and are not attracted to topics about Him, but instead worship demigods to attain dreamlike, heavenly pleasures (23-35).

Vedic sound is unlimitedly deep and potent, with many subtle levels of understanding. It manifests from Krsna, spreads in thousands of directions, and is later withdrawn into Him (36-41).

No one but Krsna knows the purpose of the Vedas, and here He says that that purpose is to know Him. Vedic worshipers ultimately worship Krsna, and Vedic philosophers discover Him as the ultimate truth (42-43).

\[The final goal of all Vedic processes is to achieve His devotional service. Through the descriptions of karma, jnana, and yoga in the Uddhava-gita, Krsna wishes to establish Himself as the Supreme Lord and the natural object of worship. He also wishes to establish bhakti as the process by which one attains Him. Krsna has now accomplished these goals.\]

**Chapter 22: Enumeration of the Elements of Material Creation**

Uddhava asks Krsna four questions: (1) How many elements are in the material creation? (2) How does one distinguish between nature and the soul? (3) How does the soul accept and give up bodies as a result of its activities? (4) how does one become tolerant and completely detached from body and mind? In response to Uddhava’s first question, Krsna defines the Supreme Lord’s spiritual energy (purusa) as distinct from the material manifestation (prakrti). Answering the second question, Krsna parses the purusa category into two - the Lord and the jiva - both of whom are fully spiritual and eternally distinct. In response to the third question, Krsna delineates the reasons the eternal jiva transmigrates from one body to another. The response to Uddhava’s fourth question is discussed in the next chapter.

**Summary**

In chapters 19 and 21, Krsna presented the universe’s twenty-eight elements as the Supreme Lord, the jiva, the mahat-tattva, false ego, the five gross elements, the ten senses, the mind, the five subtle objects of perception, and the three modes of nature. Now Uddhava asks Krsna to explain why great sages calculate the number of elements in various ways (1-3).

Krsna explains that each material element contains within itself all the elements derived from it. All the derived elements also contain subtle forms of the elements that caused them. Thus all material elements are found within each other in gross and subtle forms. Great sages are under the shelter of the internal potency of the Lord and may calculate the number of elements in the universe differently. These calculations do not really contradict one another, as they simply describe the same phenomena using different systems of categorization. However, philosophers argue over such apparently contradictory viewpoints because they are affected by Krsna’s external energy. If instead they fixed their intelligence on Krsna, differences of perception would disappear and they would see reality and the reasons to disagree dissolved (4-9).

\[By enumerating various ways in which one can count the elements, Krsna rejects philosophies that identify the soul with the Supreme. The jiva can be covered by illusion, but the all-knowing Lord is always free of illusion. The soul is also distinct from material nature, which has no consciousness.\] Krsna presents a similar list of elements to the one given in previous chapters, a list which includes the Supreme Lord as an element (10-16). Krsna next delineates the counting methods of several great sages (17-25).

Uddhava asks Krsna to clarify the difference between material nature and the living entity (26-28). Krsna says that nature is unconscious and continuously transformed by the three modes, while both the Supreme Lord and the Jiva are conscious, eternal, and unchanging. Moreover, it takes three interdependent factors to perceive a material object: the senses, the objects of perception, and the presiding deities of the senses. The Supreme Lord is the source of these interdependent relationships and is thus completely independent of matter. The jiva, who is also non- material, is influenced by false ego and so perceives itself as identical with the material body (29-34).

Uddhava asks Krsna how and why the nonmaterial conditioned soul identifies fully with the body and so transmigrates from one body to another (35-36), and Krsna replies that the material mind is shaped by one’s previous actions. This mind, along with the subtle senses, is what travels from body to body. The soul follows the mind into a new body and, by the mind’s influence, misidentifies with the body. The soul experiences pleasure and pain as if they belonged to it. At birth the soul identifies with the new body completely, and at death the soul forgets the material identity it just lived (37-42).

Material bodies change constantly under the force of time, but because the changes are subtle they are difficult to perceive. The soul identifies with the body and considers each stage the body passes through as true to itself. This conception of continuous material identity is only an illusion - like river water that is ever flowing and yet considered to be the same water. Those who become free from bodily identification realize themselves as separate from the body (43-50).

Those who consider the body the self are bound by the cycle of birth and death. They receive bodies according to the mode of nature with which they associate, and experience imaginary sense gratification that is, in reality, not gratification but suffering. Krsna warns Uddhava not to try to enjoy matter with the material senses; meditation on material sense objects reduces one’s ability to become self-realized (51-57).

The Lord assures Uddhava that even if harassed or offended, great souls can tolerate and remain on the spiritual platform. Uddhava then asks Krsna how one can attain such an amazing state of consciousness, adding that it seems possible only for those fixed in devotional service (58-61).

**Chapter 23: The Song of the Avanti Brahmana**

Krsna tells the story of the Avanti brahmana to show how it’s possible to tolerate difficulties, break one’s identification with the subtle body, and cross the ocean of material existence by controlling the mind and taking shelter of the Lord. The Avanti brahmana suffered severe reactions due to his being a miser. These reactions caused him to develop a deep sense of renunciation. Understanding that his suffering was actually the Lord’s mercy, he accepted sannyasa and wandered the earth, tolerating insults and harassments as the fruit of his karma. He realized that it was not the external circumstances that were causing his distress but his false ego exhibited through his mind. Only by fixing his consciousness on Krsna’s lotus feet could the mind be subdued. Krsna concludes that the paths of renunciation and sannyasa, like all others, culminate in devotional service.

**Summary**

In the previous chapter Uddhava asked Krsna how to cut the soul’s misidentification with body and mind, naming devotional service as a potent method for this purpose. The Lord responds by telling him the story of the Avanti brahmana. Krsna tells Uddhava that it is difficult to tolerate insults, but it’s possible if one understands that they are the result of one’s own karma (1-5).

Once, there was a wealthy but miserly and hardhearted brahmana from Avantipura. This brahmana never allowed himself or his family members to enjoy his accumulated wealth. He gave no respect to others but focused only on increasing his wealth. His family members gradually became inimical toward him, and the demigods also became angry with him. Due to his impiety and disrespect, the brahmana lost everything and was then neglected by his family. He experienced unbearable misery. This suffering purified and transformed his consciousness, leading him to feelings of renunciation (6-13).

The brahmana realized that miserliness and greed destroy all good qualities and lead to unhappiness. Men waste their lives in striving to accumulate wealth. As a result, they become contaminated by bad qualities. Actually, no material situation can award true satisfaction. \[One should therefore utilize one’s energy for spiritual advancement.\] The brahmana lamented the time he had lost in chasing wealth and contemplated how best to use his remaining time (14-27).

The brahmana further realized that his new circumstances were Krsna’s mercy - allowing him to become detached and giving him a way out of material existence. This made him joyful, and he decided to subsist only on the bare necessities while directing his full attention to spiritual life (28-30). Krsna then describes how the Avanti brahmana cut the knots of material attachment and accepted sannyasa. The brahmana humbly begged for his maintenance, controlled his senses and intelligence in all circumstances, and took full shelter of the Lord. Uncultured people considered him a dirty beggar and humlilated him by stealing his possessions, mocking him, insulting him, hitting him, and tying him up. The brahmana understood deeply that his suffering was unavoidable because it was allotted to him by providence. No matter what happened, he remained fixed in the Lord’s service while tolerating his fate (31-41).

The Avanti brahmana revealed his realization that the cause of all suffering is not one’s external circumstances but the mind alone (42). The soul identifies with the mind and so is forced to consider the mind’s desires as its own. The contents of the mind - its desires and tendencies - are the result of one’s previous karma, the specific configuration of the three modes of nature that encase the individual soul. These desires cause one to engage in material activities and thus to take birth again in the material world. Therefore it is essential to bring the mind, which is powerful and unsubmissive, under control. The prime purpose of prescribed duties, regulative principles, and pious rituals is to subdue the mind and focus it on the Supreme. Those who fail to control the mind are bewildered. They think in terms of friends and enemies and identify themselves with body, relatives, and property (43-49).

People generally attribute their suffering to other people, the demigods, the body, the movements of the planets, their past karma, and/or time. The brahmana analyzes these alleged causes and rejects them all. The actual cause is false ego, which resides in the subtle body, which is predominated by the mind. The false ego gives shape to one’s illusory material existence. As the brahmana states, the cure for this disease of misidentification is to serve the Lord purely and to practice full dependence on Him (50-57).

Krsna summarizes the life and lessons of the Avanti brahmana and then describes the essence of the brahvmana’s path: to control the mind fully by fixing one’s intelligence on the Supreme. Krsna concludes by blessing those who want to deeply comprehend the meaning of the brahmana’s teachings (58-61).

**Chapter 24: The Philosophy of Sankhya**

Krsna describes Sankhya philosophy, the analytical study of creation, maintenance, and annihilation in connection with the Supreme Lord. According to Sankhya, Krsna, through his expansion Maha-visnu, is the cause, maintained and annihilator of all material ingredients and objects. Those who realize this can free themselves of illusory, material dualities and see themselves as souls distinct from matter. Ultimately, they attain the Lord’s devotional service.

**Summary**

In the previous chapter, Krsna described how suffering can be alleviated by controlling the mind and dissolving one’s false identification with the subtle body. To better understand how to achieve these goals, Krsna now presents Sankhya philosophy, which analyzes the creation, maintenance, and annihilation of the material world in connection with Him.

First, Krsna describes the creation of the universal ingredients. When the creation is not yet manifested, only He exists, and the material ingredients are contained within Him. Matter evolves from the Lord’s material potency, and the living entities appear from His marginal potency. When the unmanifest form of material nature is agitated by His glance, the three modes become manifest, and from them appear the sutra and then the mahat-tattva. From the mahat-tattva comes false ego, which binds the living entities to matter. False ego combines with each of the modes to form the other foundational ingredients of creation. These ingredients are combined by the Lord’s potencies into a universe, and the Lord enters into it. As the Lord floats on the causal water at the bottom of each universe, a lotus grows from His navel and Brahma is born (1-10).

Brahma performs austerities, and the Lord empowers him to create the three planetary systems. Thus appropriate residences are made for the conditioned souls according to the reactions to their previously performed fruitive work. The Supreme Lord, through His time potency, arranges the movements of the living entities within the mighty river of the modes of nature (11-15).

The Lord next points to Himself as the foundation on which all material existence rests. Besides the living entities, all the objects in the material creation are based on the primal elements. Material nature is the original ingredient and final state of these elements, and Maha-visnu is the resting place of nature. As the Supreme Lord is ultimately the origin and end of all objects in material creation, these objects, although temporary, should be considered real. Due to the Lord’s continued glance, the material world continues to exist and manifest varieties, which are products of the Lord’s universal form (16-21).

During annihilation, the processes of creation are reversed, and all that was created merges back into the element from which it emanated. All the foundational ingredients merge back into false ego, the first physical element. False ego, the mahat-tattva, the three modes, material nature, and time successively dissolve one into the other. Time merges into Maha-visnu, and ultimately, the material creation returns to the Supreme Lord (22-27).

Through knowledge of Sankhya one can learn to discriminate between matter and spirit, free oneself from all illusory dualities \[and finally attain devotional service\]. And so Krsna, the perfect seer and knower of everything, establishes Himself as the cause, maintainer, and annihilator of the material creation (28-29).

**Chapter 25: The Three Modes of Nature and Beyond**

Krsna describes how the three modes of nature influence the living entities and bind them to repeated birth and death. By understanding each mode’s symptoms and areas of influence, one can elevate oneself and eventually transcend the modes. Therefore Krsna explains the observable effects of each of the modes under various conditions, and describes the qualities and activities of pure devotees who have overcome the modes’ influence. Finally, Krsna states that the goal of human life is to transcend the modes and develop love for Him. This can he accomplished by performing devotional service and taking shelter of Krsna’s holy names.

**Summary**

In the previous chapter, Krsna presented Sankhya philosophy, by which one can distinguish soul from body. However, as long as one has not conquered the actions of the three modes, one will continue to identify with the body despite his knowledge. So in this chapter Krsna describes the influences of the modes and how to become free of them (1).

The modes affect all beings and all circumstances in the material world. They influence how one sees oneself, the types of endeavors one becomes inclined to perform, one’s religiosity, methods of making money, faith, wealth, preferred sense pleasures, desires, family attachments, and duties. The modes combine in their influences, but there is almost always one mode that is dominant. When a particular mode is dominant, qualities related to that mode appear (2-8).

It’s possible to discern which mode most influences a person by looking at his or her qualities and activities. When the mode of goodness is dominant, one would expect a person to be happy, virtuous, knowledgeable, and able to control the mind and senses. When passion dominates, persons work hard to acquire wealth and prestige. When ignorance dominates, persons become dull, tend to lament, fall into illusion, sleep excessively, and act violently toward others. If we wish to elevate ourselves, we must allow a higher guna, especially goodness, to dominate our consciousness. Therefore practices that encourage goodness are favorable for spiritual advancement. It’s also important to notice the symptoms of passion and ignorance when they are dominant in order to avoid their respective influences. Unlike the living entity, Krsna is completely free of the modes (9-18).

Krsna next describes the observable effects of the three modes in the categories of strength, consciousness, future births, working mentality, knowledge, residence, faith, food, and one’s conception of happiness. In each category Krsna also mentions the qualities and activities of His pure devotees, who are not bound by the modes. These include their consciousness of the spiritual nature, attaining the Lord’s planet, performing work as devotional service, knowledge of the Absolute Truth, residence near where the Lord resides, faith in bhukti, honoring only prasada, and a conception of happiness related only to performing bhakti (19-29).

All material situations, acts, and internal and external perceptions are related to the interaction of the enjoying soul and material nature.

Therefore everything we experience in material life is a construct of the three modes, including the conditioned soul’s destination after death (30-31).

After describing the mode’s all-pervading influence, Krsna states that the goal of human life is to transcend the modes and develop love for Him. One can, again, accomplish these goals by practicing devotional service, because bhakti is beyond the modes. Living in the mode of goodness helps one conquer passion and ignorance, but eventually one must transcend all three modes in order to give up one’s conditioned life and attain the Supreme. One who has transcended the modes can experience Krsna’s transcendental form and find complete satisfaction, with no desire for material enjoyment (32-36).

**Chapter 26: The Aila-gita**

Krsna stresses the importance of avoiding materialistic association and accepting Vaisnava association. He offers the vivid example of Emperor Aila’s desire to enjoy Urvasi, and the emperor’s bewilderment and lamentation when he loses her. Krsna explains how materialistic association, especially with the opposite sex, degrades one’s consciousness and diverts one from one’s spiritual life.

On the other hand, serving and associating with devotees is extremely valuable because it gives one the opportunity to chant and hear about Krsna and thus become purified. This purification gives one the opportunity to develop the desire to serve Krsna. Pure devotees, free from false ego and surrendered to the Lord, are the only hope and shelter for those drowning in the ocean of material existence.

**Summary**

In the previous chapter, Krsna described the modes of nature and their control over the world of matter. Now He instructs Uddhava to free himself from the contamination of the modes by offering Him loving service. To achieve this, one must always avoid materialistic association and accept only the association of bhaktas (1-3).

\[The greatest obstacle to achieving freedom from the modes of nature is tho desire for sex.\| Krsna gives the example of Emperor Aila, who desired the association of the heavenly woman Urvasi. On winning her, Aila became completely attached to her; when she left him, he could only lament. Finally realizing the foolishness of his attachment, Aila, now in a detached mood, composed a song describing the dangers of association with women (4-6).

Aila describes his degraded consciousness as he tries to fulfill his sexual desires. Because of the close association he had with Urvasi, he was unaware of anything but her. Although an emperor in name, he became a weak, powerless fool, a toy animal in Urvasi’s hands. The lusty desires in his heart increased continuously, and when Urvasi abandoned him, he became completely bewildered (7-14).

Aila realized that only Krsna, the controller of the modes of nature, can save one’s consciousness from addiction to sense gratification. Ultimately, he realizes, the cause for his degraded consciousness was not Urvasi hut ignorance of his spiritual nature and his own failing to control his senses. The attractiveness of the material body, which is actually composed of polluted, filthy substances, is an illusion created by maya. Aila’s desire to possess Urvasi was but another type of illusion, as the body has many potential owners (15-21).

It’s not enough to understand only theoretically that the material body is a conglomeration of substances. Because of our continued association with women and wealth from time immemorial, the senses and mind cannot be trusted. The contact of the senses with their objects agitates the mind and can easily overpower the intelligence. Thus the association of materialists - which increases this agitation - should be avoided. Restraining sense gratification, especially intimate contact with the opposite sex, helps pacify the mind and remove previous, unfavorable, material impressions (22-24). Understanding all this, Emperor Aila gave up the position he had achieved on Urvasi’s planet and regained his previous spiritual realization (25).

Krsna next states that one must always keep oneself within the association of devotees. Krsna’s devotees are free from false ego, always surrendered to Him, and expert in severing the mind’s material attachments. In Vaisnava association one can chant and hear about Krsna, become purified of one’s sinful reactions, and develop loving service to Krsna. There is nothing else to be gained beyond this (26-30).

The opportunity to serve the Lord’s devotees is extremely valuable. Pure devotees can remove all obstacles to spiritual advancement and provide shelter for those drowning in material existence. Pure devotees are the sole protectors of and guides for the process of devotional service, and they are one’s real worshipable deities and one’s family.
