They alone can grant one an accurate spiritual vision, and ultimately they are nondifferent from Krsna (31-34).

Krsna concludes by describing how Emperor Aila freed himself from all material association and began wandering the earth, completely self-satisfied (35).

**Chapter 27: Lord Krsna’s Instructions on the Process of Deity Worship**

Krsna recommends Deity worship as a means to purify the heart from material attachment and to develop a loving relationship with Him. He presents three basic methodologies for Deity worship, describes the basic principles of Deity worship, and explains practical elements and procedures. He is most pleased by appropriate offerings made with love and devotion and simply for His pleasure. Krsna also describes the concluding steps of worship, the importance of faith, the need for temples, and how to maintain worship of the Deity.

**Summary**

\[In order to make spiritual advancement, one must become detached from matter and attached to Krsna. Aila was able to detach himself fully from materialistic association, but most people find such detachment difficult. For such materially attached persons, therefore, Krsna recommends Deity worship. Krsna is so beautiful and attractive that all material attractions fade when one serves Him. Thus the heart is purified. Coming to the temple and offering something for the Deity’s pleasure helps one come to love the Lord.\] Uddhava therefore asks Krsna to describe the qualifications, bases, and methods of Deity worship (1-5).

Krsna replies that there are innumerable prescriptions for worshiping the Deity. The basic methodologies, however, are three: performing Vedic sacrifices, performing tantric sacrifices, and a mixture of the two. The most important principle is to make appropriate offerings, simply for the Lord’s pleasure, with love, devotion, and sincerity (6-9).

Krsna then describes some basic principles of Deity worship, such as cleanliness, fixing the mind on the Lord while worshiping him through one’s prescribed duties, how Deities can be made of any of eight elements, temporary and permanent manifestations of the Deity, bathing the Deity, worshiping with the most excellent paraphernalia one can afford, and offering items pleasing to the particular Deity one is worshiping. The essence of the worship and what pleases Krsna most is the devotee’s loving sentiment (10-18).

Krsna next presents the practical elements of and procedures in Deity worship. These include sanctifying the body, place, and items of worship with water and mantras, sitting properly before the Deity, doing meditations that prepare one’s consciousness, offering the Lord water to wash His feet and mouth, worshiping His paraphernalia and associates, decorating Him, offering Him oils, flowers, incense, and lamps, offering Him palatable foods, performing festivals for His pleasure with special offerings, singing and dancing for His pleasure, and performing a fire sacrifice while meditating on His form (19-43).

One should become absorbed in singing, dancing, chanting, hearing stories about Krsna, and enacting His pastimes. At the end of the worship one should offer the Lord prayers, understanding deeply one’s desperate situation in the material world and begging Him for His mercy and protection (44-47).

Krsna is present everywhere, but one needs faith in order to realize that presence. When one develops faith in a specific form or manifestation of the Lord and worships that form, the Lord appears in that form. Without faith, one can see the Lord only as matter (48).

People are encouraged to worship the Deity and support Deity worship. Those who are wealthy can build temples and donate property for the Deity’s maintenance - by doing so one can gain one’s desired perfection, opulence, a high position, and elevation to higher planets. However, when such worship is done without material desires, one can achieve its real result: love and devotion for Krsna (49-53).

Finally, Krsna warns against stealing the property of the Deity, devotees, or brahmanas, for that will bring horrendous results to all those who participate (54-55)

**Chapter 28: Jnana-yoga**

Krsna gives a brief summary of jnana-yoga in order to emphasize that bhakti-yoga is the easier process. Krsna describes the cause of the soul’s compromised predicament in matter and presents the philosophical basis for the prescribed cure. He then offers guidance to jnanis, describes the consciousness of perfect jnanis, and delineates methods for overcoming obstacles. Only by taking shelter of the Lord can one truly overcome all obstructions to spiritual life and attain Him.

**Summary**

In the previous chapter, Krsna described devotional service in the form of Deity worship. To show the difference between the easy practice of bhakti-yoga and the much more difficult practice of juana-yoga, and to help devotees deepen their practice of bhakti through knowledge, Krsna now presents a brief summary of jnana-yoga.

Krsna first explains that all activities in this world are but interactions between eternal but illusioned souls and Krsna’s bewildering material energy. From this perspective, one should not praise or condemn another person’s qualities and activities, as this only entangles one further in illusion. Whatever seems good or bad has no true value; like a shadow, it only resembles reality. Rather, one should see everything in relation to the Absolute Truth and His energies (1-5).

Nothing in existence is separate from the Supreme. He is within everything and at the same time distinct from everything. Those free of duality understand that the material world is not the ultimate reality, and so they can wander freely and unattached throughout the world (6-9).

Uddhava notes that the soul is transcendental to matter, whereas the body has no awareness. How is it, then, he asks, that we experience material existence (10-11)?

Krsna’s reply places the responsibility for material existence on the eternal soul. By misuse of free will, He explains, the soul enters the material body, thinking that the body will help it control the material nature and thus enjoy. The soul falsely identifies with the dreamlike material world and experiences enjoyment and suffering, conditions that are actually external to it. But under the strict control of time the soul is forced to accept different material positions (12-16).

The cure for this misidentification is to understand that the only reality is the Absolute Truth and then focus one’s consciousness on Him. When one perceives an object as having no relationship to the Absolute Truth, one can know one is in illusion. Such perceptions are driven by the false ego and mind. It’s possible to have a focused view of reality if one absorbs the transcendental knowledge received from one’s spiritual master and then fine-tunes one’s ability to discriminate by studying scriptural evidence, practicing austerity, and using logic. When one gives up the tendency to enjoy and becomes detached and self-satisfied, one can become fixed in his true identity as soul, free from any material designation (17-24).

When perfected jnanis realize the Lord as a person, they no longer need to focus on sense control and meditation. The Supreme Absolute Truth, these jnanis’ object of meditation, is never contaminated by the three modes or their material transformations (25-26).

However, jnanis who have not yet attained such perfection and therefore still have contaminated hearts, should be careful not to associate with the modes of nature. Their material attachments may recur and cause them to take birth again. Unlike ordinary persons, however, who have a different destination, such progressing jnanis will resume their spiritual progress in the next life (27-30).

Krsna next describes what perfected jnanis perceive as reality. They don’t identify with the body, remain fixed in the Supreme even when confronted with material duality, see themselves as nonchanging and eternal, have direct perception of the Supreme Lord, and understand that all material forms are transformations of the Lord’s potencies (31-37).

Finally, Krsna makes some recommendations meant to help aspiring yogis overcome obstacles on the spiritual path. Through yogic meditation, sitting postures, controlled breathing, austerities, and mantras, these yogis can improve body and mind. But only those who also take shelter of the Lord, remembering Him, chanting His holy names, and following in the footsteps of His pure devotees can truly overcome all material hankering and attain the Supreme (38—44).

**Chapter 29: Bhakti-yoga**

Krsna concludes His teachings to Uddhava with a summary of bhakti' yoga, which He has shown step after step to be the culmination of all other paths. Krsna describes three major principles of bhakti and then presents a way to strip envy and rivalry from the hearts of those inclined toward jnana. Finally, Krsna glorifies the unique position of bhakti, which is the crown jewel of all spiritual processes.

After completing His instructions, Krsna glorifies the Uddhava-gita and then asks Uddhava if he has understood what has been said. Immensely grateful to Krsna, Uddhava confirms that his illusion has been dispelled and asks Krsna for undeviating attachment to His lotus feet.

Krsna then gives Uddhava his final instructions, which are intended to satisfy the sages at Badarikasrama as well as to teach the general populace: Uddhava should fix his mind on Krsna and meditate on the instructions he has just heard. Uddhava, his heart breaking, cries and places his head on the Lord’s feet. Then, in the great pain of his separation, he departs.

Sukadeva Gosvami concludes his narration of the Uddhava-gita by offering his respects both to the Uddhava-gita itself and to Krsna.

**Summary**

In the previous chapter, Krsna gave an overview of jnana-yoga. But Uddhava considers the practices of jnana too difficult, as they require an extreme level of detachment and a rigorous control of the mind. He thus asks Krsna to describe bhakti, which is easier to perform and more certain in its result (1-2).

Uddhava recommends taking shelter of the Lord’s lotus feet instead of trying to depend on one’s own strength. Krsna is very affectionate to His devotees and reciprocates with their sincere attempts at service. He makes them all-successful by His mercy. To help them, He comes externally as the spiritual master and internally as the Supersoul. The devotees feel immense gratitude for the Lord’s appearance and instructions and remain eternally indebted to Him (3-6).

Krsna smiles and describes three major principles of devotion: performing one’s duties as an offering to Him, mind fixed on Him; taking shelter of a holy place where bhaktas reside and then following in their footsteps; and celebrating holy days and festivals dedicated for the Lord’s worship (7-11).

Krsna next describes in theory and practice how through seeing Him within the heart of all beings one can remove envy and rivalry from the heart. By offering respects to all living beings in the form of obeisances, one develops equal vision. This dissipates one’s bad tendencies. Even if one is ridiculed, one should continue to offer obeisances with body, mind, and words until the ability to see Krsna in all living beings develops. This method is the best process for jnana-yogis but can also help others realize and serve the Lord’s personal feature (12-19).

Finally, Krsna glorifies the unique position of bhakti, which He Himself has established and which is free from all material motivation. Activities performed for the Lord’s pleasure, even if bereft of external value, can elevate one to perfection. Using body and mind, which are temporary and unreal, one can attain Krsna, the eternal reality. Therefore bhakti is the crown jewel of all spiritual processes (20-22).

With these words Krsna completes His instructions to Uddhava. The Uddhava-gtia is a complete survey of the science of the Absolute Truth. There is immense value in studying, reading, and hearing it, and Krsna is indebted to those who share its knowledge. Those who receive this knowledge with faith and attention while performing devotional service will not be bound by material reactions (23-28).

Krsna asks Uddhava if he understands the transcendental knowledge he has been given and whether his confusion has been dispelled (29).

Then, ascertaining that Uddhava has understood, Krsna declares the knowledge in the Uddhava-gita to be the most perfect, and then states who should and should not hear it. The perfection of all processes is to offer everything to the Lord with a desire to serve Him. Anything one can attain through other processes and more can be achieved simply by practicing bhakti (30-34).

Uddhava then offers his obeisances but cannot speak. He remembers the Lord’s kindness with love and gratitude. At last Uddhava confirms that the Lord’s instructions and association have dispelled his illusion. Krsna has given him so much in exchange for his surrender - divine knowledge and His constant presence. Uddhava declares that his material attachment to his family members is now finished, and he asks Krsna to instruct him how to gain everlasting attachment to His lotus feet (35-40).

\[Uddhava is already a pure devotee of Krsna and so needs no further instruction. However, Krsna has a mission for Uddhava to complete. His exemplary behavior will help instruct the people in general, and his association and knowledge will satisfy the sages at Badarikasrama.\] Krsna then tells Uddhava to go to Badarikasrama, purify himself in the waters of the Alakananda River, perform austerities, and maintain a pure, deep consciousness. He should fix his mind on Krsna, meditate on the instructions he has received, and deepen his realization of Krsna’s nature and qualities. By following these instructions, Uddhava will again receive Krsna’s association (41-44).

Uddhava then places his head on Krsna’s lotus feet and cries, his heart broken, out of his fear of separation from Him. Finally, in pain, he offers obeisances to the Lord and departs. Placing the Lord deep in his heart, he goes to Badarikasrama, performs the austerities Krsna prescribed for him there, and later attains the eternal land \[of Dvaraka\] in the spiritual world (45-47).

Sukadeva Gosvami concludes by blessing those who hear the Uddhava'gita with faith. He then offers respects to the conclusive knowledge of the Uddhava-gita and to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krsna, who has collected this nectarean knowledge and bestowed it on His loving devotees (48-49).

## Appendix 2. Karma, jnana, bhakti, and yoga in the Uddhava-gita

**Canto Eleven: Chapters 6-29**

In the Uddhava-gita, Sri Krsna ultimately presents the different spiritual disciplines - karma-yoga, jnana-yoga, astanga-yoga, and bhakti-yoga - to show that all spiritual paths lead to bhakti-yoga. That is, practicing a bona fide spiritual path that suits one’s inclinations and conditioning gradually advances one toward devotional service. Thus bhakti-yoga is the topmost process.

To illustrate this, we have mapped the verses in the Uddhava-gita according to which of the four categories - bhakti, karma, jnana, or yoga - is emphasized in that verse. We have also noted when a verse belongs to more than one category.

We have created a graph to represent these categories - to offer an overview of the Uddhava-gita chapters and how the four categories connect throughout the text. We can see clearly, for example, that in a number of cases the concluding verses of each chapter emphasize bhakti.

The rows in the table that follow the graph are divided according to the dialogues in which they appear and the categories present in each section.

## Appendix 3. Elevation to the mode of Goodness

Devotees wishing success in their service must cultivate the mode of goodness. But wait a minute! Am I hearing protests from hard-pressed devotees sincerely striving to serve their Lord with a passion? Are they not crying out that there’s no need for goodness? Are they not emphatically stating that devotees are transcendental to the three modes of material nature?

Srila Prabhupada once addressed this last question after a Sunday feast lecture at 26 Second Avenue. Prabhupada had just finished speaking, and I raised my hand and spoke my first words to my spiritual master. They were not submissive ones. “Swamiji, in your lecture you said that devotees were in the mode of goodness. But I thought devotees were transcendental to the mode of goodness?” Although I had no concept of the mode of goodness and did not care about transcending it, I was foolishly seeking to challenge an apparent contradiction. Prabhupada gently replied, “Yes, devotees are transcendental to the mode of goodness, but generally, they act in the mode of goodness.”

To understand the ramifications of this statement, we must first consider the position of every conditioned soul in the material world. According to Srila Prabhupada’s purport to *Bhagavad-gita* 18.60, “If one refuses to act under the direction of the Supreme Lord, then he is compelled to act by the modes in which he is situated. Everyone is under the spell of a particular combination of the modes of nature.” Contrarily, a pure devotee, one who is continuously engaged in the Lord’s service, does not fall under the control of the three modes of material nature. The *Bhagavad-gita* (14-26) states:

*mam ca yo* ’ *vyabhicarena*  
*bhakti-yogena sevate*  
sa gunan *samatityaitan*  
*brahma-bhuyaya kalpate*

One who engages in full devotional service, unfailing in all circumstances, at once transcends the modes of material nature.

Most devotees, however, are neither completely controlled by the modes of material nature nor completely transcendental to them, serving the Lord in all circumstances. It is the merciful spiritual master who considers such devotees transcendental and who offers their mixed service through the disciplic succession to Krsna.

But just because devotees are transcendentally situated due to sincerely serving their spiritual master and their spiritual master’s accepting their service does not make every act they perform transcendental. That an immature Vaisnava transcendentalist is sometimes adversely infected by the modes of material nature and thus comes under their control was confirmed by Srila Prabhupada in 1976 in Vrndavana: “Vaisnava is not so easy, or why are they falling down?”

In his purport to Bhagavad-gita 2.45 Prabhupada states:

As long as the material body exists, there are actions and reactions in the material modes. One has to learn tolerance. This transcendental position is achieved in full Krsna consciousness when one is fully dependent on the good will of Krsna. As tiny spirit souls, we are eternally *prakrti* and are always controlled either by Krsna or by *maya’s* agents, the three modes of material nature. *Krsna*-*surya-sama; maya haya andhakara:* “Godhead is light; nescience is darkness. Where there is Godhead, there is no nescience.”

As the current near the bank of a river is stronger then the current in the middle of the river, so *maya,* through the modes of material nature, acts stronger on those souls who are seeking to escape from the rushing river of material life. Therefore, it is in dark periods of nonsurrender - when we are controlled by the modes of material nature - that our position is most precarious. The Bhagavad-gita (14.9) states:

O son of Bharata, the mode of goodness conditions one to happiness; passion conditions one to fruitive action; and ignorance, covering one’s knowledge, binds one to madness.

Thus due to the strong dictates of the modes, an impure soul acquiesces to the demands of goodness, passion, and ignorance and neglects his own true desire for loving devotional service to Krsna. Although all three modes are binding, the modes of passion and ignorance bind more tightly, filling us with intense desire, foolishness, and improper discrimination. The Bhagavad-gita (18.30-32) confirms this when describing the understanding each mode allows:

O son of Prtha, that understanding by which one knows what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, what is to be feared and what is not to be feared, what is binding and what is liberating, is in the mode of goodness.

O son of Prtha, that understanding which cannot distinguish between religion and irreligion, between action that should be done and action that should not be done, is in the mode of passion.

That understanding which considers irreligion to be religion and religion to be irreligion, under the spell of illusion and darkness, and strives always in the wrong direction, O Partha, is in the mode of ignorance.

Although, we who are practicing Krsna consciousness are certainly performing devotional service, we tend to stir into the brew of our devotional service the pinches of passion and dashes of ignorance left over from our conditioning. History has shown that recently conditioned souls are capable of neglecting the entire transcendental process coming down through the previous *acaryas* and given to them by their spiritual master in order to satisfy the dictates of the modes of nature. We should guard against this danger by taking seriously to Krsna consciousness and simultaneously guarding against passion and ignorance. By examining the qualities of passion and ignorance mentioned in the Bhagavad-gita, we will see why these two modes should be avoided.

**Passion:** great attachment, fruitive activity, intense endeavor, uncontrolled desire and hankering, and the tendency to speculate; one is never satisfied with one’s position; one feels family attachment, greed, a desire for respect and honor (and is willing to perform sacrifices simply to gain that respect and honor).

**Ignorance:** whimsy, purposelessness, inactivity, madness, foolishness, misery, distress, intoxication, illusion, excessive sleep, degradation, laziness, renunciation of activities meant for spiritual welfare, and the seeking of happiness without considering its effects on one’s self-realization.

Discerning the qualities of passion and ignorance from those of true devotion is as important for a devotee as is discerning a flowering creeper from a weed for a gardener. Without such discrimination, a devotee may find himself nurturing weeds of *karma* and *jnana* instead of the creeper of devotional service.

By strictly practicing the rules and regulations of *sadhana-bhakti,* all devotional qualities will develop automatically. But if we allow the weeds of *maya* to grow along with our devotional service, the *bhakti-lata* will not grow properly. Devotees should uproot any weedlike tendencies caused by their conditioning and, while continuing to act only in the mode of goodness, strictly adhere to the process of Krsna consciousness. Srila Prabhupada writes in his purport to *Bhagavad-gita* 14.15:

Therefore, those who are actually serious about human life should take to the mode of goodness and in good association transcend the modes and become situated in Krsna consciousness. This is the aim of human life.

Having examined the qualities born of passion and ignorance, it is easy to see how these modes, if embedded within our devotional service, cause a disturbance. Krsna always directs His pure devotee, but because that pure devotee is not disturbed by the intense desires of passion or the foolish dullness of ignorance, he can neglect the modes and surrender to Krsna’s promptings. As long as the interplay of passion and ignorance interferes with our devotional service, our surrender will be incomplete. Therefore, as Prabhupada said to me that day at 26 Second Avenue, devotees “generally act in the mode of goodness.”

In his purport to *Srimad-Bhagavatam* 1.2.19, Srila Prabhupada confirms how necessary the mode of goodness is to the general consciousness of a devotee: “The effect of devotional service becomes manifest by complete elimination of these effects of passion and ignorance.”

But it is not that contamination by passion and ignorance disqualifies us from rendering devotional service; rather, the expert spiritual master deals with it in such a way that we become elevated to goodness. *Srimad-Bhagavatam* 1.2.24 states: “Of the modes, goodness is the best because by the mode of goodness one can come to realize the Absolute Truth.” Srila Prabhupada writes in his purport to this text:

As explained above, one can get release from the conditioned life of material existence by devotional service to the Personality of Godhead. It is further comprehended herein, that one has to rise to the platform of the mode of goodness *(sattva) so* that one can be eligible for the devotional service of the Lord. But if there are no impediments on the progressive path, anyone, even from the platform of *tamas*, can gradually rise to the *sattva* platform by the expert direction of the spiritual master.

Thus by serving Krsna through the spiritual master, the disciple’s consciousness gradually becomes elevated from ignorance to passion to goodness.

We should not become bewildered and think ourselves transcendental and thus relieved of having to act in goodness. Instead, we should recognize that the mode of goodness is the desirable general consciousness in which we should serve. We should cultivate the mode of goodness by strictly following the principles of *sadhana-bhakti,* regularly reading Prabhupada’s books *(srnvatam sva-kathah krsnah punya-sravana-kirtanah),* and weeding out remnants of unwanted passions and ignorant desires. We should also keep in mind that rather than denigrating goodness as “just a material quality,” Srila Prabhupada often equated the mode of goodness with Krsna consciousness.

The Bhagavad-gita (18.10) states, “The intelligent renouncer, situated in the mode of goodness, neither hateful of inauspicious work nor attached to auspicious work, has no doubts about work.” Of course, to cultivate the mode of goodness for its own sake is just as dangerous as cultivating any other mode, because one may become conditioned or limited by it. Therefore one must always keep in mind that his business is simply to serve Krsna. Becoming “good,” a *brahmana,* or anything other than a pure servant of Krsna is simply *maya. Srimad-Bhagavatam* (7.7.51-52) clearly states:

You cannot please the Supreme Personality of Godhead by becoming perfect *brahmanas,* demigods, or great saints, or by becoming perfectly good in etiquette or by vast learning. The Lord is pleased only if one has unflinching, unalloyed devotion to Him.

The *Bhagavad-gita* explains another danger of cultivating the mode of goodness for its own sake: one can become conditioned by the happiness that the mode of goodness offers, or one can become proud, thinking himself better than others, or complacent, satisfied in one’s intellect.

Despite these dangers, devotees must follow Krsna’s instruction to pursue goodness over passion and ignorance. So while goodness is rejected as an end in itself, devotees should embrace it as a jumping-off point for pure devotional service.

In conclusion, to show how the mode of goodness can aid our Krsna consciousness, here is a compilation of some of the qualities of goodness the *Bhagavad-gita* lists. It’s easy to see how these qualities are essential for devotees wishing to render pure devotional service.

**Qualities of Goodness**

Austerities practiced with faith, for the sake of the Supreme, and without expectation of material benefit are, according to the *Bhagavad-gita,* being performed in the mode of goodness:

Austerity of the body:

1\. Worship of the Supreme Lord  
2\. Worship of the *brahmanas*  
3\. Worship of the spiritual master  
4\. Worship of the parents  
5\. Cleanliness  
6\. Simplicity  
7\. Nonviolence  
8\. Celibacy

Austerity of the speech:

1\. Speaking words that are truthful  
2\. Speaking words that are pleasing  
3\. Speaking words that are beneficial  
4\. 4. Speaking words that are not agitating to others  
5\. Regularly reciting Vedic literature

Austerity of the mind:

1\. Satisfaction  
2\. Simplicity  
3\. Gravity  
4\. Self-control  
5\. Purification of one’s existence

Devotees in the mode of goodness are brahminical. They are:

1\. Peaceful  
2\. Self-controlled  
3\. Austere  
4\. Pure  
5\. Tolerant  
6\. Honest  
7\. Knowledgeable  
8\. Wise  
9\. Religious

Those in goodness give charity:

1\. At a proper time  
2\. To a suitable person  
3\. In a worthy place

Those in goodness have unbreakable determination. They:

1\. Control the mind  
2\. Control their actions  
3\. Controls their senses

Those in goodness discriminate between what should and should not be done. They perform their duties:

1\. Without false ego  
2\. With great determination  
3\. With enthusiasm  
4\. Without wavering in success or failure  
5\. Only because it ought to be done  
6\. Without fearing the troublesome effects

They also dutifully go to the temple simply to offer respect to the Deity. Those in goodness are attracted to foods that:

1\. Increase the duration of life  
2\. Purify the mind  
3\. Give the body strength

Those in goodness are happy because:

1\. They aren’t affected by material miseries  
2\. They know they are free from material reactions  
3\. They associate with things that awaken them to self-realization

Those in goodness are free of illusion and have knowledge about the soul beyond the body.

Those in goodness are not:

1\. Hateful of things that trouble the body  
2\. Hateful of inauspicious work  
3\. Attached to auspicious work

Those in goodness have no doubts about work. They renounce:

1\. All material association  
2\. All attachment to the fruits of their work

They perform sacrifices:

1\. According to the direction of scripture  
2\. As a matter of duty  
3\. Desiring no reward

And they understand things in the correct perspective.

Part two of this pastime - the actual destruction of the Yadu dynasty and Lord Krsna’s disappearance - is told in chapters 30 and 31 of Canto Eleven.

Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.1.4 refers to hearing the Bhagavatam as “the right medicine for the conditioned soul undergoing repeated birth and death.” Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.1.14 notes that topics concerning Krsna are “the remedy for all sufferings in this Age of Kali.” Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.1.16 informs us that hearing about Krsna benefits “the speaker or preacher, he who inquires, and the people in general who listen.”

The events precipitating Krsna’s descent are described in Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.1.17-26.

Krsna’s disappearance pastime, including the sages leaving for Pindaraka, is narrated in the Visnu Purana. Pindaraka still exists as a tirtha in Gujarat, along the Arabian seacoast, about two miles from Dvaraka.

See Srimad-Bhagavatam 6.5.43.

Srimad-Bhagavatam 9.13 describes the great Maharaja Nitni and his descendants. The lineage of Maharaja Rsabhadeva, as well as those of the nava-yogendras, is given in Bhagavatam 5.1-4.

Saunaka Rsi asked this same question of Suta Gosvami at the beginning of Srimad-Bhagavatam (1.1.9): “Please, therefore, being blessed with many years, explain to us, in an easily understandable way, what you have ascertained to be the absolute and ultimate good for the people in general.”

Kavi’s reply (SB. 11.2.33-43) strongly emphasizes that the supreme good is devoted service to Krsna. Yet as a santa-bhakta, he speaks from the standpoint of a devotee whose practices are mixed with those typically found in jnanis. These practices are different from the standard practices of devotional service beginning with sravanam kirtanarh visnoh smaranam, as prescribed by Prahlada Maharaja in Srimad-Bhagavatam 7.5.23.

“This knowledge is the king of education, the most secret of all secrets. It is the purest knowledge, and because it gives direct perception of the self by realization, it is the perfection of religion. It is everlasting, and it is joyfully performed.”

*bhayam dvitlyabhinivesatah syad*  
*isad apetasya viparyayo ’smrtih*  
*tan-mayayato budha abhajet tam*  
*bhaktyaikayesam guru-devatatma*  
*evam-vratah sva-priya-narrui-kirtya,*  
*jatanurago druta-citta uccaih*  
*hasaty atho roditi rauti gayaty*  
*unmada-van nrtyati loka-bahyah*  
*bhaktih paresanubhavo viraktir*  
*anyatra caisa trika eka-kalah*  
*prapadyamanasya yathasnatah syus*  
*tustih pustih ksud-apayo ’nu-ghasam*  
*sa vai pumsam paro dharmo*  
*yato bhaktir adhoksaje*  
*ahaituky apratihata*  
*yayatma suprasidati*

According to Srila Jiva Gosvami (Bhakti Sandarbha, anuccheda 198), we can understand texts 48-55 as naming the characteristics of the topmost devotee. If we accept that understanding, then text 55 is the summation of all of a pure devotee’s characteristics: he or she possesses love that controls the Lord. But Sri jiva also explains that this same series of texts (and including 45-47) can be seen as distinct definitions of various levels of topmost devotees. Taking this understanding, text 55 expands the meaning of text 45, which describes the all-inclusive nature of the topmost devotee’s love.

Srila Jiva Gosvami comments on the idea of having many gurus: “\[O\]ne’s worshipable spiritual master will instruct one in many departments of knowledge by giving lessons gleaned from ordinary objects. As recommended by the brahmana avadhuta, one can strengthen the teachings received from ones deary a and avoid transgressing his orders by observing ordinary things in nature. One should not mechanically receive the teachings of one’s guru. The disciple should be thoughtful and, with his own intelligence, realize in practice what he has heard from his spiritual master by observing the world around him. In this sense one may accept many gurus, though not those who preach against the knowledge received from the bona fide spiritual master.”
